story: Officials and residents in Okinawa have celebrated the restoration of Shuri Castle's main hall, marking a significant return of the island's cultural symbol

TOKYO -- Officials and residents in Okinawa celebrated the restoration of Shuri Castle's main hall on Sunday, its deep red exterior and dragon ornaments marking the return of a symbol of the island's heritage seven years after it was destroyed in a fire.

The fire on Oct. 31, 2019, destroyed several buildings at the castle complex in Naha, Okinawa’s prefectural capital, as it was hosting a festival. Firefighters struggled for nearly 12 hours to contain the blaze as it spread from building to building in strong winds. Investigators could not determine the cause but considered an electrical fault the likeliest explanation.

“The fire was a tremendous shock to the Okinawan people," Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja said at Sunday’s ceremony in the courtyard outside the main hall. "Seven years after the major loss, as we mark this milestone of the main hall restoration, I am deeply moved and delighted.”
The castle is a symbol of Okinawa’s cultural heritage dating to the Ryukyu Kingdom, which lasted about 450 years from 1429 until 1879, when Japan annexed the island.
It also represents Okinawa’s recovery from World War II. The castle burned down in 1945 during the Battle of Okinawa, which killed about 200,000 people, many of them civilians.

Koja thanked historians, artisans and other experts from across Japan who contributed to the restoration, as well as donors at home and abroad. He called for rebuilding the rest of the castle, saying the opening of the main hall, known as Seiden, is "not the end.”
The 2019 fire destroyed Seiden and two adjacent halls, as well as four nearby structures, while two other structures were heavily damaged.
Shuri Castle's main hall opens to the public Monday. The other parts of the castle are being restored in stages in a process experts say could take more than a decade.

After its earlier loss 80 years ago, the castle was largely restored in 1992 for the 20th anniversary of Okinawa's reversion to Japan to mark the end of the island's 27-year U.S. occupation. The island still hosts a large U.S. military presence. Work on other parts was still underway when the 2019 fire struck.

Kurayoshi Takara, a historian who also helped with the previous restoration, said the main hall was reproduced to more closely resemble the original building, based on new findings including the ingredients of the red pigment and other details from historical documents.

Experts traced the pigment to iron bacteria found in northern Okinawa. After lengthy experiments, artisans recreated the deeper red by blending the bacteria-derived pigment with a commercial product, Takara said in an interview with Japan’s NHK public television.

“We still have a long way to go,” said Takara, who led the latest restoration effort. “I hope Shuri Castle will remain for a long time so that many people come visit and learn rich history and culture on this island ... as a symbol of peace."
Shuri Castle is a major tourist attraction and reconstruction raises hopes for more visitors to the island, whose economy has long lagged behind the rest of Japan.

Koja, who took office at the end of September, has pledged to double Okinawa’s per capita income and tourism revenue within the next decade and make the prefecture a more attractive place for young people.

title: Indonesian rescuers race to find 34 missing workers after a deadly candy factory fire
summary: Indonesian rescuers are searching for 34 missing workers after a deadly fire swept through a candy factory west of Jakarta
story: Indonesian rescuers are searching for 34 missing workers after a deadly fire swept through a candy factory west of Jakarta
JAKARTA, Indonesia -- Indonesian rescuers searched Monday for 34 missing workers after a deadly fire swept through a candy factory west of Jakarta.

Saturday’s fire broke out at the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia factory in Banten province. Firefighters battled flames for about 14 hours before largely containing the blaze tearing through the three-story building.

About 300 workers were inside the factory when the fire erupted, officials said. Of those, 63 were believed to have been in the hardest-hit area, mostly on the second floor where the flames originated from a cooling unit.

Indonesia’s National Search and Rescue Agency, or Basarnas, did not immediately offer a death toll, but said they collected human remains in 24 body bags for identification through forensic examination.
Meanwhile, rescuers saved 29 workers, five of whom were hospitalized, and continue to search for the missing.

More than 500 rescue personnel, including soldiers, police, Indonesian Red Cross personnel, and volunteers, joined the emergency response, according to Basarnas, to locate the victims within an area of about 2,000 square meters (21,527 square feet), while anxious relatives awaited news.
The factory produces Milkita, an Indonesian brand of milk-based candies and snack products exported to more than 40 countries worldwide.
Indonesia has experienced a series of deadly industrial fires in recent years, raising concerns about workplace safety standards and emergency preparedness at manufacturing facilities.

title: European Commission warns EU Academy users of data leak after AI-driven cyberattack
summary: The European Commission is warning of a data leak from a major AI-generated cyberattack on its EU Academy website
story: The European Commission is warning of a data leak from a major AI-generated cyberattack on its EU Academy website

BRUSSELS -- The European Commission on Monday warned users of one of its websites that personal data has been leaked in a major AI-generated cyberattack that was launched on the EU institution last month.

The European Union’s executive branch said the EU Academy website had been caught up in the cyberattack. The site offers courses and information about the 27-nation bloc’s policies to people outside EU institutions.

“The exact scale of the data leak remains under investigation as a precautionary measure,” spokesperson Thomas Regnier said. Names and email addresses were among the data taken, he said, but did not specify how many people were affected.
The commission confirmed last week that it had first detected incidents involving its databases on Oct. 22 and that its cyber experts had taken “preventive measures” to limit the damage.
Regnier declined to confirm whether the month-long cyber campaign has been brought under control.
“As long as the investigation is ongoing, I will not make any conclusive statements at this stage on where we are,” he said.

A message on the EU Academy website said that access had been disabled and measures taken to contain the incident and limit its impact. It warned users to watch for suspicious or unsolicited emails and messages and to avoid sharing personal information with anyone contacting them about the website or its activities.
The CERT-EU agency oversees the digital security of the EU institutions, which employ about 40,000 people just in Brussels.

In a Nov. 4 blog post, the agency warned about threats from a specific AI tool called ARTEX. While designed to use AI to identify vulnerabilities in digital systems, it has been linked to recent attacks across the globe.
The agency said it was “highly likely” that ARTEX had been used in AI-driven activities in “its constituency.” It did not confirm any attack on the commission.

“We assess that ARTEX’s public availability will likely accelerate adoption by threat actors, resulting in more frequent, faster, and more scalable automated attacks with a higher success rate,” the agency said.

title: In Ukraine, the fight to keep winter outside begins with a broken window
summary: As the winter cold sets in, Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities face a growing shortage of window installers as Russian attacks leave homes shattered and families exposed to the cold
story: As the winter cold sets in, Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities face a growing shortage of window installers as Russian attacks leave homes shattered and families exposed to the cold
KYIV, Ukraine -- For weeks after a missile exploded in front of her apartment block, Oleksandra Horban found pieces of glass in her small apartment.

She threw out her 2-year-old son’s plush toys which were covered with glass shards. Outside her ground-floor home, mangled window frames were piled onto a mountain of debris awaiting removal. Pieces of glass were mixed with autumn leaves on the muddy ground.
“Even now we still find glass,” Horban said. “If we vacuum three times, wash the floor and clean up, we’ll still find those microscopic pieces somewhere, in the bed or in the toys.”

As winter sets in, Ukraine is facing a severe shortage of replacement windows with Russian missile and drone attacks continuing to damage buildings, leaving residents exposed to the cold. Temperatures in Kyiv fell to minus 20 degrees Celsius (minus 4 degrees Fahrenheit) last winter.
Government assistance can take months, skilled installers are in short supply and replacement costs have soared, hitting low-income districts near industrial zones hardest.

Horban lives in a Soviet-era “groundscraper” - an enormous horizontal apartment block in the Ukrainian capital. A missile blast in October damaged a vertical section of apartments and shattered hundreds of facade windows.
Most shattered windows have been temporarily covered with fiberboard or tarps. Some boards have small openings fitted with Plexiglas to let daylight into apartments.
New windows in Horban’s apartment would cost about $1,700, more than three times the country’s average salary. Government compensation can take three to four months.
Many cannot afford to wait. Without proper windows, apartments are exposed to cold, damp and mold, particularly during power outages.

Housing damage is among the largest costs of the war. An estimated 3 million housing units were destroyed or badly damaged by the end of last year, adding $90 billion to Ukraine’s reconstruction needs, according to the World Bank.
Ukraine’s window manufacturers can meet demand for replacement windows. The bottleneck is the shortage of skilled installers.

Mykhailo Orlenko, executive director of the Association of Ukrainian Manufacturers of Transparent Structures, said businesses were unable to exempt their employees from military service, including many installers.
“The market lost a large number of these specialists,” he said.

Factories can manufacture windows in about 10 working days, but installation can be delayed for a lot longer as customers wait for a crew to become available. High demand means installation bills have at least doubled over the past year.

Oleksandr, a 42-year-old installer who has worked in the industry for 25 years, said power outages add to the challenges. His team relies on battery-powered tools and normally has to carry heavy materials up stairs with elevators out of service.
On one recent job, his team replaced balcony doors and windows in a fourth-floor apartment, carrying the materials up by hand.

“That was 18 trips up and down the stairs, carrying heavy loads. It would have been easier with a working elevator, but we didn’t wait for the power to come back on — we got straight to work,” he said.
Oleksandr asked to be identified only by his first name, citing security concerns following Russian attacks on private businesses.

To address the shortage, the industry is investing in training. A vocational college in Kyiv opened a European Union-funded facility in March, where 26 10th graders have started a three-year program to become window, door and facade installers.
Teenagers in new overalls practice around mock window openings built from brick, cinder block, wood and synthetic materials. Their classes are frequently disrupted by missile and drone alerts.

The program was established after professional associations lobbied the government to formally recognize window installation as a profession, allowing the industry to access grants and create structured training courses.
Graduates can expect starting salaries of around $900, on par with law graduates due to Ukraine’s acute skill drain, Orlenko said.
Instructor Volodymyr Tserbii hopes the apprentices will help rebuild the country, their training offering students a path into a profession needed for reconstruction.
The massive task of repairing Ukraine’s damaged homes, schools, roads, power plants and other infrastructure will take at least a decade, according to government planners.
For Horban, the wait for new windows is added to a long list of her household’s problems.
Her apartment has no gas, forcing the family to cook on a portable cylinder. They heat their son’s room when electricity is available. A leaking kitchen roof has added to the damage.
The blast also left her toddler son, Viacheslav, frightened. The sounds of war have become part of his vocabulary.
Pressing his nose against a windowpane that survived the attack, he waves to passersby and asks his mother whether more bombing is coming, using the words “bam bam” to describe the explosions.
“Bam bam?” he asks.
“No bam bam,” she answers.
“This is not life, this is surviving,” Horban said. "This is dragging out an existence, not a life.”
Vasilisa Stepanenko, Evgeniy Maloletka and Susie Blann in Kyiv contributed.
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: Air alert sounds hours after attack on Russia-bound ship in the Gulf of Finland
summary: The governor of Kaliningrad says a rare air alert sounded in the Russian exclave near Poland and Lithuania
story: The governor of Kaliningrad says a rare air alert sounded in the Russian exclave near Poland and Lithuania

KYIV, Ukraine -- A rare air alert sounded in Kaliningrad, the Russian exclave near Poland and Lithuania, according to the local governor, as claims circulated online of drone activity near a major naval base there.

The alert late Saturday in Kaliningrad came hours after a drone strike in the Gulf of Finland set fire to a Russian cargo ship bound for the region, which is a key base for Russia's Baltic Fleet. Finnish emergency services were still working to extinguish the blaze on Sunday.

Photos and video posted online show drone activity around the city of Baltiysk, where much of the fleet is stationed. But The Associated Press couldn't immediately verify the authenticity of the images.
According to local media, air raid sirens were heard in Kaliningrad for the first time since Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022.

The Kaliningrad governor, Alexei Bezprozvannykh, said that “a suspicious object coming from the direction of Lithuania” triggered the alert in the Nemansky district near the Lithuanian border, about 170 kilometers (105 miles) northeast of Baltiysk.

On Russian Telegram channels, posts by users saying they were Baltiysk residents described air defenses working there during the night. They featured photos and videos of bright streaks against the night sky, with crackling sounds heard in the background.

Kaliningrad authorities on Sunday denounced as fake one photo, supposedly from Baltiysk, that showed clouds of smoke rising into the night sky, while an orange haze glowed on the horizon. They told Russian state media that the photo “had nothing to do with the region.”
As of Sunday morning, Russian authorities reported no casualties or damage in Kaliningrad.
Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys wrote on X that Lithuania “categorically rejects false claims” regarding the country’s involvement in a drone attack against the region.
“The Republic of Lithuania has never authorized the use of its airspace for attacks against targets in the Russian Federation, including in the present case.”
Lithuania's authorities also said they hadn't recorded any drones or similar objects flying through the country’s airspace the previous night.
Meanwhile, emergency services tried to extinguish the fire aboard the Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland on Sunday morning, authorities in Finland said.
The Sparta II drifted into Finland's territorial waters following the attack, the Finnish Border Guard said. The contents of the ship’s cargo remain unknown.

A Border Guard representative told Finnish broadcaster Yle that the crew had been transferred to a Russian rescue ship. Once the fire is extinguished, the boat would be moved out of Finland's waters, the official said.
Both Finland and Russia have suggested that the drones that struck the ship were Ukrainian. As of Sunday morning, Ukrainian officials hadn't provided any comment.

title: Police evacuate 12,000 from rapper Don Toliver concert after substance release
summary: British police have evacuated over 12,000 fans from a Don Toliver concert after an unknown substance was released in the crowd
story: British police have evacuated over 12,000 fans from a Don Toliver concert after an unknown substance was released in the crowd

LONDON -- More than 12,000 fans were evacuated from a concert by American rapper Don Toliver and over 80 were treated by medics after an unknown irritant was released in the crowd, authorities in the English city of Manchester said Monday.

Greater Manchester Police said officers were called around 10 p.m. (2200 GMT) Sunday to the Co-op Live arena after reports of people being affected by a substance, initially believed to be tear gas. Footage shared on social media appeared to show concertgoers coughing and covering their mouths as they left the venue.
The force declared a “major incident,” which allows different emergency services to coordinate their response.
Concertgoer Ben Stevenson told the Manchester Evening News he was in the standing area of the arena when he “started coughing and (my) eyes were kind of itchy.”

He said Toliver left the stage and the venue lights came on, but it was not until almost an hour later that an announcement said, “due to an unforeseen issue, the show is over, and please make your way out at your own pace.”
Joey Howe, a concertgoer, told BBC Radio Manchester that there was a “horrible smell” and people rushed out of the venue.
“People were coming through in wheelchairs, choking. It was really distressing,” he said.
One person was taken to a hospital and more than 80 were assessed at the scene, with some reporting eye and respiratory symptoms, the North West Ambulance Service said.
It said “decontamination is being carried out as a precaution” at the venue.
Police Assistant Chief Constable Steph Parker said: “Anyone who has left the event and since become unwell is advised to attend their local hospital.”
“We will now begin to fully understand what this substance was and how this incident came about,” she said.
Co-op Live, which opened in 2024, is about 2 miles (3.2 kilometers) from Manchester Arena, where 22 people were killed when a bomber blew himself up during an Ariana Grande concert in 2017.
Co-op Live said in a statement that venue bosses were working with police to identify the cause of the incident.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham's spokesman, Tom Wells, said the incident was “deeply worrying” and "many families will understandably be anxious this morning.” He urged people to let police conduct a full investigation.

Grammy Award- nominated trap and R&B rapper-singer Toliver, who features on the soundtrack to the new “Grand Theft Auto” game, is scheduled to perform at London’s O2 Arena on Monday and Wembley Arena on Tuesday as part of his Nitrous tour.

title: What to know about tear gas and reproductive health, as concerns are raised in France
summary: French activists and lawmakers are demanding after recent protests that police stop using tear gas because of rising concerns about menstrual changes and reproductive health issues
story: French activists and lawmakers are demanding after recent protests that police stop using tear gas because of rising concerns about menstrual changes and reproductive health issues

PARIS -- French activists and lawmakers are demanding after recent street protests that authorities suspend the use of tear gas to disperse crowds over concerns it's caused menstrual changes and other reproductive health problems, though scientists have not confirmed a medical connection.

The demands come after police used tear gas during student protests and demonstrations over the cost of living, some marred by violence. Some women reported painful cramps, unexpected bleeding and disrupted menstrual cycles after exposure, and an advocacy group says it has collected more than 10,000 complaints. Opposition lawmakers are seeking a ban and independent research into possible health effects.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has rejected the calls, saying police use of tear gas is essential to crowd control as an alternative to using more dangerous weapons.
Here’s what is known — and what is not — about tear gas and reproductive health.

Tear gas grenades used by French police contain CS, a chemical irritant that affects the eyes, skin and respiratory tract. CS is a crystalline powder dispersed into the air as fine particles. Its effects depend upon how much is used and how long people are exposed to it.
Those exposed during the protests include peaceful demonstrators — including children, pregnant women and older people — and residents near the sites of protest marches.

Mélina Galland, 24, was working as an independent photographer during Oct. 17 protests in Paris that were marred by rioting and looting. She wore a double surgical mask along with a diving mask when tear gas grenades were fired.
“Heading back home, I felt intense belly pain which was unusual because I never experience pain that intense at that stage of my period,” she said.

Chloé Baroux, 25, also a photographer, first noticed pain and irregular periods after covering protests against a security bill in 2020 and 2021. She said her menstrual cycles eventually became more regular, and she didn't think of a potential link to tear gas until she covered the recent protests, noting, “over the past two months, it’s become irregular again.”

Eva-Luna Tholance, a former journalist who investigated the issue six years ago, decided to found the “Lacrymos de sang” ("Tears of blood") advocacy group during the protests to raise awareness about possible effects on menstrual cycles and pregnancies. The group asked people last month to complete a questionnaire describing their exposure and symptoms. Its collection of accounts doesn't establish how common symptoms are among those who say they were exposed to tear gas, and they were not reviewed by independent doctors.
Still, Tholance said, many women described pain or unexpected bleeding, and thousands are asking questions about what’s happening in their bodies.

“Some people experience mild cramps, but a huge number tell us about cramps that are far worse than what they normally experience during their periods,” she said, adding that bleeding reports range “from spotting to extremely heavy bleeding lasting several days. Some people bleed for weeks.”
Others reported bleeding despite being postmenopausal or taking hormonal contraception that normally prevents menstrual bleeding, Tholance said.

An Associated Press investigation during the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests in the U.S. found there had been limited study and oversight of tear gas, though it did raise concerns about tear gas exposure in confined spaces, excessive use and canisters fired directly at people.

A recent study collected accounts of symptoms reported after the BLM protests. It found a “potential relationship” between exposure and “adverse reproductive health outcomes” but did not prove cause and effect.

That’s in part because the study relied on self-reported information collected at one point in time — similar to the French group’s questionnaire — and because people who felt most impacted may have been more likely to respond.
“There’s a lot of theories. We don’t really 100% know,” said the study’s lead author, Asha Hassan of the University of Minnesota Medical School. The study calls for more research “urgently.”
Hassan said much early research on tear gas involved healthy young men in military settings, which could help explain why menstrual and other reproductive health effects have gone undocumented.
Alsetex and Nobel Sport, two leading suppliers of tear gas grenades to French law enforcement, did not respond to requests for comment.

The Interior Ministry says no published scientific studies show that CS causes menstrual changes or miscarriages. It said other effects of tear gas generally resolve within hours, although it acknowledged that some longer-lasting symptoms affecting the skin and eyes “cannot be ruled out.”
Some other possible effects in the body “have been suggested, but not demonstrated,” it said.

The ministry said it conducted several studies in 2021 and 2022 assessing individual exposure to tear gas, particularly among law enforcement personnel. It did not respond to an AP request for copies.
AP journalist Teresa Suarez contributed to this story.

title: Turkish authorities search for lioness spotted on outskirts of Istanbul
summary: Police and animal welfare teams in Istanbul are searching for a lioness seen prowling the city’s outskirts
story: Police and animal welfare teams in Istanbul are searching for a lioness seen prowling the city’s outskirts
ISTANBUL -- Police and animal welfare teams in Istanbul are searching for a lioness seen prowling the city’s outskirts, Turkish officials said Monday.

A resident spotted the animal Sunday evening in Uskumrukoy, an upmarket neighborhood on the northern edge of Istanbul’s European side, surrounded by forests. The lioness was later captured on security camera footage.
“The location of the lion has been identified, and the necessary care is being taken to capture it alive,” the Istanbul governor’s office said in a statement posted on social media.

Grainy images published by the Demiroren News Agency showed the lioness walking through a grassy area. It was unclear where the animal came from, though some media reports suggested it had escaped from a nearby home. The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office launched an investigation focused on identifying its owner.

The National Parks Directorate said specialist veterinarians and teams equipped with thermal imaging cameras were assisting in the search. More than 70 personnel, supported by drones, were searching in and around the nearby Belgrade Forest, which covers 54 square kilometers north of Istanbul. The forest was closed to vehicles and pedestrians.
Local resident Arda Koc said he saw the lioness after joining the search on Sunday evening.

“I took my car and went out for a drive hoping to see it,” he said in comments reported by the Cumhuriyet newspaper. “While I was driving, it suddenly jumped out in front of me. At first I was scared. After that, I immediately notified the gendarmerie.”

The big cat's appearance has gripped the public’s imagination, drawing people to help with the search. Yusuf Yalcin arrived wearing a lion costume beneath a jersey of local soccer team Galatasaray, nicknamed the Lions.
“Hopefully, the lion will be tranquilized and neutralized without anyone getting hurt,” he told Demiroren.
Residents were warned of the danger, and police were stationed on roads leading into and out of the neighborhood.

Sariyer District Mayor Mustafa Oktay Aksu noted that the lioness had not harmed chickens she passed at night, indicating she had been hand-reared. However, he warned that she should still be treated as dangerous.

Turkey has become a hub for the illegal trade in wild animals as traffickers exploit its air links to Africa and Asia. In December 2024, a young gorilla was rescued after being discovered at Istanbul Airport on a flight from Nigeria to Thailand.

title: Poland says Russia twice tried to kill a Ukrainian American rapper
summary: Denmark expelled a Russian official after it said it thwarted an alleged plot.
story: Denmark expelled a Russian official after it said it thwarted an alleged plot.

WARSAW, Poland -- Denmark has expelled a Russian official after it said it had thwarted an alleged plot to kill a Ukrainian American citizen on Danish soil. The case took a new twist Sunday when Polish authorities revealed that the same man was allegedly targeted by Moscow's intelligence services last summer in Poland.

Denmark is expected to ask the European Union this week for more decisive action stemming from the case, perhaps restricting Russian citizens from entering and traveling freely within the EU. Poland said it would support such measures.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Russia’s threats were becoming more real, reaching EU soil as the bloc continues supporting Ukraine as Moscow's full-scale invasion nears the five-year mark.
The case involves Albert Vasiliev, a rapper who performs under the name Kyivstoner and holds Ukrainian and U.S. citizenship, according to Danish media.

The assassination attempt in Denmark was planned for Sept. 25 during a concert north of Copenhagen, according to the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, known by its acronym PET. It said the plot was “planned and initiated by Russian intelligence services.”

The plot was thwarted by authorities, the Danish prime minister’s office said Friday. PET said two men were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service in operating in Denmark. They were linked to Loyal to Familia, it said, a banned gang known for “extensive, serious and violent criminal activity.”
Russia dismissed the allegations through its embassy in Copenhagen, saying the accusations were unsubstantiated.
Denmark responded by expelling Russia’s defense attaché.

“In our assessment, the individual concerned was a particular target of the Russian intelligence services," said Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen, director general of PET. “The case demonstrates that Russian intelligence services are both willing and capable of initiating an assassination attempt on Danish soil — at a public event and using individuals from Danish criminal gangs. This is a concrete indication of the heightened threat posed by Russia.”
As Denmark announced the plot against the rapper on Friday, the Polish Foreign Ministry posted on X that it was noting the news with “outrage and concern."

“This is another assassination attempt against this person — the first took place on Polish territory in August 2026 but was thwarted thanks to the efforts of the Polish services and the would-be perpetrator, a Russian citizen, was detained,” the ministry said.
The suspect, who was allegedly recruited by Russia’s secret services, was detained by Polish authorities on Aug. 7.
Maciej Wewiór, a Foreign Ministry spokesman, confirmed to The Associated Press the previous attempt to kill Vasiliev in Poland.

On Aug. 13, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk disclosed the plot to kill a Ukrainian American citizen in Warsaw was thwarted, noting it was the first time that “someone on the order of Russia” sought to attack a U.S. citizen on the territory of another NATO country.
Tusk did not, however, disclose Vasiliev's name, saying only that the target “was uncomfortable” for Russian President Vladimir Putin's government.

Vasiliev was born in Kyiv in 1991, according to Polish media. He posted online comedy sketches and was a former member of the Ukrainian band Hryby. He also was popular in Russia before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
But he left Ukraine after the war broke out and lived for two years in the U.S. before moving to Slovakia. He has expressed his support for Ukraine against Russia.
He performed across Europe this year before his concerts were cancelled for security reasons.

Russia's domestic security service, the FSB, accused Vasiliev of being involved in supplying drones for an alleged Ukrainian attack on a defense enterprise in the Moscow region. It said he was “acting under the patronage” of Ukraine's internal security service, the SBU.
Danish broadcaster DR reported that Vasiliev denied the FSB accusations

He did not comment on social media about the plot against him in Poland, but DR reported that he announced on Instagram that “the intelligence service banned us from holding the concert” referring to the cancellation of his event in Denmark.
Western officials have accused Russia and its proxies of staging dozens of attacks and other incidents across Europe since the invasion of Ukraine.
“Russia’s hybrid threats are becoming less and less hybrid, and more and more real,” said von der Leyen, the EC president, who condemned the alleged plot against Vasiliev in Denmark.

The Polish Foreign Ministry said in a statement that "the events in Denmark are another example of Russia’s criminal activity on the territory of an EU member state, aimed at intimidating and destabilizing our societies.”
Russia has denied accusations by Western officials that it was conducting a sabotage campaign in Europe.
Joanna Kozlowska in London contributed.

title: India announces a $1.6 billion aid package for Nepal’s flood recovery
summary: India has announced a $1.62 billion aid package to help Nepal rebuild after devastating floods
story: India has announced a $1.62 billion aid package to help Nepal rebuild after devastating floods
NEW DELHI -- India announced Monday a $1.62 billion economic assistance package to help Nepal rebuild areas devastated by floods, providing a major boost to the country’s recovery efforts.

The Aug. 26 floods in Nepal destroyed roads, bridges, power plants, farms and homes, causing an estimated $4.7 billion in losses, according to Nepali authorities. The U.N. Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage has also pledged about $20 million to support Nepal’s recovery.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the aid after meeting Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah in New Delhi. Shah is on his first visit to India since taking office in March, six months after a youth-led uprising over corruption and nepotism forced former Prime Minister K.P. Sharma Oli from power.

Modi said the assistance would help restore infrastructure, rebuild communities and support people who lost their homes and livelihoods. The floods killed 1,500 people and left more than 5,200 missing.
Modi and Shah also virtually inaugurated a hydropower project and an oil storage facility in Nepal, as well as an oil pipeline and a cross-border train service connecting the two countries.

Nepal shares an open border with India, allowing people to cross without passports or visas. India has traditionally wielded considerable influence in the Himalayan nation, but ties have been strained by territorial disputes and accusations of political interference.
China, meanwhile, has expanded its presence in Nepal in recent years, investing in airports, highways and hydropower projects.

Despite growing Chinese influence in Nepal, the landlocked country remains heavily dependent on India for fuel and other essential supplies. At the same time, energy ties have become increasingly reciprocal, with India importing around 1,200 MW of electricity from Nepal.

title: Carney enlists fake Trump for laughs at Canada's annual press gallery dinner
summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney shared the stage with a fake Donald Trump and two versions of himself Saturday, enlisting comedians to help roast the U.S. president and Canadian politicians at an annual dinner with journalists
story: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney shared the stage with a fake Donald Trump and two versions of himself Saturday, enlisting comedians to help roast the U.S. president and Canadian politicians at an annual dinner with journalists

OTTAWA, Ontario -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney shared the stage with a fake Donald Trump and another version of himself this weekend, enlisting comedians to help roast the U.S. president and Canadian politicians at an annual dinner with journalists.
“I am pressing the emergency comedy button,” Carney said Saturday as comedian Mark McKinney appeared impersonating the prime minister, followed by Mark Critch playing Trump.
Critch recreated Trump’s trademark forceful handshake, exchanging grips with Carney and McKinney onstage.
Carney also poked fun at Trump’s lavish makeover of the Oval Office.
“This is a tough room. And I’ve been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator,” Carney said.
Since returning to the White House, Trump has filled the Oval Office with gold accents, gilded decorations and portraits.
The annual Parliamentary Press Gallery dinner is Canada’s version of a Washington political roast, where politicians and journalists trade jokes and insults.

Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre took aim at former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau’s relationship with American pop star Katy Perry, joking that Trudeau was doing to a “faded pop princess” what he had done to Canada during his decade in power.
The remark drew criticism online as sexist and demeaning toward Perry.
Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour, a former Supreme Court justice who represents Britain’s King Charles III as Canada’s head of state, mocked Carney’s extensive international travel.
“Do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he’s supposed to be,” she said.

title: Suspected Ukrainian sea drones hit Russian warship at Benghazi naval base, Libyan officials say
summary: The sea drone strike triggered an explosion and fire in Benghazi.
story: The sea drone strike triggered an explosion and fire in Benghazi.
CAIRO -- A suspected Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship Sunday at a naval base in Libya, officials said, the latest attack in the North African nation linked to the Russia-Ukraine war.
The strike at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette, and ignited a fire at the facility, two Libyan military officials said.

They said that several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya, according to an initial investigation into the attack. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, they said.
The officials, affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya, spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to talk with reporters.

Libya has been divided since a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime dictator Moammar Gadhafi, who was later killed, in 2011. A U.N.-supported government is based in Tripoli and a rival administration is located in the east. The oil-rich nation remains a focal point for a long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.
The eastern Libya-based government said in a statement that the strike Sunday caused an explosion and fire at the base, which was later extinguished.

The Almasar satellite television channel aired footage showing a vessel erupting into flames. It said the Libyan navy rescued the crew of the Maltese-flagged ship. A corvette warship is smaller than a frigate or destroyer and is built to patrol coastal waters and escort other ships.

The vessel had docked at the Libyan base for refueling and supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said, without providing details on the vessel or its cargo.
A joint investigation was launched with Russia to “uncover the circumstances of the attack, its source, and the party behind it,” the statement said.
No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack. There was no immediate comment from either Russia or Ukraine.

A European official said the reports of an explosion at Benghazi Port involving a Russian vessel appeared to be credible. The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record, said the vessel has been identified as a Russian corvette, adding they had no assessment of cause at this time.

On Sunday evening, local media said that another sea drone hit a Maltese-flagged commercial vessel off the port of Benghazi in a separate attack. No further details were given. Almasar said that naval and air forces destroyed at least 12 other sea drones off the Mediterranean city.
The western Libya government expressed concerns about “dragging Libyan ports and civilian facilities into external conflicts,” in an apparent reference to the war in Ukraine.
“The government reaffirms its categorical rejection of turning Libya into an arena for international conflicts or a theater for external powers to settle scores,” it said in a statement.

In March, Ukrainian forces operating in western Libya under a covert deal struck a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean in a suspected sea drone attack near Maltese waters, Libyan officials said at the time.

The Ukrainian forces, most of them drone experts, operated mainly at an air base in the coastal city of Misrata, but also at other military facilities in the capital, Tripoli, and the coastal town of Zawiya, the officials told The Associated Press.
Associated Press writer Emma Burrows in London contributed to this report.

title: Thai court upholds royal defamation conviction for opposition lawmaker and cuts sentence to 3 years
summary: An appeals court has upheld the conviction of an opposition lawmaker for defaming Thailand’s monarchy in social media posts but reduced her prison sentence from six years to three
story: An appeals court has upheld the conviction of an opposition lawmaker for defaming Thailand’s monarchy in social media posts but reduced her prison sentence from six years to three
BANGKOK -- An appeals court Monday upheld the conviction of an opposition lawmaker for defaming Thailand's monarchy in social media posts but reduced her prison sentence from six years to three.

Rukchanok Srinork of the People’s Party was initially charged with lese majeste and violating the Computer Crime Act. In 2023, she was convicted and sentenced to six years in prison over two social media posts.

The appeals court said in a statement that it upheld the conviction in connection with one post but dropped the charges related to the other, halving her sentence. It said the three-year penalty was imposed under the lese majeste law, which carries a heavier penalty than the Computer Crime Act, a broad law regulating online activities.
Rukchanok was accompanied to the hearing by several fellow party members. Supporters greeted her outside the Bangkok court and gave her red roses before she entered.
People’s Party leader Natthaphong Reungpanyawut said the court dropped the charges on one post due to insufficient evidence.

The court later granted Rukchanok's release on bail. If she had been denied bail, she would have been immediately removed from her seat in Parliament. Rukchanok said afterward that she would appeal the ruling with the Supreme Court.

The two posts were shared in 2021 on X, then known as Twitter. One reportedly criticized the monarchy over its links to a coronavirus vaccine, while the other was a repost of an anti-monarchy message. Rukchanok has denied writing the posts herself.

The court’s decision, though expected, underlines that Thailand’s political establishment remains conservative and is sensitive about any perceived threats to the status of the country’s monarchy. The progressive People’s Party is now the main opposition in Parliament after finishing second to the conservative Bhumjaithai Party in this year’s election.

The lese majeste law, also known as Article 112 of the Criminal Code, is controversial not only because it has been used to punish things as simple as liking a post on Facebook, but also because anyone — not just royals or the authorities — can lodge a complaint that most of the time leads to detention during lengthy legal proceedings.
A conviction of defaming the monarchy carries a prison term of up to 15 years, and critics say the law has often been used to quash political dissent.
Student-led pro-democracy demonstrations starting in 2020 sought reforms of the lese majeste law, but the protesters became targets of the law.
Thai Lawyers for Human Rights, a law advocacy group, says more than 290 people, many of them student activists, have been charged with violating Article 112 since early 2020.

title: Tourists evacuated after fire destroys 6 hotels in Zanzibar's Nungwi Beach area
summary: A fire engulfed six hotels along a popular beach in Tanzania’s Zanzibar archipelago over the weekend, causing widespread damage but no deaths
story: A fire engulfed six hotels along a popular beach in Tanzania’s Zanzibar archipelago over the weekend, causing widespread damage but no deaths
ZANZIBAR, Tanzania -- Investigations continued Monday into the cause of a huge fire that engulfed six hotels along a popular beach in Tanzania ’s semiautonomous archipelago of Zanzibar.
Several hotel workers were injured in the blaze over the weekend. Authorities said about 180 tourists were safely evacuated.

The fire broke out Saturday afternoon at Makofi Hotel on Nungwi Beach, at the northern end of the island, and spread rapidly to neighboring properties, fueled by strong winds and thatched roofs. Firefighters battled the blaze for about three hours before bringing it under control.
Preliminary reports suggest the fire may have started in an oven used to bake bread, though officials have cautioned against speculation.
Tourism Minister Nasra Nassor said Saturday that the government would conduct a rapid assessment and establish the cause of the fire before taking “necessary measures.”
Zanzibar’s white sand beaches and tropical climate draw tourists to the archipelago, where tourism is a major contributor to the economy.

title: A silver soup tureen once owned by JP Morgan could fetch $8M at a Christie's auction
summary: A massive silver soup tureen once owned by financier J
story: A massive silver soup tureen once owned by financier J
LONDON -- It's a perfect gift for the host with the most.
A huge silver soup tureen once owned by financier J.P. Morgan up for sale, with an estimated price of up to 6 million pounds (almost $8 million).
More than a foot and a half long (46 centimeters) long and weighing in at 44 pounds (20 kilograms), the Meissonnier Tureen is the star of a Dec. 1 auction at Christie’s in London.
Made in the 1730s by the French artist and goldsmith Juste-Aurèle Meissonnier in a flamboyant rococo style, it was “designed to astonish,” according to Christie’s specialist Isabelle Cartier-Stone.

Shaped like a stylized shell, it has a cover encrusted with detailed silver plants and animals, including “a duck, a crab, a fish, an oyster, and a snail among an artichoke and other leafy vegetables,” according to the catalog.

The tureen’s owners have included British aristocrats, Russian statesmen and the American banker John Pierpont Morgan. It is one of a pair split up after they were auctioned together in 1977, with the other in the Cleveland Museum of Art in Ohio.

It is being sold as part of a trove of silver owned by the Blaquier-Arrieta family of wealthy Argentine collectors and has a presale estimate of between 4 million pounds and 6 million pounds ($5.25 million and $7.86 million).

A group of a dozen paintings owned by the same family sold at Sotheby’s last week for $412 million, with the Vincent van Gogh painting “Châtaigniers en fleurs” (Chestnut Trees in Flower) fetching $190.4 million.

title: More remains recovered in the search for 34 workers missing after an Indonesian candy factory fire
summary: Rescue teams searching for 34 missing workers after a candy factory fire in Indonesia have recovered remains in 24 body bags
story: Rescue teams searching for 34 missing workers after a candy factory fire in Indonesia have recovered remains in 24 body bags

JAKARTA, Indonesia -- Rescue teams searching for 34 missing workers after a fire swept through a candy factory in Indonesia recovered human remains in 24 body bags, though authorities said Sunday it was too early to determine the death toll.

The National Search and Rescue Agency earlier said the fire killed at least three workers. However, in its latest statement, it said the recovered remains and body parts still required forensic examination and identification.
The blaze at the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia factory in Banten province was largely contained Sunday, but some areas were still inaccessible.
The fire started around 5 p.m. Saturday and flames engulfed the three-story building in the Serang district of Banten province, which borders the capital, Jakarta.

Fifteen fire trucks, supported by water cannons, were deployed to battle the flames in several parts of the facility more than 12 hours after the fire began, said Rizky Dwianto, an operations official at the Banten Search and Rescue Agency. A joint rescue team, including police, the military, the Indonesian Red Cross and volunteers, was at the scene.
Debris littered the floor of the burned-out structure, including twisted metal and blackened, corrugated iron roofing.
The cause of the fire wasn't immediately known. Survivors said the flames originated from a cooling unit on the third floor, local media reported.
The factory produces Milkita, an Indonesian brand of milk-based candies and snack products exported to more than 40 countries worldwide.

The company's chief executive, Steven Wijaya, told a joint news conference with authorities in Serang on Sunday that about 300 workers were inside the factory compound, with 65 workers believed to have been in the affected area when the fire broke out.
He said as of Sunday afternoon, 24 workers had returned home.

“We are deeply concerned by this tragedy,” Wijaya said. “We have established a hotline for relatives seeking information on missing family members and are maintaining regular communication with affected families.”

Wijaya said that the factory regularly conducted emergency and evacuation drills in conjunction with local firefighters. He said that the facility had adequate evacuation routes and fire protection systems, including hydrants and water reserves, that complied with applicable safety standards and were functioning at the time of the fire.

In a statement released late Sunday, authorities said 63 people were believed to have been in the area at the time. Of those, 29 were confirmed alive, including five hospitalized with injuries, while 34 workers remained missing.

The condition of the victims made visual identification impossible, prompting authorities to urge family members to provide DNA samples and other information that could be used to identify their loved ones, said Wahyu Hidayati Dwi Palupi, who heads the National Police’s victim identification division.
She said that body bags containing the remains of the victims were transferred to a hospital for identification.

Although the blaze had largely been contained Sunday, firefighters were carrying out intensive cooling operations before they could access all parts of the factory, said Tubagus Mahfud, operations chief of the Serang fire department.

“We are conducting sweeps in the areas that have already been brought under control,” Mahfud said. “Parts of the structure had collapsed, while poor lighting conditions required firefighters to proceed cautiously.”
He also said that the factory’s production materials could cause the fire to reignite, making it critical to complete cooling operations.
Anxious relatives waited for news outside the burned-out factory.
Indonesia has experienced a series of deadly industrial fires in recent years, raising concerns about workplace safety standards and emergency preparedness at manufacturing facilities in the country.

title: Missile attack on Zelenskyy's hometown in central Ukraine kills 2 and wounds scores
summary: A Russian strike on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown, Kryvyi Rih, has killed two people and wounded 60 others
story: A Russian strike on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown, Kryvyi Rih, has killed two people and wounded 60 others
KYIV, Ukraine -- A Russian strike on the center of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s hometown, Kryvyi Rih, killed two people and wounded 60 others, local officials said Saturday.

A 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman were killed in the attack Friday night on the city in central Ukraine, Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of the city administration, wrote on Telegram. Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional military administration, said 60 people were wounded, including six children.
The strike caused four fires and damaged about 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and an industrial facility, as well as businesses and vehicles, Vilkul said.
The attack fits the pattern of Moscow’s heavy responses to eye-catching Ukrainian attacks, such as the ones this week on the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to illegally annexed Crimea.

The missile attack came hours after two Russian missiles and a suspected drone came down in Poland, in what its prime minister said was likely a provocation timed to coincide with European military exercises in his country for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine.

European troops were taking part Friday in an unprecedented two-week military exercise that began Nov. 9 in southeastern Poland. Forces are preparing for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine aimed at helping to stabilize the country and rebuild its military. European countries previously have expressed alarm at what they deem to be Russia’s attempts to destabilize the continent.

The development stoked tensions between Europe and Moscow just as the U.S. tries to add momentum to talks it is mediating on ending the war that began with Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine nearly five years ago.

U.S. President Donald Trump discussed the war with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a summit in China on Thursday, according to his envoy Steve Witkoff. Trump called Putin his “friend” during the meeting and continued to tout their relationship at a White House news conference Friday.
Asked about Trump’s remarks in an interview with CNN, Zelenskyy called Putin “a killer.”
“For us, he is an enemy. And of course, for us, he is a killer,” Zelenskyy said Friday. He warned that describing the Russian leader in friendly terms could mean “he doesn’t feel enough pressure.”

Elsewhere in Ukraine, 11 people, including two children, were wounded when a Russian drone attacked a five-story apartment building in the Kharkiv region, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said Saturday. One person was wounded in a Russian attack on the capital, Kyiv, according to the service.
In Russia, local officials said Saturday that Ukrainian drone attacks wounded three people in the Bryansk and Belgorod border regions.
Morton reported from London.
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: Sydney man charged with car bomb plot and downloading Islamic State group material
summary: Australian police have arrested a man in the greater Sydney area on charges of researching how to build a car bomb and downloading violent material inspired by the Islamic State group
story: Australian police have arrested a man in the greater Sydney area on charges of researching how to build a car bomb and downloading violent material inspired by the Islamic State group

MELBOURNE, Australia -- Australian police on Friday arrested a man in the greater Sydney area on charges of researching how to build a car bomb and downloading violent material inspired by the Islamic State group.

Police stressed they found no evidence of a link to the upcoming first anniversary of an IS-inspired attack at Sydney’s Bondi Beach. Two gunmen opened fire on a Dec. 14 Hanukkah celebration, leaving 15 people dead and 40 wounded.

Nowroz Rayed Amin, 35, from Ingleburn on Sydney’s southwestern outskirts, was charged with collecting documents likely to facilitate terrorist acts and possessing violent extremist material obtained online, Australian Federal Police Deputy Commissioner Hilda Sirec said.
“It will be alleged in court that the man was researching how to build a vehicle-borne, improvised explosive device, which we allege, for use in a potential terrorist act,” Sirec told reporters.
Amin appeared in the Campbelltown Local Court later Friday on the two charges, which carry a potential combined maximum penalty of 20 years in prison.
Amin did not enter pleas or apply for release on bail. He was remanded in custody to appear in court on Thursday next week, court documents show.

Investigators decided to make the arrest Friday because there was sufficient evidence and not because of any imminent threat to the community, according to Sirec, who said police suspected he had acted alone.

“I want to stress this point because we acknowledge we are just weeks away from the first anniversary of the Bondi Beach attack,” Sirec said. “There is no information to suggest that this alleged offending is connected to the anniversary of that attack. However, we know the fear that this will cause.”
The attack at Bondi Beach was Australia's worst mass shooting since 1996.

Police killed one gunman, Sajid Akram, at the scene. His son, Naveed Akram, was wounded and faces trial next year on 78 charges including 15 counts of murder, 43 of attempted murder and one of committing a terrorist act. Akram has yet to enter any plea.
Police executed 10 search warrants in the greater Sydney area Friday and made three arrests.
As well as Amin, police arrested a 33-year-old man for weapons offenses and a 34-year-old man for hindering police, Sirec said.

title: At least 24 dead in Nigeria when boat going to funeral capsizes
summary: Authorities haven't said how many passengers were believed to be on board.
story: Authorities haven't said how many passengers were believed to be on board.
ABUJA, Nigeria -- A boat carrying people to a funeral has capsized in southern Nigeria, killing at least 24 people, emergency services said on Saturday.

The boat was taking passengers from one community to another for a burial ceremony when it sank on Friday in Bayelsa State in the country’s South South region, Nigeria’s National Emergency Management Agency spokesman Manzo Ezeki said in a statement.
He said that search and rescue operations were ongoing without specifying how many people were missing.
Police spokesman Musa Mohammed said on Friday that another 24 people had been rescued and sought medical assistance.
Authorities haven't said how many passengers were believed to have been on board.
Mohammed said that preliminary reports suggested that the boat suffered a mechanical problem.

Passengers asked the boat operator to steer toward land, but he allegedly declined, according to Mohammed. The boat operator then reportedly fled the scene, while the manager of the boat was taken into custody.
The Bayelsa state government responded by urging boat operators and passengers to adhere to safety regulations.

“Overloading, speeding, recklessness and traveling without life jackets must stop. No journey is worth a life,” Bayelsa Commissioner for Information Ebiuwou Koku-Obiyai said in a statement on Saturday.
Boat tragedies are common in Nigeria. A lack of enforcement of safety regulations means faulty boats without life jackets sometimes operate in the country.

title: Saudi Arabia intercepts more Yemen Houthi missiles and drones, and other Mideast news
summary: Saudi Arabia says Iran-backed Houthi rebels have fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom
story: Saudi Arabia says Iran-backed Houthi rebels have fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom
Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom, days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen.

Meanwhile, in Iraq, troops deployed to a militia stronghold south of the capital Baghdad after the government apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Friday. Read our full coverage here.
Iraqi security forces set up a command headquarters on the outskirts of the Jurf al-Sakhar area south of Baghdad, long a stronghold of an Iran-backed militia, Kataib Hezbollah, on Friday.
The area had been the source of rising tensions, with the government calling for the militia to withdraw amid allegations that it was using the area for oil smuggling.
Kataib Hezbollah had threatened to fight security forces if they attempted an incursion.

Two Iraqi officials, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly, said the government and Kataib Hezbollah had reached an agreement under which security forces could enter but the militia would not immediately withdraw.

The deal followed negotiations facilitated by Esmail Qaani, commander of Iran’s Quds Force, a branch of the paramilitary Revolutionary Guard that's responsible for operations outside Iran and is key to Iran’s influence and ties to allies across the Middle East.

Under the agreement, the Iraqi army, federal police and police tied to the energy sector will be deployed in the area. In a compromise, the deployment will also include fighters from the Popular Mobilization Forces, a collection of mostly Shiite armed groups close to Iran that are officially part of Iraq’s security forces.
Kataib Hezbollah would withdraw its fighters within a month.
— By Qassim Abdul-Zahra

The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said the kingdom intercepted five drones and one ballistic missile that targeted it on Friday morning. Riyadh, the kingdom's capital and largest city, was among the targets.

The interceptions marked the latest Houthi attempts to strike Saudi territory and came a day after the Iran-backed rebels said they had targeted Saudi airports, air bases and Riyadh’s financial center.
Saudi Civil Defense has sent out 13 emergency alerts since Thursday, warning the public of potential incoming strikes or debris from interceptions.

The Houthis did not immediately comment or claim Friday’s attacks. But they traded threats Friday to strike key ports in each other’s territories, marking the latest escalation between the rebels and the kingdom.
Earlier this week, Saudi Arabia launched a major air campaign across Houthi-held territory in Yemen.
Abdul-Zahra reported from Baghdad, Khaled from Cairo and Metz from Jerusalem.
This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.

title: Taiwan warns Canada’s Carney that deeper ties with China come with risks
summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has tried to deepen trade ties with China.
story: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has tried to deepen trade ties with China.

HALIFAX, Nova Scotia -- Taiwan’s deputy foreign minister warned on Saturday that Prime Minister Mark Carney risks exposing Canada to the very economic coercion he has cautioned against by deepening trade ties with China, saying that Taiwan has learned the hard way that dependence on Beijing comes with consequences.
“We worry. We worry,” Chen Ming-chi told The Associated Press in an interview at the Halifax International Security Forum when asked about Carney’s efforts to improve relations with China.

Carney has warned that major powers are using economic integration as a weapon, citing U.S. tariffs and China’s restrictions on critical minerals. He has urged middle powers to diversify their trade relationships to avoid economic coercion.
Chen praised Carney’s speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, but questioned whether Canada should deepen ties with countries that don’t share its democratic values.
“Who do you want to choose as your partners?” he asked.

“You have your own history. You have two Michaels,” Chen said, referring to former Canadian diplomat Michael Kovrig and businessman Michael Spavor, whose ne arly three-year detention in China prompted accusations of hostage diplomacy.

The two were arrested in 2018 shortly after Canada detained Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou on a U.S. extradition request. They were released in September 2021, the same day Meng returned to China. Beijing denied their detention was politically motivated.

Chen’s warning came days after Carney met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen and agreed to additional tariff reductions as Canada seeks to diversify trade during U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war.

Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if negotiations with Washington fail to preserve a viable Canadian auto industry. Trump has threatened 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles and auto parts beginning on Jan. 1.
Chen warned that Chinese electric vehicles could threaten Canadian manufacturers and pose surveillance risks because of their connected technology, even if manufactured in Canada.

Carney has argued that Canada’s trade relationship with China differs from Washington’s more complicated ties with Beijing. Canada primarily exports agricultural products, energy and other commodities rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
Chen said that Taiwan had dramatically reduced its economic dependence on China after experiencing Beijing’s use of trade restrictions to exert political pressure.
“They are very good at weaponizing interdependence,” he said. “They are very good at leveraging our dependence to reach political goals.”

Taiwan reduced the share of its outbound investment going to China from more than 80% in 2010 to 3.8% last year, Chen said. Its exports to China and Hong Kong fell from nearly 44% of total exports in 2020 to about 27% last year, according to Taiwanese government figures.

Chen also accused Beijing of exploiting a striking photograph from this week’s summit in Shenzhen showing Xi seated prominently between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin to project China as the world’s leading power.
“The main idea is to prove not only to his domestic audience that he is the world leader,” Chen said. “They are so good at propaganda."
He described the summit as “more symbolic than substantial.”

Chen said China was intensifying military operations around Taiwan, despite the potentially enormous costs of an invasion. He warned that Chinese vessels could be rehearsing for a maritime quarantine of the self-governing island.
Despite his concerns about Beijing, Chen praised Carney’s international leadership and welcomed his commitment to sign a long-delayed trade cooperation arrangement with Taiwan.
“We have a high respect of Prime Minister Carney’s vision. And we want to be part of this vision,” he said.

title: Xi projects China’s global influence after hosting Trump and Putin at APEC
summary: China’s President Xi Jinping has emerged from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with a diplomatic win, reinforcing his global standing despite limited substantive progress
story: China’s President Xi Jinping has emerged from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with a diplomatic win, reinforcing his global standing despite limited substantive progress

BANGKOK -- Results matter in the international arena, but so do optics. This week’s high-level meetings in China gave President Xi Jinping a win, reinforcing his image as a central player in global diplomacy.

As host of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday and Thursday, Xi welcomed the leaders of 21 nations representing some of the world’s largest economies that account for about 60% of global economic activity. He also convened the first formal gathering of the three biggest nuclear powers: the United States, Russia and China.

“History tells us that when major powers live in harmony, the world is at peace, and when they engage in confrontation the world is thrown into turmoil,” Xi said on Thursday before the start of closed-door discussions with U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“Our three countries should set an example by working together to address global challenges, jointly safeguard world peace and stability and make greater contributions to human progress,” he added.

The summit in China's capital city was seen as emblematic of the nation's superpower status. The trilateral meeting on Thursday produced no major breakthroughs, but the image of the three leaders seated at an enormous round table with Xi at the center and Trump to his left and Putin to his right will become part of diplomatic history.

“For most, the image was a suggestion that the world increasingly revolves around Beijing’s power and preferences,” Rush Doshi, director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations, wrote in an article for the council. “And for U.S. allies in particular, it was unsettling because it suggested that Washington will prioritize engagement with the other great powers over that with its own partners.”
“Xi’s clearest diplomatic gain in Shenzhen was bringing Trump and Putin to the same table,” said Yaqi Li, a Chinese foreign policy researcher at the ISEAS — Yusof Ishak Institute.

China positioned itself as a force for global stability and a go-to talking point in recent years. Xi started the meeting with Trump and Putin with a reminder of how the three countries fought together in World War II.
“History is the best textbook,” Xi said, presenting the talks as a way to push for peace for humanity. “We must remember history, learn from it and work together to shape the future.”
The meeting resulted in a joint declaration that was light on commitments and did not tackle major issues in a substantive way.

“They're using this opportunity … to highlight that China is a great power, and they're in a different status relative to other countries,” said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University.

Xi and Trump held their third meeting this year, highlighting the personal rapport they have built that both men said was important to the bilateral relationship between their nations. China's government highlighted the “constructive strategic stability” of the relationship while Xi commended the U.S. president for his role.
“The efforts you have made are there for all to see and will go down in history,” Xi told Trump.

There were no announcements about existing trade issues between the countries such as U.S. complaints that China has not fulfilled its commitment to buy from U.S. farmers and export more rare earth materials. Nor were there announcements about the Board of Trade and the expected framework to allow trade in nonsensitive goods worth $30 billion on each side.

It was unclear if officials taking part in a diplomatic channel to discuss artificial intelligence issues met in Shenzhen, said Wendy Cutler, senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
However, “AI seems to be the one area where some progress has been made, with China affirming its concerns about safety and security and welcoming bilateral work,” Cutler said.

Whether the personal rapport between Xi and Trump can persist will be tested soon, according to Craig Singleton, senior fellow and senior director of the China Program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.
“Xi treated Trump with respect in Shenzhen. He will test his resolve in Miami next month, when the bill for Beijing’s trade commitments comes due,” Singleton said in an email.
Castillo reported from Shenzhen, China.

title: Russian missile crash in Poland likely an intentional provocation, Polish leader says
summary: Russian missile crash in Poland likely an intentional provocation as European militaries hold drills, Polish leader says
story: Russian missile crash in Poland likely an intentional provocation as European militaries hold drills, Polish leader says
WARSAW, Poland -- Russian missile crash in Poland likely an intentional provocation as European militaries hold drills, Polish leader says.
THIS IS AN APNewsAlert. Check back for updates. AP's earlier story is below.

The Polish military is investigating a “suspected violation” of the country's airspace near its border with Ukraine after officials sought to retrieve an unidentified object that had apparently crash-landed in Poland on Friday morning.

The incident came against the backdrop of Russian attacks in Ukraine that killed three people, injured nine others and damaged bridges and transport infrastructure. Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said he believes the incident was another provocation by Russia and timed to European military exercises underway in Poland.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he would convene a meeting with government ministers, military commanders and the head of security services in response. Officials said it was too early to tell what the object was.

The potential crash site is near the village of Nowy Lipowiec, roughly 60 kilometers (37 miles) from the Poland-Ukraine border. Nearby schools suspended classes for the day, according to Polish news agency PAP.
Images from closed-circuit cameras and a mobile phone in the region collected by PAP showed a large, loud explosion in a bright flash that appeared to take place in a wooded area.
Military helicopters and rescue vehicles were spotted in the vicinity, and police set up temporary roadblocks as an investigation was underway.

The location is also about 75 kilometers (47 miles) from where thousands of European troops were taking part on Friday in an unprecedented military exercise in southeastern Poland to prepare for a potential postwar mission in Ukraine aimed at helping to stabilize the country and rebuild its military once the war ends.

title: Haiti strikes deal with El Salvador to build new prisons after minister visit
summary: Haiti announces an agreement with El Salvador for the construction of a new prison
story: Haiti announces an agreement with El Salvador for the construction of a new prison

PORT-AU-PRINCE, Haiti -- Haiti announced an agreement with El Salvador Friday for the construction of new prisons as the two countries increase cooperation following the Central American country's deployment of troops to fight gangs in Haiti.

This announcement by Haitian Minister of Justice and Public Security Patrick Pélissier follows his official mission to El Salvador. The first prison will be launched soon with the prime minister ordering it to be expedited. It will be one of three prisons built by a Salvadoran company in collaboration with a Haitian firm, the minister said.
Gangs control an estimated 70% of Haiti’s capital and swaths of land in the country’s central region.

Pélissier praised the notorious Salvadoran maximum security prison CECOT, which he visited while in the Central American country for an international conference. El Salvador has been under a state of exception since 2022 that has imprisoned more than 90,000 people with no access to family visits. The U.S. has also deported Venezuelans and Salvadorans to the CECOT and they have denounced torture there after release.
“Once you enter, there is no hope of ever seeing the outside world again,” Pélissier said.

Haiti has struggled to find proper infrastructure to hold those arrested after powerful gangs raided the country’s two biggest prisons in 2024 and released thousands of inmates. Haiti's prisons have long been notorious for severe overcrowding, with human rights experts warning that prisoners sleep standing and hundreds have died in recent years. A 2023 visit by The Associated Press to one of Haiti's prisons revealed horrid conditions with prisoners thirsty and starving.
Pélissier did not say how much the projects would cost, whether El Salvador would help finance them and whether it would play any kind of management role.

The announcement comes as El Salvador’s armed forces said Friday that two of its soldiers were killed and two others injured in a detonation while handling explosives at a camp in Haiti, where Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele has sent troops to fanfare from many Haitians.
“We express our deepest condolences and solidarity with the families of those who died. We stand with their loved ones during this difficult time,” the armed forces said on X.
The military said the two injured soldiers were receiving medical care but did not disclose their condition.

The soldiers killed were among the 2,500 Salvadoran soldiers deployed in Haiti in a military operation to rescue four technicians who disappeared in the Caribbean nation on Oct. 18, 2026, after coming under fire from gangs in the Croix-des-Bouquets area northeast of Port-au-Prince.
Some Haitians have celebrated Bukele's decision to send troops to fight gangs, but experts have said it is a political gamble for the leader running for his third term that poses risks to civilians.

The missing technicians were part of the gang suppression force in Haiti, an international force authorized by the U.N. Security Council in October 2025 to have 5,500 security personnel work to dismantle and neutralize Haitian armed gangs, protect infrastructure and facilitate humanitarian access in collaboration with the Haitian National Police. The force replaced the Kenya-led multinational security support mission and has not yet deployed the full 5,500 security personnel.
The gang suppression force has the power to arrest suspected criminals, something that members of the previous Kenyan-led mission were not authorized to do.
The additional troops deployed by Bukele are not part of the U.N.-backed force.
Haiti has not had an elected government since President Jovenel Moïse was assassinated in 2021. Elections are set to take place next year.
Magaña reported from San Salvador, El Salvador and Brigida from Mexico City. Associated Press reporter Dánica Coto reported from San Juan, Puerto Rico.
