The “Suneung,” or the College Scholastic Ability Test, is a crucial annual event for which the education-obsessed country goes to extraordinary lengths to create an ideal testing environment. The start of work hours and stock trading are delayed to ease traffic for test-takers, and flights are halted during the English listening section. Police often use cars or motorcycles to escort test-takers who are running late, while the military sometimes suspends training near testing sites.

Growing public concerns about AI-assisted cheating have drastically raised the stakes for this year’s exam, with some experts and politicians even calling for the government to postpone the test until reliable anti-cheating measures are in place.

President Lee Jae Myung, who is in the Philippines for a regional summit, chaired an emergency meeting by video to review the government’s exam preparations and vowed a stern, “zero-tolerance” response toward anyone caught cheating. He also instructed officials to consider sending more text alerts at unpredictable times during the exam.
“Would even the boldest student risk getting dragged out during the test because their telecommunications device went off?” Lee said on his X account.

Vice Education Minister Choi Eun-ok said that “there could be critics who say our measures are excessive, but a failure to conduct Suneung in a strict and fair manner will bring a (major) disruption to our society that would really be worse than a disaster.”
“We believe we are in a situation where excessive measures are necessary,” Choi said.

Government officials scrambled to strengthen anti-cheating measures this week after a 34-year-old man who topped a national tax accountant exam confessed in a video posted on his lawyer’s YouTube channel Sunday that he had used a hidden microcamera and smartphone to obtain answers from AI.

Han Won-seok’s unusually high scores had drawn suspicion after he discussed them during recent media interviews. The case follows other incidents involving AI-assisted cheating in the past several months, including test-takers caught using AI-powered smart glasses on an English standardized test in June and on some university essay exams in October.
Han Won-seok told reporters he would cooperate with the criminal investigation into his actions as he arrived for questioning by Seoul police on Tuesday.

title: Measles is surging in the US. Here’s how the Trump administration has responded
summary: International health experts have decided that the U.S. has lost its status as a country that eliminated the continuous spread of measles
story: International health experts have decided that the U.S. has lost its status as a country that eliminated the continuous spread of measles

WASHINGTON -- With the U.S. experiencing its worst year for measles in decades, international health experts have decided that the U.S. has lost its status as a country that eliminated the continuous spread of the disease.
The U.S. has racked up more measles cases than in any year since 1991, with confirmed cases surpassing 5,000 in 2026, according to the latest data. Pennsylvania alone has seen more than 1,500 cases.
The Pan American Health Organization 's decision underscores a significant public health setback for the United States as the Trump administration reshapes federal vaccine policy.

Experts say that while the Trump administration did not create the underlying vaccination problem — which predates President Donald Trump’s return to office — the Republican administration's policies and public messaging may have exacerbated it.

Asked about the administration's response to the outbreak, the Department of Health and Human Services referred to a statement by Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Erica Schwartz, which said it would remain focused on stopping outbreaks, despite losing the measles designation.

Nationally, 92.4% of kindergartners received their required measles-mumps-rubella shots in the 2025-26 school year, down from 92.5% the previous year and 95.2% in 2019-20, according to data from the CDC. That is below the approximately 95% coverage needed to prevent measles outbreaks, and some communities have substantially lower vaccination rates.
Here's a look at how the Trump administration has handled the worst year for measles in more than three decades:

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has a long record of questioning vaccine safety, has repeatedly promoted claims that vaccines are associated with autism, despite extensive scientific evidence finding no causal relationship.

And he has delivered mixed messaging on measles specifically. He has occasionally endorsed the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine as “effective,” but also continues to raise unfounded safety concerns about the shots. In August, he told CNN: "I believe that the MMR vaccine prevents measles.” In that same interview he questioned the safety of the vaccine.

Trump reinforced those doubts at an event over the summer where he signed an executive order calling for splitting up the MMR vaccine. He said falsely that taken together the shot was “quite lethal.” Doctors say, and years of real-world evidence prove, that the combination MMR vaccine is both safe and effective at protecting children from illness.
Separate vaccines for measles, mumps and rubella are not available in the United States and producing them that way would be a logistical feat for drugmakers.

Josh Michaud, associate director of global and public health policy at healthcare research nonprofit KFF, said past administrations back to the 1990s, when confronted with measles outbreaks, were aggressive in telling the public how important vaccination is against the disease. That’s not happening now, he said.
"What we’re not seeing from the administration is strong communications about the need for vaccinations,” he said.

During the most recent measles outbreak, Kennedy promoted vitamin A as a possible treatment, which created concern among medical professionals that the administration was giving undue attention to alternatives rather than emphasizing vaccination.
Throughout the surge of measles cases, Kennedy has repeatedly challenged health officials’ accounts of deaths from the disease.
In August, Pennsylvania officials reported two measles-related deaths. The county coroner later said they involved infants too young to be vaccinated, with the virus itself causing one of the deaths.

After Gov. Josh Shapiro stressed that vaccinations could have averted the deaths, Kennedy said the deaths “may even have been altogether fabricated.” He later acknowledged that one of the deaths was due to measles.
The remark echoed similar statements he made after last year, when three measles-related deaths were recorded. Kennedy questioned whether one of the children who died was killed by measles.
Medical experts said the political quarreling over the deaths diverted focus from an exploding public health threat.

As health secretary, Kennedy has spearheaded an overhaul of the nation's vaccine policy. Last year, he fired all 17 members of a key vaccine advisory committee and hired vaccine critics among the replacements. In January, his department downsized the childhood immunization schedule. The moves were temporarily halted by a judge earlier this year.
Kennedy also acknowledged personally directing the CDC to update its website late last year to contradict its longtime guidance that vaccines don’t cause autism.
Critics say the overhaul and the administration's overt questioning of immunization safety have fueled skepticism about vaccines.

Surveys indicate growing public wavering over support for the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine. An August 2025 Annenberg survey found that 82% would be “very” or “somewhat” likely to recommend that an eligible child in their household get the MMR vaccine, compared to 90% in November 2024.

Kennedy has defended his upending of federal health policy by saying the changes will restore trust in America’s public health agencies. Doctors counter that the false and unverified information he promotes and the vaccine policy changes undermine confidence in vaccination and leave more people vulnerable to preventable disease.

Along with freezing and canceling billions in research under Kennedy’s leadership at the start of the Trump administration, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services laid off more than 10,000 workers and shut down entire offices and programs. Experts say those cuts may have impacted state and local health departments’ ability to adequately respond to outbreaks.

PAHO officials expect the U.S., along with Bolivia and Mexico which also lost their elimination status, to each submit a plan “in the coming weeks” for how they will go about trying to stop transmission for at least a year and regain measles elimination status, said Dr. Daniel Salas, PAHO’s executive manager for immunizations.
A decision to strip the U.S. of its measles elimination status will not change how federal health officials are addressing outbreaks, Schwartz said.
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans,” she said. “Vaccination does.”

She said federal officials have invested $100 million to help state and local health departments to reach communities with measles outbreaks. “Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.”
Michaud said the designation change is “a marker for how we backtracked on public health, particularly related to measles prevention, and particularly related to vaccines.”
“It encapsulates this idea that the United States is more vulnerable than ever to infectious diseases," he said.

title: LeBron James sues makers of AI sports-betting app, saying they used his likeness
summary: NBA superstar LeBron James has sued the makers of an AI sports-betting app, saying they deliberately violated his publicity rights and trademarks by calling it “Bron” and using artificially generated images of him in their marketing
story: NBA superstar LeBron James has sued the makers of an AI sports-betting app, saying they deliberately violated his publicity rights and trademarks by calling it “Bron” and using artificially generated images of him in their marketing

NBA superstar LeBron James sued the makers of an AI sports-betting app Tuesday, saying they have deliberately violated his publicity rights and trademarks by calling it “Bron” and using artificially generated images of him in their marketing.
In a lawsuit filed in U.S. District Court in New York, James' attorneys called it “a willful, bad-faith tactic” to use the player's fame, likeness and nickname to promote “a new and unknown product.”

The complaint asks the court to block the makers from using the Philadelphia 76ers star's name, to give up any money they've already made, and to award damages — including fair market value for the use of his name as well as punitive damages.

“Defendants did not care that they had engaged in illegal conduct to gain notoriety for their previously unknown app,” the lawsuit states. “They intentionally created the false impression that Mr. James endorsed and was affiliated with their Bron App, in an effort to drive downloads and paid subscriptions."
Messages sent by The Associated Press through the app’s website and to email addresses for its founders seeking comment were not immediately returned Tuesday.

The app’s developer, PlayVision Inc., is based in California. It was launched by Chief Executive Anish Gupta and Chief Technology Officer Marc Zoghby in 2025, with backing from the startup accelerator Y Combinator, as a program that would use artificial intelligence to analyze game and practice footage for sports teams and fans.

This year, the company released its “Bron” app, which it says does not take direct wagers but charges a subscription fee for services like bet tracking and odds comparisons. It launched a marketing campaign this month that featured an image of a person resembling James — down to his tattoos, voice and number 23 jersey — sitting in a locker room and scrolling through the app.

James' lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter, as previously reported by Front Office Sports. The company took the ad down, but not before it had been reposted and viewed about 1 million times, the lawsuit said.

Gupta responded to the attorneys' demand on social media by writing that the app would get a new name, but no new name had been adopted by the time the lawsuit was filed, leading James' legal team to suggest the company was milking the controversy for attention. Gupta wrote on social media this week that the new name will be announced Wednesday.

The lawsuit notes that James typically commands tens of millions of dollars for such endorsement deals, and that he already has an exclusive deal with the prediction market platform Polymarket. It alleges that the app's marketing was especially harmful in part because it showed the AI-generated James scrolling through bets involving NBA players.

“The integrity of NBA competition — and the public’s confidence that players are not betting on the games they play — is of paramount importance to the league, its players, and its fans,” the lawsuit said. “Any suggestion that an active NBA player is betting on NBA games is therefore far from a trivial matter, and it should not be used for clicks and views."

title: Chinese tech firms fear AI hits from US curbs after Nvidia fallout
summary: Chinese tech firms are facing challenges as the U.S. tightens restrictions on access to advanced chips
story: Chinese tech firms are facing challenges as the U.S. tightens restrictions on access to advanced chips
HONG KONG -- Chinese technology firms are bracing for impacts on their ambitious artificial intelligence plans as the U.S. tightens restrictions on China's access to the world's cutting-edge chips.

Chinese tech giant Alibaba, which on Thursday announced another quarter of strong revenue growth for its global AI cloud and compute services, warned that the new U.S. rules could affect some of its global data center expansion plans. It said it was still assessing the repercussions.

The Trump administration this week issued new rules in the wake of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, following the news that he’d had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.

The rules now restrict remote computing access through data centers in third countries, the latest U.S. move to curtail China’s abilities to use advanced Nvidia chips to train its increasingly capable AI models.
As the technology race between the two superpowers intensifies, existing U.S. export restrictions already barred China from getting the world’s most powerful chips.
But some Chinese companies have been able to bypass those restrictions by renting remote computing access to train AI models, pushing the U.S. to close what some policymakers called a loophole.

As global AI usage grows, Alibaba has been expanding its capabilities across chips, cloud infrastructure and AI models. It launched its flagship Qwen4-Max AI model earlier this week. In September, Alibaba's CEO called its new Zhenwu V900 chip the “most powerful” AI chip in China, while it announced massive data center investment plans in China and abroad.

Alibaba Cloud’s AI-related revenue currently comes significantly from China and there’s still a lot of “untapped demand” from Chinese enterprises, said Jacob Cooke of the Beijing-based consultancy WPIC Marketing + Technologies.

For the latest July-September quarter, Alibaba reported a 53% year-on-year revenue surge for its AI cloud and compute services to nearly 61 billion yuan ($9 billion). Total revenue for the quarter rose 10% from the year before to almost 272 billion yuan ($41 billion), slightly better than what analysts had expected.
While the company has a strong cash buffer, capital expenditures jumped 60% during the quarter to 50.5 billion yuan ($7.6 billion) thanks to its increased spending on AI infrastructure buildout.
Chinese tech giant Tencent on Wednesday said the new U.S. rule on chip access “sets everyone back in China.”

“Everyone is actually having less compute, advanced compute, to work with, no matter when you actually started leasing or building capacities outside of China,” Tencent President Martin Lau said on an earnings call. Training timelines for Tencent’s next versions of its AI models would probably be impacted, he said.

“Chinese AI firms are still heavily dependent on the most frontier Nvidia chips," said James Chai, a researcher at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, with new U.S. rules on remote access cutting off a huge portion of Chinese firms’ access to compute.

A study released in October by the Institute for Progress, a U.S. think tank, estimated that remote access to AI chips through overseas data centers could account for roughly one-third of China’s AI compute by the end of 2027.

Nvidia, meanwhile, said it is now “no longer shipping” chips including the H200, one of its more powerful chips, though not the most advanced, although the Trump administration greenlighted some sales to China, reflecting how Nvidia has toughened its stance on China following Huang’s ouster.

Analysts expect the U.S. will step up its chip export control policies against China after Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a former senior executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, raised U.S. national security concerns. Earlier reporting by The New York Times suggested that U.S. officials suspected Alice Huang was a Chinese spy recruited in part to potentially influence Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available to Chinese companies.
Beijing has rejected claims that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, and has called the new U.S. rules blocking Chinese companies' remote access to computing power overseas “economic coercion.”
Analysts and industry leaders in China say the U.S.’s tightening of chip export control measures would ultimately accelerate China’s push to make its domestic chip industry self-sufficient.

“Over the longer run, we believe all Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips, which we actually see the industry is actually progressing very fast,” said Tencent's Lau.

title: Cambridge Dictionary chooses 'human' as word of the year in response to AI fears
summary: The Cambridge Dictionary has chosen "human" as its word of the year, reflecting concerns about artificial intelligence
story: The Cambridge Dictionary has chosen "human" as its word of the year, reflecting concerns about artificial intelligence
LONDON -- Fears of artificial intelligence inspired the Cambridge Dictionary to flip back to the 15th century for the word that best captures the 2026 cultural zeitgeist.
“Human,” the dictionary's word of the year, is not just a throwback but also a backlash of sorts that reflects the debate over how AI has blurred the lines between machines and people.

“AI is changing how we talk about being human," said Colin McIntosh, the dictionary's lexicographer. “Fears about what humans may lose when we outsource our thinking have made us reconsider the extent to which we rely on AI: from top mathematicians to teachers of young children."

The adjective derived from the Latin “humanus” and in use since the 1450s is defined by Cambridge as “having the qualities, faults and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals or machines.”
Dictionaries typically choose a novel word — sometimes slang that has crossed into the mainstream — or an existing word that has taken on a new meaning.
Artificial intelligence has factored heavily in Word of the Year distinctions across several dictionaries in recent years.

“AI” itself was chosen by Collins Dictionary in 2023 — a year when Cambridge picked “hallucinate,” in reference to the tendency of AI to fabricate information. Merriam-Webster last year named “slop” its word of the year for low quality content produced by AI while Collins went with “vibe coding” for the AI-assisted software development method.

“AI is making us think harder about what it means to be human," Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, who has promoted the smart use of AI, said in a comment on the Cambridge Dictionary selection. "The measure of AI’s success should be how much it improves human lives.”

Other word contenders for 2026 included “agent,” for an AI system that can make decisions and operate without human control and “analogue” for experiences or objects not involving the internet or digital technology.
Editors note: This story was produced by a human.

title: In closings, Chinese tech giant Huawei is cast by prosecutors as a villain as its lawyer disagrees
summary: The racketeering conspiracy trial of Huawei Technologies is drawing closer to an end after two days of closing arguments
story: The racketeering conspiracy trial of Huawei Technologies is drawing closer to an end after two days of closing arguments

NEW YORK -- The racketeering conspiracy trial of Huawei Technologies approached its end Tuesday after a prosecutor told jurors that the Chinese telecommunications giant helped Iran spy on its citizens and steal from U.S. companies and a defense lawyer accused the U.S. of embracing a false narrative.

Defense attorney Brian Heberlig said in a closing argument in Brooklyn federal court after a two-month-long trial that federal prosecutors “decided Huawei was a criminal enterprise” and built a case from that premise.
“They began with guilt and worked backwards,” Heberlig said. “When the evidence didn't fit, they moved the goalposts.”

He spoke a day after Assistant U.S. Attorney Meredith Arfa said the company for two decades encouraged a workforce of over 200,000 workers in 170 countries to lie, cheat and steal “for a competitive advantage to grow and protect its business.”
She said Huawei had committed crimes targeting American companies, the U.S. financial system and the American government while providing Iran with the equipment to spy on its citizens.

Huawei is the world’s largest supplier of gear for wireless telecom networks, but it is not allowed to sell equipment to U.S. carriers over fears it poses a security risk. It has also been blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and Britain.
Heberlig credited Huawei’s remarkable growth to its success in engineering, investment, innovation and competition.
He said prosecutors built their case in part by focusing on acts of wrongdoing by a few employees who were fired after their misdeeds were discovered.
Prosecutors sometimes blamed the company for gaining access to the intellectual property of competitors when the materials were already public, he said.
“You can't steal a secret that isn't secret,” Heberlig said.

Huawei makes phones and other consumer electronics, but it has been cut off from other lines of business. More recently, it has expanded into chipmaking as the boom in artificial intelligence fuels demand for microprocessors.

During President Donald Trump’s first term, his administration raised national security concerns about Huawei and began lobbying Western allies against including the company’s products in their next-generation high-speed wireless networks. The U.S. announced the criminal charges in early 2019 and has since expanded the allegations.
Chinese officials said the U.S. has engaged in “economic bullying” and improperly used national security as a pretext for “oppressing Chinese companies.”
The jury was expected to begin deliberations sometime on Wednesday.

title: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
summary: Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO, the company announced on Monday.
story: The announcement comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned.
Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO, the company announced on Monday, less than two weeks after Huang resigned amid reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese asset.
Huang will also hold a seat on the company's board, according to Nvidia.

The company's board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA," Nvidia said.

"In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk," the company added.
Nvidia will continue to carry out an investigation into reports of a foreign intelligence operation targeting Huang, the company said, noting the investigation would be completed as planned.
Huang "fully supports" the investigation and is "committed to cooperating with it," the company said.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said in a statement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment."
President Donald Trump celebrated Huang's reinstatement, calling this the "correct and proper decision" in a social media post.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

title: Ukrainian naval drones sank Russia's Merkury warship in Libya, Zelenskyy confirms
summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on Monday morning that Kyiv was responsible for the sinking of a Russian warship docked in the Libyan port of Benghazi.
story: Ukrainian forces also attacked a Russian cargo ship, the president said.

LONDON -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on Monday morning that Kyiv was responsible for the sinking of a Russian warship docked in the Libyan port of Benghazi on Sunday, describing the attack as "an exemplary Ukrainian operation."

The Russian corvette Merkury, which was commissioned in 2023, was at port when it was hit by several explosions. "Our warriors deployed seven Ukrainian-made naval drones. Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk," Zelenskyy wrote.

"I received detailed briefings on the operation's steps yesterday and today -- the targets we set were achieved," Zelenskyy wrote, adding that a Russian Ka-27 helicopter was also destroyed along with the corvette.

"Our second target was the Russian dry cargo vessel MV ANGARA, which the enemy used to transport weapons. Result: target hit," the Ukrainian president added. "We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons."

Zelenskyy also posted Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) videos of the attack, showing maritime drones striking both the Merkury and a cargo ship at sea. In a post to Telegram, the SBU said it coordinated the attack with the Ukrainian military.

"Both vessels were legitimate military targets for Ukraine, as they directly contributed to Russia's war capabilities," the SBU wrote. "Seven unmanned boats of Ukrainian manufacture were used in the operation. These boats were transported to the designated location and launched from a 'mother ship,'" the SBU said.

"Despite attempts by the enemy to destroy Ukrainian drones from the air, sea, and land, the unmanned boats of the Security Service of Ukraine successfully reached their targets and struck them," the service added.

The attack on the Merkury occurred in the Mediterranean port city of Benghazi which is the capital of Libya's Government of National Stability -- the eastern rival of the country's internationally-recognized Government of National Unity, which is based in the western city of Tripoli.

The GNS said in a statement that the docked Russian ship was hit by "unmanned vehicles." The ship was on its way back to Russia and had docked at the base for refueling and supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the Benghazi government, the statement said.
The administration said it had opened a joint investigation with Russia, "to uncover the circumstances of the attack, its source, and the party behind it."
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Monday that Russia had "taken note of Zelenskyy’s statement about an attack on a Russian warship at a Libyan port."
ABC News' Victoria Beaule, Oleksiy Pshemyskiy, Anna Sergeeva, Jamie Dorrington and Rashid Haddou contributed to this report.

title: Tom Jackson, Broncos star and ESPN 'Sunday NFL Countdown' analyst, dead at 75
summary: Tom Jackson, a cornerstone of the Orange Crush defense with the Denver Broncos who went on to even more fame as an ESPN broadcaster, has died at 75
story: Tom Jackson, a cornerstone of the Orange Crush defense with the Denver Broncos who went on to even more fame as an ESPN broadcaster, has died at 75

Tom Jackson, a fiery cornerstone of the Orange Crush defense with the Denver Broncos who went on to even more fame as a beloved broadcaster on ESPN, has died, his family and the network announced Sunday. He was 75.

Jackson's family informed ESPN that he died Friday, but it was their wishes that his death not be announced until the start of the network's “Sunday NFL Countdown” show by Jackson's longtime friend and on-air partner Chris Berman. A cause of death was not given.

“Tom was so much more than an accomplished NFL analyst. There was nobody kinder, more thoughtful, more loyal or more engaging than him. And when it came to laughter, Tom’s was frequent and unmistakable,” Berman said. “Tom was my best friend professionally and personally. If you ever met him or just knew him from watching ESPN, he was your best friend, too.”
Berman said Jackson made a surprise visit a couple of weeks ago to ESPN, where he worked for 32 years over two stints after playing 14 seasons for the Broncos, and that the two talked on Tuesday.

A fourth-round draft pick out of Louisville in 1973, Jackson was an inspirational leader of Denver’s first Super Bowl team in 1977. He started 177 games for the Broncos between 1973-86, retiring after the team's second Super Bowl appearance. He was a first-team All-Pro in 1977 and a second-team All-Pro the following season; he also was a three-time Pro Bowler.

The Broncos held a moment of silence and showed a video tribute to Jackson before their game against the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday. After the Broncos won 38-24, coach Sean Payton said the team would give a game ball to Jackson's family.
Following his playing days, Jackson had a second career at ESPN from 1987-2016 and was featured on “Sunday NFL Countdown” and “NFL Primetime.”

Before the internet, and before NBC took over the Sunday night package in 2006, “NFL Primetime” was must-see viewing for fans and players because it showed highlights from all the games, as well as the interaction between Berman and Jackson, who often finished each other’s sentences.

“I can remember coming from games and waiting in a rush to get home, to watch ‘Primetime’ because all I wanted to know was, what were you and Tom Jackson gonna say about one, the team?” ESPN analyst and Hall of Fame wide receiver Randy Moss said to Berman.

NBC's “Football Night in America” paid tribute to Jackson Sunday night. Host Maria Taylor said: “Before there was a ‘Football Night in America’, there was ‘NFL Primetime,’ where TJ and Chris Berman set the standard for an NFL highlight show. It’s a standard that we look to every single Sunday.”

NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell, who was in Mexico City for Sunday night's game between the San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings, said Jackson was “an outstanding player whose toughness and leadership helped define an era of Broncos football. He brought credibility, passion and humor to everything he did, and generations of fans came to know him through his work at ESPN.”

Jackson briefly returned to ESPN in 2019 and reunited with Berman to do an online version of “NFL Primetime.” He was awarded the Pete Rozelle Radio-Television Award from the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2015.

“In my lifetime there was Howard Cosell doing ‘Monday Night Football’ halftime highlights and then there were Boomer and TJ doing ‘Sunday NFL Countdown.’ I am not here as a colleague but as one of million who watched, learned from and idolized the two of you,” ESPN host Mike Greenberg said during Sunday’s show.
ESPN’s studio crew wore orange ties in honor of Jackson during the three-hour show.
Berman said Jackson was the last of seven people interviewed for the studio analyst job and that the last person rarely gets the job. But Jackson nailed the interview.

“Tom Jackson was one of the most influential and beloved figures in ESPN’s history. He brought the credibility of an All-Pro NFL player, the insight of a gifted analyst and a warmth and authenticity that connected with generations of football fans. Alongside Chris Berman, he helped make ‘NFL Primetime’ an iconic part of our football weekends,” ESPN chairman Jimmy Pitaro said in a statement. “Away from the set, Tom was a trusted colleague, generous mentor and dear friend to many. ... His legacy at ESPN, throughout the NFL and among the countless fans who admired his incredible work will endure.”
ESPN’s NFL studio in Bristol, Connecticut, is named the Chris Berman-Tom Jackson Studio. It is the only named studio on ESPN’s campus.

“The Denver Broncos are heartbroken by the passing of Ring of Fame linebacker Tom Jackson, a cornerstone of the legendary Orange Crush defense and one of the most beloved players in franchise history,” the Broncos said in a statement.

“An inspirational leader and fierce competitor, TJ was a proud member of the Broncos’ first Super Bowl team that helped establish a winning tradition in Denver. Off the field, Tom carried himself with class, warmth and humility, forging deep connections and lifelong friendships with teammates and throughout Broncos Country.”
Jackson is survived by his wife, Jennifer, and daughters Taylor and Morgan.
AP Pro Football Writer Arnie Stapleton in Denver contributed to this report.
See AP’s full NFL coverage here

title: Iran live updates: Iranian attacks spike over past week, Trump says
summary: President Donald Trump announced "major combat operations" against Iran on Feb. 28.
story: Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February. The opening strikes killed a host of top Iranian officials and commanders, among them Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though have not returned to the intense fighting seen in the early stages of the conflict. The U.S. says it is enforcing a naval blockade of the country's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway.

Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military, oil infrastructure and transport facilities.
See the most recent developments below.
Key Headlines

2 hours and 49 minutes agoTrump says Iran launched more attacks in past week than at any time 'for over a year'4:27 AM ESTTehran says Strait of Hormuz will be safe if its demands are metNov 22, 2026, 12:47 PM ESTUKMTO reports incident 'involving tanker and military forces' in Gulf of Oman
2 hours and 49 minutes agoTrump says Iran launched more attacks in past week than at any time 'for over a year'
4:27 AM ESTTehran says Strait of Hormuz will be safe if its demands are met
Nov 22, 2026, 12:47 PM ESTUKMTO reports incident 'involving tanker and military forces' in Gulf of Oman
Trump says Iran launched more attacks in past week than at any time 'for over a year'
President Donald Trump said in a social media post on Sunday night that "Iran has launched more drones and missiles in the last week than at any time for over a year."
"Don't worry, they've all been knocked down, and done no damage," Trump said of the Iranian attacks.

Reported attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz have been higher in number in October and November than any previous months since the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran began in late February, according to data compiled by maritime organizations and analyzed by ABC News.
Iranian forces have also been launching fresh missile and drone attacks on regional nations like Kuwait and Bahrain.
-ABC News' Isabella Murray
Tehran says Strait of Hormuz will be safe if its demands are met

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said at a Monday press conference that safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz can be restored quickly if the U.S. agrees to Iranian conditions for a full peace deal.
"We are serious about fulfilling our commitments, upholding our rights and maintaining the conditions we have set," Baqaei said, as quoted by the state-run IRNA News Agency.
"If the American side fulfills its commitments, security can be restored to the Strait of Hormuz and the region in the shortest possible time," he added.

"This does not mean overlooking the complexities surrounding the issue; rather, it simply underscores that the Islamic Republic of Iran knows what it wants, understands the rights of the Iranian people and their full scope, and will under no circumstances back down on this matter," Baqaei said.

Baqaei said that Iran's conditions include the removal of what he called "cruel and unlawful sanctions," the lifting of the ongoing U.S. naval blockade and all other terms set out in June's memorandum of understanding.
UKMTO reports incident 'involving tanker and military forces' in Gulf of Oman
U.K. Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) says they have received a report of an incident "involving a tanker and military forces in the Gulf of Oman."
Authorities are aware of the incident and investigations are ongoing, the UKMTO said.
Separately, the IRGC navy, per official Iranian state media, say two tankers have "exploded and stopped due to collision with sea mines north of Ghanem Island and east of the Strait of Hormuz."
The IRGC navy claims the tankers were passing through "unauthorized routes" and did not comply with instructions.
It is not confirmed whether these two incidents are the same.
-ABC News' Jamie Dorrington
Regional nations condemn Iranian attack on Bahrain
Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Qatar issued statements on Sunday condemning Iran's attack on Bahrain on Saturday, which Manama said injured two people and caused a fire at a civilian industrial facility.

Qatar's Foreign Ministry said the attack constituted a "flagrant violation of its sovereignty and territorial integrity, and a blatant breach of international law, the United Nations Charter, and the principles of good neighborliness."
The Saudi Foreign Ministry described the attack as "heinous" and said it holds Iran responsible for the consequences of its continued perpetration of these flagrant attacks."
Kuwait's Foreign Ministry said that Iranian attacks on Bahrain "threaten the region's security and stability."

title: Rahm Emanuel: Schumer should commit to stepping down as leader after next Congress
summary: Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, joined "This Week" to discuss what Democrats should do after their historic midterm victory.
story: Democrats should also support Jeffries' House speaker nomination, Emanuel said.

Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel said Sunday that longtime Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer should commit to stepping down from the role after the next Congress, where Democrats are set to hold 56 seats after a strong midterm election showing.

"If I was Chuck Schumer, what I would say is, 'I'm going to secure the majority, I am not going to run for majority leader next cycle, and I'm going to make sure the other -- the young voices and faces of this party grow. That would take that tension out of this," Emanuel, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, said on ABC's "This Week."
"So he should serve as majority leader for these next two years?" co-anchor Jonathan Karl followed up.
"Yeah, just get it over with," Emanuel said. "Chuck Schumer is a friend, as is [Sen.] Chris Van Hollen, but this is not what people voted for. They voted to get their lives better, not yours."

Emanuel, who also served as U.S. ambassador to Japan under President Joe Biden and chief of staff to President Barack Obama, has previously called for instituting a mandatory retirement age of 75 for federal public officials, including members of Congress. Schumer turns 76 on Monday.

Van Hollen announced on Nov. 14 he was officially challenging Schumer for the role of majority leader in the congressional session beginning in January. On last Sunday's episode of "This Week," Van Hollen told co-anchor Martha Raddatz that maintaining the status quo is not how Democrats will "earn the people's trust."
The vote for majority leader, which is a secret ballot, is scheduled for Dec. 1.

While Democrats’ Senate leader is still undecided, House Democrats voted Wednesday to officially nominate Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York to be their candidate for speaker of the House. If he wins a majority of votes among all House members in January, as he’s expected to do, he will become the first Black speaker in U.S. history.

Nearly all Democrats supported Jeffries’ nomination, but there were 11 defectors. Of the eight individuals ABC News has confirmed voted against his candidacy, all were elected for the first time in November.
Emanuel had a message to Jeffries’ naysayers, most of whom identify with the progressive wing of the party, including some who are democratic socialists: “Give me a break.”

“Hakeem Jeffries is history, OK? … First Black speaker, number two in line for the presidency. And as somebody who was chief of staff to President Obama, that is a statement about America that we should take pride in,” Emanuel said. “We're a coalition. You're going to tell the most loyal coalition partner, the African American community, that the moment in history, you're not going to get it?”

"The Black vote is the most significant, most loyal, most dedicated part of the coalition," Emanuel continued. "You voted against Hakeem Jeffries, who made history and earned it when we were in the minority. You just came along and literally hadn't earned this election. He literally over the years built a majority here that should be affirmed and not only affirmed. It tells me when you vote against him, you don't understand the politics of the Democratic Party.”

Emanuel outlined lofty policy goals he thinks the incoming Democratic majorities should try to achieve, including raising the federal hourly minimum wage to $20 by 2030 and reducing or completely undoing tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump. He also called for a major ethics reform package that would impact all three branches of government.

“Ban all stock trading … ban all prediction market participation. Mandatory blind trust, mandatory age and term limit mark out, and what I call the Jared Kushner rule: no foreign money while you're in and for two years out of government,” Emanuel said.

Karl also asked Emanuel what he thinks the next Democratic president should do about the still-under-construction White House ballroom that has been one of the president’s prized projects this term. The White House has said the goal is to finish it before Trump leaves office.

“I think the opening floor should be dedicated to the history of our democracy and what we built: the good, the bad, the ugly,” Emanuel said. “And so you have a version of what the president has done, which is -- I think is horrendous, both substantively and in style that he did, but dedicate a major portion as you walk in, the guests will walk in, to the democracy of this country.”
Emanuel also said that the Rose Garden, which Trump turned into a stone patio, should be reverted back to the design that dates back to the Kennedy administration.
As for whether he'll seek the Democratic presidential nomination for 2028, Emanuel was tight-lipped.
"When do you make this decision-slash-announcement?" Karl asked.
"As soon as I get out of here," Emanuel quipped.

title: DNI Clayton: Putin is 'not America's friend in Ukraine'
summary: The director of national intelligence appeared on ABC's "This Week" Sunday.
story: The director of national intelligence appeared on ABC's "This Week" Sunday.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said Sunday that President Donald Trump's use of the term "friend" to describe his relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin was "entirely appropriate" in the context of last week's summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, but said Putin "is not America's friend in Ukraine."

"That conversation, that picture -- historic, historic picture -- was in the context of the three nuclear powers, the three main nuclear powers, getting together and saying, 'We cannot have a nuclear incident,'" Clayton told ABC "This Week" co-anchor Jonathan Karl. "In that circle of that conversation, using the term 'friend' is entirely appropriate."

After Trump greeted Putin as his "friend" at the summit in China, he declined to say whether the Russian president is a friend to the U.S. at a White House press briefing Friday, saying he "can't speak to America." On Saturday, the president posted a photo on his social media platform of himself and Putin with the text "My Friend" bolded above the photo.
"Is Vladimir Putin America's friend? Because Trump said he couldn't answer that question," Karl pressed Clayton.
"Is Vladimir Putin America's friend? He is not America's friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all," Clayton responded.

Michael LoSapio, Trump's nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Agency, made headlines earlier this this week at a congressional hearing with his refusal to say whether the Capitol was attacked on Jan. 6, 2021.
Karl asked Clayton the same question. Clayton also refused to directly answer, telling Karl, "I'm not going to relitigate that issue here."
Pressed to respond, Clayton said, "The American people saw what happened that day. It was a very unfortunate day for America."
"Does everybody who saw that wish it never happened? Absolutely, but I'm not going to get into the political characterizations in the hearings like that," Clayton continued.
"We all condemn violence," Clayton said when pressed further, adding, "There is no place for violence in America."
"There was violence. You can call it what you want. Every American can call it what you want. There was clearly violence," Clayton said.

After a slew of high-profile tech outages, sources told that the FBI and the U.S. Department of Agriculture were hit with cyberattacks late last week. Clayton told "This Week" on Sunday that he could not "get into the specifics" of those incidents.

"We have highly professional people at the FBI who handle both private sector and public sector incidents like this, and I'm sure we'll get the answers in due course, just as we've gotten the answers to the incidents that happened this past week at the NSA, at Microsoft, at other places," Clayton said.
As the Trump administration has explained, many of the outages in recent weeks have come during repairs to infrastructure patches identified by artificial intelligence.

"We have a step change in technology that we're facing with super intelligence and computing power that is expanding exponentially. And we have a dated digital infrastructure. The need to improve our digital infrastructure is clear, and that is the dynamic that we have today," Clayton said.
Clayton maintained that the recent outages were not coordinated or state-sponsored.
"The incidents that we saw during the course of this week, we know that they were not coordinated and that they were not state-sponsored," Clayton said.

"Companies and the government, we should all be transparent with the American people that we have dated systems in a highly-evolving environment where they need to be upgraded in order to have cybersecurity," he added.
Clayton said there has been an increase in cyberattacks, "but this is something that we have had for a long time."

title: Democrat Chuck Hubbard wins recount, flips North Carolina US House seat
summary: Democratic Chuck Hubbard will win the election in North Carolina's 5th congressional district, the Associated Press projects.
story: The victory gives Democrats their biggest House majority since 1992.

Democratic Chuck Hubbard will win the election in North Carolina's 5th congressional district, the Associated Press projected on Sunday, flipping the seat held by longtime Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx.
With Hubbard's victory, the Democrats are set to have their biggest majority in three decades in the House of Representatives when the next Congress is sworn in in January.
With 99% of the estimated vote reported, Hubbard leads Foxx 48.7% to 48.6%. Fewer than 300 votes separate the two.
Hubbard wrote in a social media post on Sunday that Foxx, who had requested a recount, called him earlier Sunday to concede.
"Let me be the first to thank Congresswoman Foxx for her decades of service and countless sacrifices," wrote Hubbard, a former local journalist who ran unsuccessfully against Foxx in 2024.

“After a hard-fought and thorough election process, the voters of the Fifth Congressional District exercised their Constitutional rights and made their voices heard," Foxx said in a statement Sunday in part, acknowledging Hubbard's victory. "I recently called to congratulate Chuck Hubbard on his victory in this election, and I sent him my best wishes as he represents this wonderful district in the 120th Congress."
Foxx, first elected to the U.S. House in 2004 after serving in the North Carolina state Senate, is currently the chair of the powerful House Rules Committee.

Democrats have had major successes this year in North Carolina. In addition to Hubbard's win, Democrat Roy Cooper, the former North Carolina governor, flipped the U.S. Senate seat currently held by retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis.

As of Sunday, based on the current ABC News House estimate, which tracks the expected balance of power based on results in U.S. House races, Democrats are on track to have at least 258 members in the U.S. House, with at least 173 for Republicans. Four races have not yet been projected.
Hubbard's win will secure the largest majority Democrats have had in the U.S. House since 1992, when they also elected 258 members, according to U.S. House records.

title: Trump touts relationships with Putin and Xi after historic Asia trip
summary: Trump said the three countries made strides in advancing denuclearization talks.
story: Trump said the three countries made strides in advancing denuclearization talks.

President Donald Trump touted his historic trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday following his trip to Asia earlier this week, claiming that there was "great electricity" between the three leaders of the world’s superpowers.

"I have a fantastic relationships with Putin. That's a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That's a good thing. And our country is safe because of that," Trump said during a Friday news conference.

During the trip, Trump called Putin his "friend." Asked on Friday about whether Putin, who leads a country that is Iran's biggest ally, is a friend to America, Trump said they have a "very good relationship."

Trump has insisted that Putin wants an end to its ongoing war with Ukraine, now in its fifth year, but Russia has continued to launch deadly attacks. Asked by ABC News Senior Political Correspondent Rachel Scott about whether Putin was stringing Trump along, as he has said in the past, the president said "that it's a very hard thing" to end the war.

"To be honest, you have two guys that don't know how to end it. We're trying to help them," Trump said of Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, later adding, "you're very lucky to have somebody that has a relationship with the heads of the most powerful countries."
Trump had promised to end the war within 24 hours of taking office for his second term in 2024.
"It's a tough job. The problem is President Zelensky and President Putin have tremendous hatred, and that's never easy. I thought that would be one of the easier," Trump said Friday.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who delivered brief remarks after Trump and Vice President JD Vance, defended the president’s meeting with Xi and Putin after he garnered criticism for establishing such warm relations with authoritarian leaders.

"These three countries, the United States, Russia, and China, between these three countries, possess the overwhelming majority of nuclear weapons on this planet. The idea that these three leaders should not engage on a regular basis is not just absurd, it's dangerous," Rubio said at the news conference where several other Cabinet members were in attendance. "And if these leaders can't get along and can't engage with one another and don't have a positive relationship, it is impossible to get anything good done for the country and the safety of the world."
Trump said that Russia, China and the U.S. agreed to a "first-of-its-kind trilateral peace declaration."

Trump said that the trilateral meeting made strides in advancing discussions around denuclearization, but he also discussed how "hard" it is for him to give up nuclear weapons. Overall, there appeared to be no major diplomatic breakthroughs.
"I'm the one that keeps talking about the denuclearization of the world, but it's very hard," the president said.

Trump also claimed that he and Xi agreed on "some joint guardrails" on artificial intelligence, despite previously saying this is not something he would do. The president did not offer specifics on what those guardrails entail.

On Sept. 29, Trump declined to partake in a "joint venture" with China on AI despite others encouraging him to do so. He has also been adamant about not curtailing AI, even when some tech CEOs have sounded the alarm on the need for federal guardrails.
Trump also touted trade agreements with Thailand and the Philippines.
The president said he is pushing U.S. tech companies to build controversial data centers in the U.S. -- threatening a "tremendous tax" on those that build in other countries.

"We're not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can. But we're going to put a tremendous tax on them," he said, without offering details about the tax.

Following Republicans' bruising midterm losses, Vance said the Trump administration's ongoing war with Iran was to blame. Asked about Vance's comments on Friday, the president said it was a "very accurate statement," acknowledging the role of rising fuel prices.

"I thought the statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing that if it were asked, I would have said that, 'Would you do it again?' And absolutely. The answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon," Trump said.
Vance was later asked about his previous comments about whether losing the Senate for the next six years was worth the war. The vice president responded that he follows the president's orders.

"I think the president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again," Vance said Friday. "And my view is that my goal is and my job is to support the president of the United States."
A week after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop, Trump said the nation's air traffic control system is "obsolete," but still safe.
"We have an obsolete system. Now, with that being said, it's safe, but it's very safe," he said.

Trump repeated calls from Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy for more funding to fix the air traffic control system they say is broken. Department of Transportation on Thursday officially submitted its $50.1 billion budget funding request -- a marked increase -- to fix the system.
Trump again asserted on Friday that he previously directed the FAA not to spend $12 billion in congressionally appropriated funds.

"Let's not spend the 12, spend as little as you can to keep it going, until we get to 12. So we're asking for $50 billion from the Senate, from government, so that we can have a system better than any system,” Trump said.
Trump made similar comments during his trip to Asia earlier this week, telling reporters in Manilla that he told the agency to save the money.
Trump notably referred to House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries as "smart," despite the president previously calling the Democrat a "thug" with "low IQ."
He also suggested he might prefer working with a Democratic-controlled Congress over his own party.
"But I just want to tell you, he's smart, and your new speaker," Trump said.
He later said Sen. Chuck Schumer, the Senate's top Democrat, is also "smart."

"If they want to get things done, I want to get things done too. You know, there are those that say we might get more done because we had some Republicans that were just impossible to deal with," Trump said.
But the president also said there’s a "real possibility" he can work with Democrats "because of the power of the veto."

"There's a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done, especially on healthcare, I'm open to great healthcare. Now, can it be what they want? No, but it can be a combination of what we all want, and we could end up with great healthcare in our country. We could end up better than dealing with the Republicans,” he said.
Trump also said he is going to wield his veto power to accomplish legislation he wants and that he believes he could use this to reach compromises with Democrats.

"So they're going to send things my way, and I'm going to veto them. And then they're going to send more things, and I'm going to veto them. And they could go two years and one month because that's what we have. And I'm going to veto them," Trump said. "But I think after a month or so, they're going to send things that I'm going to say, 'I'm going to veto unless you want to do this and this and this.'"

title: FBI's national crime database targeted in hack, Trump says
summary: President Donald Trump confirmed on Saturday that the FBI’s National Crime Information Center database was targeted in a hack.
story: A law enforcement source confirmed to ABC News that the database was hacked.
President Donald Trump said in an interview Saturday that the FBI’s National Crime Information Center database was targeted in a hack.
Trump made the claim during a phone interview with Fox News.
"Well, we just heard about it, and I will say that it's not good. I don't like that," he said during the interview.
A law enforcement source confirmed to ABC News that the database was hacked.
The NCIC is a repository of criminal justice information, including data on criminal record history, current fugitives, stolen property, and missing persons, according to the FBI.
The FBI declined to comment.
The perpetrators behind the hack and the scale of the intrusion are currently unclear.
Federal, state, and local law enforcement use the database for their investigations, according to retired FBI Supervisory Special Agent Jason Pack.

"Whether you’re a deputy sheriff in rural Tennessee, a state trooper working the interstate or an FBI agent investigating a fugitive, NCIC is how you check wanted persons, stolen vehicles, missing persons and other critical information," Pack told ABC News.
"The FBI maintains the system, but it’s connected to law enforcement agencies all across the country. And that’s important when we start talking about how somebody might have gotten in," he added.

Pack said that he believed the FBI will have its best cyber investigators on the case. "Officers need to know that when they run somebody through NCIC, the information coming back is accurate," he said. "Because sometimes that information can mean the difference between an officer going home at the end of a shift or not."

During the interview, the president implied without providing evidence that the hack might include information related to the investigations into Russian interference into the 2016 election, which he has repeatedly called a "hoax," and the phone call he made to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy that led to his first impeachment by Congress.
The NCIC would not have information regarding those investigations in its database.
Russian hackers allegedly hacked Democratic National Committee emails during the summer of the 2016 campaign.
Then presidential candidate Trump said at the time he hoped Russian hackers reportedly responsible would also find thousands of private emails deleted by former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton.
"Russia, if you're listening, I hope you're able to find the 30,000 emails that are missing," he said. Later, Trump said he was being sarcastic.
The White House hasn't immediately commented about the incident.
ABC News' Ivan Pereira contributed to this report.
Editor's note: This story has been updated.

title: White House replaces national cyber director amid widespread tech outages
summary: White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross has been fired, according to a source close to the White House.
story: DOD Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will replace him, per a source.

The White House has replaced National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, the administration's top cybersecurity adviser, amid a wave of technology outages that hit major companies and government agencies.
Cairncross, who served as President Donald Trump's principal adviser on national cybersecurity policy and strategy, will be replaced by Pentagon Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies.
President Trump fully supported replacing Cairncross, with one source telling ABC News that the president believed he "lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job."
The official rapid response account for the White House acknowledged Davies' appointment.

"With nearly two decades of leadership experience in the technology space, Kirsten Davies will be a strong asset for the Trump administration in her new position with the Office of the National Cyber Director. It has been my pleasure to work closely with Kirsten on national security matters, and I look forward to now working with her to navigate an increasingly dynamic and fast-moving cyber landscape,” said United States Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton in the statement on social media.
Axios was first to report the move.

The move comes after a week of tech outages across a variety of U.S. sectors sparked public alarm, but the Trump administration has maintained the technical issues are not the result of a cyberattack or state-sponsored activity, but likely the result of upgrades and system patches.

title: Trump says he plans to penalize companies that build data centers in other countries
summary: President Donald Trump says U.S. tech companies will face “a tremendous tax” if they build artificial intelligence data centers in other countries
story: President Donald Trump says U.S. tech companies will face “a tremendous tax” if they build artificial intelligence data centers in other countries
WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump says U.S. tech companies will face “a tremendous tax” if they build artificial intelligence data centers in other countries.

Trump did not provide details Friday and he said he hadn’t yet told his own officials about his plan. The Republican president urged Americans to welcome data center construction in their communities and extract concessions from the developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.
Trump says, “You ought to take advantage of the data centers. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off.”

With host communities across the U.S. turning against their gargantuan data centers, America’s technology giants are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts, keep fewer secrets or shower more money onto the communities willing to allow the server warehouses.
The new raft of promises from the world’s richest companies came as anti-data center sentiment was a potent issue in the midterm elections, in which Democrats took control of Congress.

Despite backing from Trump, the data centers powering the artificial intelligence boom have become politically toxic. Community opposition that blocks municipal permits has become a bottleneck, and tech giants could face even more challenges if voters next month elect more public officials who are skeptical of data centers.

title: Nidal Hasan is set to be executed. The military's other death row cases are in limbo
summary: There are three other former soldiers who are on the military’s death row.
story: There are three other former soldiers who are on the military’s death row.
The U.S. military hasn't executed anyone in 65 years.

Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan is set to be put to death next month. The Army has no immediate plans to carry out any other executions at this time, according to two sources with direct knowledge of the matter.

The Army's three other inmates sentenced to die have spent decades on death row for crimes that include murder, rape and an attack on fellow troops in the opening weeks of the Iraq War. None of them have an execution date. Military courts can impose a death sentence, but the case must go through the Pentagon before the president gives final approval to carry it out.
It's unclear why the Trump administration singled out Hasan, the former Army major who killed 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009.
Both the Pentagon and the White House declined to comment on whether they plan to execute any of the other death row inmates after Hasan.

Hasan is scheduled to face a firing squad Dec. 3 at the same base where he committed the attack, a method the military has not used since 1945. The Army originally planned to use lethal injection, internal documents reviewed by ABC News show.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth initially planned to livestream Hasan’s execution, which would have been the first public execution in the U.S. in nearly a century. Republicans and Democrats questioned the decision to broadcast the shooting death of a prisoner who uses a wheelchair and warned it could fuel anti-American propaganda and ultimately become a spectacle that has been associated with dictatorships in the past century. The plan was scrapped after President Donald Trump intervened.
The four men on the military's death row -- including Hasan -- are imprisoned at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

Ronald Gray, a former Army specialist who served as a cook with the 82nd Airborne Division at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, was convicted in a 1988 military trial on 12 charges, including two counts of premeditated murder and three counts of rape. The attacks involved five women, two of them soldiers. A civilian court separately convicted him on 22 charges and sentenced him to eight life terms.
President George W. Bush approved Gray’s execution in July 2008. It was scheduled for that December, but a federal judge halted it. Another judge lifted the stay in 2016.

Timothy Hennis, a former Army master sergeant who worked on parachutes with the 82nd Airborne Division, was convicted in civilian court in 1986 for raping and murdering a woman and killing her 5-year-old and 3-year-old daughters. His conviction was overturned on appeal, and a second trial ended in acquittal in 1989.

Years later, investigators retested evidence using new DNA tools. The acquittal barred another prosecution, but the Army could bring its own charges. The service recalled Hennis, who had retired in 2004, to active duty. A court-martial convicted him and sentenced him to death.

The fourth inmate, former Army Sgt. Hasan Akbar, attacked fellow soldiers at Camp Pennsylvania, Kuwait, in March 2003, during the opening days of the U.S. invasion of Iraq. Akbar, a combat engineer, wounded 14 soldiers and killed two officers. Akbar was convicted in a military court in 2005 on two counts of premeditated murder and three counts of attempted premeditated murder; he was sentenced to death.
In May, Hegseth awarded Purple Hearts at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, to nine veterans wounded in the attack.
It's unclear whether the other three death row inmates have maintained legal counsel.
Tim Jon Semmerling, the mitigation expert on Hasan’s defense team at his 2013 trial, said he believes the number of people Hasan killed at Fort Hood played a part in why he is being executed.
“If you believe in the death penalty, it's really difficult to argue against so many people being killed by one person,” Semmerling said.

Semmerling said he believes Hasan’s Muslim faith may also have figured into the administration's decision, as may Hasan’s stated motive for the attack, which he described as a protest against the U.S. wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Semmerling, who conducted dozens of interviews with Hasan and his family over four years, described Hasan as a devout Muslim who spends much of his time in prayer and studying the Quran and Muslim scholars.
Hegseth invoked Fort Hood in a 2015 appearance on Fox News where he argued that troops should be allowed to carry weapons on military bases, saying "Islamics are at war with us."
Hegseth told The Hill in September 2025 that he is "100% committed to ensuring the death penalty is carried out for Nidal Hasan" because the "victims and survivors deserve justice without delays."
As Hasan's execution approaches, Army officials say they are revising the outdated firing squad procedures, which date back to 1959.

John Galligan, a retired Army colonel who has long represented Hasan, said officials at the U.S. Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth promised to provide him with the execution protocols, but haven't done so yet. He wants to know how many soldiers will serve on the firing squad and whether Hasan can make a final statement.

“Those kind of details -- details about how you're going to kill someone during their execution -- are important for defense counsel to know -- particularly when, as here, the governing regulation is totally silent on the subject,” Galligan said.
The Army declined to comment when asked detailed questions about how it plans to carry out Hasan's execution.
Hasan could still file a habeas corpus petition, or a judge could delay the execution. It’s unclear whether either will happen.
The Army will have to assemble and train the soldiers who will carry out its first firing squad execution since World War II. It’s unclear what rehearsals they will undergo.

The 1959 procedures allowed prisoners to make reasonable final requests, including a meal, writing materials and access to a chaplain of their faith. On the day of the execution, the prisoner could make a final statement before being hooded and could ask the chaplain to stay until the firing squad was prepared to fire.
Hasan was partially paralyzed after police shot him during the Fort Hood attack. It’s unclear how the Army plans to account for his use of a wheelchair.

In Killeen, Texas, outside of the base where Hasan in set to be executed, officials plan to close city offices and public facilities on the day of the execution as a precautionary measure. Schools will also close, and the city has rescheduled trash collection. It’s unclear whether officials expect any significant protests.
Hasan told a military mental health panel during his trial that he wished he had been killed during his rampage and said he would still consider himself a martyr if the military put him to death.

title: Immigration officers make arrests at Seattle airport in 'distressing' scene, delaying flight
summary: Masked U.S. immigration officers have detained two people on a jet bridge at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as passengers were boarding
story: Masked U.S. immigration officers have detained two people on a jet bridge at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as passengers were boarding

Masked immigration officers detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, causing what the airline called a “distressing” scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight.
Video of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as a woman screams that her daughter is being taken and she has a work permit.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who “overstayed his visa in violation of our nation’s laws.”

During the confrontation, another passenger “hurled hot coffee on the officers,” the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer.
Online flight data showed that Alaska flight 1306, which had been scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m., was delayed.
Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

“We are concerned by this morning’s law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306,” the airline said. “We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests.”
It added that the airline is committed to “treating every guest with dignity and respect.”
The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The video showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases look on.
ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns “directly with the appropriate authorities.”

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would “engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred.”
Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE's tactics were “deeply un-American” and called for the agency's abolition.

“The video is horrific and it is chilling,” Ferguson said at an afternoon news conference with labor leaders and local elected officials. “We need a system of immigration enforcement and border security that is effective, ethical and humane. And ICE is not it. It is beyond reform.”
Ferguson also said he was looking into how ICE agents accessed the jet bridge and he believes they violated a state law he signed in March limiting facial coverings on law enforcement officers.

April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, representing over 600,000 workers, said union members were aboard the flight. She said the action disrupted travel during one of the busiest times and only days after flights were grounded nationwide due to a communications problem. “Airport workers are already managing extraordinary stress, passengers are already anxious and instead of restoring calm and confidence, federal agents introduced more fear and more chaos,” she said.

title: Miley Cyrus marries rock drummer Maxx Morando in an intimate Palm Springs wedding
summary: Singer Miley Cyrus has married rock drummer Maxx Morando in an intimate ceremony in Palm Springs, California
story: Singer Miley Cyrus has married rock drummer Maxx Morando in an intimate ceremony in Palm Springs, California
Pop culture icon Miley Cyrus married rock drummer Maxx Morando in an intimate weekend wedding in Palm Springs, California, according to a post on the singer’s Instagram account.

The post said Cyrus, 33, and Morando, 28, were wed on Saturday. Photographs show the couple embracing in front of a white backdrop with a palm tree characteristic of the Palm Springs desert in the background, a large dog lying at their feet. In one photo, the couple kisses standing in an aisle of white roses.

The “Party in the U.S.A.” singer wore a long-sleeve silk Saint Laurent gown by Anthony Vaccarello and elegant white silk kitten heels, according to a statement from Saint Laurent. The dress had a low back, and she wore flowers in her hair, which was pulled back into an updo.
Morando wore dark, square shades. His single-breasted tuxedo was also made by the French luxury fashion brand.

The pair have been together since 2021, meeting after they were set up on a blind date, according to an interview Cyrus gave Vogue in 2023. Morando proposed to her while the couple were in Japan late last year, he said in a separate interview with Wonderland Magazine.
“I could feel my heart pounding” before popping the question, Morando said for a profile in the magazine.
Morando is the drummer of the rock band Liily.

title: 9 people shot at a central California concert; 1 in critical condition
summary: Nine people have been shot at a concert in central California, leaving one person critically injured
story: Nine people have been shot at a concert in central California, leaving one person critically injured
Nine people were shot at a concert in central California, leaving one person critically injured with a chest injury, the local sheriff said Sunday.

The shooting broke out around 7:30 p.m. Saturday at a concert attended by about 150 people in Strathmore, a small town in Tulare County, a mountainous region in the center of the state, the county sheriff's department said in a statement. An unspecified number of suspects opened fire on the crowd. No arrests were announced.

One 26-year-old man was shot in the chest and required surgery. He remained in critical condition, the sheriff's department said. Two other victims ages 19 and 22 also required surgery, while six people sustained minor injuries.

Authorities said that they believe the shooting “may be gang-related” but didn't elaborate. The show in the town of roughly 3,000 people featured performers from neighboring states, the department said.
The department didn't immediately respond to emailed questions seeking further details but said there was no longer any immediate threat to the public.

title: 3 killed, 1 wounded in shooting at Ohio baby shower, police say
summary: Authorities say an apparent domestic dispute turned deadly at a baby shower.
story: Authorities say an apparent domestic dispute turned deadly at a baby shower.
PARMA, Ohio -- Three people were killed and one was injured at an Ohio baby shower during an apparent domestic dispute, authorities said.
Officers responded to a shooting Saturday evening at Pandora’s Magical Events Venue in Parma, about 10 miles (16 kilometers) south of Cleveland, a police news release said.

Authorities said one of the shooters, a 29-year-old man, was taken into custody, but he wasn't immediately charged. Detectives were trying to determine whether the man was the aggressor or acting in self-defense, police spokesman Scott Traxler said. A second suspected shooter, a 19-year-old man, was one of the people killed, police said.
