Officials have identified two of the victims as 17-year-old Leasia England and 45-year-old Jayson Townsend. Police said Townsend was the father of the woman for whom the baby shower was being held; she was not injured.
Officials haven't released the names of the 19-year-old suspected shooter who was killed, or a 39-year-old woman who was shot in the leg.

Preliminary information indicates that the 19-year-old man was the father of the unborn baby, and witnesses told police that he was not invited to the shower, Traxler said. The man in custody appears to be a relative of the expectant mother.

Both firearms involved in the shooting were recovered by police, officials said. Detectives were reviewing surveillance video and witnesses' statements on Sunday to determine what led to the violent confrontation, Traxler said. Ballistics testing might be required to determine which gun shot each victim.
Prosecutors will eventually determine whether the man in custody should be charged with a crime, officials said.

title: Natural gas pipeline fire shoots flames in Alabama, cause under investigation
summary: A pipeline in rural Alabama sent a column of flames high into the night sky.
story: A pipeline in rural Alabama sent a column of flames high into the night sky.

WARD, Ala. -- A fire on a natural gas pipeline lit up the night sky in rural Alabama late Saturday with a towering column of orange flame, prompting the operator to shut down part of the line but causing no injuries, the company said.
The cause of the fire is under investigation and customer deliveries were not impacted, Southern Natural Gas Company said in a statement Sunday.

Photos and videos posted on social media appeared to show flames rising dozens of yards (meters) above the trees near Ward, with smoke billowing into the air. People said on social media that the fire was visible from miles (kilometers) away across the state line in Mississippi.

Southern Natural Gas said it “experienced a natural gas release and fire” on the segment of the pipeline at around 11:30 p.m. CST Saturday. Emergency responders and company personnel secured the area and the blaze was extinguished, the company said. The impacted part of the pipeline was shut down and depressurized.
The Sumter County Emergency Management Agency did not immediately respond to a voicemail seeking information.

title: Nations at UN talks on AI killer robots agree to more talks but no firm commitment to rein them in
summary: Efforts to establish rules for AI-powered killer robots and drones have run aground
story: Efforts to establish rules for AI-powered killer robots and drones have run aground
GENEVA -- Efforts to set firm rules on AI-powered killer robots and drones ran aground Saturday as U.N.-backed talks in Geneva produced a softened agreement to extend discussions for two more years.

Scores of countries ended the week-long U.N. conference on weapons by agreeing to “elaborate” a possible accord on such lethal autonomous weapons systems by 2028. But they didn’t commit to binding rules sought by U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, many countries, and activists.
The outcome underscored the difficulty of achieving concrete results in diplomacy amid global conflicts and major military powers jockeying for dominance.

Izumi Nakamitsu, the U.N. high representative for disarmament affairs, hailed a “significant achievement” but acknowledged a “glass half full or half empty” scenario, citing Guterres’ hopes for a legally binding deal this year.
Activists accused military powers like Russia and the United States of blocking stronger language.

Stop Killer Robots lamented a “watered-down mandate,” and Beatrice Fihn, founder of international law advocacy group Lex International, said the decision amounts to “pushing the can down the road for two more years."

They noted most countries supported work toward a new treaty, and Max Tegmark, a machine learning specialist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and founder of the Future of Life Institute, said: “States have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about the issue, for the 14th year, while these weapons enable atrocities.”

Before the meeting, seven countries proposed launching negotiations on a rulebook that could prevent or limit the ability of machines to kill without human control or accountability. That effort fell short.

“Technology is moving faster than diplomacy,” said Ambassador Frederico Meyer of Brazil, which joined Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama in proposing such negotiations. “Diplomats are very slow.”

After years of talks on the issue, advocacy groups bemoaned obstructionism largely by Russia, which, like other top AI weapons-developing countries such as the United States, wants a freer hand to develop such high-tech weapons.
Guterres, who leaves office at the end of the year, set a 2026 deadline for launching negotiations toward an agreement on autonomous weapons systems.
Pope Leo XIV and many advocacy and humanitarian groups have framed the issue as an existential debate, urging quick action to rein in AI weapons before they become too commonplace to regulate easily.
Activists say armed drones that can independently strike targets have already been deployed in some select instances in conflict zones, but widespread rollout hasn’t happened.

Talks this week centered on the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, ratified by 128 countries, where decisions are made by consensus. That means any single country can thwart an agreement, and that any deal was likely to be based on a low common denominator.

title: San Francisco braces for massive tides, mayor urges residents to reconsider travel
summary: Scattered rain is exacerbating the impacts of historic flooding across central Florida, as Northern California braces for an unprecedented deluge accompanied by high tides ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday
story: Scattered rain is exacerbating the impacts of historic flooding across central Florida, as Northern California braces for an unprecedented deluge accompanied by high tides ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday

Scattered rain continued to exacerbate the impacts of historic flooding across central Florida on Saturday, even as officials in Northern California braced for an unprecedented deluge during high tides heading into the heavy Thanksgiving travel week.

San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie warned that an “extremely serious” situation was about to hit the city, based on National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and National Weather Service forecasts, and urged people to consider not traveling for the holiday.

“We are expecting tides that the National Weather Service told us they have never seen before in recorded history here in San Francisco,” Lurie said via the social platform X. “Take this weekend to get yourself ready, please stock up on supplies, get your shopping done, and know that the city will be out all weekend doing everything possible to protect our residents and our small businesses.”

Storm systems impacting Florida and California are an offshoot of El Niño, the natural warming of the Pacific near the equator that warps weather patterns worldwide. Florida typically experiences its dry season from October to May, for example.

The expected deluge in California coincides with the highest tides of the year, called king tides. Forecasters said up to 2 feet (0.6 meters) of flooding would be likely in low-lying areas near shorelines and tidal waterways through 6 a.m. Monday, and through 4 p.m. Thursday along other areas of the Pacific coast.

Forecasters also warned of dangers Saturday along Florida's Atlantic coast. The weather service issued marine warnings to boaters tied to thunderstorms capable of creating destabilizing waterspouts, and advised beachgoers to beware of rough surf and dangerous rip currents.

NWS meteorologist Melissa Watson in Melbourne said that while the heaviest rains have passed, water levels were expected to continue to rise along the St. Johns River, Florida’s longest, due to continued lighter showers. Near the city of Cocoa, the river rose above a 1953 record Thursday.
“Regardless of any additional rainfall, we are expecting these river floods to continue for an extended period of time,” Watson said.
Heavy rain earlier this week submerged large swaths of Florida’s Atlantic coast, trapping people in floodwaters in the northeastern part of the state.
Associated Press journalist Donna Warder contributed.

title: Trump administration use of encrypted messaging apps like Signal is scrutinized by House Democrat
summary: A Democratic lawmaker is investigating the use of encrypted messaging apps by Justice Department employees for official business
story: A Democratic lawmaker is investigating the use of encrypted messaging apps by Justice Department employees for official business

WASHINGTON -- A top House Democrat is demanding that multiple government agencies preserve communications created on nongovernment messaging apps and investigate whether any records related to official business have been deleted.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee and the panel's incoming chairman, said in a series of nearly identical letters made public on Friday that he was concerned that President Donald Trump's administration was circumventing record-keeping requirements by using apps like Signal that can be configured to automatically delete messages after a certain time period.

Raskin noted in the letters, which were sent to top officials at the FBI, the Justice Department, the Department of Homeland Security, the Bureau of Prisons and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, that the agencies were legally required to preserve all records related to their official business, policies and decisions.

But he said: “There is significant evidence that Trump Administration officials have engaged in the widespread destruction, mutilation, and concealment of government records, seemingly with the express purpose of circumventing federal record preservation laws. This attempt to evade transparency extends to the highest levels of federal agencies, including top-ranking law enforcement officials.”

The Maryland Democrat cited as an example a Signal exchange that he said he had obtained between the FBI’s general counsel and an associate of the Republican president's oldest son, Donald Trump Jr., in which a potential or ongoing healthcare fraud investigation was discussed.

The Justice Department said in a statement Friday that it “follows all legal requirements for the management of federal records involving its official functions and decisions.” The other agencies cited by Raskin did not immediately return messages seeking comment.

Signal is an app that can be used for direct messaging and group chats as well as phone and video calls. It uses end-to-end encryption for its messaging and calling services that prevents any third party from viewing conversation content or listening in on calls.
Encrypted messaging apps are increasingly popular with government officials, an Associated Press review from last year found.

Their prevalence was demonstrated in vivid fashion last year when journalist Jeffrey Goldberg revealed that he had been inadvertently added to a Signal group chat of U.S. national security officials coordinating plans for airstrikes.

The White House and the Pentagon have said that disgruntled former employees were spreading false claims about the use of Signal, a commercially available app not authorized to be used to communicate sensitive or classified national defense information.

title: Northeastern Florida faces flood threats from devastating storms
summary: Heavy rains that left large swaths of Florida’s Atlantic coast under water and led to dozens of rescues moved further north on Friday
story: Heavy rains that left large swaths of Florida’s Atlantic coast under water and led to dozens of rescues moved further north on Friday

Heavy rains that left large swaths of Florida's Atlantic coast under water and led to dozens of rescues moved further north on Friday as forecasters warned flooding threats could stretch into next week when a major river is expected to crest well above record levels.

The National Weather Service posted flood warnings and watches stretching around 200 miles (320 kilometers) from just south of Melbourne to the Jacksonville area. Additional rainfall of 2 to 6 inches (5 to 15 centimeters) was expected through Saturday, while some areas could see an extra 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 centimeters).

“Severe, widespread flash flooding is expected,” the weather service said in a Friday morning forecast. “In addition, areas that normally do not experience flash flooding will flood. Furthermore, lives and property (are) in great danger.”

The St. Johns River, Florida's longest, rose above a record level Thursday near Cocoa that was set in 1953. The river is forecast to stay at least 2 feet (61 centimeters) above flood stage through early next week, the weather service said.

Also Friday, a nontropical low-pressure system was expected to form and could become a subtropical or tropical storm along the southeastern U.S. coast, the National Hurricane Center in Miami said. The southeast and mid-Atlantic coasts should expect strong winds, dangerous surf and coastal flooding into early next week ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

Parts of Florida's east coast have been deluged with rainfall totaling more than 17 inches (43 centimeters) in some spots since Tuesday, according to preliminary totals by the weather service. That's in addition to heavy rains that fell earlier this month. Several places have already seen their wettest November on record.

The storms shifted north to the Space Coast on Thursday, sending rivers over their banks and prompting water rescues of people and horses during what is supposed to be Florida's dry season that runs from October to May.
“Never seen such a thing like this in Florida,” said Jazmin Foster, whose Melbourne home was inundated with water for the second time in two weeks.

In Brevard County on Thursday, people with trailers braved knee-deep water to rescue dozens of horses and other animals at the Blue Lake Equestrian Center, an animal hospice and boarding facility in Cocoa. The animals were taken to a dry pasture elsewhere.

First responders conducted nearly 100 high-water rescues across the county, and those numbers continued to climb, Sheriff Wayne Ivey said. The city of Palm Bay conducted mandatory evacuations for some residents of a mobile home community. Shelters were opened for residents forced from their homes.

Nearly 200 Florida National Guard personnel with 50 high-water vehicles have been deployed to help up and down the coast, the Division of Emergency Management said. Other responding agencies included about 235 officers with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission.

This week’s storms have been fueled by persistent high pressure over Virginia and a low-pressure system and an associated stationary front in the Gulf, which together have pushed a steady onshore flow across the Florida Peninsula. They're an offshoot of El Niño, the natural warming of the Pacific near the equator that warps weather patterns worldwide.
Forecasters said El Niño conditions are expected to persist through the spring, meaning the soggy extreme weather in Florida and California will likely continue through the winter.

The California coast, from the Los Angeles to San Francisco areas, was also swamped with flooding in many areas this week, leaving neighborhoods under water and forcing some drivers to abandon stalled vehicles in floodwaters. A long stretch of the coastal Highway 1 was closed south of the Monterey Peninsula due to rock and mud slides.
Associated Press writers Amy Taxin in Santa Ana, California, and Jessica Hill in Las Vegas contributed to this report.

title: FBI investigating apparent hack of a key criminal justice information database, AP source says
summary: The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of its National Crime Information Center database
story: The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of its National Crime Information Center database
WASHINGTON -- The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of a national law enforcement database that it maintains, a person familiar with the matter said Saturday.

The National Crime Information Center, known as the NCIC, is a computerized database of criminal justice information that is available to local, state and federal law enforcement agencies and includes records on fugitives, missing persons, criminal history data, stolen property and other topics.

The FBI declined to comment Saturday on the apparent hack, which was first reported by CNN and confirmed to The Associated Press by a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak by name and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
The scope of the problem was not immediately clear.
Asked about the subject on Saturday, President Donald Trump said in a Fox News Channel interview: “We just heard about it and I will say that it’s not good.”

News that the NCIC was targeted comes as the country has encountered a series of digital outages in the government and private sector that Trump administration officials have said were caused by routine efforts to upgrade computer systems and fix vulnerabilities, rather than a cyberattack. There was no immediate indication that the FBI incident was related to those outages.
The bureau has historically been a frequent target for hackers.

In September, for instance, the FBI said it was investigating a hack of its job portal website after a criminal hacking group known as ShinyHunters claimed it had obtained a massive trove of data on bureau employees and applicants.
And in March, the FBI disclosed that it was investigating “suspicious activities” on an internal system that contains sensitive information related to surveillance operations and investigations.

title: Fans near and far mourn Fiona the hippo
summary: Fans of the Cincinnati Zoo’s beloved Fiona the hippo are mourning
story: Fans of the Cincinnati Zoo’s beloved Fiona the hippo are mourning

CINCINNATI -- Fans of Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo's hippo, draped a hippo statue with flowers and notes written in crayon Friday, a day after she died from complications caused by swallowing a knit hat accidentally flung into her enclosure.
A little girl held up a drawing of Fiona while a woman left behind a watermelon, one of Fiona's favorite treats.
“She brought so much love in her lifetime,” said one note.

Born prematurely almost a decade ago and given slim odds of survival, Fiona became not only a source of hometown pride but also a worldwide symbol of hope and inspiration for many — from teachers to parents to children.

“I have never known an animal so beloved in all my life. From the day she was born, she was like lightning in a bottle,” Thayne Maynard, the zoo board's executive chair, said in a statement. “And, she will be remembered and beloved many years from now.”
Zoo officials have yet to release the specific medical cause of Fiona's death or details surrounding her final hours. Fiona was 9 years old.
“Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn’t fight anymore,” zoo director Dave Jenike said.
At first, Fiona showed no signs of distress after swallowing the hat 11 days before her death. A zoo visitor tossed the hat, which a ceiling fan caught and flung into the hippo habitat.
But a few days later, her appetite started to decline, zoo officials said. By Monday, the zoo announced Fiona was undergoing veterinary care.
The zoo's animal care team gave her fluids through an IV, conducted a colonoscopy and tried to shake the obstruction loose with a vibration table borrowed from a horse farm.
They said they were cautiously optimistic she could pass the hat.
“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome,” the zoo said.
The zoo's director said Fiona's death came as a shock. “We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn’t anymore,” Jenike said.
Fiona captured the hearts of millions in her first months and final days, uniting people across all boundaries and political spectrums.
Usha Vance, the wife of Vice President JD Vance, posted a photo of one of their children face-to-face with Fiona through the glass wall of her enclosure.
Former first daughter Chelsea Clinton posted photos of her behind-the-scenes encounter with Fiona, writing that she would treasure “the smiles she gave me.”
Speaking outside the zoo Thursday, Amy Haacke, a teacher from Dayton, said that she was a “huge fan” of Fiona because she likes underdogs. She said she uses the Fiona book series in her classroom.
“It kind of means a lot to be here,” she said.
Fiona was born six weeks premature, weighing just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms), far below the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at the time.
The zoo's staff went to extraordinary lengths to keep her alive, raising her by hand. She couldn't nurse, so a zoo staffer hand-milked her mother to feed her.
She became a celebrity during her nine years. Hippos typically live 40 to 50 years in zoos.

Her story marked an uplifting turn for the Cincinnati Zoo after months of backlash over the 2016 shooting of Harambe. The gorilla became a pop culture phenomenon after he was killed because a child got into his enclosure.

title: Federal judge denies a request to release man shot by immigration agents in New York
summary: A federal judge has denied a request to release a man shot and wounded by immigration officers in New York
story: A federal judge has denied a request to release a man shot and wounded by immigration officers in New York
NEW YORK -- A federal judge on Friday declined to release from custody a man who was shot and wounded by immigration officers as they arrested him in New York last month.

U.S. District Court Judge Hector Gonzalez said in a written ruling that agents may have made a procedural error in serving an arrest warrant on Oscar Belgal before he was given a notice to appear in immigration court. However, he wrote, that was merely a technical error that does not require Belgal to be released from federal custody pending deportation proceedings.

Belgal, a 28-year-old Dominican national, entered the U.S. illegally in 2021, and about two years later he was arrested on robbery and other charges and eventually pleaded guilty to grand larceny. He was given a sentence of probation, and in 2025 he was arrested again, this time on allegations that he attempted to sell controlled substances. That case remains pending.
On Oct. 8, amid President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents found him as he was driving his 5-year-old son home from school.

Security camera footage released by New York City police shows an officer dressed in plainclothes running up to the car with his gun pointed at Belgal, then immediately using the barrel of his gun to bash the driver’s side window. A second officer then draws his gun as Belgal pulls out, away from the two officers. The chase ends moments later, with Belgal’s bullet-riddled car coming to rest.
Belgal was struck in the shoulder and neck. His son was not injured. His attorneys said he didn’t learn the men were ICE officers until he awoke later in the hospital.

“It is unconscionable that Mr. Belgal should have to endure another day in detention, separated from his family, particularly given everything he has already suffered,” The Legal Aid Society, a nonprofit law firm that represents him, said in a written statement.

Federal officials maintained that ICE officers fired their weapons because they believed their lives were in danger. They said Belgal smashed his car into two government vehicles and “accelerated toward other officers.”

His attorneys said the agents did not have a valid warrant and never identified themselves before running up to Belgal’s car, smashing a window and firing several shots inside. The lawyers also argued in their filings that Belgal's due process rights were violated because he was subjected to “unreasonable use of extreme force” during his arrest.

The judge disagreed that the agents did not have a valid warrant. And the petition Belgal filed for release from custody was not an appropriate venue for arguing that the agents used excessive force, he said.
Gonzalez noted that Belgal can still ask the immigration court to release him on bond.
Johnson reported from Seattle. Associated Press writer Michael R. Sisak in New York contributed.

title: Leaders of Mexican drug cartel and 19 others indicted for smuggling guns, drugs and people
summary: A federal grand jury in Texas has indicted the leaders of a powerful Mexican drug cartel and 19 others
story: A federal grand jury in Texas has indicted the leaders of a powerful Mexican drug cartel and 19 others

A federal grand jury indicted the leaders of a powerful Mexican drug cartel and 19 others Wednesday, accusing them of a range of crimes, including drug trafficking and smuggling firearms from the U.S. into Mexico.

The indictment accuses Mexican nationals Johnny Hurtado Olascoaga, alias “El Pez,” and Jose Alfredo Hurtado Olascoaga, alias “El Fresa,” of leading La Nueva Familia Michoacana cartel. The two are currently at large.

La Nueva Familia Michoacana, or LNFM, is one of nearly two dozen Latin American and Caribbean gangs designated by the Trump administration as a foreign terrorist organization. The cartel, founded in 2006, operates in the Mexican states of Michoacan and Guerrero, and authorities say it produces and distributes drugs. The brothers took control of the cartel in 2011.

The brothers are charged with conspiring to distribute and import cocaine, heroin, and methamphetamine, trafficking firearms — including .50-caliber rifles — international money laundering and human smuggling. The brothers, along with 14 others accused in the case, are at large and believed to be in Mexico, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas. The U.S. is offering rewards of $5 million and $3 million for information leading to the brothers' capture.

The indictment, which was filed in federal court in Western Texas, also accuses 19 others of being members or associates of the cartel and committing related crimes. All 21 are charged with racketeering.

Edgar Aguilar Cruz of Mexico, for instance, orchestrated the purchase of firearms “by numerous straw purchasers throughout Texas and the Southeastern United States,” according to the indictment. The guns were eventually transported to Mexico by couriers. He is also accused of overseeing the cartel's human smuggling operations.

U.S. citizens are among the accused, including a 23-year-old man who is alleged to have been a “mid-level drug trafficker who coordinates drug trafficking logistics” for the cartel, primarily in Texas and North Carolina. Another U.S. citizen, a 35-year-old man, recruited people to buy firearms for the cartel, authorities said.

Cash profits from drug trafficking and human smuggling were often transported together with firearms back to the cartel in Mexico, according to the indictment. Members and associates of the cartel discussed obtaining military-grade weapons, such as rocket-propelled grenades, and cartel leaders customized their guns with gold plating and cartoon and religious figures, authorities said.

Only five of the accused are in federal custody, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas. Gregory Torres, an attorney for Rogelio Ponce Esquivel, a 33-year-old Mexican national who is charged in the indictment and is in custody, declined to comment. It is unclear if the other four who were detained have lawyers.

In addition to its drug and firearm trafficking operations and for-profit human smuggling, the cartel has expanded to control mines and barter with Chinese companies to trade Mexican minerals for chemicals used in drug distribution, the indictment said. ___
Kelety reported from Phoenix. Associated Press writer Fabiola Sanchez in Mexico City contributed.

title: Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
summary: The man accused of sparking last year’s deadly Palisades Fire has been found guilty of arson charges
story: The man accused of sparking last year’s deadly Palisades Fire has been found guilty of arson charges
LOS ANGELES -- The man accused of sparking last year’s deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.

Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.

Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges.
With little apparent reaction, Rinderknecht gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. The verdict was delivered on the third day of deliberation.

Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in LA, said the verdict was a “testament of the hard work” his team put into the case. He said he was “intimately familiar” with the strength of the evidence and was happy with the jury that convicted Rinderknecht.
Rinderknecht’s attorney Steve Haney said in a statement they were disappointed in the verdict but respected the jury process.
“After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration,” Haney said. Regarding an appeal, he said they would review all the options at the right time.
Rinderknecht is set to be sentenced March 17, 2027. Each count carries a mandatory minimum of five years and a maximum of 20 years in federal prison.

Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht’s first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial. Essayli said he believed the first jury acted improperly and appeared to consider things in their decision that weren’t presented as evidence during the trial.

Juror No. 3, who only wanted to be identified by his first name Cameron, said he was the only person who felt Rinderknecht was not guilty at the start of deliberations. Another person was undecided, and the rest of the 10 jurors believed Rinderknecht was guilty.
“It took a lot for me to be convinced otherwise,” he said. “After listening to every single point, I do now agree that he’s guilty.”

Cameron said he initially had concerns about a technical review conducted by a defense expert witness, who argued the government had gotten the origin area of the fire wrong. He said there was a “lack of information” presented to the jury about the technical review.
In the end, it was Rinderknecht’s own testimony that was the strongest piece of evidence pointing to a guilty verdict, he said.
“Stating that he was up on the hill, didn’t smell a fire, didn’t see fireworks … no one else was on the hill that night,” Cameron said.

During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organized case that presented digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht’s state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. They did not focus as much on his resentment toward the rich and powerful to present the crime as arson motivated by “societal revenge” like they previously did.

Prosecutors zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire’s origin area, such as photographs that showed his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and cellphone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks.
They established that Rinderknecht was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.
“He was mad at everything, and frustrated,” said Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams.

After the fire began, Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times as he walked down the hill. Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: “Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?”
These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said.
They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was a holdover fire from the initial blaze Rinderknecht sparked.
Haney cast doubt on the government’s case, saying the fire scene could have been compromised because the area was publicly accessible until the Palisades Fire started Jan. 7.
The defense called their own expert witnesses, including a retired fire investigator for the U.S. Forest Service who argued the fire origin area was different from what the government concluded.

Prosecutors attacked the fire investigator during cross examination and at one point accused him of perjury, alleging he did not disclose all records related to the case. The judge ultimately rejected prosecutors’ request to strike his testimony.

Haney argued the government could not conclusively say there was no one else by the fire ignition point that night because of missing cell data records, and pointed to a neighbor’s testimony that he saw a group of teenagers running away from the direction of the trailhead.
He told jurors to disregard any evidence related to Rinderknecht’s character, such as his angry text messages, because they were “evidence of the man, not evidence of the act.”

Finally, Haney presented an alternate explanation for what ignited the fire — fireworks. Multiple witnesses, including two neighbors and a local firefighter, all said they heard a loud bang or explosion from the direction of the hill the fire purportedly started on.
In the thousands of images of the evening collected from cameras in the area, none showed fireworks in the sky above the hill where the fire started, prosecutors said.

title: Rights groups urge sanctions after top UN court finds Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
summary: Rights groups are urging military and economic sanctions against Myanmar after the United Nations' highest court ruled that its government committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in 2017
story: Rights groups are urging military and economic sanctions against Myanmar after the United Nations' highest court ruled that its government committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in 2017

UNITED NATIONS -- Rights groups are calling for military and economic sanctions against Myanmar after the United Nations' highest court, in the first ruling of its kind, determined that its government committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation.

The International Court of Justice has no power to enforce Thursday's ruling, which orders Myanmar’s military-supported government to allow those who fled the violence to return home safely, to pay reparations to the Rohingya Muslims and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide.

Myanmar’s government has denied committing genocide, claiming it acted against insurgents, and is considered unlikely to fulfill any of the court’s demands. President Min Aung Hlaing, the former military leader, was in charge of the 2017 operation. The court said evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 100,000 Rohingya.
Khine Khine Soe, the president's spokeswoman, noted the International Court of Justice decision handed down Thursday had been the result of a nine-to-six vote of the judges.
“Not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” she told reporters in the capital Naypyitaw. “So it was not a decision made unanimously. I would say that it was unfair.”
While the World Court’s rulings are final and legally binding, it has no recourse beyond reporting noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council.

The Security Council scheduled closed consultations on the ruling next Wednesday and a private meeting on Dec. 7 at the request of the United Kingdom, which expelled Myanmar's defense attache after Thursday's ruling.

But Daniel Forti, the International Crisis Group’s head of U.N. affairs, said it’s unlikely there will be any immediate action from the 15-member Security Council, which could impose sanctions on Myanmar. He said any action would likely be blocked by China and Russia, both permanent members with veto power.

“China has discouraged the Security Council from acting on the Myanmar file since 2021, as it is reluctant to cede any influence in its own backyard,” Forti told The Associated Press. “The ICJ ruling will not alter China’s calculations, and it is hard to imagine that either Beijing or Moscow would support any potential Security Council resolution that attempts to enforce the court’s recommendations.”

Forti said Gambia, which launched the court proceedings, may eventually pursue a resolution in the 193-member General Assembly calling on Myanmar to comply with the ICJ’s demands, even though its actions are not legally binding, unlike those of the Security Council.

Justice for All, an American human rights organization that advocates for the rights of Muslim minorities, called on the Trump administration to support a General Assembly resolution demanding Myanmar’s compliance with the judgment, and establishing international monitoring and follow-up.

Justice for All, which has a task force of 38 U.S. and Canadian Muslim organizations that have advocated for Rohingya rights since 2017, argued that sanctions should target Myanmar’s oil and gas sector and the networks that provide weapons and other support to its military.

Amnesty International’s Secretary General Agnes Callamard urged governments not to welcome the president “on the international stage, especially as grave violations continue unchecked inside Myanmar.”

“Instead, they should stop any transfer of all weapons, security and surveillance equipment, and military and security assistance to Myanmar,” she said. “The U.N. Security Council should impose a global arms embargo and refer the entire situation in Myanmar to the International Criminal Court.”
That court, however, is under U.S. sanctions along with many of its judges and staff, so any action by the Security Council would face an almost certain U.S. veto.

Prosecutors at the ICC requested an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing in late 2024 alleging he was responsible for crimes against humanity against the Rohingya. There has been no public announcement on a decision by judges at the court who would have to issue a warrant.
The court's Office of the Prosecutor did not immediately respond to a request Friday for comment.
Human Rights Watch urged governments to step forward to help the Rohingya.

“Concerned governments should strongly support the Rohingya and promote justice for atrocities, press Myanmar’s junta to comply with the judgment, and ensure the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar,” Maria Elena Vignoli, the group's senior international justice counsel, said in a statement.

Justice for All called for global support for a Rohingya reparations fund and measures to advance their education, protection, pursuit of citizenship and safe voluntary return from Bangladesh, where some 1.2 million Rohingya now live in overcrowded camps.

Myanmar, which is majority Buddhist, has long claimed the Rohingya are “Bengali” migrants from Bangladesh, even though their families have lived in the country for generations. Nearly all Rohingya have been denied citizenship since 1982, effectively rendering them stateless, and they are denied freedom of movement and other basic rights.
Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya rights activist who listened to the court ruling in The Hague, Netherlands, said the judgment “will only mean something if governments act on it.”
“So, I say to every U.N. member state, take robust steps to implement the ICJ judgment,” she said, starting with sanctions against the president.
“Make Myanmar pay reparations to the people it destroyed,” she said. “Give us back our lives. Give us a future. We want to be part of a stable, prosperous and thriving Myanmar.”
Associated Press writer Mike Corder in The Hague, Netherlands, contributed.

title: 2 men cleared in South Carolina road rage shooting now face charges after family finds new evidence
summary: Two men initially cleared in a South Carolina road rage shooting three years ago now face murder charges
story: Two men initially cleared in a South Carolina road rage shooting three years ago now face murder charges

COLUMBIA, S.C. -- Two men initially cleared of criminal charges in a South Carolina road rage shooting three years ago now face murder charges after the victim's family uncovered evidence of police officers influencing the investigation.
Two of the Horry County officers also were indicted this week on obstruction of justice and misconduct charges for their role in investigating the shooting of Scott Spivey in September 2023.
The charges came after another independent look at the case pushed by Spivey's family. After prosecutors first decided not to charge Weldon Boyd and Kenneth Williams, they filed a civil lawsuit.

The family received recordings Boyd made of his own phone calls where he bragged about the shooting and asked a police officer friend to intervene. It also got body camera footage of another officer writing a note to the men the day of the shooting that said “act like a victim camera.”

The case started with Boyd and Williams chasing Spivey for several miles after Spivey pulled a gun on them in a road rage incident, authorities said. Both pickups reached speeds over 100 mph (160 kph) before Spivey pulled off a side road and got out of his truck with a gun and told the men to stop following him, investigators said.
The men shot through the windshield of the pickup, hitting Spivey in the right side of his back near his armpit, authorities said.

The local prosecutor in the case turned it over to the South Carolina Attorney General's Office after Boyd posted a message on Facebook thanking police and prosecutors for their work on the case a week after the shooting.

The Attorney General's Office decided not to prosecute Boyd and Williams in the shooting seven months later, ruling they were threatened and therefore justified to fire on Spivey under the state's stand your ground law.

That led to the civil lawsuit, which unearthed Boyd's phone calls. In one, he talks to Williams about them getting teardrop tattoos since they killed a man. In another, he told someone Spivey figured out during the chase he could drive faster than them and was terrified. In another, he said about the shooting, “I know it’s (expletive) up to say, but I had a (expletive) blast."

The officers were fired after the new evidence and the Attorney General's Office brought in prosecutor Barry Barnette from Spartanburg to review the case. He called for another grand jury that led to Thursday's indictments.

Lawyers for all four men charged said publicity has tainted the case. They all said their clients were innocent and Boyd's lawyer Shaun Kent said the charges should be dropped in part because the evidence from the civil case was used to build criminal charges — a tactic that led to the dismissal of sexual assault charges against Bill Cosby.
There are reasons prosecutors initially cleared the men including findings that Spivey had alcohol in his system, Kent said.
“He was intoxicated. He had a firearm. He was pointing it at other individuals," Kent said in court Thursday.

Boyd and Williams were both indicted on murder charges, while former Horry County Deputy Chief Brandon Strickland and Sgt. Damon Vescovi were charged with misconduct in office and obstruction of justice.
Boyd called Strickland several times from the scene and after, and Strickland told his friend he talked to investigators and prosecutors, according to Boyd's phone calls.
Strickland's lawyer said at a Thursday bond hearing that his comments may have been inappropriate but there is no evidence he influenced the investigation.
Vescovi passed along the note about the camera. His lawyer said he made a poor choice but at that point he thought Boyd and Williams were victims of a road rage incident.

Jennifer Spivey, who pored over the evidence in her brother's killing until she found the note and heard Boyd's phone calls, was at Thursday's hearing and asked the judge to make sure justice is finally served.
"Scott tried desperately to escape the violence that ultimately took his life," she said.

title: Mamdani sets plan to close NYC's notorious Rikers Island jail
summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani plans to shutter New York City’s notorious Rikers Island jail complex by 2032
story: Mayor Zohran Mamdani plans to shutter New York City’s notorious Rikers Island jail complex by 2032

NEW YORK -- New York City's Rikers Island jail complex would close by 2032 under a plan announced Friday by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose strategy for finally shuttering the notorious facility hinges on substantially reducing the number of people kept behind bars.
The city is all but certain to blow past a legal requirement to close Rikers and replace it with four smaller, more modern jails by 2027.

For years, Rikers Island has stood as a symbol of dysfunction, with the network of jails so plagued by violence and overcrowding that a federal judge, citing “ abnormal and unacceptable " conditions, appointed an outside manager to restore order and implement reforms.

Mamdani, a Democrat, has been a vocal proponent of closing Rikers, though the longstanding plan to build new jails has met pushback, including from his predecessor, former Mayor Eric Adams, who opposed federal oversight and borough jails.
“It is time to finally close Rikers Island,” Mamdani said in a statement. “For decades, New Yorkers have demanded a correctional system that is safe and humane."
The plan hinges on lowering the city's inmate population from the more than 6,500 people housed at Rikers to around 4,500.

The Mamdani administration is proposing a new slate of diversion and supervised release programs, expanding housing and social services to prevent recidivism, along with restoring an online bail payment system and reducing case delays through various measures.

“We have a legal and moral obligation to close Rikers. Working alongside the City Council, Courts and nonprofit partners, we will meet it — for the people in our custody, the staff who serve them, victims of crime, and every New Yorker,” Mamdani said.

Instead of housing prisoners at Rikers — an island in the East River near LaGuardia Airport — the city will shift people to jails in the Bronx, Queens, Brooklyn and Manhattan, as well as a handful of medical facilities for people who need healthcare or psychiatric treatment. The city also plans to reduce the number of beds for women, diverting them into community-based programs.
The borough jails are expected to open in Brooklyn in 2029; the Bronx and Queens in 2031; and then Manhattan in 2032, according to City Hall.
Criminal justice activists have pushed for decades to close Rikers Island, which has housed jail inmates since the 1930s.

In 2019, the New York City Council voted to close the jail complex and replace it with newer jails located in the city's boroughs, with local lawmakers invoking the names of former prisoners who died, including Kalief Browder, who took his own life at age 22 after being held for three years at Rikers.

At the time, city officials had also called for shrinking the jail population to accommodate the closure, but ran into opposition from critics who argued doing so would mean more violent criminals on city streets.

title: Famed Marine Corps veteran under federal investigation over undisclosed allegations
summary: The Naval Criminal Investigative Service says it is investigating a famed Marine Corps veteran over undisclosed allegations
story: The Naval Criminal Investigative Service says it is investigating a famed Marine Corps veteran over undisclosed allegations

LAS VEGAS -- A celebrated Marine Corps veteran who became famous for his heroism during the Iraq War is under criminal investigation for undisclosed allegations, the Naval Criminal Investigative Service confirmed Friday.

CBS News first reported that retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal is under investigation over allegations stemming from his time as an ROTC assistant at a high school in Henderson, Nevada. The Naval Criminal Investigative Service, which is the Navy’s lead for felony-level criminal investigations, declined to provide further details to The Associated Press.

Kasal is a well-known veteran who earned the Navy Cross — the second-highest award for heroism for members of the Navy and the Marines — for his actions during combat operations in Fallujah, Iraq. Kasal was wounded in 2004 while fighting and shielding an injured Marine from a grenade. An iconic photo capturing the moment that soldiers helped carry Kasal inspired sculptures that were displayed at Marine Corps base camps.

The Clark County School District, which oversees hundreds of schools in the Las Vegas area, confirmed that Kasal worked at the Basic Academy of International Studies as an ROTC assistant. He was hired in August 2018 and resigned in August 2025, the district said.

In an email to Basic Academy families, the district said it was aware of the investigation into the former employee and said the former employee is no longer on campus. The district added that it will “cooperate fully with any investigation.”
The AP left text and voicemail messages Friday at a cellphone number for Kasal. CBS News said he did not respond to its own attempts to seek comment.

Some former students interviewed by CBS News praised him as a caring instructor who devoted time, energy and resources to his students. Other cadets claimed to the outlet that Kasal would take a select group of female cadets to get Starbucks.

Damien Greenwell, a 22-year-old who participated in the program from 2018 to 2022, told CBS News that he questioned some of Kasal’s conduct over the years and his behavior toward students could be interpreted as inappropriate by an outside observer.

Estella Deleon, a cadet who graduated in 2022, told the AP she was “baffled” by the investigation into Kasal and she never witnessed inappropriate behavior by him. Kasal always made himself available to cadets if they needed someone to talk to, she said, and he taught them important life lessons she still thinks about.

Deleon, 22, said Kasal would take everyone to get coffee or bring it to cadets if they were staying late after school or arriving early in the morning. One day he brought everyone in the class tamales, she said.
Deleon said she can understand the thinking that he should have kept a more professional relationship, “but he was like a father figure to a lot of us, and he was a great role model.”

title: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year as rout in tech stocks tanks the market
summary: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year as rout in tech stocks tanks the market
story: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year as rout in tech stocks tanks the market
NEW YORK -- S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year as rout in tech stocks tanks the market.
THIS IS AN APNewsAlert. Check back for updates. AP's earlier story is below.
Wall Street's losses mounted Friday, pulling the S&P 500 10% below its record high set last month, as the sell-off for AI stocks accelerated and the market headed for a sharp weekly loss.

The S&P 500 index fell 2.8%. If it closes down more than 10% from its Oct. 6 high, it will have entered what professional investors call a “correction.” The benchmark index is on track for a seventh straight day of losses, which would mark the longest such streak since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.

The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 4.2%, dropping it into the red for the year. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 549 points, or 1.1%, as of 2:46 p.m. Eastern time.
The technology sell-off spread around the globe: Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well.

AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.

AI stocks have been losing ground partly over worries that their big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level.

“The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that’s what’s being priced right now,” said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. "But I don’t think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over.”
Chip stocks, big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centers, led the way lower. Advanced Micro Devices dropped 12.6% and Broadcom fell 12.1%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 9.2%.

Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, is falling for the ninth day in the last 10, down 10.6%. The chip company's stock was caught up in the market's anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25%.

The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled on Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.3% to $88.14. It is still above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value.

As of early afternoon trading on Friday, Anthropic’s stock had fallen about 23% from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That’s an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO.

Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later.
While the stock market’s mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year.

The University of Michigan's latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists' expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran.
Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills jumped 4.4% and homebuilder Lennar rose 2.5%.
Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.91% from 5.04% late Thursday.

Brent crude oil, the international standard, dipped 0.1% to $92.10 per barrel, despite continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.
AP Business Writers Yuri Kageyama and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

title: House to debate slightly tweaked version of Protect College Sports Act
summary: The House of Representatives will soon consider a slightly tweaked version of a bill already passed in the Senate that needs to be signed by the end of the year to become law
story: The House of Representatives will soon consider a slightly tweaked version of a bill already passed in the Senate that needs to be signed by the end of the year to become law
The House of Representatives will soon consider a slightly tweaked version of a bill already passed in the Senate that needs to be signed by the end of the year to become law.

One key change in the House version of the Protect College Sports Act released Friday would allow conferences to expand to as many as 22 teams — two more than allowed in the Senate version. The bigger number appears designed to cater to teams in Florida and the Carolinas that play in the Atlantic Coast Conference.
The House version would also forbid schools with $50 million or more in media-rights revenue from using student fees to subsidize sports.
The NCAA sent a letter to members pushing them to advocate for the bill, which it said could start to be considered as soon as Nov. 30.
“Given the short time period, it is imperative member schools contact their representatives as soon as possible,” the letter said.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Republican colleagues Tim Walberg and Brett Guthrie released a statement saying, “Congress needs to pass strong antitrust protections to end the Wild West atmosphere that exists today.”
In a news conference, President Donald Trump reiterated his support for the bill, saying without it, “you’re going to have these colleges all go bankrupt.”
The bill, which among other things locks in rules that regulate how athletes are paid and builds in protections for Olympic sports, passed the Senate 77-22 last month.

But it faces a tougher road in the House where Democrats have expressed several concerns, including over athletes' rights in the face of the bill's proposed antitrust exemption. That exemption would prevent many lawsuits, including those over eligibility, the likes of which have been streaming through courts around the country since the start of this school year.
See AP’s full sports coverage here

title: A decade after shooting Harambe, the Cincinnati Zoo is reeling from Fiona's death
summary: The Cincinnati Zoo is once again facing the tragic death of a beloved animal
story: The Cincinnati Zoo is once again facing the tragic death of a beloved animal

CINCINNATI -- Months of international backlash cast a shadow over the Cincinnati Zoo after workers decided to fatally shoot a beloved endangered gorilla named Harambe in response to a little boy falling into his exhibit in 2016.

That outrage faded the following year with the premature birth of an adorable hippo named Fiona, this time bringing positive attention to the reeling zoo, which shared her miraculous survival story in videos and blog posts. They showed her taking a bottle, splashing in a pool and learning to run. She captured hearts around the world and helped restore the zoo’s image.
Now, though, the zoo is dealing with another tragedy: Fiona died Thursday more than a week after eating a visitor’s hat.
“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome,” the zoo said.

Fiona's death at age 9 led to an outpouring of grief as well as comparisons to the end of Harambe's life, as both were untimely and involved zoo visitors. Some social media users were quick to condemn the zoo, saying it needs to better protect its animals. Others called for compassion.

“As devastated as we are, we cannot begin to fathom the grief that Fiona’s keepers, veterinary team, and the entire Cincinnati Zoo family are experiencing today,” Dino Buddies, a local wildlife outreach company, said in a statement. “We hope that everyone extends these incredible individuals the compassion, kindness, and grace they deserve as they mourn the loss of an animal they loved so deeply.”

After Harambe was killed at age 17, the zoo reopened its gorilla exhibit with a higher, reinforced barrier. Tongue-in-cheek online petitions circulated seeking to add his face to Mount Rushmore and the dollar bill. There was also a more somber “Justice for Harambe” petition that sought to hold the mother of the boy who fell into the enclosure responsible for the gorilla's death. The county prosecutor determined there was no cause for charges.

Fiona swallowed the hat about 12 days ago after a zoo visitor tossed it in the air, it struck a ceiling fan and deflected into the hippo enclosure through a small opening above the viewing windows. It was an accident, a zoo spokesperson said.

She was not the first zoo animal to die from eating a non-food item that found its way into a pen. Zoos around the world have been warning for years about the dangers posed by objects that are tossed or blown into animal habitats.

Two years ago, a rare antelope choked to death after eating the plastic lid from a squeezable fruit pouch at a zoo in Tennessee. A polar bear at a German zoo died in 2014 after swallowing a jacket dropped into his enclosure by a visitor.
But the accidental nature of Fiona's death hasn't dampened the despair.
“The two saddest days in all my time here in Cincinnati come from the Zoo,” Facebook user Marianne King posted Thursday. The first was Harambe's death and the second was Fiona's, she said.

Joanne Prater, who lives in the Cincinnati suburb of Loveland, was attending a high school fundraiser Thursday evening and said every person she spoke to talked about how sad they were about Fiona's death and compared it to Harambe's.

“They are tokens of Cincinnati. You can’t say Fiona or Harambe without everybody knowing who that is here in Cincinnati," she said. "I guess both of their deaths could have been prevented, but unfortunately accidents do happen.”

title: ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ sets record with $3.79B in first-day retail sales, Rockstar Games reports
summary: Rockstar Games announces that “Grand Theft Auto VI” has generated a record $3.79 billion in first-day retail sales
story: Rockstar Games announces that “Grand Theft Auto VI” has generated a record $3.79 billion in first-day retail sales

NEW YORK -- Sales of “Grand Theft Auto VI” generated a record with $3.79 billion in first-day retail sales, maker Rockstar Games said Friday, underscoring the enormous demand for the first new installment in the blockbuster series in 13 years.

The worldwide figure was based on company estimates through the end of the day Thursday, the day the game launched. Rockstar also said in a release that it sold 32.5 million units prerelease, setting a record across platforms.

“We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you,” Sam Houser, Rockstar’s president and founder, said in a release.
The launch far eclipsed that of its predecessor.

“Grand Theft Auto V,” released in 2013, generated $1 billion in retail sales in its first three days. It went on to become one of the bestselling video games of all time, accounting for more than 230 million of the franchise's more than 470 million units sold globally, according to publisher Take-Two Interactive.

Earlier Friday, market research firm Sensor Tower estimated “GTA VI” had generated $2.36 billion in revenue on approximately 24.6 million units sold. Rockstar's figures, released later in the day, were based on the company's own estimates of worldwide, day-one retail sales.
The standard edition of the game retails for around $80 in the U.S.

Earlier this month, the PlayStation blog said that “GTA VI” was the most preordered game in the history of its namesake store. Due to the demand, PlayStation said that it was teaming with Rockstar Games to allow players to start preloading the game nine days early, so that they'd be ready to play on launch day.

“GTA VI” is the latest installment in the hyperviolent, open-world video game series that has skewered American culture with fictionalized versions of New York and Los Angeles and is now returning to its sun-baked version of Miami — Vice City.

It's the first new “GTA” game in 13 years, with the story of “GTA VI” centered on Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple trying to improve their circumstances through crime across the fictional state of Leonida.
Early reviews for the game have noted a greater emphasis on relationship building that goes beyond the violent stickups, bank robberies and mayhem that have long defined the franchise.

The game's release also ended years of secrecy around its cast. Manni L. Perez plays Lucia and Dylan Rourke portrays Jason, while Bobby Moynihan, Stephen Root, Taryn Manning, Roselyn Sanchez and rapper Denzel Curry are among the familiar names in Rockstar’s sprawling credits.
The enormous launch comes after more than a decade of anticipation around a series that has become one of the biggest properties in entertainment. ___
This story has been corrected to show that Sensor Tower on Friday estimated “GTA VI” had generated $2.36 billion in revenue, not $2.36 million.
Jonathan Landrum Jr. is an Entertainment Writer reporting from Los Angeles.

title: US senator says Pentagon restrictions on Canada focus on think tanks and social events
summary: A Republican senator says Pentagon restrictions on Canada largely target U.S. military officials’ participation in think tank events and social engagements rather than military operations or intelligence sharing
story: A Republican senator says Pentagon restrictions on Canada largely target U.S. military officials’ participation in think tank events and social engagements rather than military operations or intelligence sharing

HALIFAX, Nova Scotia -- Pentagon restrictions on Canada largely target U.S. military officials’ participation in think tank events and social engagements rather than military operations or intelligence sharing, a Republican senator said Saturday, as Canada’s defense minister described military cooperation as “business as usual.”

The Washington Post reported Friday that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth circulated a classified memorandum last week imposing new restrictions on military cooperation with Canada. The report comes as U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and repeated threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state have strained relations between the longtime allies.

The Trump administration had already barred Pentagon officials from attending the Halifax International Security Forum under restrictions imposed in 2025 on participation in think tank events. Previous Republican and Democratic administrations sent senior U.S. military officials, including defense secretaries.
Republican Sen. Mike Rounds said the latest guidance appeared consistent with existing practices and was not expected to affect joint military operations or intelligence sharing.
Speaking at the Halifax International Security Forum, Rounds said his assessment was based on information from the delegation’s Pentagon liaison.
“They’re basically limiting some social engagements, and they’re asking people to get permission before they come in and do think tanks and so forth,” he said.
“We don’t expect any real changes over the way it has been going for the last year or a year and a half,” he said.
Rounds said the disclosure was unfortunate as Washington sought to reassure Canada and other allies of its commitment to longstanding security relationships.
Canadian Defense Minister David McGuinty said he had not seen the document and had detected no change in military cooperation.
“I’ve seen no evidence of any kind of change. I’ve heard about the existence of a document. I’ve not seen the document,” McGuinty told reporters.

He cited Canadian vessels working alongside American ships to intercept drug trafficking in the Caribbean. “So that cooperation remains ongoing. And as far as we’re concerned, it’s business as usual,” he said.
Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine called the directive’s tone “bad” and “unnecessary,” while Sen. Chris Coons said it risked worsening relations with a close ally.
“The United States should be doing nothing to further aggravate some of the distance and division between the United States and Canada,” Coons said.

title: A California billionaire tax proposal faced a major setback despite big wins for progressives
summary: A first-in-the-nation effort to pass a billionaire tax in California faced a major setback when voters rejected the measure and passed a policymaking it much harder to enact such a tax in the future
story: A first-in-the-nation effort to pass a billionaire tax in California faced a major setback when voters rejected the measure and passed a policymaking it much harder to enact such a tax in the future

SACRAMENTO, Calif. -- In an election with major wins for Democrats and progressives nationwide, California voters not only rejected the biggest test yet for a state wealth tax, they also approved a measure making it much harder to enact one in the future.

Proposition 40 would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion, with most of the money dedicated to healthcare. Just more than half — 52% — of voters rejected it. Meanwhile, they narrowly approved Proposition 42, which bans the state from enacting future taxes on people’s financial assets. State lawmakers can't override that; it can only be undone by voters with a future ballot measure.

“I don’t think you’re going to see such a good Democratic electorate in the near future,” said Wesley Hussey, a political science professor at California State University, Sacramento. “This was the time to pass something that was pretty lefty and progressive and had a lot of opposition.”

Nationally it was a good year for so-called “tax the rich” measures in other states, including Washington, where voters upheld a 9.9% tax on household income over $1 million. But California's measure was different because it would have taxed the assets, not the income, of the ultrarich.

And it targeted billionaires, who are significantly wealthier than millionaires and have far more assets to spend. A committee that opposed Proposition 40 and backed Proposition 42 raised more than $333 million, including large donations from tech billionaires such as Google co-founder Sergey Brin and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. Collectively, the fight over taxing billionaires was one of the most expensive ballot battles in state history.

Outside observers say the fact that it failed in California, a heavily Democratic state often viewed as a liberal leader, is not surprising because of the sheer amount of money spent opposing it and the big-name Democrats who lined up against it. Gov. Gavin Newsom was among those warning it was a bad financial deal for the state. Opponents outspent supporters by 10 to 1.

But proponents of the wealth tax, which included SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna, are trying to frame the loss as progress toward holding billionaires accountable in the future. They have teased bringing the idea before voters again in 2028.
“The game is up, people have had it and this election is just the beginning,” Khanna said on election night.

Faced with pushback from Newsom, SEIU UHW offered to scale back its proposal in June just before it qualified for the ballot. The union proposed a 2% levy, down from 5%, but Newsom's office said the proposed tax remained fundamentally flawed. Efforts to make a deal fell apart, and the union proceeded despite a growing coalition of groups opposing the tax.

Opponents of the tax said its failure affirmed that voters understood the risks associated with it. They warned it would have driven billionaires and their tax money out of state, causing budget problems down the road. California relies heavily on the rich for its income tax revenue.

“We were hopefully optimistic based on the polls that voters would agree with us that Prop. 40 was just a horrible idea for the state and Prop. 42 provides some important protections going forward," said David Kline, a spokesperson for the California Taxpayers Association.

California voters didn’t completely repudiate the concept of taxing the wealthy at higher rates in this year’s election. They approved a measure to indefinitely extend a tax increase on individual incomes exceeding $371,000 to raise money for education.

Besides Washington, Colorado voters adopted a graduated income tax that imposes higher rates on people with higher income, including an 8.4% tax on income over $1 million. The revenue from both states' taxes will go toward education, healthcare and other services. Spending on the Washington and Colorado measures paled in comparison to the billionaire tax battle. Legislatures in Hawaii, Maine and Rhode Island also approved new taxes this year on people with incomes over $1 million.
California has a 1% income tax on millionaires that voters approved in 2004 to raise money for mental health services.

Carl Davis, research director at the nonprofit Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, said the results indicated “a really good batting average” for backers of higher taxes for the wealthy. California's billionaire tax effort was hurt by divisions among organized labor over the measure, he said.
“I think the pendulum is swinging toward increased interest in taxing the rich,” he said.

Advocates for higher taxes on the wealthy plan to expand their push next year in a half-dozen states where Democrats recently won control of both legislative chambers and the governor's office, said Amber Wallin, executive director of the State Revenue Alliance, a nonprofit advocacy group for progressive tax policies.
“I think that the movement will only continue to grow,” Wallin said.

California's Proposition 42 bans new taxes on people's financial assets, business interests and intellectual property, as well as taxes that apply retroactively. The billionaire tax, for instance, would have applied to people living in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026, even though it would have taken effect the following year. That will now be prohibited.

California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who will take over from Newsom in January, opposed the billionaire tax. But he said recently that the amount of support it received sent “a clear signal” that people “don’t believe everybody in California is paying their fair share.” He said he wanted to correct that but didn’t specify how.

Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions, which supported Proposition 40, said opposition from groups like the California Teachers Association and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California made it harder to pass the measure than if supporters had been fighting billionaires alone.
But she said this year’s ballot fight was just the start.
“We have to go back to the ballot,” Gonzalez said. “We’ve got to keep fighting.”
Associated Press writer David A. Lieb in Jefferson City, Missouri, contributed.

title: Senate approves bill to speed up permitting reviews, force data centers to pay for energy costs
summary: The Senate has approved bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower...
story: The Senate has approved bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower...

WASHINGTON -- The Senate approved bipartisan legislation Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices.

The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.

The 62-33 vote is the first major action by Congress since midterm elections that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans. The bill now goes to the House, which approved a more limited, industry-friendly version last year.

The Senate bill would overhaul several environmental laws to make it easier to build energy infrastructure, drawing criticism from Democrats and environmental groups about limits on judicial review and changes to bedrock laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act.

Trump urged approval of the bill, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” in a recent social media post. The bill, formally known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, will ensure the U.S. can build pipelines, mines and power plants more quickly, “lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote.
Fifteen Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, voted for the bill. Two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, voted no.

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and the oil and gas sector support the bill as a way to deliver more electricity to the grid and avoid delays for infrastructure projects that can stretch a decade or more.

However, many environmental organizations have denounced the measure, saying it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

“Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centers, oil and gas pipelines and (liquefied natural gas) terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the U.S.,” said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project.

Benefits for renewable energy are outweighed by likely increases in greenhouse gas emissions and air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry, Duggan and other critics said. She called the bill “a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America” and complained that it was being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without public hearings or sufficient debate.
A final vote on the measure was held up this week as Oregon's two Democratic senators pushed to add amendments, including one to ban data centers on public lands.
