title: Transcript: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 22, 2026
summary: The following is the transcript of the interview with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 22, 2026.
story: The following is the transcript of the interview with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 22, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We begin with the Secretary of the Treasury, Scott Bessent. It's good to have you here and in person, sir.
U.S. TREASURY SECRETARY SCOTT BESSENT: Margaret, good to see you.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So there were thousands of customers across America who, when they went to some of the biggest banks, had issues this past week with tech outages, and it caused a bit of a panic with people pulling out cash. In this age of AI, what should Americans be prepared for, and should they worry about their financial institutions?

SEC. BESSENT: It's a good good question, Margaret. And no, they shouldn't. The banks have been at the forefront of cybersecurity for decades. They experience attacks every day, every week, every month, and they are by far the most resilient companies in the U.S. economy. What we are seeing as they, because of the SI, as they go into patch their security systems, the patches may cause a glitch, which is what happened last week. J.P. Morgan went in, and I think the American people should think of it as a vaccine. Your arm may hurt, you may feel a little bad the next day, but it increases your long-term immunity and resiliency.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay. Well, there's other concerns about AI, as you know, and we've seen in the stock market anxiety, a real sell-off over the past week. Nvidia is sometimes referred to as the central bank of AI, since it uses its cash to finance things like data centers and essentially boost demand for its own sales. We have a graphic there, sort of showing the gist of that. I mean, when you look at its size and how interwoven it is in the tech industry. Do you worry that this kind of circular financing means that one company is becoming so hugely important that it could have ripple effects if something goes wrong?

SEC. BESSENT: Well, look, Nvidia is one of our great companies with the management chains. The board has slowed things down. The CFO is now in charge, so you know, I believe that she understands the financing quite well. And no, as Nvidia continues to be fantastically profitable, and there is near unlimited demand for their chips worldwide.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Do you—how do you understand what happened in the markets this past week?

SEC. BESSENT: Well, I think it's a combination of things. You know, we could see that the market sell-off actually began as the Democrats moved ahead in the polls and then accelerated after Election Day. The Democratic position on the SI buildout has spooked a lot of investors in terms of slowing it down. We've also seen some very hawkish remarks from the Federal Reserve. Many people believe that they may be making a policy mistake if they over-tighten. We've seen a substantial tightening in financial conditions over the past few months. So, you know, I think it was a combination of these things.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, President Trump gave that 90-minute or so press conference on Friday, and he did talk about things in AI. Among many things, he said, take a listen to this.
[START SOUND ON TAPE]

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen, and we're going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.
[END SOUND ON TAPE]
MARGARET BRENNAN: How is that policy going to work, and won't that also inhibit the sector?

SEC. BESSENT: Well, I haven't spoken to the president about that. I was sitting in that press conference, and I didn't get a chance to speak to him after that. But look, I think the president's very concerned that we don't do a big technology transfer offshore. What we've seen, that the U.S. used to be the leader in the chip industry, and now we see that 97% of the high-end chips are made in Taiwan, which creates a strategic vulnerability.
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's been the case.

SEC. BESSENT: Well, this administration is working to bring them back. There are large fabs being built by TSMC in Arizona, and we hope to have substantial onshoring of the chip business by the end of this administration. So, I think he's worried about the same thing happening with data centers.

MARGARET BRENNAN: With data centers, so one of the arguments against this, and the Wall Street Journal editorial board was pointing out a challenge here, is that if American companies can't build data centers and their AI models close to the markets they're trying to sell into, it will basically give their competitors, the Chinese, an edge.

SEC. BESSENT: Well, look, I think that the SI is very fungible. That companies access U.S. centers. There are many centers in Southeast Asia. They get access from around the world. So I think the real thing here is going to be, and I've said it many times before the election. The industry has done a terrible job of explaining themselves to the American people, and I think they need to have a conversation with the American people, with the communities where these centers are built, and rebuild public trust. And I think once we see that, then we could see a more substantial build out here in the U.S.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, so what the president announced was not reversing, for example, what the U.S. was encouraging in the United Arab Emirates with these data centers being built in some of our Gulf allies.
SEC. BESSENT: No, he's talking about American companies doing it.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, let me ask you about Nvidia in particular and what's been happening in terms of the ongoing revelations. Multiple congressional committees, federal prosecutors, and presumably regulators here in the United States are probing the role Nvidia played in sending advanced AI computer chips to China. On Fox last Sunday, I watched your interview. It was pretty extraordinary. You did not parse words. You referred to a culture of non-compliance at Nvidia. The possibility that they were quote "pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings." You said you needed answers to what was going on within 10 days. That was seven days ago. Have you gotten the answers you need?

SEC. BESSENT: We don't, Margaret. And I think the important word there is possibility. And we have seen. We've been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers, and we do need answers. And back to your question about the centrality of Nvidia to the SI system, it behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was. Was there promiscuous attitude toward this, and where—if it happened—where were the faults, and then they can move on.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So when you say we, you mean to Treasury? You're expecting those answers to go to Treasury, or they're expecting to go to the White House?
SEC. BESSENT: To the administration.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Because there was a lot of reporting that Nvidia's business deals were often based on handshakes. That doesn't leave a lot of a paper trail. How challenging is this for regulators to get to the bottom of what the CEO was doing? I know you said the CFO is at the helm, but last Sunday you said basically they need to clean up shop and get someone from the outside to run the place.

SEC. BESSENT: Well, what I said was we do need to see who was in charge of compliance there. Normally, it's the legal department, the general counsel's office. So we'll see what they have to say. But you know, in terms of handshake deals, for deals that size, there's no such thing as an untraceable handshake deal, there are bills blading that movement. There are money movements, so you know, they may not be the 100-page documents, but there, it will be possible to understand what has gone on here.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I mean, that's an extraordinary charge though, a culture of non-compliance.
SEC. BESSENT: Well--
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's not just the foibles of one man.
SEC. BESSENT: Well, again, I said the possibility.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SEC. BESSENT: So we will see, and that's why I think the board is moving very quickly to establish whether this did or did not exist.

MARGARET BRENNAN: The president of the United States said Jensen Huang should get his job back. You said the board of directors needs to go to the outside. Does the president understand the national security risk and the regulatory risk that you're pinpointing here?
SEC. BESSENT: Well, Jensen is on the outside now, so you know.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I know the president said he should come back.

SEC. BESSENT: Well, I said they should go to the outside, but he's on the outside now. But I think what we need to see, because the other thing I said was we will see which level of the business knew about this. Was it at the lower levels? Was it the middle levels? Did it go all the way to the top? And I have confidence that the Nvidia committees are moving very quickly on this and will come up with some very fulsome and robust answers.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I understand Mr. Huang is no longer at the helm, but are you saying that you think it would be a good idea for him to go back and run the company?
SEC. BESSENT: I think we have to see where the buck stops. You know, what were these malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for the non-compliance.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, so you see that as almost separate and apart from the relationship with Alice Huang, who's reportedly linked to Chinese security?
SEC. BESSENT: Yeah, I think that is kind of a canard that the, you know, was their culture of compliance versus the one person's foibles
MARGARET BRENNAN: With a Chinese spy, allegedly.
SEC. BESSENT: Well, I assume he didn't know that she was an alleged spy.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Senator Tom Cotton, the Republican chair of the Intelligence Committee, told the Journal about his frustrations with Commerce Secretary Lutnick, ignoring what he said were repeated letters and information from him about Megaspeed, the company that Alice Huang was running, which is at the heart of this. Cotton said he's glad that the Trump administration is finally coming around, but we need to catalog the damage. What damage has been done? Do you know?
SEC. BESSENT: Well, again, we will see if Megaspeed was indeed a pass-through company, a front company based in Singapore, to get the high-end chips to Chinese entities.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, should it be blacklisted while that's under consideration?
SEC. BESSENT: Well, Nvidia actually took them off their vendor list or sales list in August of '25, so they wouldn't have gotten any chips since then.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Should it be blacklisted in the meantime?

SEC. BESSENT: We at Treasury and several other departments have pushed for it. I think the important thing was last week we did something called the connected, or the remote access rule, which prevents certain countries, certain entities from accessing chips via lease capacity, which I actually think may be more important.
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil. You're trying to tighten the licensing there.
SEC. BESSENT: Yes.

MARGARET BRENNNAN: But in the meantime, it was pretty extraordinary to have the Republican chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee release publicly documents showing that the Commerce Department had approved the sale of more than 800,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips to China. The approvals included two companies highlighted here as known to be linked to the Chinese military. I know there's a threshold set on the type of chips, but is any sale to the Chinese military really advisable?
SEC. BESSENT: The president's been very clear that the H- and drawn a very hard line at the--
[CROSSTALK]
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah, the H200s.

SEC. BESSENT: The H200s. So I think, and you know, these are companies, I think one of them is Alibaba, which is in general social media and online platform. So I think once you draw the threshold, then I don't know if you have to differentiate.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So some sales to the Chinese military are okay.
SEC. BESSENT: Well, again, this isn't Chinese military. These are companies that do business with the Chinese military.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Understood. And there's a very, very thin line there, but Secretary Bessent, I appreciate your time today. Face the Nation will be back in a minute. Stay with us.

title: Home-cooked meals, to go
summary: In California, more than 1,300 small kitchens are licensed to make and sell food. These MEHKOs (short for "micro enterprise home kitchen operations") are run out of homes, allowing home chefs to turn family recipes into culinary passion projects.
story: If you're looking for some of the most sought-after, fresh-baked buns in Los Angeles, you better get to Sofia Draco's house early. Every other Sunday, Draco lowers baskets full of fresh-baked pastries from her kitchen window to a line of customers who've ordered from her website, all made by hand in her 55-square-foot kitchen.

This home operation, which she calls Bun Bun, is one of more than 1,300 small kitchens licensed to make and sell food in California. They're called MEHKOs – short for "micro enterprise home kitchen operations," emphasis on the micro.

Draco's kitchen features two tiny ovens from which she bakes everything. "I've always baked from, like, the day I was born pretty much," she said. "My grandma has been, like, my inspiration when it comes to hosting and cooking."

Since moving to L.A. from her native Sweden. Draco has played music, and worked in home design, which comes in handy for running a MEHKO out of her living room, which converts into a Bun Bun staging area when her custom-made sofa comes apart like the leaves of a dining room table.
Draco says starting small is what's made all of this possible. "I can take a little idea and just like make it happen out of my house without having to spend $150,000," she said.
Recipe: Hastkaka ("Speed Cake") (from Sofia Draco's Bun Bun Bakery)
Recipe: Hastkaka ("Speed Cake") (from Sofia Draco's Bun Bun Bakery)

Roya Bagheri runs Cook Alliance, a group that helped pass California's bill legalizing home kitchens in 2018. She said, "We see a lot of immigrants, a lot of women, people of color, a lot of people who just want to share family recipes that have been passed down for generations."

MEHKOs get inspected, and they need to clear menu items with the health department, as well as abide by caps on their businesses: No more than 30 meals per day, and no more than $100,000 in gross sales over the year.
When Adreana Obienu's grandson, Deuce, was on the way, she wanted to be at home so she could spend time with him. So, Obienu retired after 30 years working for the phone company.

Last year, she and her daughters, Charmaine and Patrice, opened Village Gate Kitchen in her Nigerian husband's converted home office. Obienu developed the menu based on what she cooked at home regularly. The hallmarks of Nigerian food, said Patrice, are the spices, and tons of flavors.
Charmaine said, "When I was pregnant, I would call like every other week: 'Mom, can you please make me a pot of egussi?' And egussi soup is, like, the most popular thing on her menu now."

For Obienu and her daughters, Village Gate is about much more than making money. It's a family affair, allowing Obienu to also spend time with her grandson: "Absolutely, and it was great to be there when he came into the world," she said.
And with her daughters helping out with the business, it has come full circle.

"Because no matter what, she retired for my baby," said Charmaine. "So that's why, as soon as she's like, 'I wanna do this,' I'm like, 'Come on, let's do it for you!' 'Cause that's my mom for all of us, and that's what she puts into her cooking, that love."

title: Taking on credit card debt to buy food
summary: According to a recent survey, about 35% of Americans are using credit cards to buy increasingly expensive groceries – and many are having trouble paying off that food debt.
story: Those beeps at the checkout counter aren't music to anyone's ears these days. Each one is an ear-piercing reminder of how just much more we're paying for groceries this Thanksgiving – 32% more, to be exact – than we paid in 2020, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. One mother shopping with her daughter told us, "Feels like all my money goes to food."

The USDA doesn't report food insecurity figures like they used to; that survey was discontinued last year. What we do know is, in 2024 nearly 14% of Americans said they were struggling to eat, making this Thanksgiving yet another exercise in the art of the possible.

First, consumers are changing where we shop. Discount grocery chains like Aldi, Lidl, and Food 4 Less are reporting greater and greater market shares, giving traditional supermarkets, like Kroger, a real run for their money.

David Rinaldo, chief operating officer at Aldi, says there used to be a stigma around discount stores. Now, Aldi is on track to open 150 stores this year alone. "I never would have dreamed we'd ever get to the point that it would be that mainstream, that people would come to a limited assortment discount grocer to be where they shop," Rinaldo said.

Part of the draw? Cheaper in-house brands, contracted out to manufacturers that make them for stores like Aldi and others – assembly lines tailored to a specific market. They aren't the no-name generic brands you might remember from the 1970s and '80's.  These are different. It's what fills 92% of what's on Aldi's shelves.

Private labels, says Rinaldo, aren't the exception; they're now the trend.  "I think there's been a movement with private label," he said. "Nine out of the last ten years, private label has grown faster than national brands."

But it's not just where American are buying groceries; it's how they're paying for them that is changing. According to a recent survey by the Urban Institute in Washington, D.C., about 35% of us are using credit cards to buy groceries. But unlike past years, 1 in 4 customers is having trouble paying off that food debt.

"That's a substantial share of families that are needing to turn to credit to purchase their groceries, and then taking on debt in the process of doing so," said Cassandra Martinchek, a senior researcher associate at the Urban Institute. She says it's not just credit cards we should be concerned about – it's digital lay-away services (like Klarna, Splitit, Affirm, Sezzle and Zip) that people are increasingly using to buy food.

They're called BNPL, or Buy Now Pay Later apps, that often charge little to no interest. According to the same survey, 1 in 10 is using them to buy groceries, but more than a third of those shoppers also missed a payment.
Martinchek said, "This strategy can help them meet their needs right now, but it could be consequential for their future financial stability and also mobility."

Jordan Williams is mom to two-year-old Micah, and fiancée to Julian Morgan. She was using a Buy Now Pay Later app for her groceries before she got engaged, but as a single mom she fell behind.  "It felt a bit like a rat race for a little while, like I couldn't keep up," she said.

Williams stressed to be on a rotating line of credit where she was always owing: "I really could never just afford to just buy the groceries I needed, because I was busy paying off the last groceries I needed," she said.

Her delinquent payment meant her account was locked. Before she could go shopping for more groceries again, she had to pay off the entire balance. "I couldn't afford $200 in groceries the first time, I can't afford $160 today, all of this, and you can't use the app anymore," Williams said. "And after 30 days, it starts to take a hit on your credit as well."

Like millions of others this Thanksgiving, Williams feels like she shouldn't be struggling to eat, least not on her salary. She has a master's degree, teaches English at the University of North Carolina at Greensboro, and has a second job as a social media influencer to boot. "If it was just like, you know, 28-year-old poor money management issues, that's one thing," she said. "But if this is what it looks like for me, what does that look like for everybody else?"
The answer? Not all that great. Unlike the price of gas, which is finally starting to come down, for now, the price of groceries hasn't.
And Williams feels it at the end of the month: "I'm like, okay, payday is on the 28th. If it's like the 24th, we are stretching to get by," she said.
She is planning to do a potluck-style Thanksgiving this year – it seems, few can afford feeding family, extended family, and friends of family as well without everyone pitching in.

If there IS something to be thankful for, the increase in grocery prices is expected to slow by next Thanksgiving. But even so, that Norman Rockwell image of the holiday is still for so many more the ideal than reality.

title: Trump vows to work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates
summary: President Trump says he will work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates.
story: President Trump said he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates, hoping to fulfill a promise he made on the 2024 campaign trail but couldn't deliver on because of industry pressure and a lack of interest from his fellow Republicans.
"I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot," Trump told Fox News Channel's "Saturday in America."

Democrats and the Republican president have both backed capping credit card interest rates, with the standard proposal being capping rates at 10%. It would substantially reduce what credit card companies can charge customers. The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve.
With rates at 10%, a cardholder with a $5,000 balance would pay about $42 per month in interest. At the current average rate of 22%, they would owe about $100 per month.

Mr. Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates in January, as part of the White House's affordability push. Banks and credit card companies immediately and aggressively opposed the proposal, saying any interest rate cap would force them to cancel cards for the poor and less creditworthy customers or substantially cut back on the rewards they offer when customers spend on their cards.
The proposal also did not sit well with Republicans, and there was little effort by the GOP-controlled Congress to fulfill Mr. Trump's promise.

That could change now that Democrats will control both the House and Senate. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who is expected to be the next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has said repeatedly she wants to cap rates.

In response to the Fox News interview, Warren said: "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money." Warren told CBS News in January 2026 that she believes Congress could work with Mr. Trump to cap rates.

Researchers who studied Mr. Trump's campaign pledge after it was first announced found that Americans would save roughly $100 billion in interest a year if credit card rates were capped at 10%. The same researchers found that while the credit card industry would take a major hit, it would still be profitable, although credit card rewards and other perks might be scaled back.
About 195 million people in the United States had credit cards in 2024 and were assessed $160 billion in interest charges, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says.
Americans are now carrying more credit card debt than ever, to the tune of about $1.23 trillion, according to figures from the New York Federal Reserve for the third quarter last year.

title: Stocks enter correction territory, driven by deepening tech rout
summary: The tech-heavy Nasdaq tumbled more than 1,200 points, putting it on track for its second-worst day of the year.
story: Technology stocks plunged on Friday, dimming investor cheer over Anthropic's high-profile IPO this week amid mounting concerns about the health of the artificial intelligence sector.

The Nasdaq Composite Index fell 1,261 points, or 5.3%, to close at 22,618, the tech-heavy index's second-worst day of 2026 and erasing all of its gains for the year. The S&P 500 declined 3.7%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.9%.

Both the  S&P 500 and Dow entered "correction" territory, meaning the indexes have fallen more than 10% from their most recent highs. The S&P 500 is set for its seventh consecutive day of losses, its longest losing streak since February 2020, when the pandemic caused investors to sell in a panic.

Investors are fretting over the value of AI stocks, which drove much of Wall Street's gains earlier this year but are now driving the slide. Microchip companies like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom led Friday's losses over concerns about a possible slowdown in data center construction and over tighter federal policies on exporting chips outside the U.S.

"The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. "But I don't think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over."

The S&P 500's decline into correction territory was largely driven by investors selling AI-related companies, but the underlying U.S. economic and business fundamentals remain solid, said Chris Larkin, managing director of trading and investing at E*TRADE from Morgan Stanley, in an email.

"It's impossible to know when any selloff will run its course, but history shows most moves like this don't turn into bear markets —only five of the past 15 corrections from all-time highs since 1983 have done so," he said, referring to when stocks decline 20% or more from the market's most recent peak.
Anthropic can't buck the market

Thursday's big market debut for Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI chatbot, fizzled on Friday, along with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.3% to $88.14, although it remains above its IPO price of $83 per share.

As of early afternoon trading on Friday, Anthropic's stock had fallen about 23% from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That's an even bigger drop than the dive Facebook (now Meta) saw shortly after its May 2012 IPO.
Shares of Nvidia, considered practically synonymous with the AI boom, are falling for the ninth day in the last 10, down 13% in late Friday trading.

The chip company's stock was caught up in the market's anxiety about the strength of the AI buildout, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its co-founder and former CEO. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has shed more than 25% of its value.
Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills jumped 4.4%, and homebuilder Lennar rose 2.5%.

title: 6 reasons stocks are falling, and what you should do about it
summary: The S&P 500 is on track for a seventh consecutive day of losses, marking its longest losing streak since February 2020. Here's what's taking the shine off stocks.
story: The stock market is having its roughest patch since the early days of the pandemic.

Stocks renewed their slide on Friday after tumbling the previous day, with the S&P 500 racking up a seventh consecutive day of losses. The Nasdaq Composite Index fell 1,261 points, or 5.3%, to close at 22,618, the tech-heavy index's second-worst day of 2026 and erasing all of its gains for the year. The S&P 500 declined 3.7%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.9%.
Here are six factors souring investors' mood, and what experts say you should do about it.
Fears that AI investments might not pay off

Investors are increasingly concerned that the enormous spending on data centers and other infrastructure needed to power artificial intelligence may not deliver the hoped-for returns. Anthropic, the first AI lab to go public, has shown rapid revenue growth, but its regulatory filings also point to massive losses — about $104 billion for the first nine months of 2026 alone.

"Those figures explain both the frenzy and the nerves," said Nigel Green, CEO of deVere Group, an investment advisory group. "From here, the market will judge whether the software layer can turn breathtaking growth into lasting profit, and Friday's wobble shows the judging has already begun."
Anti-data center laws could take root

With Democrats set to gain the upper hand in Congress, investors are bracing for new laws that could restrict data center construction when newly elected officials take office in January. Although the shifting political winds aren't expected to halt that buildout, even a modest slowdown could impact the financial results for a range of big tech companies investing heavily in AI.
"The Blue Tidal Wave win and fears about an anti-AI/anti-data center DC" are contributing to the selloff, said Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, in a report on Friday.
The Fed raising interest rates

The Federal Reserve is expected to hike interest rates at its December meeting, as inflation remains well above the central bank's 2% annual target. Raising rates tamps down inflation, but it also makes borrowing more costly, tempering consumer spending and business investment.
"The evidence does not suggest we are on a path back to 2%" without intervention from the central bank, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago President Austan Goolsbee told reporters on Thursday.
A crackdown on chip exports

The revelation that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a spy for the People's Republic has sparked calls for stricter export rules to China. The ensuing turmoil at Nvidia, including Huang's resignation, has prompted the Commerce Department to move to restrict sales of advanced AI chips to China.
"The chip industry globally is witnessing a far larger impact from Washington's new export restrictions than initially expected," Adam Crisafulli, an analyst at Vital Knowledge, said in a report.
Fears over President Trump's saber-rattling

Israel and the U.S. are considering launching a new assault on Iran in the short term, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News. That's raising fears that new hostilities could cause a renewed spike in oil prices, adding to inflationary pressures.
"The Iran war remains in a dangerous liminal stage," Crisafulli said.
Government shutdown risks

Lawmakers face a Dec. 11 deadline to extend funding for most federal agencies and prevent a U.S. government shutdown. But there's a risk that efforts in Washington, D.C., to broker a deal could break down, as some congressional Democrats are pushing to block any funding bill that doesn't restrict funding for the Iran war.

Shutdown risks could also intensify next year under a divided government, according to Oxford Economics. The Democratic-controlled Congress could "bring bruising fights over shutdowns and the debt limit, while doing little to curb tariff, immigration and geopolitical uncertainty," analysts with the investment adviser said in a report this week.
What experts advise

Investment pros say that while it's important to stay informed, it's best not to sell stocks in a panic, as that can lead to losses that are tough to recover from. For instance, investors who sold in February 2020 may have lost out on the sharp market gains that followed as the economy recovered from the pandemic.

"We have seen so many peaks and valleys over the decades, with many investors asking us over the last few weeks, is this a March 2000 moment (pre-dot.com bubble) or Fall 2007 vibe (financial crisis buildup)," Ives wrote. "This is a painful tech sell-off that is heavily discounting [that] this 4th Industrial Revolution thesis will take place over the next few years, and that is the wrong move in our view."

title: Trump signs Common Cents Act
summary: The Common Cents Act established guidelines for businesses and consumers when conducting cash transactions.
story: President Trump on Friday signed the Common Cents Act, which lets businesses round cash transactions to the nearest nickel, into law.

It sets standards for cash transactions that businesses and consumers can use when exact change isn't available, as the penny is phased out. The legislation calls for cash transactions to be rounded up or down to the nearest 5 cents. For example, if a purchase costs $10.02 after tax and a customer is short 2 cents, the tab would round down to $10 under the act. A charge of $10.04 would round up to $10.05.
Before its passage, businesses could be sued if they failed to give customers exact change, even when rounding up in a patron's favor.
Business advocacy groups cheered its passage. NACS, which represents the convenience and fuel retailing industry, said it creates reliable guidelines for conducting cash transactions.

"Retailers have been looking for federal guidance on processing cash transactions since penny production ended," Brennan Duckett, NACS' director of regulatory and policy, said in a statement to CBS News. "NACS members benefit directly from this law, and we are pleased to see President Trump make it official with his signature."
Business owners said they faced confusion and were vulnerable to litigation before the act passed.

"As a retailer, I am grateful to have established legal guidance on rounding cash transactions," Scott Zietlow, CEO and president of Kwik Trip, said in a statement Friday. "Every cash transaction that we processed in recent months was a reminder that we needed more clarity from the federal government. We've now got that clarity."

title: Americans need help affording homes. Can Congress deliver?
summary: Lawmakers may face more pressure in 2027 to focus on bipartisan housing proposals that would lower the cost of buying a home.
story: With voters pressing for relief from high costs in the midterm elections, lawmakers may face more pressure in 2027 to focus on bipartisan housing proposals that would lower the cost of buying a home.

In recent years, rising home prices, tight inventory and high mortgage rates have locked out many would-be first-time homebuyers. Three-quarters of prospective property buyers said that financial hurdles, such as rising borrowing costs, have prevented them from buying a home this year, according to a July survey from financial services firm FICO.

Some lawmakers from both parties have already introduced bills aimed at helping Americans achieve homeownership, with the proposals focused on reducing upfront costs. The midterm elections, which flipped control of both the Senate and House to the Democrats, could give those proposals fresh momentum in 2027.
"This is kind of one of those rare pockets where everyone can agree housing is expensive — 'We got to do something,'" Kate Wood, a lending expert at NerdWallet, told CBS News.

One Democratic-led proposal would provide up to $20,000 to first-generation homebuyers and up to $25,000 to low-income households to cover down payments. Another bipartisan bill, introduced in February, would permit first-time homebuyers to funnel unused education savings toward a down payment.

Experts outside of Congress are also pitching possible solutions. Lael Brainard, who served as the director of the National Economic Council during the Biden administration, has advocated for lowering the down payment on a federal loan to $1,000, while Ted Tozer, president of Ginnie Mae under former President Obama, has argued for zero-down mortgages for certain borrowers.
Inspiration from the ROAD Act
Lawmakers are likely to want to build on the success of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a landmark bipartisan housing bill passed last year to boost housing supply and bring down costs.

Given that much of the regulatory and zoning action occurs at the state and local levels, Wood expects Congress to focus, in part, on offering incentives to local governments to encourage more construction and affordable housing, as it did with the ROAD Act.

One proposal that housing analysts are watching is the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, a bill introduced in September that focuses on permitting reform, including making it easier to receive permits for some housing developments.
"At its core, the bill is about permitting energy and infrastructure projects and getting them approved faster," said Jake Krimmel, a senior economist for Realtor.com.
The Senate voted to approve BAAJA, as it is known, earlier this week.
Political obstacles

Democrats have historically been more focused on providing direct support for first-time homebuyers and on increasing federal spending on housing programs, Dennis Shea, a housing policy expert at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said in an email to CBS News.
"Expect more substantial appropriations for housing than a Republican-controlled Congress would deliver, and more 'demand-side' initiatives like down payment assistance," Shea added.

Aside from the bill that would provide down payment assistance for first-generation and low-income homebuyers, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, a Democrat from Illinois, has proposed a new refundable tax credit of up to $25,000 for qualified first-time homebuyers, delivered in up to $5,000 chunks over five years.
Even with Democrats vowing to tackle housing affordability, however, they may be limited in what they can achieve, experts said.

Despite having a Democratic majority in the Senate and House as newly elected lawmakers are sworn in next year, President Trump could veto anything they pass. Lawmakers would need a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override a veto, which would require them to muster bipartisan support.

"Despite their significant electoral gains during the recent election, Democrats still need buy-in from the White House and at least four Republican senators to move legislation over the legislative finish line," Shea said.

title: Can Anthropic win hearts and minds by curing hearts and minds?
summary: Anthropic says Claude Science can drive breakthroughs in drug discovery. It could also open lucrative commercial opportunities, experts say.
story: Fresh off its record-setting initial public offering, Anthropic now must show investors that it can sustain growth and generate profits. The company has a plan for that: curing some of the world's gnarliest diseases.

In its IPO prospectus, Anthropic states that AI holds the potential to "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine, potentially curing diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia, including cancer, Alzheimer's disease, heart disease, rare genetic diseases, and the major infectious diseases."

Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei said in a post on X in August that he believes "it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!)."
Speeding in the right direction

Developing breakthrough drugs is among the most promising avenues of research for AI, potentially bringing treatments for a range of conditions to market much faster than is currently possible, according to scientists and industry analysts.

"AI can accelerate research. It will help you get there faster, but it's not just speed — it's directional speed," Neerav Kaushal, an AI and molecular biology expert at Michigan Technological University, told CBS News. "Let's say you're at the top of the mountain and your aim is to find a drug for cancer that lies in the valley. AI will not just help you get down there faster — it will help you get down to the right valley where the drug is."

For Anthropic, meanwhile, developing drugs could open up potentially enormous commercial opportunities. The company has partnered with biotech and pharmaceutical companies that use its Claude Science model for various purposes. Anthropic also operates its own AI-powered biology wet lab in San Francisco that has already made scientific discoveries.
"If you can use a large language model to condense any part of the timeline, it is very economically valuable," Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan told CBS News.
The challenge for Anthropic will be how it turns its life sciences research into profits. That could take time, Khan told CBS News.

"How this becomes lucrative for Anthropic is a very important question, and I think it's a question Anthropic hasn't figured out yet," Khan said. "Coding is its best-proven use case, followed by cybersecurity applications, then financial and legal research."
But the potential to move the needle for both Anthropic and its pharma partners is significant.

"If you improve your drug's efficiency by a couple of percentage points, that can make a world of difference," Khan added. "You'll get asymmetric payouts in the sense that if a model can help with any part of the process, it's very economically valuable."

For example, he expects a drug developer like Eli Lilly and Co., which partners with Anthropic to give its employees access to Claude, would be willing to pay "hundreds of millions or billions of dollars to make its arthritis drug 2% better than it is."
A way to win hearts and minds by curing them?

Developing potentially lifesaving drugs could have other benefits for Anthropic. By applying tools to the life sciences and using them to improve human life, the company could help shift the narrative around AI to a more positive one, according to experts.

"If you are the AI company that helps advance some kind of cure or solution to a sickness or illness that's prevailed for quite some time, I think that gets you a ton more trust with consumers and end users," Khan said. "Because you end up becoming the company that is actually improving the quality of life for humans at large."

title: Musk said he'd "look into" this disclosure law. Now it heads to court.
summary: Two county prosecutors say the Trump administration broke the law when it exempted U.S. companies from ownership reporting.
story: In March 2025, a conservative comedian named Terrence K. Williams had a plea for Elon Musk: ask President Trump to scrap a "ridiculous" federal rule that forced companies to disclose their true owners.
"I'm begging you!" Williams posted on X, Musk's social media platform. "It's targeting conservatives and small businesses!"
The billionaire replied, "I can look into it."

A day later, the Trump administration took action. In a post on X, the Treasury Department announced it would no longer enforce penalties or fines against U.S. citizens, domestic companies or their owners under the law, known as the Corporate Transparency Act.
Now, two local prosecutors are suing to stop the administration from erasing roughly 15 million company ownership records it has already collected, CBS News has learned.

On Thursday, the top prosecutors in Hennepin County, Minnesota, and Pima County, Arizona — Mary Moriarty and Laura Conover — alleged in a lawsuit that the Treasury Department violated the law when it exempted American companies from the disclosure rules and let foreign companies leave out their American owners.

Moriarty and Conover, both Democrats, say the ownership records would help their offices pursue cartel money laundering, wage theft, fraud and organized retail theft carried out through shell companies. The suit also names Attorney General Todd Blanche and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, whose departments had to sign off on the exemptions.

Deleting the records would make it "easier than ever for criminals to use shell and front companies for illicit activities and evade detection," the lawsuit, filed in federal court in Washington, D.C., says. It argues that "because law enforcement cannot know in advance which companies will warrant scrutiny, the value of beneficial-ownership reporting lies in collecting that information before the need for it arises."

In a statement to CBS News, a Treasury spokesperson said removing the reporting requirement was "a victory for common sense," adding that the department made the change "after careful consideration of the costs to small business owners and the benefit to national security."
The agency did not respond to questions about whether Musk reached out to Treasury about the rule. A spokesperson for Musk did not respond to requests for comment.

The lawsuit escalates a fight between Democrats and the Trump administration over the rollback, which critics have scrutinized for its timing. The complaint cites Musk's exchange with Williams, saying he had "set his sights on" the disclosure rule while leading the Department of Government Efficiency. Democrats in Congress have questioned Musk's possible role since April 2025, when they wrote to the Treasury Department that the decision was "seemingly triggered by a single Elon Musk social media comment."

Democratic Sens. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, along with California Rep. Maxine Waters, said in a March 2026 letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that Musk "uses a network of dozens of secretive companies" that could potentially be required to share ownership information under the law.

"This rule started with an Elon Musk post on X and will end with 15 million documents in the shredder," said Brendan Ballou, a former Justice Department prosecutor whose firm, the Public Integrity Project, is representing the plaintiffs.
The Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security declined to comment.
A plan to delete millions of records

The Corporate Transparency Act became law in January 2021 with bipartisan support, after Congress included it in a defense bill and overrode Mr. Trump's veto of the broader package. Then-Florida Sen. Marco Rubio, one of its champions and now Mr. Trump's secretary of state, called it in 2020 "the most significant anti-corruption [and] money laundering law in decades."

The law's aim was to combat money laundering and illicit finance by requiring companies to report their true owners to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, a Treasury Department office known as FinCEN. The reporting requirement took effect in 2024, covering nearly 33 million companies, until the Trump administration narrowed it to foreign firms.
By then, U.S. companies had filed about 15 million reports with FinCEN, according to the Treasury Department.
In August 2026, the agency said it plans to delete them in "one sweep of the database" and will notify the public on its website once it's done.
Supporters of the law say it helps investigators follow the money behind crimes like sanctions evasion, drug trafficking and smuggling.

"The only way that you can actually create an easy chain to examine these flows is if you're able to unmask who's behind all these types of transactions," said Max Meizlish, a former career Treasury sanctions official who is now a fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a foreign policy think tank.

In its final rule, the Treasury Department argued the requirement placed "costs of time and money" on "law-abiding American small businesses," and said the rollback would save billions of dollars a year. The department concluded that requiring domestic companies to report their owners "would not serve the public interest," and that "indiscriminate collection" of that information "would not provide law enforcement with highly valuable information."

A number of Republicans have long said that the law buried mom-and-pop companies in paperwork and threatened them with steep financial penalties. In January 2025, Alabama Sen. Tommy Tuberville and Ohio Rep. Warren Davidson reintroduced a bill to repeal the law entirely. Tuberville called it "big-government overreach at its worst."

Not all Republicans welcomed the rollback, though. Iowa Sen. Chuck Grassley, who co-sponsored an earlier version of the law with Whitehouse, urged Treasury in 2025 to scrap its initial rollback. When the final rule came out in August 2026, the two senators said in a joint statement that it "undermines the clear intent of the law."

Without the corporate records, the lawsuit argues, investigators must subpoena bank after bank to learn who is behind a shell company, a slow process that often yields thin or inaccurate answers. The prosecutors are asking a judge to throw out the rule and stop the deletion.
"Wage thieves and fraudsters hide behind shell companies because it works," Moriarty said in a statement. "The only people who benefit are the ones we are trying to catch."
This story published first on CBS News at 8:28 a.m. on Nov. 20, 2026.

title: Stocks plunge as investors take cover amid growing uncertainty
summary: The Dow tumbled 1,100 points, while other stock markets also swooned, as Wall Street frets over AI growth and other market risks.
story: Stocks crumbled on Thursday as investors confronted a number of headwinds that could hurt corporate profits and heighten economic uncertainty.

The Dow tumbled 1,101 points, or 2.2%, to close at 49,097, while the S&P 500 slipped 2%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index fell 2.3%. The swoon in markets was broad, with more than 90% of S&P 500 stocks nosing down.
Stocks were mixed when trading opened on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 370 points, or 1.5%, early in the session, the S&P 500 dipped 0.4% and the Dow gained 0.6%.

Wall Street analysts said no single catalyst accounted for the plunge, but rather pointed to a slew of factors weighing on investor sentiment. Those include ongoing concerns about whether the heavy spending on AI will boost profits, renewed fears that the U.S. and Israel are planning attacks on Iran, and the specter of a potential government shutdown as early as December.

"The slump has set off a scramble of headline searching as people scour the wires to find the most negative sounding news flash," Adam Crisafulli, an analyst at Vital Knowledge, said in a research note. "People just don't have much enthusiasm for this market, and rallies tend to bring out sellers instead of chasers (there is still a lot of hesitation when it comes to being long AI-linked names, especially picks-and-shovels, and the defensive stuff is quite extended after the recent rally)."

For weeks, investors have fretted about the financial strength of the AI sector amid concerns that the torrent of capital pouring into data centers may not deliver the productivity and profit growth companies are counting on.

More recently, investors were shaken by the resignation earlier this month of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after the revelation that he had a relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Some lawmakers have increased scrutiny of Nvidia's sales to China and to companies in southeast China, while the Commerce Department this week signaled it plans to tighten export controls on AI chips.

Despite those concerns, Anthropic had a successful stock market debut, with its shares rising as much as 34% in Thursday trading after the company staged the largest initial public offering in history.

On Thursday, shares of AI-related stocks went from morning gains to afternoon losses. Micron Technology, whose sales of memory for computers have soared amid the AI boom, initially rallied 7.8% before swinging to a 1.8% loss. CoreWeave, a company that buys AI chips and rents access to them to customers via the cloud, went from a 10.5% morning gain to a 5.5% drop.

Nvidia erased an early gain of 4.7% and flipped to a loss of 2.7%. The chip company has been the face of the AI boom, and its stock has struggled with the worries that have been dogging the entire industry.

It wasn't only tech stocks that tumbled on Thursday. Williams-Sonoma dropped 15.3% after the company behind Pottery Barn and West Elm reported revenue for the latest quarter that was just below Wall Street's forecast.
Walmart sank 1.2% even though the retailing giant reported profit and revenue for the latest quarter that edged past analysts' expectations.

title: Meet Anthropic's 7 co-founders, now worth about $20 billion each
summary: Dario Amodei and the company's other six co-founders instantly joined the ranks of America's richest citizens with the AI giant's initial public offering.
story: Anthropic's seven co-founders are in for a massive payday.

Each of Anthropic's co-founders is now worth about $20 billion, based on their stock holdings and the initial price of its record-setting initial stock offering. Their individual wealth, at least on paper, will put them in the same ranks as Rupert Murdoch and his family, worth a combined $20 billion, and famed inventor James Dyson, who is worth $19.9 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Anthropic, the AI developer behind the popular Claude chatbot, started trading shortly before noon on Thursday on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol "ANT." Its shares were priced at $83 each, well above the targeted range of $70 to $78 apiece, suggesting strong investor demand.
That came to pass as its price quickly surged to nearly $115 once trading began. Shares later lost some of their early gains and wound up at $97.17 — still 17.1% higher.
The IPO was the largest in U.S. history, surpassing SpaceX's $75 billion public offering in June.

The IPO also turned many Anthropic employees into instant millionaires. The typical worker at the company could be worth more than $40 million after the initial stock sale, CNBC reported, citing regulatory filings and investors.
Here's what to know about the seven Anthropic founders.
Dario Amodei: $19.7 billion

CEO Dario Amodei, 43, co-founded Anthropic in 2021 after working at OpenAI, its chief rival in the race to dominate the artificial intelligence space. He has said he was prompted to launch Anthropic because he wanted to build an AI model aligned with broader human goals, such as advancing scientific knowledge.
His 237.3 million Class A shares are worth about $19.7 billion, based on the $83 per-share price reserved for Anthropic insiders and early investors.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco's Mission District with his sister, Daniela, another co-founder set to realize billions in wealth. Their father was a leather craftsman, while their mother managed public library renovations, according to the New York Times.

Amodei, who earned a Ph.D. in biophysics from Princeton and a bachelor's degree from Stanford, also completed a postdoctoral fellowship at Stanford's medical school, and also worked at Google Brain, the search giant's AI research lab.
Daniela Amodei: $19.8 billion
Daniela Amodei, 39, co-founded Anthropic with her brother after also working at OpenAI, where she held positions including vice president of safety and policy.
Her 238 million shares will be worth about $19.8 billion, based on the $83 per-share IPO price.

Amodei, who holds a bachelor's degree in English literature from the University of California, Santa Cruz, told Stanford University's business school that she hadn't planned to focus on AI. "I really think of myself as a generalist," she said.
She told Stanford that she and her brother decided to leave OpenAI to form Anthropic based on their values.

"We were running towards something versus running away from something. We had this vision in our heads of wanting to create an organization where the values that matter to us around safety and around responsibility were at the forefront of what we were doing," she said.
Tom Brown: $20 billion
Tom Brown, 39, another of the seven co-founders of Anthropic, serves as the company's chief compute officer.
His 240.8 million shares are valued at $20 billion, based on the $83 per-share IPO price.

Before co-founding Anthropic, Brown led the engineering of GPT-3 at OpenAI, according to his company bio. He has a master's degree from MIT, where he majored in computer science with a focus on how it applied to cognitive science.
Jack Clark: $19.8 billion

Clark, 37, co-founded Anthropic with Dario and Daniela Amodei, and now serves as the head of the Anthropic Institute, which the company describes as a think tank focused on researching the societal implications of AI.
Clark's 242.3 million shares are worth about $19.8 billion.

Clark served as policy director of OpenAI before co-founding Anthropic, and is a former tech journalist who covered supercomputers, neural networks and advanced technology for publications including BusinessWeek.
Jared Kaplan: $19.8 billion

Kaplan, 42, serves as Anthropic's chief science officer and is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University, where he has taught courses on the foundations of deep learning, according to his company bio.
His 239 million shares are worth $19.8 billion, based on the IPO price.

Kaplan, who has a Ph.D. in physics from Harvard University and a bachelor's degree in physics and math from Stanford, spent the first 15 years of his career in academia as a theoretical physicist, according to Anthropic. He was also "instrumental in building GPT-3 and Codex at OpenAI," his bio states.
Sam McCandlish: $19.9 billion
McCandlish, 36, is Anthropic's chief architect, focusing on large-scale AI model training, leading pretraining and research productivity, according to his company bio.
His 240 million shares are worth about $19.9 billion, based on the IPO price.

Before co-founding Anthropic, he led a team at OpenAI, where he focused on the science and scaling of machine learning. He has a Ph.D. in theoretical physics from Stanford University and a bachelor's degree in math and physics from Brandeis University.
Christopher Olah: $19.9 billion
Olah, who is in his early 30s, is the interpretability research lead at Anthropic. Olah previously led interpretability research at OpenAI, according to his company bio.
His 239.5 million shares are worth about $19.9 billion, based on the IPO price.

title: Here are the GTA 6 songs you'll hear cruising around Vice City
summary: Grand Theft Auto 6 players carry out missions to songs by artists such as Cardi B, Lana Del Rey and Travis Scott.
story: Grand Theft Auto 6 relies on a murderer's row of musical hitmakers to provide the backbeat for cruising around Vice City.

The latest installment in the video game franchise, which officially launched on Thursday, features 34 original songs from a range of artists, including Cardi B, Lana Del Rey, Travis Scott and Morgan Wallen. The game's official album was created in partnership with Atlantic Records, and will be available on music platforms such as Spotify and Apple Music beginning on Nov. 20.
Rockstar Games, the company behind the GTA series, is also offering fans limited-edition vinyl and CDs featuring the original tracks.
Music is an essential part of the GTA experience for players like 34-year-old Kansas City resident Cameron Logan Cox, who credits the game's music over the years with helping springboard his career.
"I went on to become a filmmaker and director for a hip-hop label," he told CBS News. "I really don't think I would have had that musical affinity if not for GTA."

In addition to the official GTA 6 soundtrack, gamers will be exposed to countless other tracks through "in-game radio," a feature in GTA 6 that allows players to listen to songs from fictional radio stations while they carry out their missions. They can turn on a station while they drive through Vice City, or via their phone.
"My favorite thing in GTA has never been a mission," Cox told CBS News. "It's the car, the radio and nowhere I have to be."

GTA 6 offers 22 stations, according to industry media outlet GameStop. Some have DJ personas, such as the Cocoteo FM station, which is hosted by characters voiced by Puerto Rican singers Bad Bunny and RaiNao, according to Rolling Stone.

GameStop has a list of some of the songs in Vice City. Among the hundreds of tracks are old hits like "Let Your Love Flow" by the Bellamy Brothers and "Pour Some Sugar on Me" by Def Leppard, as well as more recent hits like Chappell Roan's "HOT TO GO!".

title: AI fueling "disturbingly high" inflation, Chicago Fed president says
summary: A boom in data center construction across the U.S. and broader investment in AI are contributing to hot inflation, according to Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee.
story: The boom in AI data center construction is adding to the nation's "borderline disturbingly high" inflation, with the sector's massive business investment indirectly contributing to rising service prices, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago President Austan Goolsbee told reporters on Thursday.

"The AI boom is contributing to the potential of overheating in the economy," Goolsbee said. "I find it hard to look at it any other way when you are getting major business investment, almost an unprecedented level of business investment."

Goolsbee, who will become a voting member of the interest rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee in January, declined to forecast the central bank's next moves on interest rates. But he said the Fed's decisions will be determined by whether U.S. inflation is on track to return to the central bank's annual 2% target.
"The evidence does not suggest we are on a path back to 2%," Goolsbee added.

Consumer prices around the U.S. rose faster than economists had expected in October, climbing 0.4%, government data shows. While inflation in recent months has largely been driven by higher energy prices, the figures showed that the costs of other goods and services also increased.

Goolsbee's comments come after the Fed's October minutes showed that nearly all officials expect the central bank to raise its key interest rate by a quarter point in December. Others had supported a hike in October, although the committee kept the rate steady, and two members suggested a half-point increase at its meeting next month.

The risks and promise of artificial intelligence were in the spotlight on Thursday with Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering, the largest in history. Shares of Anthropic jumped 17% in their first day of trading on Nasdaq, even as the broader market suffered a major selloff, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average shedding more than 1,100 points.
The wealth creation unleashed by the Anthropic IPO, which has made its seven co-founders multibillionaires, bears watching, Goolsbee added.
"The question of what are people going to do with the money ... will become a macro relevant statistic," he said.

Even so, consumer sentiment remains low despite relatively strong economic trends, a puzzle that economists have sought to explain. One reason is tied to inflation, with Americans generally feeling "very sour" about higher prices, Goolsbee added.
Most Americans are neither benefiting from the AI boom nor Anthropic's IPO, meaning that they are experiencing higher inflation without seeing the upside of the sector's growth.
"The consumer sentiment about inflation hasn't been wrong," Goolsbee said.

title: Consumers stock doomsday pantries as tech outages cause jitters
summary: Companies such as Costco and Walmart are seeing a surge in sales for generators, canned goods and other disaster-preparedness staples.
story: Public anxiety over a string of technology failures is driving some Americans to plan for the worst.

Jittery shoppers are stocking up on generators, shelf-stable canned goods, bottled water and other disaster-planning supplies at retailers such as Costco and Walmart, according to businesses and Wall Street analysts.
What's usually perceived as fringe behavior is starting to spread into the mainstream, according to RBC Capital Markets retail analyst Steven Shemesh.

"We've seen some evidence of it happening across the consumer retail space," he told CBS News, citing recent concurrent tech outages affecting online banking platforms, the Federal Aviation Administration's air traffic control system and even the National Security Agency. "Right now, on the margins, people are preparing more than they have in the past."
"People want to be comfortable knowing that if we did have an outage for a couple of days, they'd have food in the house," Shemesh added.

Data from market research and analytics firm Circana show that purchases of common emergency-prep staples rose for the four weeks ending Nov. 1. Sales of water germicidal tablets, which remove contaminants from drinking water, surged 154% compared with the same period a year ago. Sales of disinfecting wipes rose 72%, while moist towelette sales increased 20%, according to data from RBC Capital Markets.
Shemesh said that Walmart, which reported its third-quarter earnings on Thursday, told RBC that it is seeing a spike in sales of doomsday staples such as soup, water and ready-to-eat foods.

"It's not enough to move the needle for a company that does $8 billion in sales per year, but they are seeing those kinds of behaviors play out," Shemesh said. "Things could need to escalate quite a bit for this to go from level one to level three, which would maybe start to move the needle for some companies."
Nik Modi, global consumer and retail research co-head at RBC Capital Markets, is also seeing signs of panic shopping by consumers.
"A convergence of government action and social media anxiety has pushed 'doomsday prepping' into mainstream consumer behavior over the past several months," Modi said in a research note this week.
He traces the shift in purchasing behavior to a Pentagon military readiness initiative in late September that was misinterpreted and amplified on social media as an impending "blackout."
Government officials have said the recent tech incidents are not connected and were not caused by cyberattacks.

"The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These issues that we've seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated one from another," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday during a news conference in the Philippines.

Yet many consumers aren't taking any chances. Earlier this week, investment firm Mizuho Securities said that consumers flocked to Costco after tech vulnerabilities heightened concerns about the risk of a major cybersecurity incident.

"Consumer anxiety following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at Costco," Mizuho analyst David Bellinger wrote in a report.
He added that shoppers are "pantry-loading" and also depleting the retailer's inventory of "high-ticket generators," which were sold out online as of Sunday night.

Tractor Supply, which sells a range of tools, clothing, and heating and cooling equipment, told CBS News that it has seen increased demand across "several preparedness-related categories." It's selling more generators, liquid storage tanks, propane and accessory tanks than it did during the same period last year.

title: Gamers, start your engines. Grand Theft Auto 6 is ready to roll.
summary: The latest, long-awaited version of the hit video game franchise launches at midnight local time on Nov. 19 in countries worldwide. Here's what to know about GTA 6.
story: In the immortal words of Carl "CJ" Johnson from an earlier edition of Grand Theft Auto, "Ah s***, here we go again." After 13 years and two delayed launches, video game fans are finally getting their hands on Grand Theft Auto 6.

GTA, as it's widely known, has evolved since its launch in 1997 into one of the biggest franchises in entertainment and one of the few sure hits in the ferociously competitive video game world. Tens of millions of people globally are expected to pick up their joysticks as Rockstar Games, the company behind the series, rolls out GTA 6 on Nov. 19 in countries around the world.

As fans eagerly await the latest GTA installment, Rockstar has whipped up interest with a series of trailers and even an extended look on Netflix. In typical fashion, however, the company has kept the hype simmering by withholding key information about the game ahead of its official launch this week.

"Having been over a decade since the last full release of a Grand Theft Auto game, all that energy just keeps getting bottled up and bottled up, and people are reading into every tweet and every little piece of news that's coming out of Rockstar to try and glean all the details of this game," Andrew Marok, director of equity research for digital media at financial firm Raymond James, told CBS News.
Here's what to know about the long-awaited release of GTA 6.
What is GTA 6 about?

The latest GTA installment centers on the stories of Lucia Caminos, the game's first-ever female protagonist, and Jason Duval. Jason, who has been working for drug runners, craves a quieter life but keeps getting dragged back into crime, according to Rockstar's synopsis of GTA 6. Lucia, meanwhile, has recently left Leonida Penitentiary, where she landed after "fighting for her family."

When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair becomes entangled in a wider conspiracy. The series is based in Vice City, inspired by Miami, in the fictional state of Leonida. Rockstar has touted the location as the most detailed version of the game yet, with architecture, beaches, roads and bars all inspired by South Florida.
There's "this concept of GTA 6 being just bigger than the game," Marok said.  "It's also about the immersion in the world of Vice City."
What equipment do I need to play the game?

Players will need a PlayStation 5 or an Xbox Series X/S console to play GTA 6. Rockstar told players who are preloading the game to plan ahead, as they may need up to 212 GB of storage space, depending on their device.
When can people start playing?

The game officially debuts worldwide on Thursday, Nov. 19. Rather than a single launch time, GTA 6 is rolling out at midnight local time in countries around the world, giving some users access before others. This website shows the countdown time by country.

Pre-orders for the game began back in June. But users weren't allowed to start pre-downloading on their PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S consoles until Nov. 10, according to Rockstar. Gamers were also able to purchase a "code-in-box" version, a physical case that contains a code users can input to download the game from the PlayStation Store or Xbox.
How much does it cost?
Grand Theft Auto 6 costs $79.99 for the "standard edition" and $99.99 for the "ultimate edition." The latter contains an exclusive collection of cars, weapons and apparel.
What are players saying?

New Zealand was among the first countries where players could access the game. One 25-year-old told CBS News he set up his PlayStation account to appear as if he were in New Zealand — where the game is already live — rather than his home in the United Kingdom, to access it as soon as possible.
"It's definitely more immersive than previous entries," he told CBS News, requesting anonymity because he is taking a day off from work to play GTA 6. "Visually, it's incredible."
Other gamers were also quick to praise GTA 6's visual quality and action-packed plot.

"The gameplay dynamics are just amazing, and the graphics are great, and you can tell that the storytelling is really deep, which is impressive," Adam Simmons, a 50-year-old in Wellington, New Zealand, where the game has already rolled out, told The Associated Press.

On Metacritic, a review aggregator website, players gave GTA 6 a score of 99 out of 100. "Grand Theft Auto VI, against all odds, has somehow managed to not only meet but surpass all my expectations," one user wrote.
How long does it take to play?
Insider Gaming, a website focused on the video game industry, said it takes an average of roughly 50 hours to complete all of the missions in GTA 6.
When will online play launch?

The online, multiplayer version of the game introduces new missions and allows players to stay immersed in the world of GTA after completing the more linear single-player version. It's free with the option of in-game purchases, according to Marok of Raymond James.
Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar's parent company, hasn't confirmed GTA Online's availability, though it seems likely given its enormous revenue potential.
"That's where GTA 5 made so much of its money," Marok said.
Will there be a PC version?

Rockstar Games did not respond to a request for comment about whether it will release a desktop version of the game. Historically, a PC version has been released about 12 to 18 months after the console version, according to Marok. However, the company could decide to launch it sooner.

"I think that there are reasons why Rockstar and Take-Two would want the PC version of the game out sooner than usual, and a lot of that has to do with the Grand Theft Auto Online component of the game, which is the multiplayer, ongoing monetization piece of it," he told CBS News.
Who plays GTA?
Male millennials and Gen Zers represent the key demographic playing GTA 6, according to a recent report from Sensor Tower. The company estimates 72% of players are male, while 57% are under 35.
What music is featured in the game?

GTA 6 features an original adaptive score from Justice, the Grammy-winning French electronic duo featuring Gaspard Augé and Xavier de Rosnay. The music is "dynamically tuned to the different ways players engage with the world of Vice City and Leonida throughout Jason and Lucia's story," Rockstar Games said on its website.
The 30-track "Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score" is scheduled for release Dec. 11 and includes collaborations with Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein.
Who are the voice actors?

Rockstar has not disclosed the full voice cast. However, actress Manni Perez was nominated for her voice acting in the "Best Performance" category at The Game Awards, an annual ceremony that celebrates the video game industry. Actor Stephen Root has also confirmed to the AP that he appears in the game, though Rockstar has not publicly disclosed his participation.
How many GTA 6 units have already been sold?

The company had sold 19 million units, including pre-order copies, and generated $1.84 billion in revenue by Thursday, according to Sensor Tower. The market intelligence and digital analytics platform said earlier this month that GTA 6 is the "most pre-ordered game in history."
Raymond James projects that Rockstar will sell 50 million units of the game from launch through the end of Take-Two's fiscal year 2027, which runs until March 31.
"That would be by some distance the biggest launch in video gaming history," Marok said.

GTA 5, released in 2013, has sold nearly 235 million copies, according to Take-Two. The game has generated more than $10 billion in revenue over the last 13 years, according to Victor Matheson, an economist at the College of the Holy Cross who studies sports and major events.
How much did GTA 6 cost to make?
Rockstar hasn't disclosed the exact figure, but analysts estimate GTA 6 cost upward of $1 billion to produce, which would make it the most expensive video game in history.
"I would be shocked if it was under a billion dollars because they've been working on this for the better part of a decade," Marok said.
Asked about the price tag during a recent Wall Street Journal event, Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick didn't offer an exact figure, saying only, "It was expensive, and it took a long time."
