story: The following is the transcript of the interview with Microsoft president and vice chair Brad Smith that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 22, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Welcome back to Face the Nation. We turn now to the president and vice chairman of Microsoft, Brad Smith, who joins us from Seattle. Very early morning. Thank you for joining us.
MICROSOFT PRESIDENT & VICE CHAIR BRAD SMITH: My pleasure. Thank you.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So we've been talking about these outages at companies. Microsoft had a global outage for 24 hours, hobbled corporations. It was tough for us here in the news business not to have our email working on November 12 or so. Microsoft said it was linked to a technical issue, not a cyber hack. What is the company doing to make sure this doesn't happen again? And did AI play a role here?

SMITH: Well, the first thing we always need to do when this happens is apologize, and we have, and I want to do so again. And you're right; it was not linked to AI. It wasn't a cyberattack. It was basically a perfect storm of software that was updated four months earlier, and then it interacted with a new update and a shift in network traffic. You know, we have taken steps. We've published two reports in the last 10 days. We've worked to be transparent, showing minute by minute to the public what happened. We've taken nine steps already, as we laid out in our report. There's 13 more steps we're going to take. We've learned a lot. It was painful, especially for everybody who relies on us. We get it, and I think this combination is going to make us stronger going forward. It's just constantly what we have to do in an age of such complex technology.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, as you know, it was a series of events. It wasn't just Microsoft, but we saw tech outages and all sorts of complications. It's raised questions about what AI's role is generally. I heard you say it wasn't a factor for Microsoft, but when you look across the country right now, I mean, do you think that we are applying AI tools to look for vulnerabilities and then doing these automated updates in such a way that, frankly, like our old infrastructure, just isn't prepared for.

SMITH: I think that is part of the really important question, and you can think about what's happening with all of these outages, at least in substantial part, as sort of AI ripple effects. What AI did earlier this year was basically make it much easier for people to find vulnerabilities in code, and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you're a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems. So what happened is we've set off, in effect, a race. Around the world, people who have technology are using these systems to identify the vulnerabilities and patch at a pace we have never seen before, to beat the bad actors so they can't use them to hack in, but especially when you have older infrastructure, especially when you're trying to patch at such a pace, especially when you have to go so fast that you can't take as much time to test what you're changing in the code, you do increase the risk of something going wrong, and that's what we've seen over the last week. I think we have to be prepared, frankly, for the coming months because this isn't the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks. The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But that makes it sound like there are some pretty big risks that we may not yet be anticipating. What are Americans supposed to do?

SMITH: Well, what I would say for all of us is three things. First, if you get an update on your phone or your laptop with a patch, apply it because I think that's going to keep your technology far safer. Second, for all the organizations in the world, people are having to update their patching practices. They're having to change the way their IT teams work together, they're having to upgrade their- their legacy infrastructure, and I think there's a huge opportunity for the government and the tech sector to work more closely together. Jay Clayton is really, I think, focused on advancing this in the administration. I think that's critical, and we're going to need better sharing of threat intelligence, better concerted action.

MARGARET BRENNAN: I want to ask you about something I asked the Treasury Secretary about just a few moments ago. On the Microsoft website, it says your company has more than 600 data centers in 34 countries. The president said that he wants to put a tremendous tax on companies that build data centers abroad, and he'd like to stop them from building abroad. I know Bessent said he didn't have the details, but when you hear that from the president of the United States as a new policy, what impact does that have on your business?

SMITH: Well, my sense is that the president is making an important point, but there's some critical nuance we need to think about as well. The point is sort of analogous to the chip industry. I think the administration might want to see the most advanced frontier models trained in the United States, and- and there's room to have that kind of conversation. The nuance is that there's lots of different kinds of data centers. Most data centers actually don't have AI. They're cloud services to stream a video, play a video game, run your business, and those have to be located close to customers. They often now have AI because the business applications, even your video games, have an AI element, and the president talked about say, data centers in Finland. You can't support Helsinki from New Jersey any more than you can keep the lights on in Helsinki from an electricity power plant in New Jersey. Those have to be located locally.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah, he might have been referring to a Chinese project there. It wasn't clear. I heard that line too. TikTok owner ByteDance is reportedly spending significantly on Microsoft's AI and cloud services, and that has gotten the attention of the Republican chair of the committee on the Communist Party. He said, given Microsoft's crucial Pentagon contracts, it's unacceptable for your company to sell AI tools to arm ByteDance, which works with the Chinese Communist Party. That's his opinion. But why do you think it's a good idea?
SMITH: Well, take TikTok. It's a social media service. It's a social media service today that uses AI to make it easier for TikTok users to find what they're looking for. As Secretary Bessent said--
MARGARET BRENNAN: There's social media and there's surveillance state, right?

SMITH: Well, there's TikTok services around the world. You know, in the United States, it's now a separate company. So I think the question is always, what technology is being provided? How is the technology being used? We always go up to Capitol Hill to provide information when these kinds of news stories arise. I'm sure we'll be going up to Capitol Hill to answer the questions of- of that committee.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, we'll watch for that. And before I let you go, we had Speaker-Designate Jeffries on the program. He was talking about this idea of accountability. There's been a lot of focus, as you know, on the president's projects, including this ballroom. Microsoft donated $10 million to it, according to the Journal and the Post, so that makes your company one of the top donors to the ballroom. I know that was a decision that you must have weighed in on. Why did you come to that conclusion? And are you worried now about risk from a Democratic-controlled Congress looking to focus in on companies like yours?

SMITH: We always have the same philosophy for every administration, regardless of which political party it comes from. We partner where we can. We stand apart when we should. We looked at the ballroom. We didn't know, obviously, that it was going to involve any demolition of the East Wing. That was- we put in the first category, and we've disagreed where we thought that was important, including suing this administration, as we have previous administrations, to stand up for the free press to make sure that the privacy of journalists are protected. We always have to make judgment calls. We never expect to get everything perfect, but I think that is the right philosophy for us.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Brad Smith, thank you for your time today. We'll be right back.

title: Bessent: We "need answers" on Nvidia role in sending China AI chips
summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says the government wants to know if Nvidia had "malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for the noncompliance" with chip export controls.
story: Washington — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that the administration needs answers from Nvidia as questions swirl about whether it has complied with export restrictions, after revelations surrounding its CEO's alleged affairs sent the chipmaker into crisis.
"We do need answers," Bessent said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

After Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO amid revelations about extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged spy, the U.S. is investigating how Nvidia may have given China access to advanced AI computer chips, despite government restrictions.

Last week, Bessent referenced a possible "culture of noncompliance" at Nvidia, questioning whether the company was "pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings." In an interview on Fox News, Bessent said he needed answers from Nvidia on its compliance with export restrictions within 10 days. On Sunday, he told Brennan the administration has not yet received those answers.

"We've been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers," Bessent said. "It behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was."

Nvidia's CFO, Colette Kress, has taken the helm after Huang's departure. But Bessent has urged the company to bring someone in from the outside to run the company. The treasury secretary said Sunday, "We do need to see who was in charge of compliance there."

Asked how challenging it could be to get to the bottom of what Jensen Huang was doing, given reporting about Nvidia's "handshake" business approach, Bessent said, "For deals that size, there's no such thing as an untraceable handshake deal."
"There are bills ablating that movement, there are money movements," he said. "They may not be the 100-page documents, but it will be possible to understand what has gone on here."
On his call for an inquiry into whether Nvidia had a culture of noncompliance, Bessent said that it's simply a possibility that the dynamic was at play.
"We will see, and that's why I think the board is moving very quickly to establish whether this did or did not exist," Bessent said.

The comments come as President Trump has called for Jensen Huang to return as CEO of Nvidia. Asked whether the president understands the risks that Bessent has pointed to, Bessent replied that it remained to be seen "which level of the business knew about this."

"Was it at the lower levels? Was it at the middle levels? Did it go all the way to the top? And I have confidence that the Nvidia committees are moving very quickly on this and will come up with some very fulsome and robust answers," he said.

When pressed on whether he thinks it would be a good idea for Jensen Huang to return, Bessent said, "I think we have to see where the buck stops — Were these malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for the noncompliance?" He also drew a distinction between this possible dynamic, and Jensen Huang's alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang.
"I think that is kind of a canard," Bessent said. "Was there a culture of compliance versus one person's foibles?"
Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee and will also be interviewed by House panels in early December.

title: Transcript: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 22, 2026
summary: The following is the transcript of the interview with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 22, 2026.
story: The following is the transcript of the interview with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 22, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We begin with the Secretary of the Treasury, Scott Bessent. It's good to have you here and in person, sir.
U.S. TREASURY SECRETARY SCOTT BESSENT: Margaret, good to see you.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So there were thousands of customers across America who, when they went to some of the biggest banks, had issues this past week with tech outages, and it caused a bit of a panic with people pulling out cash. In this age of AI, what should Americans be prepared for, and should they worry about their financial institutions?

SEC. BESSENT: It's a good good question, Margaret. And no, they shouldn't. The banks have been at the forefront of cybersecurity for decades. They experience attacks every day, every week, every month, and they are by far the most resilient companies in the U.S. economy. What we are seeing as they, because of the SI, as they go into patch their security systems, the patches may cause a glitch, which is what happened last week. J.P. Morgan went in, and I think the American people should think of it as a vaccine. Your arm may hurt, you may feel a little bad the next day, but it increases your long-term immunity and resiliency.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay. Well, there's other concerns about AI, as you know, and we've seen in the stock market anxiety, a real sell-off over the past week. Nvidia is sometimes referred to as the central bank of AI, since it uses its cash to finance things like data centers and essentially boost demand for its own sales. We have a graphic there, sort of showing the gist of that. I mean, when you look at its size and how interwoven it is in the tech industry. Do you worry that this kind of circular financing means that one company is becoming so hugely important that it could have ripple effects if something goes wrong?

SEC. BESSENT: Well, look, Nvidia is one of our great companies with the management chains. The board has slowed things down. The CFO is now in charge, so you know, I believe that she understands the financing quite well. And no, as Nvidia continues to be fantastically profitable, and there is near unlimited demand for their chips worldwide.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Do you—how do you understand what happened in the markets this past week?

SEC. BESSENT: Well, I think it's a combination of things. You know, we could see that the market sell-off actually began as the Democrats moved ahead in the polls and then accelerated after Election Day. The Democratic position on the SI buildout has spooked a lot of investors in terms of slowing it down. We've also seen some very hawkish remarks from the Federal Reserve. Many people believe that they may be making a policy mistake if they over-tighten. We've seen a substantial tightening in financial conditions over the past few months. So, you know, I think it was a combination of these things.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, President Trump gave that 90-minute or so press conference on Friday, and he did talk about things in AI. Among many things, he said, take a listen to this.
[START SOUND ON TAPE]

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen, and we're going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.
[END SOUND ON TAPE]
MARGARET BRENNAN: How is that policy going to work, and won't that also inhibit the sector?

SEC. BESSENT: Well, I haven't spoken to the president about that. I was sitting in that press conference, and I didn't get a chance to speak to him after that. But look, I think the president's very concerned that we don't do a big technology transfer offshore. What we've seen, that the U.S. used to be the leader in the chip industry, and now we see that 97% of the high-end chips are made in Taiwan, which creates a strategic vulnerability.
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's been the case.

SEC. BESSENT: Well, this administration is working to bring them back. There are large fabs being built by TSMC in Arizona, and we hope to have substantial onshoring of the chip business by the end of this administration. So, I think he's worried about the same thing happening with data centers.

MARGARET BRENNAN: With data centers, so one of the arguments against this, and the Wall Street Journal editorial board was pointing out a challenge here, is that if American companies can't build data centers and their AI models close to the markets they're trying to sell into, it will basically give their competitors, the Chinese, an edge.

SEC. BESSENT: Well, look, I think that the SI is very fungible. That companies access U.S. centers. There are many centers in Southeast Asia. They get access from around the world. So I think the real thing here is going to be, and I've said it many times before the election. The industry has done a terrible job of explaining themselves to the American people, and I think they need to have a conversation with the American people, with the communities where these centers are built, and rebuild public trust. And I think once we see that, then we could see a more substantial build out here in the U.S.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, so what the president announced was not reversing, for example, what the U.S. was encouraging in the United Arab Emirates with these data centers being built in some of our Gulf allies.
SEC. BESSENT: No, he's talking about American companies doing it.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, let me ask you about Nvidia in particular and what's been happening in terms of the ongoing revelations. Multiple congressional committees, federal prosecutors, and presumably regulators here in the United States are probing the role Nvidia played in sending advanced AI computer chips to China. On Fox last Sunday, I watched your interview. It was pretty extraordinary. You did not parse words. You referred to a culture of non-compliance at Nvidia. The possibility that they were quote "pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings." You said you needed answers to what was going on within 10 days. That was seven days ago. Have you gotten the answers you need?

SEC. BESSENT: We don't, Margaret. And I think the important word there is possibility. And we have seen. We've been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers, and we do need answers. And back to your question about the centrality of Nvidia to the SI system, it behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was. Was there promiscuous attitude toward this, and where—if it happened—where were the faults, and then they can move on.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So when you say we, you mean to Treasury? You're expecting those answers to go to Treasury, or they're expecting to go to the White House?
SEC. BESSENT: To the administration.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Because there was a lot of reporting that Nvidia's business deals were often based on handshakes. That doesn't leave a lot of a paper trail. How challenging is this for regulators to get to the bottom of what the CEO was doing? I know you said the CFO is at the helm, but last Sunday you said basically they need to clean up shop and get someone from the outside to run the place.

SEC. BESSENT: Well, what I said was we do need to see who was in charge of compliance there. Normally, it's the legal department, the general counsel's office. So we'll see what they have to say. But you know, in terms of handshake deals, for deals that size, there's no such thing as an untraceable handshake deal, there are bills blading that movement. There are money movements, so you know, they may not be the 100-page documents, but there, it will be possible to understand what has gone on here.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I mean, that's an extraordinary charge though, a culture of non-compliance.
SEC. BESSENT: Well--
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's not just the foibles of one man.
SEC. BESSENT: Well, again, I said the possibility.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SEC. BESSENT: So we will see, and that's why I think the board is moving very quickly to establish whether this did or did not exist.

MARGARET BRENNAN: The president of the United States said Jensen Huang should get his job back. You said the board of directors needs to go to the outside. Does the president understand the national security risk and the regulatory risk that you're pinpointing here?
SEC. BESSENT: Well, Jensen is on the outside now, so you know.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I know the president said he should come back.

SEC. BESSENT: Well, I said they should go to the outside, but he's on the outside now. But I think what we need to see, because the other thing I said was we will see which level of the business knew about this. Was it at the lower levels? Was it the middle levels? Did it go all the way to the top? And I have confidence that the Nvidia committees are moving very quickly on this and will come up with some very fulsome and robust answers.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I understand Mr. Huang is no longer at the helm, but are you saying that you think it would be a good idea for him to go back and run the company?
SEC. BESSENT: I think we have to see where the buck stops. You know, what were these malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for the non-compliance.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, so you see that as almost separate and apart from the relationship with Alice Huang, who's reportedly linked to Chinese security?
SEC. BESSENT: Yeah, I think that is kind of a canard that the, you know, was their culture of compliance versus the one person's foibles
MARGARET BRENNAN: With a Chinese spy, allegedly.
SEC. BESSENT: Well, I assume he didn't know that she was an alleged spy.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Senator Tom Cotton, the Republican chair of the Intelligence Committee, told the Journal about his frustrations with Commerce Secretary Lutnick, ignoring what he said were repeated letters and information from him about Megaspeed, the company that Alice Huang was running, which is at the heart of this. Cotton said he's glad that the Trump administration is finally coming around, but we need to catalog the damage. What damage has been done? Do you know?
SEC. BESSENT: Well, again, we will see if Megaspeed was indeed a pass-through company, a front company based in Singapore, to get the high-end chips to Chinese entities.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, should it be blacklisted while that's under consideration?
SEC. BESSENT: Well, Nvidia actually took them off their vendor list or sales list in August of '25, so they wouldn't have gotten any chips since then.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Should it be blacklisted in the meantime?

SEC. BESSENT: We at Treasury and several other departments have pushed for it. I think the important thing was last week we did something called the connected, or the remote access rule, which prevents certain countries, certain entities from accessing chips via lease capacity, which I actually think may be more important.
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil. You're trying to tighten the licensing there.
SEC. BESSENT: Yes.

MARGARET BRENNNAN: But in the meantime, it was pretty extraordinary to have the Republican chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee release publicly documents showing that the Commerce Department had approved the sale of more than 800,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips to China. The approvals included two companies highlighted here as known to be linked to the Chinese military. I know there's a threshold set on the type of chips, but is any sale to the Chinese military really advisable?
SEC. BESSENT: The president's been very clear that the H- and drawn a very hard line at the--
[CROSSTALK]
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah, the H200s.

SEC. BESSENT: The H200s. So I think, and you know, these are companies, I think one of them is Alibaba, which is in general social media and online platform. So I think once you draw the threshold, then I don't know if you have to differentiate.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So some sales to the Chinese military are okay.
SEC. BESSENT: Well, again, this isn't Chinese military. These are companies that do business with the Chinese military.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Understood. And there's a very, very thin line there, but Secretary Bessent, I appreciate your time today. Face the Nation will be back in a minute. Stay with us.

title: Transcript: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 22, 2026
summary: The following is the transcript of the interview with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 22, 2026.
story: The following is the transcript of the interview with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 22, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We turn now to the incoming Speaker of the House, Democratic Congressman Hakeem Jeffries, who joins us from New York. Good morning, Mr. Speaker-designate.
REP. HAKEEM JEFFRIES: Good morning. Great to be with you.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, you have — really a huge role to take over in January, and I want to lay out for you what we saw in our exit polls as the message sent by voters. 89% said cost of living was crucial or a major factor in their vote. 90% said the same about corruption. Given those dual messages, what is the first bill you try to pass, and will it be bipartisan?

REP. JEFFRIES: We're going to work incredibly hard to deliver on our promises to the American people around affordability and accountability. We have to drive down the high cost of living. Life is way too expensive. There are far too many people who are working hard, they're playing by the rules, they can't thrive, and they can barely survive. There are several things that we plan to do very early on in the new Congress. We need to end this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran that has skyrocketed gas prices, food prices, and diesel prices. We need to reverse the Medicaid cuts. We need to restore SNAP benefits. We need to deal with the Trump tariffs, which have also increased costs on everyday Americans by thousands of dollars per year —
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
REP. JEFFRIES: — and of course we need to extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, when I asked about whether or not it would be bipartisan, some of the things you just laid out, it really doesn't seem likely that the president, a Republican president, would sign off on. Some of the things you listed- they were part of his signature tax and spending bill that Republicans passed. Are you going to send these as messaging vehicles?

REP. JEFFRIES: No, we're committed to delivering the type of bold, dramatic, and meaningful change that the American people are demanding. When we moved earlier this year to extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits, that was bipartisan in the House of Representatives because the reality is tens of millions of people in this country, hardworking, working-class, middle-class folks, those who aspire to be part of the middle class, have experienced dramatically increased health insurance premiums. In some cases, more than $1,000 per month. That's unacceptable. Reversing the Medicaid cuts will help out people all across this country —
MARGARET BRENNAN: You don't think Trump will veto that?

REP. JEFFRIES: — rural America, urban America, small town America, the heartland of America, and Black and Brown communities all throughout America. Listen, that remains to be seen. We have three areas that we need to work on. We need to drive down the high cost of living and deal with the affordability crisis. We have a broken healthcare system. We need to fix it, and then make sure that we actually don't simply return to the status quo, but we do much better than what currently exists. And we need to fix our broken immigration system as well. And those are three possible areas to explore whether we can work together with the president and our colleagues on the other side of the aisle.

MARGARET BRENNAN: There are a lot of different ways to define accountability. Rahm Emanuel, the former congressman, mayor, and ambassador- I know you know him well, told my CBS colleague that Democrats seeking accountability should move on ethics reform. He suggested a ban on stock trading in prediction markets, mandatory blind trust for everyone with over $1 million in wealth and no foreign money when you're in government or two years afterwards. Do you have an appetite for that kind of proposal?

REP. JEFFRIES: Yes, we have promised the American people that, in addition to our affordability agenda, we know, in the face of the unprecedented corruption that has been unleashed on the American people and the country over the last two years, that we need to deal with accountability, and we've made that clear. And no one is going to get a pass because--
MARGARET BRENNAN: But how do you define that?

REP. JEFFRIES: --there's a cost to corruption that adversely impacts everyday Americans. So, well listen, we've got to clean up the mess in Washington. That means the Congress, that means the Supreme Court, and that also means with respect to the administration. And we should begin by dealing with our own House, which is why very early on in the new Congress, House Democrats are going to move to ban members of Congress from trading stock.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, we will see if that gets the bipartisan support needed. I want to ask you as well about what President Trump said he thinks he can work with you on. He said we can get a lot of great things done. Take a listen.
[START SOUND ON TAPE]

DONALD TRUMP: I'm open to great healthcare. Now, can it be what they want? No, but it can be a combination of what we all want, and we could end up with great healthcare in our country. We could end up better than dealing with the Republicans.
[END SOUND ON TAPE]
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, what would working with him on healthcare do apart from, like you said, repealing the things that have already been passed?

REP. JEFFRIES: In addition to what I've talked about in terms of fixing our broken healthcare system, of course, we can't simply return to the status quo. In my view, we should lower the age of Medicare eligibility. We should expand coverage to include vision, hearing, and dental, and we should make sure that we cover the kids so that every single child and young American in this country can afford to go see a doctor when they need one. That's a place where we can explore coming together. I know it has strong support amongst Democrats in the House and the Senate, and let's see what's possible in terms of what the president has said with respect to healthcare. Can you imagine how angry the American people will be with Washington if over the next two years, we fail to do anything--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

REP. JEFFRIES: --about affordability, fail to do anything about healthcare, and fail to do anything about immigration? We're committed to bringing about the type of dramatic change the American people are demanding.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But you also have constraints on you given the already over $40 trillion in debt America is carrying. You have constraints with the rising cost of Social Security and Medicaid. How do you pay for expanding this?

REP. JEFFRIES: Well, those are conversations that we look forward to having as members of Congress, both sides of the aisle, and certainly with the administration. But we have to do better. The economy is broken. Life is not working for far too many Americans, and it's clear we can't simply return to the status quo. This is a great country. When you work hard and play by the rules, you should be able to live an affordable life, and a comfortable life, and a good life. And that's what we're committed to bringing about for every single American in this great country of ours.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So, when you were elected as Speaker-designate, there were seven of the 11 lawmakers who voted against you who released a statement. Some of them are democratic socialists, and they said that they had secured commitments from you already. It was in a positive direction, still wasn't enough to win their vote. But can you tell us what commitments you have made to the left of your party?

REP. JEFFRIES: The only commitments that I've made is to continue to deliver upon the aggressive agenda that we've talked about with respect to making life more affordable for the American people, and that's in every area. We believe we have to drive down the high cost of healthcare, and housing, and gas, and groceries, and goods, and utilities, and caregiving, and we have plans to make sure that we aggressively engage in every single one of those areas. With respect to the House Democratic Caucus, I'm going to continue to have an open-door policy and talk to everyone. But what I believe unites us is our shared commitment to the affordability agenda and our shared commitment to making sure that if you have folks out there who've been stealing from the American people, screwing over the American people, or shortchanging the American people, we will also hold the crooks accountable.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But that doesn't mean impeachments come January? It's not an immediate plan?

REP. JEFFRIES: We haven't ruled anything in, and we haven't ruled anything out. We're focused on actually delivering and keeping our commitment. And it's my expectation that with respect to the accountability agenda that everyone involved and whatever investigations are unveiled, they're going to follow the facts, they're going to apply the law, they're going to be guided by the Constitution, and they're going to let the chips fall where they may, so we can deliver a government of the people, by the people, and for the people that's focused on actually making life better for everyday Americans.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Speaker-designate, we will watch your work. More questions for you, but we have to leave it there for today.
REP. JEFFRIES: Thank you.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We'll be right back with a lot more Face the Nation. Stay with us.
In:

Hakeem Jeffries

title: Jeffries talks about where Democrats may be able to work with Trump
summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries outlined areas where Democrats "can explore coming together" with President Trump.
story: Washington — Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who's set to become House speaker when his party takes control of Congress next year, outlined areas on Sunday where he said Democrats "can explore coming together" with President Trump.
"Let's see what's possible in terms of what the president has said with respect to healthcare," Jeffries said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

As Democrats are poised to take control of both the House and Senate in the new year, following a slew of victories in the midterm elections, Mr. Trump expressed openness to working with Democrats in recent days — citing healthcare as a possible area for compromise.

"I'm open to great healthcare," Mr. Trump said at a press briefing on Friday. "Now, can it be what they want? No. But it can be a combination of what we all want, and we could end up with great healthcare in our country. We could end up better than dealing with the Republicans."

Jeffries identified a couple of areas where Democrats and Republicans might come together, pointing to lowering the age of Medicare eligibility, expanding healthcare coverage to include vision, hearing and dental, and making sure that children get coverage, "so that every single child and young American in this country can afford to go see a doctor when they need one."

"That's a place where we can explore coming together," Jeffries said. "I know it has strong support amongst Democrats in the House and the Senate, and let's see what's possible in terms of what the president has said with respect to healthcare."

The New York Democrat repeatedly emphasized the need for action, saying, "Can you imagine how angry the American people will be with Washington if, over the next two years, we fail to do anything about affordability, fail to do anything about healthcare, and fail to do anything about immigration?"
"The economy is broken — life is not working for far too many Americans, and it's clear we can't simply return to the status quo," he said.
Jeffries said Democrats are "committed to bringing about the type of dramatic change the American people are demanding."

Beyond healthcare, where Democrats more broadly would like to see a reversal to the Medicaid cuts in the GOP's One Big Beautiful Bill last year, Jeffries said the two other key areas of focus in the next Congress will be the high cost of living and the immigration system.
"Those are three possible areas to explore whether we can work together with the president and our colleagues on the other side of the aisle," Jeffries said.

Jeffries also highlighted combating corruption as an early focus, saying that Democrats have promised the American people that "we need to deal with accountability" among lawmakers, the Supreme Court and members of the administration.
"No one is going to get a pass," he said.
Jeffries said stock trading by lawmakers will be high on the Democrats' agenda.
"Very early on in the new Congress, House Democrats are going to move to ban members of Congress from trading stock," adding, "we will see if that gets the bipartisan support needed."

The president's relationship with Jeffries still remains to be defined. But Mr. Trump has already cast doubt on his ability to work with Jeffries' expected counterpart on the other side of the Capitol, Sen. Chuck Schumer.

"It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader," Mr. Trump said in a post on Truth Social earlier Sunday. "He failed badly as 'Leader' once before, one of the worst in history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again. All he did was perpetuate the Russia, Russia, Russia Hoax, and many other Hoaxes and Scams, making my victory in 2024 an easy and glorious one. Here we go again!"
When asked whether impeachment efforts would be a focal point for the House Democrats in the new Congress, Jeffries said, "We haven't ruled anything in, and we haven't ruled anything out."

"We're focused on actually delivering and keeping our commitment. And it's my expectation that with respect to the accountability agenda, that everyone involved in whatever investigations are unveiled, they're going to follow the facts," Jeffries said. "They're going to apply the law. They're going to be guided by the Constitution, and they're going to let the chips fall where they may."

title: Trump signs executive order on federal workers' responses to Congress
summary: If they fail to comply, the White House warns their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended.
story: President Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to a new executive order issued late Friday.

The companies must also coordinate with the White House and U.S. agencies on "appropriate responses" to any such requests, the order says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended.

The order signed late Friday is the administration's latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January. Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets, noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Mr. Trump's family, particularly at the Pentagon.

It comes as White House officials have already begun taking steps to exert more control over how agencies and officials respond to congressional requests, anticipating there will be a flood of investigations once Democrats take power in January.

On Monday, White House Counsel Will Scharf told U.S. agencies that they must seek approval from his office and the White House's Office of Legislative Affairs before agreeing to appear before Congress. Scharf also suggested in a recent letter to Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, that some congressional investigations may amount to "blatant criminality."

Garcia earlier this week sent letters directing members of Mr. Trump's family and top administration officials to preserve documents. Scharf sought to dismiss the requests, noting in a letter to Democratic lawmakers that they are not yet in the majority and cannot compel compliance.

In a fact sheet, the White House framed the new requirements as "protecting executive privileges from congressional overreach," arguing that some congressional leaders have tried to intrude on executive branch privileges by "harassing private companies that contract with the federal government."

Presidents of both parties have long used executive privilege to resist congressional inquiries, but the claims can set up messy, protracted legal fights as parties dispute whether it applies. Executive privilege allows the president to keep information from the courts, Congress and the public to protect the confidentiality of White House deliberations, but the protection is far from absolute.
Friday's executive order applies to all contractors and subcontractors, a universe of tens of thousands of businesses.

title: Trump vows to work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates
summary: President Trump says he will work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates.
story: President Trump said he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates, hoping to fulfill a promise he made on the 2024 campaign trail but couldn't deliver on because of industry pressure and a lack of interest from his fellow Republicans.
"I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot," Trump told Fox News Channel's "Saturday in America."

Democrats and the Republican president have both backed capping credit card interest rates, with the standard proposal being capping rates at 10%. It would substantially reduce what credit card companies can charge customers. The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve.
With rates at 10%, a cardholder with a $5,000 balance would pay about $42 per month in interest. At the current average rate of 22%, they would owe about $100 per month.

Mr. Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates in January, as part of the White House's affordability push. Banks and credit card companies immediately and aggressively opposed the proposal, saying any interest rate cap would force them to cancel cards for the poor and less creditworthy customers or substantially cut back on the rewards they offer when customers spend on their cards.
The proposal also did not sit well with Republicans, and there was little effort by the GOP-controlled Congress to fulfill Mr. Trump's promise.

That could change now that Democrats will control both the House and Senate. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who is expected to be the next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has said repeatedly she wants to cap rates.

In response to the Fox News interview, Warren said: "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money." Warren told CBS News in January 2026 that she believes Congress could work with Mr. Trump to cap rates.

Researchers who studied Mr. Trump's campaign pledge after it was first announced found that Americans would save roughly $100 billion in interest a year if credit card rates were capped at 10%. The same researchers found that while the credit card industry would take a major hit, it would still be profitable, although credit card rewards and other perks might be scaled back.
About 195 million people in the United States had credit cards in 2024 and were assessed $160 billion in interest charges, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says.
Americans are now carrying more credit card debt than ever, to the tune of about $1.23 trillion, according to figures from the New York Federal Reserve for the third quarter last year.

title: Families frustrated with Pentagon probe of deadly drone strike
summary: The Pentagon is preparing to release findings of its investigation into the attack that killed six U.S. soldiers in Kuwait early in the Iran war.
story: Gold Star families have told CBS News that briefings about a forthcoming U.S. military report on the deadliest strike on U.S. soldiers in the Iran conflict did not, to their satisfaction, address their concerns about the military preparations and response to the attack.

Several of the families said they have been briefed about the unclassified results from the long-awaited internal probe into one of the first attacks on U.S. troops during Operation Epic Fury. Six U.S. Army Reserve soldiers were killed by a drone strike on their command post in Kuwait, known as Port Shuaiba, on March 1.
The official report has not yet been released to the public. The Pentagon has indicated it could be made public in a matter of days.
Over the past week, the Army briefed at least three Gold Star families on the investigation, and several family members told CBS News they were frustrated by what they heard.

Some of those briefed told CBS News the report does little to address the findings of an eight-month CBS News investigation, in which multiple sources said Army commanders ignored repeated warnings about the drone threat in the weeks before the attack.

Witnesses told CBS News that the facilities were not fortified to protect service members from a strike by one-way attack drones, which are a staple of the Iranian arsenal. Soldiers on the site said they had seen U.S. intelligence prior to the war showing the location was on an Iranian target list. And they argued the facilities lacked sufficient medical supplies and a plan for a mass casualty incident.

The briefings were led by Brig. Gen. Peter Glass, the deputy commander of U.S. Army Central, according to those who attended. They were individually held at either military or National Guard posts in locations close to the respective families.

"I wish I felt better," a Gold Star family member told CBS News after her briefing, which she said lasted roughly three hours. "I wish this gave me more than what I had yesterday or what I had the day before."

The briefings come just days after a U.S. Army soldier who survived the deadly Iranian drone attack filed a whistleblower complaint to Congress alleging senior military officials ignored warnings and did not plan properly for anti-drone defenses ahead of the war with Iran.

The whistleblower, Army Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom, spoke exclusively with 60 Minutes' Norah O'Donnell about his complaint, which was submitted to the House and Senate Armed Services Committees on Nov. 13 and obtained by CBS News.

In the complaint, Ramsbottom alleges that Army leaders were warned about drone threats at   the U.S. command post, and alleges the site had "no dedicated protection" against the Iranian drones. In an interview with CBS News, he identified Brig. Gen. Clint Barnes, who commanded the unit, and Maj. Gen. John Hinson, who oversaw logistics for the U.S. command, as dismissing warnings about protection at the location. Ramsbottom called for an independent investigation.
Neither official responded to multiple requests for comment from CBS News.

Another Gold Star family member described the briefing as mostly "cordial" but said the exchange grew tense when family members pressed for more answers about why the unit was moved to Port Shuaiba when most other soldiers were sent out of Kuwait ahead of the launch of Operation Epic Fury.
"We took a couple breaks because it got heavy and I needed some air," one family member said.

Joey Amor, whose wife, Master Sgt. Nicole Amor, was among those killed, told 60 Minutes he believes she might have survived if there was a better plan in place. "I think my wife had a shot, yeah," he said.
He said investigators told him that, no matter what medical resources were present, his wife's injuries were too severe for her to have survived the strike.

The Pentagon for months has declined comment to CBS News, but confirmed its internal investigation into the Port Shuaiba attack concluded in June. Still, it would take until mid-November for the Army to share its findings — another point of contention for some Gold Star family members.
"Going in I had an idea of what I wanted to know," another family member said. "I just knew I wasn't going to get answers — and I was right."

title: Marine Corps hero under federal investigation
summary: Retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal, whose bloodied visage was depicted in an iconic Iraq War photo, is under investigation stemming from his tenure as a high school JROTC instructor.
story: Henderson, Nevada — One of the most celebrated Marine Corps veterans, whose heroism during the Iraq War earned him the nation's second-highest award for combat valor and a place in military history, is the subject of a criminal investigation over allegations stemming from his tenure as a high school instructor for a Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps, CBS News has learned.

Retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal, who served in the Marine Corps for 34 years, is under investigation by the Naval Criminal Investigative Service, the primary federal law enforcement agency for matters involving the Navy and Marine Corps.

The allegations against the highly decorated Marine veteran have not been disclosed by the law enforcement agency. However, federal agencies told CBS News that the investigation concerns the period of time when he worked as a JROTC instructor at the Basic Academy of International Studies. The academy is a public high school in Henderson, Nevada, operated by the Clark County School District.

The federal investigation marks a dramatic turn for a Marine whose actions on the battlefield made him a symbol of military courage. Kasal's heroism was captured in a 2004 photograph showing him in the Second Battle of Fallujah. His uniform was soaked in blood, and he was being helped out of a building by two Marines. His right leg was shattered, and his body riddled with gunshot wounds and grenade fragments, but he still gripped a pistol and combat knife. The scene was later immortalized in statues installed at two Marine bases. He retired after 34 years of service and was the recipient of two Purple Hearts and the Navy Cross, the second-highest decoration for combat valor, behind the Medal of Honor.

On Wednesday, the Marine Corps told CBS News that the service is "aware of the allegations against a retired Marine Sergeant Major which occurred while he was employed as a civilian JROTC instructor by the Basic Academy of International Studies."
The Marine Corps also said that the Naval Criminal Investigative Service "is actively investigating the allegations, as the Department of the Navy's lead for felony-level criminal investigations."
Separately, Denise Caskey of NCIS confirmed that its field office at Camp Pendleton in California is conducting the investigation.

NCIS does not typically confirm active investigations, making this an unusual case. The agency commonly investigates matters of homicide, sexual assault, fraud and even terrorism and espionage cases. The agency also conducts counterintelligence investigations, working with other federal agencies to identify threats to national security.
Kasal did not reply to CBS News' multiple attempts to contact him.

CBS News traveled to Henderson, Nevada, and over the course of the last two weeks spoke to nearly 40 people, including former students, school district employees, city officials, parents, U.S. military service members and Marine veterans who served with Kasal. Some asked for anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly or feared reprisal.

The cadets CBS News spoke to alleged Kasal often gave rides home to a select group of female cadets. He would take them to Starbucks and spend time with certain students outside of school-sponsored functions. Some also described instances when he was alone with a cadet in a room.

A former school district employee told CBS News that Kasal was advised on several occasions about the perceptions surrounding his relationships with students and was warned against putting himself in potentially compromising situations, including being alone in a room with a cadet.

One former female cadet described developing an unusually close relationship with Kasal after meeting him in 2020, when she was 14. She said she confided in him about difficulties at home and personal matters, including her relationships with boys. After knowing her for barely a year, Kasal offered to adopt her, saying in a text message, "I'm not asking as charity. I'm asking because your [sic] wanted."

When her family members learned of Kasal's offer, she said, they made it clear that adoption was not an option. She said that her relationship with Kasal continued, and she remained comfortable confiding in him about deeply personal matters. The cadet alleged some of their conversations involved sexual rumors that had been spread about her and why Kasal believed some of the problems she was experiencing stemmed from her relationship with her father. In retrospect, she said she realizes that those conversations were inappropriate for an instructor to have with a teenage student.

She now says she thinks Kasal crossed other boundaries, alleging that Kasal invited certain cadets to spend time at his home and at his cabin, she said, including for at least one birthday celebration. He did not extend invitations to everyone in the program. She also claimed that Kasal drove one student home nearly every day.

The Clark County School District told CBS News Kasal was hired by the school district three months after he retired from the Marine Corps, in August 2018. He resigned in August 2025, the school district said.
Enrollment in Basic Academy's JROTC program fluctuates from year to year, averaging roughly 135 students. The program is overseen by a senior Marine instructor and a senior enlisted leader.
When Kasal transitioned from the Marine Corps to the high school JROTC program, he sought to restructure it to more closely resemble the military service.

Some former cadets described him as professional and organized, crediting him with establishing strict standards and bringing a sense of discipline to the program. They also praised the time, energy and personal resources he devoted to his students.

Samantha Francisco, 22, who was in the program from 2018 to 2022, said, "I can't say enough about how amazing he was," and that "he genuinely cared about everybody and taught us incredible lessons." She added that she and her husband, who was also in the JROTC program, still talk weekly about Kasal or something he taught them.

Ashley Vazquez Romo, 22, another cadet from that period, said Kasal "poured his heart and soul into the program." She recalled that he sometimes helped pay for program outings and purchased equipment, including a CPR training mannequin, so students could practice.

Damien Greenwell, 22, who participated in the JROTC program from 2018 to 2022, told CBS News that he deeply respects Kasal for his military service and mentorship, especially to cadets with a troubled home life. But Greenwell also said that over the years he questioned Kasal's conduct on several occasions, adding that even if the decorated Marine's intentions were innocent, his actions could appear inappropriate to an outside observer.

"He would mentor us on how to be a proper leader — which is his job — but he would go a bit beyond this. Sergeant Major [Kasal] helps people in a time of need and that's very honorable," Greenwell said.

"If someone couldn't eat, he would pay for their food. If someone didn't have a ride home, he would help them out. It's awesome, it's great and very commendable," Greenwell said. "But if you're regularly getting Starbucks for a girl … it looks kind of weird … and with driving people home on a consistent basis, it looks bad. You need to have a certain kind of boundary between you and students."
Greenwell told CBS News he remembers a night that still "shocks him a little." It happened in 2024, two years after Greenwell graduated.

Greenwell claimed he went to Lowe's home improvement store around 9 p.m. and saw Kasal's truck in the parking lot. In the store, he observed Kasal walking with a student who he believes was a senior at the high school or a newly minted graduate.

"It was just really weird to me," Greenwell said, recalling that he briefly exchanged greetings with Kasal and the student before the two continued down the aisle. CBS News is withholding the student's name for privacy reasons.

Greenwell said over the years of observing Kasal, he developed doubts about him. He believed the optics could be interpreted as inappropriate, but at the same time wonders if Kasal could just be trying to help students navigate the difficulties of life. But even if he found a relationship between Kasal and a student odd, he was "not gonna say anything. Like, who am I to tell [a] sergeant major?"
Daniel Gillan, who participated in the program from 2018 to 2022 and later enlisted in the Marine Corps, said JROTC was good for him and that Kasal was part of the reason he ended up joining.

The program "gave me a lot of structure and discipline," Gillan said, adding that Kasal helped him "become a better person overall, and once you become a better person, things will fall into place for you."

Gillan said he never witnessed Kasal engage in inappropriate behavior. He sees Kasal as having made an effort to create memorable experiences for students by organizing group hikes, camping trips and other activities outside the classroom. He said Kasal recognized that some students did not have a good home life, and he wanted to make the JROTC program enjoyable and inclusive, emphasizing that all cadets were invited to participate.

Still, he acknowledged that Kasal appeared to favor certain cadets, sometimes buying them coffee, for instance. Gillan said Kasal had also bought coffee for him, but he didn't think it was inappropriate, describing him as a "nice guy."

Gillan also alleged Kasal would take cadets on hikes without seeking permission from the school, but he said this was more a matter of convenience. The hiking trail was only a few minutes away from Basic Academy.
"It was about a 10-minute drive from Basic, and [about] 20 cadets would go. Whoever wanted to go, they would go. We would all carpool," Gillan said, and the hikes were just about an hour.

"Legally, you gotta get [trips] ran through the school, and they gotta approve of it, … but [Kasal is] not gonna wait for [the school] to take two weeks to [approve] an event that takes one day to get back."
One former male cadet, who joined the program in 2019 and now serves in the U.S. military, alleged that Kasal invited him to visit his cabin in Iowa over the summer.

The trip was not school-sponsored, he said, and "it was just going to be the two of us." He says he declined the invitation because he was playing a sport that summer. At the time, he said, he did not consider the invitation to be inappropriate, believing Kasal had extended it because they shared an interest in the sport.

Greenwell said that at one point, he heard a rumor that Kasal was trying to adopt a fellow cadet but that he didn't believe it was true. When CBS News told him that Kasal had offered to adopt a former female cadet, Greenwell said he was "very surprised, shocked and disappointed."
"Even if you have the best intentions in the world, it still looks bad, no matter how you put it, because she's a minor," said Greenwell.

The Defense Department and local school districts share responsibility for overseeing JROTC programs because they are federally sponsored and operate in high schools nationwide. Although instructors are employed by school districts, they must also be certified by their respective military branches, which are responsible for monitoring their professional conduct and ensuring compliance with military standards.
The military services certify and oversee instructors, while school districts handle employment decisions, classroom supervision and compliance with local education policies.

JROTC instructors must acknowledge in writing that they will not engage in prohibited activities between JROTC instructors and students. The rules ban instructors from developing personal, intimate or sexual relationships with cadets, engaging in inappropriate communications and attending social gatherings with students on a personal basis. The restrictions apply from an instructor's first contact with a cadet until six months after the student leaves the JROTC program.

Under the rules, instructors are generally not allowed to give students rides in their personal vehicles, including rides home from school. Exceptions may be made when a student's safety or welfare is at risk or for official school functions involving multiple students. The rules specifically prohibit an instructor from transporting a single student in their personal vehicles.

Instructors are also not allowed to have cadets or other students in their homes. Other interactions, such as purchasing coffee or refreshments for students, are not explicitly prohibited. But such interactions could raise questions about compliance with the rules.
Instructors must sign the acknowledgment before beginning their duties as JROTC instructors and recertify it annually.
When CBS News received the initial news tip regarding Kasal, the Marine Corps said it was aware of allegations and of an investigation, but made no mention of NCIS' involvement.

The Henderson Police Department initially said it had no record of a complaint about Kasal. The Clark County Detention Center and the Clark County District Attorney's Office also did not have any complaints about Kasal on file when contacted some two weeks ago.

Later, during that same period, a spokesperson for the Henderson Police Department said the Clark County School District Police Department was handling the matter. Multiple calls and emails to the Clark County School District and the school district's police department went unanswered. Lt. Bryan Zink of the Clark County School District police department referred inquiries to the school district.
Last week, when CBS News emailed to check in on its inquiry, an email sent in error to CBS News asked a human resources manager to "disregard the request."
When CBS News asked why the request for information was being disregarded, Bryan Callahan, the district's public information officer, emailed for the first time: "We are looking into your request."

When questioned by a CBS News reporter in Henderson earlier this week, Callahan said he was not aware of an investigation of Kasal by the Clark County School District or the school district's police department.

Before he retired from active duty, Kasal reflected on his time in Iraq. The Second Battle of Fallujah in November 2004 was the bloodiest battle involving U.S. Marines since the Vietnam War, marked by brutal house-to-house fighting against Iraqi insurgents.

In 2018, Kasal told CBS News' David Martin that he had entered the building to rescue fellow Marines trapped by insurgent gunfire during one of the war's bloodiest battles. By the time he emerged, Kasal had been shot seven times, shielded a wounded Marine from an exploding grenade and refused medical treatment until others received care.
His actions earned him his second Purple Heart and the Navy Cross.
The photograph of Kasal became an iconic symbol of Marine resilience and sacrifice. The Marine Corps Heritage Foundation named a photojournalism award for Kasal.

The photograph inspired a bronze statue called the "No Man Left Behind" monument, which is installed at both Camp Pendleton in California and Camp Lejeune in North Carolina, according to the Marine Times. The sculpture was the work of John Phelps, a Navy Vietnam veteran whose son Chance was killed in Iraq in 2004, the newspaper reported.

When CBS News first learned about the criminal investigation into Kasal earlier this month, the retired sergeant major was in New York as the guest of honor at an event hosted by the NYPD Marine Corps Association to commemorate 251 years since the founding of the U.S. Marine Corps and honor Marines who also serve as New York City police officers. The New York Post reported that Kasal was presented a framed retirement shadowbox by NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch at police headquarters in Manhattan.
James LaPorta reported from Henderson, Nevada. Julia Kimani Burnham and Eleanor Watson reported from Washington, D.C.

Editor's note: For the past three years, James LaPorta has served as a judge for the Marine Corps Heritage Foundation annual awards program. He has never judged the award category named for retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal.
Editor's note: An earlier version of this article misspelled former JROTC cadet Daniel Gillan's name. The article has been updated.

title: House Ethics aims to speed up sexual misconduct investigations
summary: The pace of the committee's investigations has come under scrutiny after several members were accused of sexual misconduct this year.
story: Washington — The House Ethics Committee on Thursday approved several changes aimed at improving how the secretive bipartisan panel handles sexual misconduct investigations.

The pace of the committee's investigations has come under scrutiny after several members were accused of sexual misconduct this year. Two lawmakers — Democratic Rep. Eric Swalwell of California and Republican Rep. Tony Gonzales of Texas — resigned before the committee could complete its work. Other members under investigation by the committee for sexual misconduct either ended their campaign or lost their reelection bids.
The panel met briefly Thursday afternoon in a rare public meeting to discuss the proposed changes, which were detailed in a news release Friday.

The committee delegated subpoena authority to the chairman and ranking member, instead of requiring that the full committee vote on subpoenas. The change should "significantly expedite" its investigations, the committee said.

The committee also codified its longstanding policy of publicly disclosing when a member has been found to have engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct, while protecting the identity of victims.

It also consolidated duplicative procedural steps and simplified the process, which it said should "accelerate the conclusion of investigations by several months or more while still providing for important due process protections."
Another change includes "expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered as appropriate sanctions."

"The House of Representatives must have a zero-tolerance policy for sexual harassment and misconduct and the Committee on Ethics is committed to ensuring that its practices and processes sufficiently hold perpetrators accountable and deliver justice for survivors," Rep. Mark DeSaulnier of California, the top Democrat on the committee, said in a statement Friday.

A bipartisan initiative aimed at addressing how sexual misconduct claims are handled within the House was formed earlier this year to propose reforms. The group, led by Reps. Kat Cammack, a Florida Republican, and Teresa Leger Fernández, a New Mexico Democrat, has yet to release its recommendations.

title: Musk said he'd "look into" this disclosure law. Now it heads to court.
summary: Two county prosecutors say the Trump administration broke the law when it exempted U.S. companies from ownership reporting.
story: In March 2025, a conservative comedian named Terrence K. Williams had a plea for Elon Musk: ask President Trump to scrap a "ridiculous" federal rule that forced companies to disclose their true owners.
"I'm begging you!" Williams posted on X, Musk's social media platform. "It's targeting conservatives and small businesses!"
The billionaire replied, "I can look into it."

A day later, the Trump administration took action. In a post on X, the Treasury Department announced it would no longer enforce penalties or fines against U.S. citizens, domestic companies or their owners under the law, known as the Corporate Transparency Act.
Now, two local prosecutors are suing to stop the administration from erasing roughly 15 million company ownership records it has already collected, CBS News has learned.

On Thursday, the top prosecutors in Hennepin County, Minnesota, and Pima County, Arizona — Mary Moriarty and Laura Conover — alleged in a lawsuit that the Treasury Department violated the law when it exempted American companies from the disclosure rules and let foreign companies leave out their American owners.

Moriarty and Conover, both Democrats, say the ownership records would help their offices pursue cartel money laundering, wage theft, fraud and organized retail theft carried out through shell companies. The suit also names Attorney General Todd Blanche and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, whose departments had to sign off on the exemptions.

Deleting the records would make it "easier than ever for criminals to use shell and front companies for illicit activities and evade detection," the lawsuit, filed in federal court in Washington, D.C., says. It argues that "because law enforcement cannot know in advance which companies will warrant scrutiny, the value of beneficial-ownership reporting lies in collecting that information before the need for it arises."

In a statement to CBS News, a Treasury spokesperson said removing the reporting requirement was "a victory for common sense," adding that the department made the change "after careful consideration of the costs to small business owners and the benefit to national security."
The agency did not respond to questions about whether Musk reached out to Treasury about the rule. A spokesperson for Musk did not respond to requests for comment.

The lawsuit escalates a fight between Democrats and the Trump administration over the rollback, which critics have scrutinized for its timing. The complaint cites Musk's exchange with Williams, saying he had "set his sights on" the disclosure rule while leading the Department of Government Efficiency. Democrats in Congress have questioned Musk's possible role since April 2025, when they wrote to the Treasury Department that the decision was "seemingly triggered by a single Elon Musk social media comment."

Democratic Sens. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, along with California Rep. Maxine Waters, said in a March 2026 letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that Musk "uses a network of dozens of secretive companies" that could potentially be required to share ownership information under the law.

"This rule started with an Elon Musk post on X and will end with 15 million documents in the shredder," said Brendan Ballou, a former Justice Department prosecutor whose firm, the Public Integrity Project, is representing the plaintiffs.
The Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security declined to comment.
A plan to delete millions of records

The Corporate Transparency Act became law in January 2021 with bipartisan support, after Congress included it in a defense bill and overrode Mr. Trump's veto of the broader package. Then-Florida Sen. Marco Rubio, one of its champions and now Mr. Trump's secretary of state, called it in 2020 "the most significant anti-corruption [and] money laundering law in decades."

The law's aim was to combat money laundering and illicit finance by requiring companies to report their true owners to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, a Treasury Department office known as FinCEN. The reporting requirement took effect in 2024, covering nearly 33 million companies, until the Trump administration narrowed it to foreign firms.
By then, U.S. companies had filed about 15 million reports with FinCEN, according to the Treasury Department.
In August 2026, the agency said it plans to delete them in "one sweep of the database" and will notify the public on its website once it's done.
Supporters of the law say it helps investigators follow the money behind crimes like sanctions evasion, drug trafficking and smuggling.

"The only way that you can actually create an easy chain to examine these flows is if you're able to unmask who's behind all these types of transactions," said Max Meizlish, a former career Treasury sanctions official who is now a fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a foreign policy think tank.

In its final rule, the Treasury Department argued the requirement placed "costs of time and money" on "law-abiding American small businesses," and said the rollback would save billions of dollars a year. The department concluded that requiring domestic companies to report their owners "would not serve the public interest," and that "indiscriminate collection" of that information "would not provide law enforcement with highly valuable information."

A number of Republicans have long said that the law buried mom-and-pop companies in paperwork and threatened them with steep financial penalties. In January 2025, Alabama Sen. Tommy Tuberville and Ohio Rep. Warren Davidson reintroduced a bill to repeal the law entirely. Tuberville called it "big-government overreach at its worst."

Not all Republicans welcomed the rollback, though. Iowa Sen. Chuck Grassley, who co-sponsored an earlier version of the law with Whitehouse, urged Treasury in 2025 to scrap its initial rollback. When the final rule came out in August 2026, the two senators said in a joint statement that it "undermines the clear intent of the law."

Without the corporate records, the lawsuit argues, investigators must subpoena bank after bank to learn who is behind a shell company, a slow process that often yields thin or inaccurate answers. The prosecutors are asking a judge to throw out the rule and stop the deletion.
"Wage thieves and fraudsters hide behind shell companies because it works," Moriarty said in a statement. "The only people who benefit are the ones we are trying to catch."

title: Too many House Republicans are missing work, Mike Johnson says
summary: Dozens of House members didn't show up to vote this week. They're still getting paid.
story: Washington — Too many House Republicans skipped work this week, and House Speaker Mike Johnson isn't happy about it. Their absences are holding up legislation in the last few days the GOP controls Congress.

In a "Dear Colleague" letter he posted on X Friday, Johnson said "we need every House Republican to remain fully engaged," and lamented that the House was forced to postpone a vote scheduled earlier this week "because we didn't have enough members in town."
"To state the obvious, barring any serious medical issue, we need every Republican to be here to faithfully complete our two-year term," Johnson wrote.
Johnson's letter comes after GOP leaders had to pull a scheduled procedural vote from the floor due to attendance issues, with 14 Republicans missing.

Members of Congress will be paid until early January. The base salary for a rank-and-file House Republican is $174,000, while those in leadership positions earn more. "The Twentieth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution specifies that our clock doesn't run out until noon on January 3rd," Johnson concluded. "LET'S SCORE EVERY POINT WE CAN AND LEAVE IT ALL ON THE FIELD!"

Both Republicans and Democrats missed votes this week, although more Republicans were absent. According to the House clerk's office, in the last six floor votes since Nov. 11, between 23 and 35 members failed to vote. On Thursday, the final day in the House session this week, 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats and one independent missed votes.

Republicans have a packed to-do list before the end of the year, which includes passing a funding bill that would avert a government shutdown on Dec. 11, as well as the annual defense policy bill. Republicans also hope to get the farm bill and permitting reform bill across the finish line during this lame-duck period.
Speaking to reporters Thursday at the Capitol, Johnson said, "Attendance is a great frustration for me right now. We'll be addressing that with members."

"I am going to be here working," he said. "The leadership team are going to be here working. We want to run through the tape and finish strong, but we can't do that unless people are present at work."
Votes were canceled on Friday to allow lawmakers to return to their districts and states for the Thanksgiving break. The House won't return until Monday, Nov. 30.
Several of those who did not show up were among the more than 30 incumbent House Republicans who lost their seats this month.

Among the 14 Republicans who missed votes on Wednesday, those who were defeated in November included Reps. Lauren Boebert of Colorado, Monica De La Cruz of Texas, Scott DesJarlais of Tennessee, Max Miller of Ohio, and Jeff Van Drew of New Jersey. Other GOP lawmakers who missed votes are not returning to Congress or lost their elections for higher office.

title: Trump touts Asia trip, meeting with Putin and Xi at news conference
summary: President Trump touted his trip to Asia this week and his meetings with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin at a press conference at the White House.
story: What to know about Trump's news conference today:

President Trump touted his trip to Asia this week and his meetings with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin at a press conference at the White House on Friday, saying the U.S. is "respected again like never before."The president said the trip was "one of the most successful presidential visits to Asia in American history."
