title: Anthropic files for IPO as it competes for AI dominance
summary: Anthropic, which developed the Claude chatbot, is barreling ahead with its public offering despite mounting concerns about AI going rogue.
story: Anthropic filed for an initial public offering on Monday, bringing the maker of artificial intelligence platform Claude a step closer to its highly anticipated public market debut and providing a key test for the rapidly emerging AI sector.
In the filing, Anthropic outlined its vision for a future profoundly shaped by AI, touting the technology's potential to transform the global economy and improve lives worldwide.

"We believe the diffusion of AI through the global economy represents one of the largest opportunities in history to improve how humans live and work, and it is just beginning," the company said in its S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The filing highlights Anthropic's rapid growth, with the company generating $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year. That staggering rate of expansion is likely to slow, with Anthropic noting that its revenue growth is expected to decline over time.

The company has yet to turn a profit. Anthropic reported a net loss of $80.7 billion for the first half of the year, more than six times the net loss of nearly $13 billion for the first two quarters in 2025.
Anthropic's founders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, pitched the IPO to investors in part as an opportunity to be part of a history-defining moment.

"We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms," the company's seven co-founders said in a letter included in the S-1. "We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history."
Referendum on AI

The IPO, which market analysts expect as early as November, could instantly rank Anthropic among the world's largest publicly traded companies. The offering could raise as much as $100 billion, according to reports. That would slingshot it past Elon Musk-owned SpaceX, which raised a record-breaking $86 billion when it went public in June.
Anthropic, which was valued at $965 billion in May, could see its value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established.
Anthropic shares will list on the Nasdaq stock exchange, according to the company's filing. The AI company will trade under the ticker symbol "ANT."

More broadly, the transaction will gauge the strength of investor demand not only for Anthropic shares, but also for the widening constellation of data center builders, chipmakers and other companies involved in developing the critical infrastructure powering AI services.

"This IPO is a referendum on the entire AI trade," Nigel Green, CEO of investment firm deVere Group, said in an email. "If it soars, expect a queue of AI listings and even more capital piling into the theme. If it stumbles, valuations across tech could reset fast."

The torrent of capital flowing into AI has helped propel the stock market to record highs. The question is whether AI can maintain its momentum amid signs that investors are fretting over when — and if — their money will eventually pay off and deliver the returns they are banking on.

Anthropic's prospectus shows that the company has funneled massive amounts of money toward building the computing resources necessary to power its AI models. The company spent $8.9 billion in the first half of the year on chips and other infrastructure to run its platform, compared to $2.3 billion over the same period last year.

"Anthropic could become the most valuable company in the world. It could also end up in bankruptcy," analysts with Lightshed, an investment advisory firm, said in a research note ahead of the IPO filing.
Potential obstacles to growth

Anthropic's IPO filing also outlines various risks that could hamper its growth or cause it to fall behind competitors. Much of the company's future growth hinges on whether it has access to sufficient capital, including debt financing, which more companies are using to finance the AI buildout.

To maintain its competitive edge, Anthropic also said it will need to use its existing AI models to design and train next-generation platforms, a process known as "recursive self-improvement," or RSI.

"If we fail to direct sufficient compute and research efforts to AI-assisted development, or if our competitors more effectively leverage AI to enhance their own innovation cycles, we risk falling progressively further behind. …" Anthropic said in the filing.

AI experts warn that using AI to build ever more powerful frontier models raises the risk of people losing control of the technology, potentially leading to disasters such as deadly pandemics or cyberattacks that cut off internet, electricity or water.
Barreling ahead despite safety concerns

Anthropic filed a confidential IPO with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, beating out rival OpenAI, which filed just over a week later. Both companies are barreling ahead with plans to go public despite concerns about the potential threats AI poses to humanity.

Reports of AI agents going rogue continue to pile up, stoking concern that the technology could escape human control and carry out cyberattacks. In September, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development after one of his company's former researchers said that there's a 10% chance the technology could wipe out humanity in the next decade.
In an interview with CBS News, Amodei said the pace of technological growth should serve as a warning sign, while making a case for continued development of AI.

title: Hawley, Durbin introduce Roblox safety bill ahead of hearing
summary: The legislation would allow families of individuals harmed by tech products to take their claims to court even if they agreed to the company's terms of service for private arbitration.
story: Missouri Republican Josh Hawley and Illinois Democrat Dick Durbin are introducing new legislation targeting sexual abuse on Roblox and online gaming platforms, CBS News has learned.

The legislation, titled the No Forced Arbitration for Child Sexual Exploitation and Cyber Injuries Act, would allow families of individuals harmed by tech products to take their claims to court even if they agreed to the company's terms of service for private arbitration. Roblox is being sued by dozens of families and state attorneys general who claim online predators have been able to groom, extort and exploit kids they meet on the platform.

The measure is being rolled out ahead of an inaugural congressional hearing Tuesday into the popular gaming portal. The hearing, chaired by Hawley, will feature witness testimony from two abuse survivors and a pair of experts.

"I am investigating allegations that Roblox, a popular online gaming platform for kids, has become a breeding ground for sexual predators," Hawley said in a statement. "This week, as my Subcommittee holds the first-ever congressional hearing on Roblox's practices, Senator Durbin and I will introduce new bipartisan legislation to give survivors justice. We must hold these platforms accountable and ensure no child is left vulnerable to exploitation online."

The bill would close loopholes to ensure a child's rights aren't limited in click-through agreements, allow class-action lawsuits and let survivors and families choose whether to bring a claim in public court or through confidential arbitration.

"In the digital age, predators can target our kids from anywhere—including online gaming platforms like Roblox. And sadly, the numbers show that they have," said Durbin. "Therefore, an 'agreement' buried in the terms of service shouldn't limit a child's or family's rights to bring their claim before a judge or jury. I'm proud to partner with Senator Hawley on this bipartisan issue, and I won't stop until this bill—and other key measures to protect children online—are signed into law."
CEO Dave Baszucki was invited to testify at Tuesday's hearing but has declined to appear.

"The claims being made about Roblox are fundamentally misleading and ignore the rigorous safeguards we have in place to help protect users," a Roblox spokesperson said in a statement to CBS News. "Roblox's mandatory age checks for chat, age-based content, prohibition on sharing photos or videos via chat, and continuous monitoring and filtering of chat, help set the standard for youth protection online."
In August, Hawley and Durbin launched a joint investigation by the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism into child safety on Roblox.

"Roblox appears to prioritize revenue and engagement metrics over the safety and well-being of our children, and the alleged criminal activity on Roblox warrants congressional scrutiny," the Senators wrote in a letter to the company at the time.

Roblox has 138 million daily active users, ranging in age from five to over 25, according to its latest shareholder letter released at the end of October. The company currently faces nearly 200 lawsuits in federal court and has reached settlements with at least six states over online child safety issues.

This month, Roblox chief safety officer Matt Kaufman wrote that the company continues to partner with law enforcement and "aggressively look for bad behavior and report it through the appropriate channels."

Last year, the company announced it would strengthen its age verification protections for minors. Roblox CEO David Baszucki described the guardrails in an interview with "CBS Mornings" as "what we believe will become the gold standard for safety and civility on the internet."

title: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
summary: Nvidia said Monday that it has restored Jensen Huang as the chipmaker's chief executive, calling him the "right person" to lead the company.
story: Nvidia's board of directors said on Monday that it has reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO.
The action comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned amid scandal over an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of spying for China. China has denied it.

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," board Chair Harvey C. Jones said in a statement on Monday. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company."
In a statement, Huang said he is "honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution."
He also thanked the company's board, interim CEO Colete Kress, and Nvidia staffers and shareholders.
"I can't wait to get back to work," Huang added.

Dan Ives, a tech analyst with Yorkville Ives, told CBS News that the board "had no choice" but to bring Huang back as CEO, saying that the executive's shock resignation earlier this month was becoming an "economic and global markets issue."
Nvidia makes advanced chips and other components that help power AI, which is driving economic growth in the U.S. and until recently had fueled record stock market gains.
"Nvidia is the linchpin to the global economy," Ives said.
After U.S. markets opened on Monday, Nvidia's stock soared nearly 30% on news of Huang's reinstatement.

title: ICE officers arrest 2 passengers boarding flight in Seattle
summary: Masked immigration officers arrested two passengers on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday.
story: Masked immigration officers arrested two passengers on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, federal officials said, causing what Alaska Airlines called a "distressing" scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight.
Videos of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as a woman screamed that her daughter was being taken and she has a work permit.
Alaska Airlines said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

"We are concerned by this morning's law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306," the airline said. "We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests."
An Alaska Airlines spokesperson told CBS News on Sunday that the flight, scheduled to depart at 8:45 a.m., left the airport at 11:03 a.m. after some crew members asked to leave.

"Immediately following the incident, some inflight crew members requested to be replaced. As we learned more about what occurred, we ultimately brought in an entirely new crew," the airline spokesperson said in a statement.

In a statement provided to CBS News Saturday evening, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, the parent agency of ICE, said that ICE officers "conducted a targeted enforcement operation" on a Mexican national identified as Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza who had "overstayed his visa."

During the arrest, a second passenger "hurled hot coffee" at the officers, the DHS spokesperson said in the statement. That second passenger, identified by DHS as Sofia Hernandez Mejia, is a Mexican national who had also been determined to have overstayed her visa, the spokesperson said.
Mejia was also subsequently arrested and will face federal charges of assaulting a federal officer, DHS said.
A DHS source told CBS News the two people arrested are a father and daughter.

Mendoza and Mejia remained in ICE custody in Washington, immigration attorney Olia Catala told CBS News on Sunday night, saying she was visiting her clients at the Northwest Processing Center in Tacoma.

Democratic Rep. Adam Smith of Washington said in an earlier statement that "masked ICE agents detained at least one passenger waiting to board an Alaska Airlines flight at Sea-Tac Airport. The masked agents forcibly dragged the individual off the jet bridge, taking them into custody."
The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants. Videos showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases looked on.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past. ICE sources told CBS News in July that the uptick in arrests stems from increased collaboration between ICE and the Transportation Security Administration.

On Thursday, a Princeton University student and Chinese national was detained by ICE at Ronald Reagan National Airport in Washington, D.C., after attending a neuroscience conference, the school and her colleagues said.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns "directly with the appropriate authorities."

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would "engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred."
Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, called the incident "just the latest example of ICE's deeply un-American tactics."

"ICE is completely and totally out of control," Ferguson said in a statement. "Like many Americans, I'm outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities."

Democratic Rep. Pramila Jayapal of Washington said in a social media post that she was "disturbed by the reports of this detention at Sea-Tac," adding that her office was "working to gather more information on the situation."

DHS numbers obtained by CBS News last week found that ICE arrested 491,000 people in FY 2026, a record, including nearly 475,000 administrative arrests, also a record. Administrative arrests are those in which alleged undocumented immigrants are arrested for civil violations rather than criminal charges.

In a "60 Minutes" interview earlier this month following the heavy losses suffered by Republicans in the midterm elections, President Trump appeared to acknowledge that his administration's immigration crackdown may have contributed to his party's poor showing.

"For getting people out, I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out," Mr. Trump told "60 Minutes." "But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally. Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out. And there's a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes."
Of his deportation policies, the president said: "I think it was too tough. A lot of people would say that it's great, but a lot of people think it's too tough."

title: Stock futures rise, erasing some losses after tech rout
summary: U.S. stock index futures regained ground on Monday, but Wall Street analysts think it's too soon to sound the all-clear.
story: Stock futures in the U.S. climbed before the opening bell as financial markets partially rebounded from a major technology sell-off on Friday that plunged the S&P 500 and Dow into correction territory.

Nasdaq Composite futures rose 3%, regaining ground after the technology-heavy index fell 1,261 points, or 5.3%, on Nov. 20, its second-worst day of 2026. S&P 500 futures gained 2.4%, while Dow Jones Industrial Average futures rose 1.8%.
Despite the signs of recovery, Wall Street analysts said investors remain on edge amid concerns that the artificial intelligence sector is unraveling.

"Stocks in the U.S. are staging a large rebound rally so far this morning, although, just to put things into context, the S&P futures aren't even reclaiming its loss from Friday, much less the entire week," Vital Knowledge analyst Adam Crisafulli said in a note to investors on Monday.
"Sentiment remains pretty bleak — most people are looking at this [Monday] uptick as nothing more than technical in nature, a partial reversal of extremely oversold conditions," he added.

Financial markets tumbled Friday as concerns swelled about a possible slowdown in data center construction across the U.S. and tightening restrictions on chip exports, both of which could hurt corporate profits.

The losses were led by microchip companies like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom, which shed 13.3% and 12.2%, respectively. Both were recovering Monday, with AMD futures up 4.8% in premarket trading and Broadcom futures gaining 4.6%.

Futures for Nvidia, which has seen a major setback since the departure of former CEO Jensen Huang, surged 8.6%. Anthropic, which made its public market debut on Thursday, was mostly flat, rising 0.3% in premarket trading.

title: Anthropic's IPO set for blastoff in key test for AI boom
summary: Anthropic's stock is poised to start trading on Nasdaq Thursday in one of the largest IPOs of all time. The AI world is watching.
story: Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering is set to launch on Thursday, a milestone that will test investor enthusiasm for the company behind the popular Claude chatbot and the burgeoning artificial intelligence sector.

"This is a case where the deal is so large and important, so central to the AI thesis, that it's going to be a turning point for the AI sector," Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at Renaissance Capital, told CBS News. "Even non-AI companies are going to feel the ripple effects, especially in the IPO market."
Anthropic shares are scheduled to start trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol "ANT" sometime after markets open Thursday at 9:30 a.m. ET.
Anthropic increases stock price amid high demand

In an announcement on Wednesday night, San Francisco-based Anthropic said it will offer 980 million shares of Class A common stock priced at $83 each. The initial public offering raised around $81 billion and valued Anthropic at $1.5 trillion, making it the largest public offering in history. Elon Musk's SpaceX raised $75 billion when it went public in June.
Anthropic is selling 956.3 million shares, although only 7.4% will be available for public trading (up to 9.8% including Class A shares held by nonfounder employees), according to Renaissance.

The company plans to raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, all of which have a stake in the AI race.

Kennedy thinks Anthropic shares could reach $100 by the end of their first day of trading, an increase that would represent a "solid pop," he said. If the stock rises closer to $140, "that would tell me that AI enthusiasm has come roaring back," he added.
Great expectations
Although many investors appear eager to own a piece of Anthropic, the IPO comes amid growing concerns about whether the torrid spending on AI will deliver the expected productivity and profit boom.

AI-related stocks have fluctuated in recent weeks following subpar earnings and the mountainous debt companies are taking on to finance data center construction. Jensen Huang's shock exit from Nvidia last week has also rattled investors, with the chipmaker's stock now down more than 35% from its October all-time high.

"The whole AI sector has sold off from its July peak. Investor enthusiasm was greatest then," Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business, told CBS News.

Although Anthropic has yet to turn a profit, the company has shown explosive revenue growth over its short time in business. Anthropic raked in nearly $17 billion in the third quarter this year, up 45% from the second quarter, a recent regulatory filing shows. Given that heady rate of expansion, Ritter expects Anthropic to reach profitability quickly.

To justify its projected trillion-dollar valuation, however, the company will need to sustain that momentum while operating under Wall Street's unsparing gaze. Compounding the challenge is how quickly the AI landscape itself is changing. For instance, Anthropic could struggle to maintain its growth rate as consumers shift from pricier AI models like Claude and ChatGPT to cheaper open-source models, Ritter noted.

Anthropic also will have to spend heavily to keep developing its AI models and stay ahead of rivals, from OpenAI, Alphabet and Meta to Chinese platforms. Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is "substantial." Meanwhile, the company has committed to spending nearly a trillion dollars on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045, according to a securities filing.

Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a national backlash against data centers, giving new impetus to a congressional effort last year to enact a national moratorium on new ones.
"The company is likely to be very successful, but the market is pricing in very lofty expectations," Ritter said. "It could be hard for management to execute."
Wall Street analysts said Anthropic's share offering has broader ramifications for the AI sector, with the IPO's pricing setting a benchmark for other tech companies planning to go public.
Even if Anthropic's stock soars on the first day of trading, it won't necessarily create a swarm of IPO activity, Kennedy said. Still, it could reinvigorate markets, he added.

Meanwhile, by going public, Anthropic is effectively asking investors to discount the threats that Anthropic founder Dario Amodei himself has identified as posed by AI. In September, he called for an industrywide slowdown in AI development after a former Anthropic researcher warned of the existential threat AI poses to humanity.

title: Anthropic shares jump in Nasdaq trading debut after record IPO
summary: Anthropic raised a record $81.3 billion, catapulting it past SpaceX, which raised $75 billion​ when it went public in June.
story: Anthropic's stock soared in early trading on Nasdaq Thursday before partly shedding those gains in the afternoon, as the artificial intelligence developer completed the largest initial public offering in history.

Trading under the ticker "ANT," Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, up 34% from the $83 offer price, and rose as high as $114.99, valuing the company at more than $2 trillion at the peak. The stock pared those gains over the course of the day, closing at $97.17, a rise of 17%.

"Both the jump from the offer price and the high volatility are not surprising, given the enormous potential of the company and the wildly different opinions about how profitable the company will become," Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business, said in an email.

Anthropic shares rose on a day when the rest of the stock market took a dive. Late in Thursday's session, the Nasdaq dropped 550 points, or 2.3%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled more than 1,100 points, or 2.2%, and the S&P 500 sank 2%.
"Seminal" moment
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei celebrated Anthropic's market debut at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York City on Thursday.
"The goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time," Dario Amodei said Thursday in an event to mark the IPO.
"The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history, and we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better," he added.

San Francisco-based Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in its IPO, catapulting past SpaceX, which raised $75 billion when it went public in June. The IPO values the company behind the Claude chatbot at roughly $1.5 trillion, more than companies such as Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway, JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Walmart.

Anthropic's IPO represents an "A-plus success," Dan Ives, a tech analyst and partner of Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News. "I think it's a vote of confidence for the market relative to the tech trade," he added.
The public offering delivered a huge payday to the seven Anthropic co-founders, boosting their worth on paper to around $20 billion each. It will also turn many Anthropic employees into millionaires.

Anthropic said Wednesday that it would offer 980 million shares of Class A common stock priced at $83 per share, allowing it to raise a record-breaking amount. Anthropic originally priced its shares in a range of $70 to $78, but raised its per-share IPO price amid strong investor demand.

The IPO price of $83 a share is what Anthropic insiders and other early investors pay to receive an allocation of stock. According to Renaissance Capital, which tracks IPOs, 7.4% of Anthropic shares are available for public trading (or up to 9.8% if Class A shares held by non-founder employees are included).
Even if Americans don't buy shares, Anthropic's IPO could still affect their 401(k), given how exposed the stock market is to AI stocks.

Anthropic has previously said it will raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, bringing its fundraising total to around $107 billion.
Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at Renaissance Capital, thinks Anthropic shares could reach $100 by the end of their first day of trading.

However, like many companies that go public in a blockbuster, and perhaps overhyped, share offering, Anthropic's stock could well waver in the months to come. In a Truist study of 32 of the biggest ever IPOs, more than half saw their shares slide by at least 50% at some point during their first year of trading.

Anthropic announced its plans to go public in October, inviting investors to be part of what it called one of the "seminal moments in human history." The company is the first frontier AI lab to go public.
Critical time for AI trade

Anthropic's IPO comes at a critical time for the AI industry, as investors are asking harder questions about the sector's growing losses, capital investments and returns, Sam Grelck, an equity strategy analyst at Truist Advisory Services, a unit of Truist Financial, told CBS News.
"I wouldn't view Anthropic's IPO as a verdict on AI, but the reception can give us another indication of investors' appetite for the AI theme after what's been a challenging few weeks," he said.

AI-related stocks have swung sharply in recent weeks as concerns mount about the mountainous debt companies are taking on to finance the data center buildout and a potential Democratic-led crackdown on the AI boom following the midterms. Jensen Huang's shock exit from Nvidia last week has also rattled investors.
At a time when investors are skittish, the robust demand for Anthropic shares suggests there is still faith that lofty investments in AI will pay off.
"Anthropic's IPO is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning," Ives said in a research note.
Financing its future

The IPO provides Anthropic with cash to finance its AI development plans. The company, which is yet to turn a profit, has said it wants to use its technology to "improve how humans live" by providing tailored financial and legal advice and speeding up scientific discovery.
"I believe sufficient and powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of medical and scientific progress into a decade," Amodei said at Nasdaq in New York on Thursday.
While the IPO will boost its coffers, Anthropic could quickly burn through cash as it works to keep its AI models on the cutting edge and stay ahead of rivals like OpenAI.

As of Sept. 30, the company had $6.2 billion in debt, according to its regulatory filing. At the same time, it has committed to spending nearly $1 trillion on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045.

title: Why the Army says it needs to detonate unstable explosives in Iowa
summary: The U.S. Army plans to detonate 68 drums of lead azide in Iowa despite local leaders and residents raising concerns.
story: The U.S. Army is moving forward with plans to detonate several tons of unstable explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa despite a court battle and community outcry about the risk of toxic lead particles spreading in a dust plume across parts of Iowa and Illinois.

Military officials have now scheduled the detonation of the barrels of lead azide for Wednesday, Nov. 25, saying it's necessary due to the public safety risks associated with the possibility of the explosives detonating on their own.

"Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized," the Army said in a statement.
But why exactly does the Army need to detonate the chemicals and what are the risks to the public?
Why does the Army need to detonate lead azide in Iowa?

In March of this year, the Army said it discovered that 68 drums of lead azide at the site had started "recrystallization." The lead was stored in bunkers at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, a munitions plant built in 1941, which produces quality medium- and large-caliber munitions.
Lead azide is a highly sensitive primary initiating explosive. Due to its extreme sensitivity, even minor external triggers, such as sparks, open flames, friction or pinpricks, can detonate it.
The recrystallization of lead azide can have a high risk of spontaneous explosion, which the EPA said creates a highly unstable and dangerous situation.

Additionally, cold weather would further destabilize the explosive materials. Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist at Army Sustainment Command, told CBS News Chicago that the risk of accidental detonation increases in cold weather.
Military officials said it's not safe to relocate the explosive materials.
The Army said it modeled four different ways to try to neutralize the chemicals, and concluded that a controlled detonation was the best method available.

"It was determined that a controlled detonation was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area," Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a statement.

Army officials said they connected with stakeholders and the public in Middletown and the surrounding area about the approved plan. Critics, however, contend they weren't made aware of the plan to detonate the lead azide until just days before the scheduled controlled explosion.
Local politicians said the decisions were made at the federal level, and poor communication contributed to the outcry and confusion from residents concerned about toxic chemicals.

"The safety of Iowans now and in the future should be the government's top concern. An unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation," Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand said.
What are the risks to residents?
One of the main concerns is that lead particles would be scattered in the dust plume created by the explosion. Lead in any amount is dangerous for humans, and in particular for young children.
"Lead is a really challenging contaminant," said David Cwiertny, a professor at the University of Iowa and director of its Environmental Policy Research Program.
He said there are essentially two ways the lead could be released: moving freely in the air and collecting on the ground.
"We do expect that air to dissipate fairly quickly as it moves with the wind," Cwiertny said.

Lead can enter the body through contaminated food, water or through dust or fumes, according to the U.S. National Institutes of Health, leading to health issues for adults and children. It can impede growth, contribute to learning disorders and damage the brain and nervous system. Children under age 6 are most susceptible to lead poisoning, the CDC says, as their bodies and brains are still developing.

Residents were told to evacuate the immediate area ahead of the planned explosion. But some are worried that afterward, lead would contaminate the environment and infiltrate their groundwater, rendering their communities unsafe.
Middletown resident Sean Byers, whose house is across from the munition plant, pointed down the street and said, "There's a playground back over there where kids in the community play all the time."
Byers, who has three young children, said he's worried about contamination.
"It's going to linger probably for decades," he said. "It's going to affect everyone."
Are there any steps to reduce the risk?
The Army said it planned to take a number of steps to reduce the risk in a controlled detonation.

The lead azide drums would be detonated inside earth-covered magazines made of concrete, and surrounded with Hesco barriers full of sand, which are approximately two stories high. Before and during the detonation, explosive experts would saturate the soil above with water. Water misters would also be spraying, the Army said.

Residents would be asked to vacate the area at that time, as the controlled detonation "will cause temporary noise, ground vibrations, and a dust plume that will contain some lead," the Army said in a statement.

Byers said he found out about the planned explosion through his neighbor a few days before the planned explosions — not from the U.S. Army. He said he plans to evacuate with his family to Branson, Missouri, where they'd stay for three or four days.
He said the Army told them it would be safe to return to their homes after six hours, but he "highly doubts" that.
Notices were sent out by the Army saying residents' windows could potentially break, and if they do, they'd be replaced by the ammunition plant.

Byers said he got the notice, but says, "The damage at that point has already been done, because it's going to let all that lead enter the house. And the question is, are they going to come in and decontaminate that? Are they going to, you know, are they going to do that? Probably not."

The Army said that due to its mitigation efforts, while there will be some lead particles in the air after the detonation, the levels will be well below the level at which the EPA requires protective actions.

title: When disaster strikes, Medicaid work rules add barriers
summary: Medicaid provides a critical safety net for people to maintain healthcare coverage. But new work requirements create barriers for those trying to recover from natural disasters.
story: PO'IPŪ, Hawai'i — A month after Hurricane Lowell hit the island of Kauaʻi, downed trees, construction crews, and damaged homes dotted the neighborhoods. At the Sheraton Kauaʻi Resort, where over 100 workers were laid off, heaps of sand blanketed the grounds, and the drained pool's concrete deck crumbled into the beach, just steps away from the ocean.

On Kauaʻi, unemployment claims jumped from 69 before the September hurricane to about 1,800 nearly two weeks afterward, with widespread layoffs in the tourism industry amid a sharp decline in visitors. The number of Medicaid applications submitted by island residents jumped by about 50% in the following month, according to the Hawaiʻi Department of Human Services.

In times of emergencies, Medicaid provides a critical safety net for people to maintain healthcare coverage. But new work rules in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which President Trump signed last year, has put Medicaid enrollees living in disaster-struck counties at risk of losing health insurance. The law requires many nondisabled adults enrolled in Medicaid in 43 states and Washington, D.C., to work, volunteer, or attend school at least 80 hours a month, with eligibility checks starting in January.

In most states, residents impacted by a disaster can be granted a short-term exemption from Medicaid work requirements. Eligibility largely relies on a federal law that allows the president to issue a disaster or emergency declaration and authorizes federal assistance, but any declaration can take months or may not come at all.

Those who live in counties affected by natural disasters may not need to comply with the work rules — one of several carve-outs intended to provide limited, short-term exceptions. However, it's unclear whether those who lost jobs after Hurricane Lowell would be eligible for that exemption so many months later. The Trump administration hasn't offered clear guidance on how long a state can apply the natural disaster exemption to enrollees.

Rochelle Ganotisi, a mother of five, and her boyfriend were laid off by Sheraton and are getting by with unemployment payments and part-time work. The union that represents the hotel's hospitality workers secured them three months of health insurance. If Ganotisi isn't hired back to her housekeeping job by then, she plans to apply for Medicaid, the federal-state program that provides health coverage to people with low incomes or disabilities.

Hawaiʻi Gov. Josh Green, a Democrat and practicing physician, emphasized the importance of quickly issuing disaster declarations, especially as changes to Medicaid are set to take effect. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services allowed states to delay enforcing the work requirements until next July, but states are still expected to implement eligibility checks by Jan. 1.

"It would be devastating if suddenly 40,000 or 50,000 people didn't have their Medicaid benefits," he said. "It could affect our rural hospitals, our nurse practitioners, our doctors, so timeliness is key."
Hawaiʻi officials said they will keep people who don't meet the work requirements enrolled until July.

At least 34 states, plus Washington, D.C., plan to adopt the optional hardship exemptions to those work requirements. So far, four states — Indiana, Iowa, Missouri, and Ohio — do not plan to adopt the exemptions, according to KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News. All four were issued disaster declarations for severe storms and flooding this summer.

CMS spokesperson Timothy Foster told KFF Health News in a statement that states can request a longer duration for a hardship exemption if they can prove that barriers to demonstrating work requirements persist in disaster areas.

Tom Cotter, CEO of Health Response Alliance, a nonprofit focused on improving healthcare access in disasters, said that when people lose coverage they end up using emergency rooms and charitable clinics, among the few places that will treat patients regardless of their ability to pay.

"All of these are really stretched thin during an emergency because their patient load goes way up," he said. "That makes it even more expensive for the healthcare system that is being otherwise also burdened for the disaster."

With additional work requirements, "it is going to slow the economic recovery of any particular community," Cotter said. "It's going to require people to be thinking about how they're paying for healthcare when they have a lot of other things to worry about."
Nebraska work requirements begin

Once the president declares a disaster or emergency, the short-term hardship exception applies for the full month the disaster took place. Eligibility can apply retroactively after a disaster declaration, and enrollees can be reimbursed for expenses from previous months.
Nebraska implemented Medicaid work requirements early, in May, offering states a preview of how the hardship declaration might provide relief. For Nebraskans, that relief was delayed.

It took three months for Mr. Trump to declare a federal disaster for March and April wildfires. For severe storms, tornadoes, and flooding that occurred in May, he didn't declare a federal disaster until August.

Six Nebraskans impacted by the disasters lost coverage because they did not comply with work requirements. In October, the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services reported it was reprocessing their eligibility now that they qualify for a hardship exemption.
Sarah Maresh, director of the Health Care Access program at the nonprofit advocacy group Nebraska Appleseed, said the early rollout of the Medicaid work requirements has been marred by uncertainty.

"This is part of the confusion that comes with the Medicaid work requirements, because it applies differently depending on your situation," she said. "I think it'll be very challenging for new applicants."

Local economies and businesses can take years to recover after a natural disaster. About 90% of businesses fail within two years after being struck by disaster, according to the U.S. Small Business Administration. Housing shortages can hamper business recovery as employees repair their homes or are displaced to areas farther from work. Three years after the 2023 Maui wildfires that killed over 100 people, recovery is ongoing, with most storefronts still shuttered in what was once a bustling area.

After CMS published rules governing the exceptions to the work requirements, several Democratic states sued the agency. Their lawsuit cited the narrow time frame for securing natural disaster exceptions. The complaint argued that the lack of guidance burdens state Medicaid agencies determining eligibility.
In its response filing, CMS wrote that the restrictions ensure the exemption applies only when a disaster affects Medicaid enrollees' ability to comply with work requirements.
Disaster delays, denials

In Mr. Trump's second term, he has denied nearly a quarter of disaster and emergency declaration requests as of mid-November, a denial rate higher than that of any other presidential administration in more than two decades, KFF Health News found. While decision wait times have increased across the country, they're more acute in states with Democratic governors. Those states experienced both significantly higher denial rates and longer decision times than states with Republican governors, according to 2026 analyses from The Associated Press and Politico's E&E News.

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis denied any politicization in Mr. Trump's decisions on disaster relief. She wrote that his response to requests from states ensures appropriate use of taxpayer money and that federal funds are used to "supplement — not substitute" states' obligations to respond to disasters.

The presidential major disaster declaration for Kauaʻi was the state's sixth disaster or emergency declaration this year. As of November, Hawaiʻi had received more disaster and emergency declarations than any other state in 2026. The president's disaster declaration for a 6.0-magnitude earthquake that damaged over 300 homes on Hawaiʻi Island took about three months.

Other states have waited longer for disaster declarations. New Mexico, where the Democratic Party controls the governor's office and majorities in both legislative chambers, had one of the longest wait times for a decision — nine months for a presidential disaster declaration for severe storms and flooding in September 2025. Illinois, which also has a Democratic trifecta, waited over seven months and was denied. The state has yet to secure any major disaster declarations during Mr. Trump's second term, despite several attempts.
Some who lost their jobs and don't qualify for Medicaid have few resources to help them.

Oscar Cardova worked at The Terrace Hanalei, a restaurant on Kauaʻi's North Shore that was significantly damaged in the hurricane. When the restaurant closed, he lost his employer-provided health insurance. Although he has a work permit visa from Peru, he was denied Medicaid because of his immigration status.
Cardova and his wife, Yesenia, live in their van. Yesenia has astigmatism and, without insurance, she will need to pay for glasses out-of-pocket, Cardova said. The cost is expected to be about $500.

The couple planned to work for two more years in the U.S. before returning to Peru. A month after the hurricane, they were still struggling to find work. In search of more job opportunities, they considered moving to Honolulu.
"Right now, we're just surviving," Cardova said. "We're waiting to see what happens before making other decisions, because we can't keep living like this."

Have you tried to prove your eligibility for Medicaid under new rules that require people to show they are working, going to school, or participating in another qualifying activity? Click here to contact KFF Health News.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

title: Army plans to carry out detonation at Iowa plant on Wednesday
summary: The Department of the Army said it plans to use an emergency munitions and explosives exclusion to the Environmental Protection Agency's permit.
story: The U.S. Army says it plans to move forward with the detonation of several tons of unstable explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa on Wednesday "to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced," the military said in a post on social media Sunday night.
The Army had earlier said in a court filing that it planned to carry out the detonation by Tuesday.

The detonation is being planned despite a federal court order that paused it indefinitely, which the Army said it does not need to follow because of the public safety risks associated with the possibility of the explosives detonating on their own.

In federal court records filed late Saturday, the Department of the Army said it plans to use an emergency munitions and explosives exclusion to the Environmental Protection Agency's permit. The government argues it needs to perform a controlled detonation to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion.

On Friday, a federal court suspended the U.S. Army's plan to detonate the explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Middletown, Iowa, after community outcry about the risk of toxic lead particles spreading in a dust plume across parts of Iowa and Illinois.
The Army originally scheduled two controlled explosions for Friday. The Army then delayed them until Monday before the court stepped in.
The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals granted an emergency motion to pause the demolition after environmental groups filed a lawsuit.
Why the Army says it needs to detonate unstable, lead-filled explosives in Iowa and what's at risk
Why the Army says it needs to detonate unstable, lead-filled explosives in Iowa and what's at risk
The military said on Friday it was working closely with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the controlled explosion would be conducted in the safest manner possible.

"Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized," the statement said.

In its filing on Saturday, the government had warned that it must conduct the controlled explosion by Tuesday because the temperature is expected to drop below 30 degrees in the next several days. It says the lead azide has deteriorated and that crystals in the waste could break as temperatures drop. It did not immediately explain if the forecast or other factors had changed to make a move to Wednesday safer.

"A controlled detonation allows the Army to implement measures to minimize the risk to the public, including the risk from the ejection of partial unexploded ordnances that can explode later from the Facility," the court filing says. "The Army intends to act consistent with the terms of the Emergency Permit and its mitigation measures even if not in effect. That includes mitigation measures to minimize the risk of the dispersal of lead dust. In short, a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion."
In response to the Army's filing, the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club filed a motion Sunday seeking to supplement their emergency request to block the planned detonation.

The filing includes three expert and local government declarations challenging the Army's assessment of the risk of delaying the detonation, as well as concerns about public notice and potential health and environmental impacts.

In a statement Sunday, the Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club and Earthjustice questioned claims that all alternatives were given appropriate consideration, saying "this emergency is of the Army's own making."

"The Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public's demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm," said Earthjustice Attorney Thien Chau.

Iowa's new Democratic Senator-elect Josh Turek said in a statement Sunday that he is "concerned about the potential health risks resulting from the U.S. Army's planned detonation in Middletown and the lack of clear communication and transparency from the U.S. Army."

"I also believe we need a full investigation into why this stockpile of lead azide, which has been at IAAAP for decades, was allowed to degrade into this critical state, why safer methods of disposal were not pursued, what other potentially dangerous materials are being stored at the IAAAP and their condition, and what procedures are needed to ensure this never happens again," he said. "The public also deserves answers as to why the U.S. Army's communication — both with the public and with Iowa officials — was delayed and inadequate from the beginning."

In March of this year, the Army said it discovered that 68 drums of lead azide at the site had started "recrystallization." The lead was stored in bunkers at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, a munitions plant built in 1941, which produces quality medium- and large-caliber munitions.

title: Tom Jackson, former Broncos star and sports broadcaster, dies at 75
summary: Tom Jackson, a former Denver Broncos player and ESPN analyst, has died at 75.
story: Former football star and famed broadcaster Tom Jackson has died, his family and ESPN announced Sunday.

Jackson rose to prominence as a Denver Broncos player and went on to build a career as a beloved NFL analyst for ESPN, becoming a mainstay of the network's Sunday football programs for three decades, including its "Sunday NFL Countdown" show. He was 75.

Jimmy Pitaro, the chairman of ESPN, praised Jackson in a statement released by the network after his death. In it, Pitaro called Jackson "one of the most influential and beloved figures in ESPN's history," who "brought the credibility of an All-Pro NFL player, the insight of a gifted analyst and a warmth and authenticity that connected with generations of football fans."

"Alongside Chris Berman, he helped make NFL Primetime an iconic part of our football weekends," Pitaro said. "Away from the set, Tom was a trusted colleague, generous mentor and dear friend to many. We extend our deepest condolences to his family, friends, former teammates and all who loved him. His legacy at ESPN, throughout the NFL and among the countless fans who admired his incredible work will endure."

Jackson's family informed ESPN that he died Friday, but it was their wish that his death not be announced until the start of the network's "Sunday NFL Countdown" show by Jackson's longtime friend and on-air partner Chris Berman.

"Tom was so much more than an accomplished NFL analyst. There was nobody kinder, more thoughtful, more loyal or more engaging than him. And when it came to laughter, Tom's was frequent and unmistakable," Berman said at the start of the show. "Tom was my best friend professionally and personally. If you ever met him or just knew him from watching ESPN, he was your best friend, too."
Berman said Jackson made a surprise visit a couple of weeks ago to ESPN, where he worked for 32 years after playing 14 seasons for the Broncos, and that the two talked on Tuesday.

A fourth-round draft pick out of Louisville in 1973, Jackson was the inspirational leader of Denver's first Super Bowl team in 1977. He started 177 games for the Broncos between 1973-86, retiring after the team's second Super Bowl appearance. He was a two-time Associated Press All-Pro and three-time Pro Bowler.
Following his playing days, Jackson had a second career at ESPN from 1987-2016 and was featured on "Sunday NFL Countdown" and "NFL Primetime."

Before the internet and NBC took over the Sunday night package in 2006, "NFL Primetime" was must-see viewing for fans and players because it showed highlights from all the games, as well as the interplay between Berman and Jackson, who often finished each other's sentences.

"I can remember coming from games and waiting in a rush to get home, to watch 'Primetime' because all I wanted to know was, what were you and Tom Jackson gonna say about one, the team?" ESPN analyst and Hall of Fame wide receiver Randy Moss said to Berman.

Jackson briefly returned to ESPN in 2019 and reunited with Berman to do an online version of "NFL Primetime." He was awarded the Pete Rozelle Radio-Television Award from the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2015.

"In my lifetime there was Howard Cosell doing 'Monday Night Football' halftime highlights and then there were Boomer and TJ doing 'Sunday NFL Countdown.' I am not here as a colleague but as one of million who watched, learned from and idolized the two of you," ESPN host Mike Greenberg said during Sunday's show.
ESPN's studio crew wore orange ties in honor of Jackson during the three-hour show.
Berman said Jackson was the last of seven people interviewed for the studio analyst job and that the last person rarely gets the job. But Jackson nailed the interview.
ESPN's NFL studio in Bristol, Connecticut, is named the Chris Berman-Tom Jackson Studio. It is the only named studio on ESPN's campus.

"The Denver Broncos are heartbroken by the passing of Ring of Fame linebacker Tom Jackson, a cornerstone of the legendary Orange Crush defense and one of the most beloved players in franchise history," the Broncos said in a statement.

"An inspirational leader and fierce competitor, TJ was a proud member of the Broncos' first Super Bowl team that helped establish a winning tradition in Denver. Off the field, Tom carried himself with class, warmth and humility, forging deep connections and lifelong friendships with teammates and throughout Broncos Country."
Jackson is survived by his wife, Jennifer, and daughters Taylor and Morgan.

title: Delta Air Lines hit with delays after baggage network system issue
summary: The Delta Air Lines delays are most impacting flights in and out of Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in Georgia.
story: A systemwide network issue affecting Delta Air Lines' baggage system that forced teams to manually process bags, resulting in nationwide delays during a busy holiday travel weekend, has been fixed, the airline said Sunday.

The airline said in a statement that the automation for departing flight weight and balance calculations is now working, several hours after it forced a temporary ground delay program to be issued at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport — Delta Air Lines' mega hub — to manage traffic backups caused by the system outage. The ground delay, which has been lifted, impacted only Delta's flights.

"Delta apologizes to customers for the delay in their travels today," the airline said. "Delta is rebooking customers to the next best itinerary and providing meals and hotel rooms where necessary. For customers facing a canceled flight and don't wish to travel, refunds are being given."
Delta warned that while teams are focused on completing the 500 Delta and Delta Connection flights scheduled for Sunday, cancellations would be a last resort if all other options have been exhausted.

As of Sunday evening, Delta Air Lines had canceled 202 flights, or 4% of the day's total, departing from the U.S., which is higher than average for the airline. Only 50% of its flights were arriving on time Sunday, which is also highly unusual for the airline, which usually operates above the 80% mark each month.
According to FlightAware, Delta Air Lines currently has more than 1,900 delayed flights, as of 6:00 p.m. EST. The airline said about 70% of these delays are connected to the automation.
"The remaining are attributable to inclement weather and ensuring ATC programs in NYC and the U.S. Northeast," the airline said.
United Airlines had a similar issue last Monday that forced the airline to hold departures for about 90 minutes.
AAA projects nearly 6 million people will take domestic flights for Thanksgiving this week.

title: Natural gas pipeline fire in Alabama lights up night sky
summary: Photos and videos posted on social media appeared to show flames rising dozens of yards above the trees near Ward, Alabama, with smoke billowing into the air.
story: A fire on a natural gas pipeline lit up the night sky in rural Alabama late Saturday with a towering column of orange flame, prompting the operator to shut down part of the line but causing no injuries, the company said.
The cause of the fire is under investigation, and customer deliveries were not impacted, Southern Natural Gas Company said in a statement Sunday.

Photos and videos posted on social media appeared to show flames rising dozens of yards above the trees near Ward, with smoke billowing into the air. People said on social media that the fire was visible from miles away across the state line in Mississippi.

Southern Natural Gas told CBS News in a statement that it "experienced a natural gas release and fire" on the segment of the pipeline at around 11:30 p.m. CST Saturday. Emergency responders and company personnel secured the area and the blaze was extinguished, the company said. The impacted part of the pipeline was shut down and depressurized.

Pleasant Hill Volunteer Fire Department said on social media that its firefighters, along with several other volunteer fire departments, responded to the blaze after midnight to assist Sumter County officials after "a major pipeline explosion that caused a secondary brush fire."
The Sumter County Emergency Management Agency did not immediately respond to a voicemail seeking information.
Ward is an unincorporated community located near the Mississippi state line. The mayor of nearby York urged residents on Sunday to remain calm and avoid the affected area.
Mayor Renee Ward Pringle said in a social media post that the city of York's gas facilities are not believed to be affected.

title: Democrats reach historic House majority not seen since 1992
summary: "House Democrats have just secured the largest majority any party in Congress has held this century. BOOM," Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York said Sunday.
story: Democrats secured their 258th seat in the House on Sunday, marking the largest majority either party has won in the lower chamber in a general election in three decades.

Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in President Trump's first midterm in 2018. It's an election sweep unseen since 1992 for either party, creating not only vast opportunities for Democrats to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.

The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. Hubbard led Foxx by 330 votes following a recount, according to the North Carolina Board of Elections.
"House Democrats have just secured the largest majority any party in Congress has held this century. BOOM," Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, of New York, wrote on X Sunday afternoon.

The milestone in the 435-member House exceeded Democrats' own expectations, and they could still gain a few more seats with four other House races remaining outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff.
Republicans will have at least 173 seats in the minority.

The blue wave, or as some have called it, "blue tsunami," sets up a divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and with a Republican president in the White House. Emboldened Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address the high cost of living while also confronting Mr. Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term.

The Democrats' majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257), yet not quite the high-water mark of the Franklin D. Roosevelt era, which saw House Democratic majorities swell past 300.
It presents opportunities and challenges ahead.

In an interview on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday, Jeffries repeatedly emphasized the need for action, saying, "Can you imagine how angry the American people will be with Washington if, over the next two years, we fail to do anything about affordability, fail to do anything about healthcare, and fail to do anything about immigration?"
Election rout creates a mandate to govern

The numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins, which spanned from the strongest Republican states to the Midwest and East Coast, as voters, angry over high prices and war with Iran and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with Mr. Trump.

Persistent negative views of the economy turned against the party in power. Those who said the economy was bad voted for Democrats in their House races, according to CBS News exit polls. This was the second straight election most voters told CBS News inflation was a hardship for them, and more said their finances are worse now compared to two years ago — these voters also backed Democrats over the Republicans for the House.

Taking control of both the House and the Senate come January, the Democrats will carry with them the backing of voters and the expectations to deliver. The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in over a decade.
The Democrats, as part of their 100-day agenda, are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans' Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire.

Democrats have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power. That includes plans to probe how Mr. Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. Jeffries, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Mr. Trump for a third time.
"This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen," said progressive leader Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at the Capitol.
The New York Democrat called the big numbers "a mandate for change."
Rep. Tom Suozzi, a centrist Democrat from New York and an accountant by profession, said the House Democrats should focus 75% of their time on affordability issues and 25% on accountability.
"Everything should be tied back to the people — and how it's affecting the people," he said.
For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Mr. Trump's financial dealings, they should be connecting the dots: "How does that affect people's pocketbooks?"

The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress — may amount to "blatant criminality."
A new generation of leaders

After House Speaker Mike Johnson struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow single-digit majority — meaning a few GOP lawmakers could derail the agenda — the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides the new leadership much more room to maneuver.

Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job on Jan. 3, 2027, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage, in the face of GOP opposition.
"We're not a monolith — people come to the caucus with different ideas — it's OK," said Democratic Rep. Troy Carter of Louisiana, who is expected to lead the Congressional Black Caucus.

Republicans saw their number of House seats fall to one of the lowest tallies in decades. They're far from the end of the Obama administration, when the House Republicans won 247 seats in the 2014 election and the rise of Newt Gingrich when they won 230 seats in 1994.
Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, who was elected by his colleagues to be the Republican leader in the minority, vowed to fight their way back to power.
"Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families," Jordan said.
The GOP's high-water marks include the 1920 election, with 301 seats for House Republicans.

title: Ossoff's broad and decisive Senate win fuels 2028 speculation
summary: Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff's commanding victory in Georgia relied on a broad coalition, and this is fueling 2028 presidential interest in him, even though he says he'll be in the Senate for the next six years.
story: Washington — Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff's commanding reelection victory in Georgia is drawing renewed attention to his potential as a 2028 presidential contender, as election data shows how he assembled a broad coalition of voters in the pivotal presidential battleground state.

Despite the growing speculation, Ossoff, 39, is for now dismissing the possibility of a White House bid. During a debate in October, Ossoff said he had "zero interest in running for president" in 2028.

Some early polls place him at the top of a hypothetical 2028 primary field. A post-election Emerson College survey showed Ossoff with the support of 17% of respondents — narrowly ahead of former Vice President Kamala Harris and New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, with former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and California Gov. Gavin Newsom rounding out the top five.

Ossoff has attracted interest from both centrists and progressives while delivering a decisive victory in a closely divided presidential battleground state. At Crooked Con, a primarily progressive gathering in Washington after the midterms, Ossoff received 38% of first-choice votes in its straw poll, ahead of Ocasio-Cortez and Buttigieg.

"I think he would make an attractive presidential contender on the Democratic side," said Jerry Gonzalez, CEO of GALEO Impact Fund PAC, a Georgia-based Latino political action committee that endorsed Ossoff in his Senate race. "He is not afraid, he won't shy away from holding the Trump administration accountable, but in a way that works towards actually building coalitions to get something done."
Democrats who can win statewide in conservative or swing states tend to be moderate, and that's true of Ossoff, too.

"He comes across, and tries to present himself, as a moderate, and he talks about issues which moderate conservatives could get behind," said Charles Bullock, a longtime political science professor at the University of Georgia. "The issues he stresses are things which are within the broad mainstream of 'These would be good things.'"

It's unclear how well a moderate would fare in the early nominating states. What is effective in a Georgia general election may be a tougher sell in a Democratic primary, where voters often reward ideological purity over swing-state caution.
"Obviously, he's successful here in Georgia," Bullock said. "How would he play elsewhere?
"I think what we will be seeing is preparation, maybe for a later run," Bullock speculated.

Ossoff's record gives rivals on both flanks openings to attack: progressives have criticized his vote for the Republican-backed Laken Riley Act and his reluctance to embrace "Medicare for All," while his votes to restrict certain weapons sales to Israel and his criticism of its military conduct in Gaza have drawn objections from some pro-Israel Democrats and donors.
All of those issues are certain to be part of the 2028 primary contest. For example, Rep. Ro Khanna, another potential 2028 candidate, last week tried to restart the debate over universal healthcare.

"Medicare for All means healthcare for everyone, like public school is free for every kid," Khanna wrote on X, arguing, "'Medicare for All who want it' is pablum. It's telling parents they have to pay for public school."

In his reelection this month, Ossoff defeated GOP opponent Mike Collins by around 18 points, two years after President Trump defeated Harris by around two points in 2024. It was a much wider margin than his last Senate election, which he won by just over one percentage point.
Powering Ossoff's win this year was a broad coalition of voters, including some swing constituencies that Democrats have struggled with in recent years, CBS News' exit polling shows.
Ossoff maintained strong support among Black voters, winning 93% of the group, which make up almost one-third of the state's eligible voters according to Pew Research Center.

He did not win the White voters who make up just over half of Georgia's electorate, but he did make significant inroads, winning 40% — after Harris had won just 28% two years earlier. He also notched some improvement in groups that have shifted hard against Democrats: He won 29% of White voters without college degrees (compared to Harris' 18%) and 19% of White evangelical or born-again Christian voters (compared to less than 10% for Harris).
Ossoff also won men by nine points after Harris lost them by 13 points.

Both Ossoff and Harris won younger Georgians, but Ossoff won them by a larger margin, securing 85% of voters ages 29 and under. Ossoff also split the 45-and-older vote roughly in half, while Harris lost that age group by a 15-point margin.

And Ossoff made gains with Hispanics — a group that makes up less than 10% of Georgia's eligible voters but which has grown rapidly and has become a swing demographic that could decide a close race in the perennial battleground. In his reelection victory, he won around two-thirds of Latino voters, up seven points from Harris' performance two years earlier.
A comparison of 19 Georgia precincts where at least 30% of active registered voters identify as Hispanic or Latino shows substantial Democratic improvement.

Ossoff won those precincts by a combined 49 points in the two-candidate vote, compared with an eight-point advantage for Harris in the 2024 presidential election and an 18-point margin for fellow Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock in 2022.
The changes were significant in areas that had supported Mr. Trump just two years earlier.

In six heavily Latino precincts in Whitfield County, the combined results shifted from a 12-point Trump advantage in 2024 to a 37-point Ossoff victory in 2026. Three similar precincts in Hall County shifted from an 11-point Trump edge to a 33-point Ossoff victory.

Those figures reflect the voting behavior of entire precincts rather than individual Latino voters, and comparisons between presidential and midterm electorates are not exact. Still, they underscore how dramatically the environment changed in places with large Latino populations.
Gonzalez attributed the shift in part to concerns over affordability and immigration enforcement, two issues he said weighed heavily on Latino voters in Georgia.

"Things are really expensive," Gonzalez told CBS News. "The price and affordability were a big driving issue." He also pointed to the Trump administration's immigration crackdown and its impact on Latino communities in Georgia. Ossoff has investigated allegations of abuses in federal immigration detention facilities as part of his Senate oversight work.
Gonzalez also credited Ossoff's success among voters across the political spectrum to his accessibility and constituent outreach.
"His office is accessible to all Georgians, and that's part of the reason why he won."

In this wave election, Ossoff wasn't the only Democrat to pick up ground in the midterms. Latino and Black voters, men, voters without college degrees and younger voters moved back toward Democratic candidates nationwide, a reversal after all four groups had shifted rightward in 2024.
In 2028, those groups could once again play a central role in both the Democratic Party's nominating process and the general election.

States with large Black and Latino populations will lead the Democratic primary calendar after the party rearranged its schedule, and Ossoff, with his strong support from both groups, would likely stand to benefit if he were to decide to run. South Carolina — where Black Democratic voters have long played an influential role in choosing the party's presidential nominee — will go first, followed by Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia.
The DNC says approximately 4.2 million Latinos live across the six early nominating states, a major increase from the party's previous early-state lineup.

In the general election, maintaining a strong lead with Black, Latino and younger voters — and preventing too much slippage among White and non-college-educated voters — will also be a core task for Democrats, as they seek to prevent the GOP's first non-Trump presidential candidate in over a decade from reassembling the Trump coalition.
Though Ossoff says he doesn't plan a White House bid in 2028, his performance in Georgia has provided an early measure of what an electoral coalition for him could look like.
"He has mentioned that he was focused on winning reelection, which he has done, so I think that gives him a little bit of latitude to think about it a little more seriously," Gonzalez said.

title: Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeats Rep. Virginia Foxx in House race
summary: Chuck Hubbard defeated Rep. Virginia Foxx, CBS News projects, adding to Democrats' sizable majority in the House next year.
story: Washington — Chuck Hubbard defeated Rep. Virginia Foxx, CBS News projected 19 days after Election Day, adding to Democrats' sizable majority in the House next year.

Hubbard, 64, is a former journalist who took on Foxx for a second time after falling short by almost 10 points in 2024. This cycle, he became the latest Democrat to overcome expectations and flip a House seat.

Foxx, who chairs the House Rules Committee, has represented the Tar Heel State in the House since 2005 and is the longest-serving member of the state's congressional delegation. Her loss comes as Democrats saw a slew of wins throughout the country, with key victories delivering them majorities in both chambers in the new Congress. And the dynamic was especially acute in North Carolina, where Democrats flipped several House seats and a Senate seat. Heading into Election Night, the Cook Political Report rated Foxx's seat as likely Republican.
Hubbard said Foxx called to concede on Sunday, after a recount had been conducted in the tight race.

"Let me be the first to thank Congresswoman Foxx for her decades of service and countless sacrifices," Hubbard wrote in a post on X. "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."
With the victory, Democrats have secured 258 seats in the House, marking the largest majority either party has won in the lower chamber in a general election in three decades.

summary: On this "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" broadcast, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries join Margaret Brennan.
