For now, the pair can enjoy their luxury accommodations and newfound celebrity status, knowing their next stop is 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue rather than the oven.
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: New York Dem addresses bizarre 'lizard people' claims after viral clip behind Mamdani
summary: New York Assemblyman Jordan J.G. Wright breaks silence on viral reptilian claims after a clip showed him rolling his eyes behind Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
story: A clip showing New York Democratic Assemblyman Jordan J.G. Wright making an unusual eye movement while standing behind Zohran Mamdani during a press conference has sparked wild "lizard people" conspiracy theories online. (Credit: Mayor Mamdani)

A Democratic New York City assemblyman addressed bizarre "lizard people" conspiracy theories after a viral video appeared to show his eyes rolling backward while standing behind Mayor Zohran Mamdani during a press conference.
Jordan J.G. Wright was spotted during a press conference behind Mamdani on Friday, when the city announced plans to eventually shut down Rikers Island.
As Mamdani spoke, Wright appeared to flash a slight grin before blinking and rolling his eyes in a circular motion toward the back of his head, prompting a wave of bizarre speculation online.
"I have no idea what was going on in that video. I’m really not sure," Wright told the New York Post in a statement.
NYC MAYOR MAMDANI ANNOUNCES DELAYED PLAN TO CLOSE CITY'S LARGEST JAIL
A New York City assemblyman is addressing bizarre speculation about his humanity after an unusual eye movement behind Mayor Zohran Mamdani went viral. (ABC 7)

He added that his work as an assemblyman speaks to his human character, pointing to a project he championed in Harlem that serves as the city's first community-based center dedicated to climate action. The five-story hub provides residents with environmental education and advocacy.

"Obviously I’m a human being, and my humanity can be seen through my legislation like the $4 million for the WE ACT environmental justice center in Harlem," he said. "I can’t speak to any reptiles or aliens."

The video sent social media users into a frenzy over the weekend, reigniting a decades-old conspiracy theory that extraterrestrial reptilians secretly control the Earth by disguising themselves as world leaders and celebrities to manipulate society.

"This is how lizards blink… I am pretty sure there is full-blown ‘Men in Black’ aliens walking among us disguised as human beings, and they are hiding in plain sight," one social media user said, according to the Post.
NYC SUSPECT IN CHINATOWN FATAL BEATING HAD 5 OPEN CASES AS MAMDANI PUSHES PLAN TO CLOSE RIKERS
Jordan Wright says he is human after a viral video from Zohran Mamdani’s Rikers Island press conference sparked a bizarre reptilian conspiracy. (ABC 7)
Another X user suggested the clip showed that aliens were becoming increasingly brazen about revealing themselves to the public.
"The ‘reptile’ is standing right behind Mamdani, as he announces a full scale-release of dangerous prisoners from NYC jails," the X user said.
"The aliens are not even bothering to hide themselves anymore. They intend to create so much chaos on Earth, that we will be unable to defend ourselves," the user added.
The discussion also spilled onto Reddit, where some users questioned whether Wright was human.
"Yes, the guy in the back is a reptilian, 100%" the Reddit user said.
MAMDANI IGNITES ONLINE FIRESTORM AFTER MOURNING DEATH OF INMATE CHARGED IN GRISLY MURDER: 'WTF ARE WE DOING?'

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks with inmates on Rikers Island on July 15, 2026, in New York. Mamdani announced plans to close Rikers Island by 2032 and move remaining detainees to four smaller borough-based jails. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig)
Wright, the son of former Assemblyman Keith L.T. Wright and grandson of former New York Supreme Court Judge Bruce Wright, represents New York's 70th Assembly District in Harlem.

He was reelected without opposition in November after defeating Democratic socialist Conrad Blackburn in the Democratic primary in June. His legislative priorities include affordable housing, health care access and public safety, according to his profile.
A lifelong New Yorker and Central Harlem resident, Wright graduated from Syracuse University in 2017 with a degree in psychology.
Wright stood behind Mamdani on Friday as the mayor announced plans to cut New York City's jail population by 2,500 inmates over the next five years and close the city’s largest jail by 2032.

title: Democrats clinch historic House majority as Chuck Hubbard defeats longtime GOP Rep. Virginia Foxx
summary: Democrats secured their largest House majority since 1992, setting up clashes with Trump over investigations, health care and Republican policies.
story: President Donald Trump expresses surprise at the results of the 2026 midterm elections after it is projected Democrats will take control of the U.S. House and Senate on ‘FOX News Democracy 26.’

Democrats have stormed back into power in the House, securing the largest majority of any party since 1992 in a sweeping midterm victory that will reshape the balance of power in Washington and leave Republicans with significantly less influence over the chamber.

The victory was cemented after Democrat Chuck Hubbard was elected to the House from North Carolina, according to The Associated Press (AP). He defeated longtime Republican incumbent Rep. Virginia Foxx, who chaired the powerful House Rules Committee, which determines which bills reach the House floor for a vote.

With several general election results still being called, Democrats have picked up 44 seats so far, giving them at least 258 seats in the House, their largest majority in more than three decades, according to The AP.
STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE
FILE — Democrats secured at least 258 House seats, their largest majority since 1992, with four races still undecided. (Chip Somodevilla)
Meanwhile, Republicans have been left with at least 173 seats.
Four House races remain undecided in Minnesota, Tennessee and two December runoffs in Louisiana, according to The AP.

The party's projected majority will surpass its post-election totals in every election since Bill Clinton first won the presidency in 1992, when Democrats secured 258 seats, the outlet said. The party's next-largest showing reportedly came in 2008, when Barack Obama was elected president and Democrats won 257 House seats.
The shift in the 435-member House will set the stage for a dramatic power struggle in Washington.
WHAT THE 2026 MIDTERM RESULTS MEAN FOR CAPITOL HILL
Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated longtime Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx (pictured), who chaired the powerful House Rules Committee. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
Democrats are also poised to take control of the Senate, where they secured a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their largest advantage in more than a decade.

Democrats scored some of their biggest victories in traditionally competitive states and Republican strongholds alike, including Texas, Georgia, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina.
BLUE WAVE NEARLY SWALLOWED SOME OF AMERICA'S REDDEST STATES AS ELECTION DATA EXPOSES GOP'S CLOSE CALLS
FILE — President Donald Trump faces a Democratic-controlled Congress poised to investigate his administration and challenge his legislative agenda. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images)

President Donald Trump will face a new legislative reality when the next Congress convenes in January, with Democrats preparing to launch a flurry of investigations targeting his administration and its Republican allies in Congress.

The party's 100-day agenda will also focus on rolling back Republican policies, with top priorities including reversing GOP Medicaid cuts and restoring Affordable Care Act tax credits that Republicans allowed to expire, The AP said.

title: Progressives unveil $25 minimum wage push to solve affordability crisis despite economist inflation warning
summary: House Democrats push a $25 minimum wage to fight the affordability crisis, but Heritage economist E.J. Antoni warns it could raise costs and unemployment.
story: Reps. Everton Blair, R-Ga., and Delia Ramirez, D-Il., told Fox News Digital that raising the minimum wage to $25 is a crucial step in solving the affordability crisis, while dismissing concerns that their desired minimum wage could raise inflation.

House Democrats are pushing to raise the federal minimum wage to $25 an hour, calling the current hourly pay a "remnant of slavery" to "oppress women," despite warnings from conservative economists that the proposal could drive up costs and threaten jobs.

The proposal from the Congressional Progressive Caucus would more than triple the current $7.25 federal minimum wage, raising questions about its potential impact on businesses and workers in states with significantly lower living costs than major cities.

"We should be rallying around (a minimum wage of) $25 at minimum, and it should be cost adjusted for inflation, so that people can have a job that enables them to survive and thrive," Rep. Everton Blair Jr., D-Ga., told Fox News Digital.
The push for higher federal wage mandates is fueling debate among economists over potential trade-offs that could harm American workers and businesses. (Kathleen Flynn/Bloomberg/Getty Images)
AOC-BACKED $25 MINIMUM WAGE PLAN SOUNDS GREAT — BUT AT WHAT COST?
Asked whether a nationwide $25 minimum wage could hurt workers and businesses in lower-cost states, Blair argued that the proposed rate should serve as a national baseline.
The congressman said $25 an hour should be "the floor" and "should be higher in places with a higher cost of living."
Blair acknowledged concerns that raising the minimum wage could contribute to inflation but said lawmakers must find a way to increase workers' earnings while "keeping people afloat."
Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., echoed Blair's support for the proposal, pointing to the high cost of living in cities such as Seattle and Washington, D.C., as justification for raising wages.
Rep. Delia Ramirez attends a news conference on June 30, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
DEMOCRATS SEIZE ON MIDTERM WINS TO PUSH MASSIVE MINIMUM WAGE HIKES, BUT ECONOMISTS SEE TROUBLE AHEAD
"The truth is that the boogeyman, the corporations, don't want to pay their workers liveable wages," Ramirez told Fox News Digital.

Heritage Foundation chief economist E.J. Antoni warned that a $25 federal minimum wage could increase costs and unemployment, arguing that the economic consequences would extend beyond major metropolitan areas.
"Whenever a price floor on labor is set above the market equilibrium, a surplus of labor is created. In this case, we call that surplus unemployment," Antoni told Fox News Digital.
DEMOCRATS PLOT MASSIVE SPENDING SPREE AFTER MIDTERM ROUT — AND TRUMP COULD HELP THEM PULL IT OFF

Despite those warnings, progressive lawmakers expressed confidence that the proposal could gain support from Democratic leadership in both chambers and potentially reach President Donald Trump's desk.
"There's a widespread coalition of folks in the Democratic caucus who have long been saying that one job should be enough to pay the bill," Blair told Fox News Digital.
Ramirez also expressed cautious optimism about the possibility of Trump signing the legislation, pointing to his previous willingness to discuss bipartisan immigration reform.
She said she "never knows what the president might or might not be willing to do."
SANDERS-AOC BACKED PROGRESSIVE DEBUTS FEDERAL $25 MINIMUM WAGE BILL WITH COALITION OF 100+ ORGANIZATIONS
The strategy reflects a broader push to drive loyalty as consumers pull back on discretionary spending, according to reports. (Eric Thayer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The Living Wage for All coalition, which joined lawmakers in unveiling the proposal, says support for a $25 minimum wage extends beyond Democratic voters.

"Not a blue wave," the coalition said, citing polling it claimed showed 63% of Republicans support a $25 federal minimum wage. "There is a blue collar demand that says that this is how we address the affordability crisis."

Coalition members also drew comparisons between the history of minimum-wage policies and slavery-era labor practices, arguing that the current wage system has historically disadvantaged women and marginalized workers.

The proposal comes as Democrats prepare to advance their affordability agenda in the 120th Congress, with progressives seeking to make higher wages a central component of the party's economic platform.

title: DHS, Dem officials clash after ICE arrest at Seattle airport
summary: DHS says a passenger threw hot coffee at ICE officers during a Seattle airport arrest of a visa overstay, as Washington Democrats blast the operation.
story: Video shows federal officials detaining illegal immigrants who allegedly overstayed their visas, leading to Democrat Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson saying enforcing the law is "out of control."  (John Gaedeke via Storyful; KOMONEWS via AP)

Federal officials and Washington state Democrats are at odds after ICE officers arrested two prospective airline travelers – both accused of overstaying visas and one accused of throwing hot coffee at agents – on a Seattle airport jetway Saturday morning.
"This violence must end," the Department of Homeland Security fired back on X, responding to Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson saying, "ICE is completely and totally out of control."

The operation began around 8:05 a.m. PT as travelers boarded an Alaska Airlines flight, according to the Department of Homeland Security. DHS says ICE officers targeted Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, whom the agency described as a Mexican national "who overstayed his visa." During the arrest, other travelers began getting in the officers' way, and one passenger threw hot coffee at the agents, DHS said.
TLAIB MOVES TO BLOCK ICE AIRPORT ARRESTS, SAYS TSA HELPING TARGET IMMIGRANTS

At his Saturday news conference, Democrat Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called video of the incident "horrific" and "chilling," adding that he told Alaska Airlines representatives that "they need to call on ICE to get out of our airports." (John Gaedeke via Storyful; KOMONEWS via AP)

"The individual who threw the hot coffee was identified as Sofia Hernandez Mejia, an illegal alien from Mexico and visa overstay," DHS wrote on X. "She was subsequently arrested as well. She will be charged with assaulting a federal officer."

The attorney representing Mejia disputed DHS' characterization in a statement shared with Fox News."She is not a U.S. citizen and was in the process of adjusting her status. It is pending with USCIS," Olia Catala said in a statement. "Yes, her entry into the United States was lawful. She subsequently had pending asylum status, later married a U.S. citizen, and was undergoing the legal process to adjust her status."
The post came in response to Ferguson, who claimed law enforcement removing suspected illegal immigrants from flights is "creating chaos in our communities."

"ICE is completely and totally out of control," Ferguson wrote on X, making no mention to the alleged assault of the officers. "Like many Americans, I’m outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities."
BORDER CZAR TOM HOMAN FIRES BACK AFTER DEMOCRAT CHRIS MURPHY CLAIMS ICE IS ‘TERRORIZING LITTLE KIDS’

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., has designs on using her leverage in Congress to curb federal immigration law enforcement, while Republicans and Trump administration officials have long rebuked Democrat efforts to curb enforcement versus changing the laws already on the books. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Ferguson even suggested airlines should push federal immigration agents out of the airport, which has been under stress from this month's nationwide ground stop and rooting out security threats during the busy holiday travel season.

"This morning, masked ICE agents terrorized our community, dragging at least one woman on the ground and arresting her as she was in line to board her flight," Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., wrote on X. "This behavior is totally unacceptable. Violent arrests are the hallmark of fascist states, not a democracy."

At his Saturday news conference, Ferguson called video of the incident "horrific" and "chilling," adding that he told Alaska Airlines representatives that "they need to call on ICE to get out of our airports." He said he plans to make the same request of every other airline operating out of the Seattle and Tacoma airport.

DHS and Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials have been agitated by protesters and efforts to halt the Trump administration's detention efforts, sometimes creating deadly circumstances and exchanges between federal officers and agitators.
DEMS SHAMED AS DHS BRINGS ICE SHOOTING RECEIPTS AFTER POLITICIAN CALLED ICE OFFICERS ‘LIARS WITH MASKS’
DHS defended the agents and pointed to what it described as a surge in violence against federal officers, citing DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin's directive on prosecutions.

"Assaulting and obstructing law enforcement is a crime and a felony," the DHS X post continued. "Secretary Mullin has been clear: anyone who assaults or obstructs law enforcement will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. Our brave law enforcement is facing more than a 1,600% increase in assaults, 300% increase in vehicular attacks, and an 8,000% increase in death threats against them. This violence must end."

Democrats ran on affordability in the midterm elections, but Jayapal vows to work to end immigration enforcement operations, taking the fight from American streets and airports to the House and Senate.
'SQUAD' DEMOCRAT SLAMMED BY TRUMP ADMIN FOR MOST 'RADICAL' PLAN TARGETING ICE YET

"Soon, Democrats will take back control of Congress and we will continue the critical work to rein in these out of control agents and hold them accountable," her X post continued, expressing concern for the illegals who overstayed their visa versus the law enforcement officers attacked during an obstruction. "My heart goes out to those directly affected, and the passengers and airline workers whom ICE traumatized today."
Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson, a democratic socialist, called efforts to enforce immigration law "un-American."
"I am outraged by videos of masked ICE agents causing chaos and dragging a woman off the jetway at Sea-Tac airport," she wrote Saturday on X. "These tactics are unacceptable and un-American."
Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., called federal law enforcement "a profound threat to our community."

"This morning, masked ICE agents detained at least one passenger waiting to board an Alaska Airlines flight at Sea-Tac Airport," he wrote on X. "The masked agents forcibly dragged the individual off the jet bridge, taking them into custody. Let me be clear: this is absolutely unacceptable.

"ICE’s conduct across our country is putting people in harm’s way, undermining public trust, and stoking fear in our communities. I am incredibly concerned about the conduct of immigration enforcement and believe that ICE is operating as a paramilitary force that is a profound threat to our community. There is no question that this agency needs to be reined in before causing more chaos and fear."
DEMOCRAT COMPARES ICE TO 'DOMESTIC TERRORISTS' AS 111 HOUSE DEMS DEMAND TEXAS DETENTION CENTER CLOSE
Alaska Airlines said it had no advance warning of the enforcement action and moved many affected passengers onto other flights.

"Alaska Airlines was not provided advance notice of the enforcement action and we are working to understand the circumstances surrounding what occurred," the airline said in a statement, adding it is "concerned" by the federal action.

Union leaders representing airport workers also criticized the timing of the arrests ahead of a busy travel week. April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, called the operation a "smash-and-grab" action that injected fear and chaos into the terminal.

"Just days after our nation experienced widespread disruptions to air travel and flights being grounded, federal agents chose to carry out this operation at one of our busiest airports, during one the busiest travel weeks of the year," Sims wrote in a statement.
Reuters contributed to this report.

Eric Mack is a breaking news reporter and writer Sunday through Thursday, 6 a.m. ET to 2 p.m. ET, with a particular interest in stories that lead the news cycle on politics, elections, foreign affairs and government.

title: 'Crazy': Moderates fear Dem leadership promised far-left reparations and ICE demands in turn of votes
summary: House Democrats are split as progressives' push to abolish ICE and reparations for descendants of slavery, while moderates warn it may hurt affordability.
story: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., told Fox News Digital she hopes to work with President Donald Trump on a stock trading ban and healthcare, while leaving the door open to a potential presidential run.

Progressive House Democrats believe party leaders could use their newly won majority to back their far-left agenda on such matters as reparations and abolishing ICE, despite pushback from moderates concerned about the party's direction.

Newly elected Democratic Caucus Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., and progressive lawmakers told Fox News Digital that proposals to abolish ICE, expand deportation protections and pursue slavery reparations will be part of the party's legislative discussions under Speaker-nominee Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., despite concerns from moderates that the agenda could distract from affordability.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and other House Democrats attend the hearing on "Americans impacted by service cuts, mass firings and healthcare price hikes," due to the government shutdown in the Capitol Visitor Center on Oct. 22, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
‘SQUAD’ MEMBER ANNOUNCES ‘MAJORITY PRIORITIES’ INCLUDING REPARATIONS, ABOLISHING ICE AFTER BLUE WAVE
"Jeffries has been very clear, he wants to make sure everyone in the caucus is well represented," Rep. Sara Jacobs, D-Calif., a member of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, told Fox News Digital.
Lieu told Fox News Digital that he is "excited" to have "discussions on everything" with members of the caucus, including proposals involving reparations and abolishing ICE.

The California Democrat said he would also be willing to consider other priorities of Rep. Ayanna Presley, D-Mass., including Medicare for All, "abortion justice" and extending Temporary Protected Status for Third World migrants.
Rep. Ted Lieu speaks during a press conference at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Feb. 3, 2026. (Matt McClain/The Washington Post)
'SQUAD' MEMBER URGES DEMS TO TAKE ADVANTAGE OF MIDTERM SWEEP BY PASSING FAR-LEFT POLICIES

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., a prominent supporter of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), told Fox News Digital that progressives and Jeffries have found common ground on several priorities outlined in Pressley's agenda, including expanding healthcare access and public housing.

"Of course, there are going to be areas where leader Jeffries and DSA are going to be in strong opposition, but there are also areas like expanding Medicaid, public housing, and housing issues in general, where there are shared values that unite everybody," Ocasio-Cortez, a potential 2028 presidential contender, told Fox News Digital.

Ocasio-Cortez has also begun working with Democratic leadership on the House Energy and Commerce Committee to advance her healthcare priorities, a senior congressional democratic staffer told Fox News Digital.

However, moderate Democrats were skeptical that party leadership would embrace the progressive agenda, with some questioning whether Jeffries and other leaders had promised to consider those demands in exchange for support during the leadership elections.

"Our agenda is to focus on costs," Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., told Fox News Digital. "What's clear is we had an overwhelming majority. I think some of my colleagues seem to be unhappy with winning in a place we've never won before."
Gottheimer accused progressive colleagues of wanting to "squawk and complain and make their demands" rather than focus on the issues that helped Democrats win the midterm elections.

The New Jersey Democrat also rejected proposals to "defund police, have open borders, or get rid of the United States Senate," arguing that neither he nor Democratic leadership would support such policies.
HAKEEM JEFFRIES REJECTS MEDICARE FOR ALL, DSA AGENDA AS RO KHANNA CALLS HEALTH PLAN 'MOST IMPORTANT PRIORITY'
Rep. Ayanna Pressley takes to the stage at an election night party for Gov. Maura Healey and Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll on Nov. 3, 2026. (Jessica Rinaldi/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)

Gottheimer, an outspoken critic of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), suggested that Pressley's priorities more closely resemble the organization's platform than the broader Democratic Party's agenda.
"The DSA, they have their own agenda," Gottheimer said.
RADICAL SOCIALIST WING'S HUGE NIGHT REVEALS ASCENDING CLOUT WITHIN DEMOCRATIC PARTY
Another Democratic lawmaker, who requested anonymity, told Fox News Digital that they and a longtime colleague viewed the prospect of leadership adopting the progressive agenda as "crazy."
The lawmaker also speculated that Lieu and Jeffries were expressing openness to progressive proposals to avoid opposition during Wednesday's leadership elections.

Jeffries and Pressley did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

title: Newsom's bid to empty California's death row collides with voters' repeated rejection of abolition
summary: A lawsuit challenges Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom's effort to commute all 548 death sentences, citing failures to notify district attorneys.
story: Zack Smith, a senior legal fellow at the Heritage Foundation, tells Fox News Digital that Gov. Gavin Newsom may be imposing his own views of the death penalty over those of other Californians.

A lawsuit challenging Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom's plan to commute 548 death sentences is raising questions about the governor's clemency powers, with a legal expert arguing Newsom is using his gubernatorial authority to circumvent the will of voters who have repeatedly rejected efforts to abolish capital punishment.

Newsom announced Nov. 5 that he intends to commute the death sentences of all 548 inmates on the Golden State's death row to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole, a move that will take effect only after the necessary legal steps are completed.

The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation (CJLF) on Sunday filed a lawsuit at the California Supreme Court seeking to block Newsom's proposed sweeping commutation, citing the governor's "failure to provide legally required notice to district attorneys and his disregard for the rights of victims and their families to be notified and heard," according to a news release.

Newsom may be using clemency to impose his own views on capital punishment despite voters repeatedly rejecting abolition, Zack Smith, a senior legal fellow for Courts and the Constitution at the Heritage Foundation, told Fox News Digital on Tuesday.
MICHAEL RUIZ: DA IDENTIFIES 49 LOCAL KILLERS SLATED FOR NEWSOM'S DEATH ROW CLEMENCY — AND THEIR CRIMES
California Gov. Gavin Newsom takes questions from the media. (Reuters/Fred Greaves)

"The death penalty remains on the books in California, and as you alluded to, California voters have repeatedly rejected efforts to abolish the death penalty," Smith said. "So Californians understand that it can be an appropriate punishment in certain circumstances. Now, [Gov.] Newsom, he does have the ability to exercise the pardon, the commutation power, the contours of that obviously are being litigated, but I think what's clear is that from a practical standpoint, [Gov.] Newsom is essentially using this to circumvent the clear will of the voters and impose his own views of the death penalty over those of ... the California populace."

"Now some of the specifics related to this suit challenging Gavin Newsom's use of the commutation pardon, that is going to vary a little bit from state to state," Smith added. "So this is going focus largely on issues of California state law and the issues specifically that I think will get the most attention is whether the California Supreme Court would essentially have to weigh in and more or less approve some of these repeat offenders before their sentences can be commuted."

California voters notably defeated Proposition 34, a ballot initiative to ban capital punishment, in 2012, according to Ballotpedia. Voters in the Golden State similarly rejected Proposition 62, the Abolition of Death Penalty Measure, in November 2016, per Ballotpedia.

The lawsuit alleges that Newsom "has claimed to himself the unfettered power to decide how clemency should be granted, ignored the Legislature’s requirement of a referral to the Board of Parole Hearings for investigation and recommendation, ignored the role of the trial court and District Attorney in providing crucial factual input to the Board of Parole Hearings, ignored the limitation of the required notice to District Attorneys, and deprived the Legislature, the public, and this Court of the information needed to determine whether he has abused his authority."

CJLF's lawsuit also requests that "the Court immediately stay any issuance, implementation, recognition, or enforcement of the challenged commutations pending further order of the Court and pending determination of this petition on the merits."

Anne Marie Schubert, president and CEO of CJLF, said in a statement that the lawsuit "is about protecting the constitutional rights of victims, defending the rule of law, and ensuring that no Governor is above the law."

"The Governor’s clemency power does not authorize mass commutations that disregard constitutional safeguards, legally required procedures, or victims’ rights," Schubert said, adding that "blanket commutation is not an exercise of discretion — it is an abandonment of it."
CJLF and Newsom's office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

The coalition suing Newsom is comprised of several law enforcement leaders and organizations, victims’ rights groups and multiple district attorneys, including Sacramento County District Attorney Thien Ho, who ran as a Democrat in the 2026 congressional primary.
Some of California’s most notorious serial killers are among the death row inmates whose sentences Newsom plans to commute, KTLA reported Nov. 8.

"Obviously, these are individuals who, again, have been convicted by a jury of their peers of committing particularly aggravated forms of murder," Smith told Fox News Digital. "Again, many of these individuals tortured their victims and included sexual violence against their victims before they were ultimately killed. And so these are individuals that their own peers thought deserved the death penalty. And, so again, to see [Gov.] Newsom circumventing this through his commutation power is very, very troubling."

Under the California Constitution, Newsom must obtain a recommendation from at least four California Supreme Court justices before commuting the sentences of 382 inmates who have been convicted of more than one felony.

The California Supreme Court has invited interested parties to weigh in on the proposed commutations, with legal briefs due Nov. 24 and Newsom's response due Dec. 4. Attorney General Rob Bonta told the court Newsom will not formally commute any death sentences until the justices act, including those of inmates with only one felony conviction.

Newsom's office has argued that the governor's broad constitutional clemency authority allows him to initiate blanket commutations without following statutory procedures governing individual applications, while separately seeking the California Supreme Court's required recommendation for inmates with multiple felony convictions.
Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks during an address on June 10, 2025. (Office of California Governor via AP)
CALIFORNIA DA SAYS GAVIN NEWSOM'S 'CRUEL' DEATH ROW CLEMENCY STABS CRIME VICTIMS 'IN THE HEART'

"District attorneys have a legal responsibility to represent the people of California and protect the rights of crime victims," Greg Totten, CEO of the California District Attorneys Association, said in a statement. "The Governor’s failure to provide legally required notice to prosecutors has deprived them of the opportunity to provide critical information and ensure that victims and their families are heard."
'BABY KILLERS, COP KILLERS' HAVE AN ALLY IN NEWSOM, MURDERED GIRL'S FATHER SAYS AMID DEATH ROW CONTROVERSY
"No Governor should be permitted to circumvent the very safeguards designed to ensure that justice is served," Totten added.

A California flag is waved outside of the Edward R. Roybal Federal Building, at left, and the U.S. Justice Department, right, in Downtown Los Angeles on June 11, 2025. (Christina House/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Newsom's proposed commutations would mark the largest mass commutation of death sentences in American history, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Newsom also issued a March 2019 executive order establishing a moratorium on executions in California, leaving the state's death penalty law and existing death sentences in place.
Democratic California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra said in a May 28, 2026, X post that he plans to extend California’s moratorium on executions when he takes office.

"Governor Newsom’s death penalty moratorium represented an important step toward a more just criminal justice system," Becerra wrote in the post. "As Governor, I will extend California’s moratorium on executions and continue moving our state away from a costly, flawed system that disproportionately impacts Black and brown communities and too often gets it wrong."
Dan Dow, district attorney of San Luis Obispo County, California, blasted Newsom's proposed commutation as "a sickening abuse of power" in a Nov. 5 statement.

"Governor Newsom just told the families of Rachel Newhouse, Aundria Crawford, Kesha Gurke and every other innocent victim of California's 548 condemned killers that the killers' lives matter more," Dow asserted. "Juries chose justice case by case, voters chose it five times, and one outgoing governor is trying to erase it all with a pen. This is a sickening abuse of power."

title: $275M Obama-era solar fraud case could net taxpayers $1B, but Trump's DOJ backs Biden dismissal
summary: Investors behind a False Claims Act qui tam lawsuit over Crescent Dunes' $275 million federal grant say the Trump DOJ is defending a Biden-era dismissal.
story: Pat Hogan, CEO of CMB Regional Centers, alleges fraud in a $275 million Treasury grant obtained by Crescent Dunes’ former owner and companies linked to Spanish construction giant Cobra.
This article is Part 2 of a Fox News Digital exclusive series investigating the Crescent Dunes solar power plant in Nevada. You can read Part 1 here.
The Trump administration has made fighting fraud and rooting out government waste a top priority, even offering cash rewards to Americans who expose wrongdoing.

Yet investors in a failed Obama-era solar plant are questioning why President Donald Trump's own Justice Department is fighting to squash their fraud lawsuit over a $275 million federal grant — a case they say could recover up to $1 billion for taxpayers.

The investors allege that Spanish construction giant ACS and companies to tied its former subsidiary Cobra, misled federal officials into approving the grant by claiming the troubled solar plant was ready for use, even though it had suffered major construction problems and was shut down for months following a molten-salt-tank failure.

The lawsuit centers on the beleaguered Crescent Dunes solar plant, a billion-dollar, government-backed project that began operating in Nevada in 2015 but was later plagued by engineering failures, repeated shutdowns and two bankruptcies before being sold for just $7 million in July.
HOW A $1B OBAMA-ERA SOLAR PLANT WENT BANKRUPT TWICE, LEAVING TAXPAYERS WITH THE TAB

An aerial view of the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada, shows thousands of mirrors concentrating sunlight onto the central tower in footage published in 2018. The billion-dollar solar plant later went through two bankruptcies before being sold for $7 million in 2026. (ferrantraite/iStock via Getty Images)

The plant was built around an emerging solar technology that used thousands of mirrors to concentrate sunlight onto a towering receiver, heating molten salt that could be stored and used to generate electricity even after sunset.

In 2020, a group of private investors who had put $90 million into the project and suffered substantial losses filed a whistleblower lawsuit, alleging the companies had misled the federal government to secure the enormous grant.
But in November 2024, just two days after Trump's re-election, Biden's Justice Department moved to shut down the lawsuit, arguing that pursuing the case would burden federal agencies.
WHITE HOUSE LAUNCHES INTERACTIVE MAP TRACKING BILLIONS IN SUSPECTED FRAUD

SolarReserve, ACS Group/Cobra and Banco Santander were original project participants in Crescent Dunes, which received a $737 million Department of Energy loan guarantee and approximately $275.6 million in Treasury grant awards. CMB investors also provided $90 million in private financing. (Fox News)
DOJ UNVEILS NATIONWIDE TAX FRAUD CRACKDOWN INVOLVING 76 DEFENDANTS, NEARLY $500M IN ALLEGED LOSSES

The incoming Trump administration could have reconsidered that position in early 2025. Instead, its Justice Department defended the Biden-era dismissal in an April filing with a federal appeals court.
CMB, an investment group headed by Pat Hogan, is appealing the dismissal. Hogan is also urging Trump’s Justice Department to ask the court to reopen the case.
"It makes no sense," Hogan told Fox News Digital in a video interview.
Hogan said he had contacted Trump's Justice Department seeking help reviving the case but had received no commitment.

"The real problem here is, why isn't the government asking for this?" he said. "All in all, I would say this has just been a fleecing of the federal government by a foreign entity. And we have the opportunity to fix it, and they're doing nothing."
Hogan argues that allowing the lawsuit to proceed could potentially net hundreds of millions of dollars for taxpayers.
Under the False Claims Act, which CMB used to bring its lawsuit, companies found liable can face damages of up to three times the government's proven losses, plus additional penalties.
"This could be a billion dollars," Hogan said.

Tonopah Solar Energy, the plant's former owner and one of the defendants, has rejected CMB's allegations as baseless in court filings. Other companies named in the lawsuit have also backed the Justice Department's effort to dismiss the case.

In an April 2026 court filing, Trump's Justice Department defended the Biden administration's decision, making the same argument that continuing the lawsuit would drain government resources and that federal law gave it broad authority to shut down the case. In court filings reviewed by Fox News Digital, neither administration put a dollar figure on the cost of continuing the lawsuit.

The decision has left Hogan and his investors questioning why the government shut down the case — and what Treasury officials knew about the plant's serious problems when they approved the $275 million grant.

Pat Hogan, CEO of CMB Regional Centers, whose investors provided $90 million in financing for the Crescent Dunes solar project, is challenging the dismissal of a federal whistleblower lawsuit alleging fraud involving a $275 million Treasury grant. (Provided)

The Crescent Dunes solar plant in Tonopah, Nevada, left, received approximately $275.6 million in Treasury grant awards. Private investors allege the plant's former owner and companies involved in its construction fraudulently obtained the funding. The allegations remain disputed, and a federal judge dismissed the whistleblower lawsuit at the Justice Department's request. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital; Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
At the heart of the lawsuit is a dispute over whether Crescent Dunes was properly completed — and whether its owner, Tonopah Solar Energy, was entitled to collect the $275 million Treasury grant.

The grant was part of a $26 billion program within the Obama administration's broader $90 billion green-energy push, launched under the 2009 economic stimulus package to create jobs and turbocharge its green energy agenda.

Known as Section 1603, the program paid developers about 30% of their qualifying construction costs once their facilities were "placed in service" — meaning ready and available for their intended use. Treasury considered several factors in determining whether a plant met that standard, including whether it had passed critical tests, begun generating electricity and come under its owner's control.
Crescent Dunes began generating electricity in 2015, but CMB alleges it had produced no more than 32% of its expected output through June 2016.
Then, in October 2016, a failure involving the plant's hot molten-salt storage tank shut it down for months.

A diagram displayed at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada, illustrates how thousands of mirrors concentrate sunlight onto a central receiver, heating molten salt that is stored in tanks and used to generate electricity. The diagram bears the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy logo. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital)

In December, while Crescent Dunes was still shut down, its builder, Cobra Thermosolar Plants, formally handed the plant over to its owner, Tonopah Solar Energy, under an arrangement known as "provisional acceptance."
But first, they changed the construction contract to allow the handover despite major defects and unfinished repairs.
That agreement came just days before the year-end deadline for solar plants to be ready for use to qualify for the Treasury grants.

In a later court filing, CMB alleged that more than 9,000 defects had been identified and grouped into roughly 500 outstanding construction items, including seven major deficiencies. The investors argue the problems showed the plant was not ready to be handed over.

The December agreement itself acknowledged that repairs to the failed hot molten-salt storage tank were still needed. The tank was central to the plant's operation, storing heat from the sun so electricity could be generated even after sunset.
CMB alleges the companies used the revised agreement to make Crescent Dunes appear ready for use and secure the Treasury grant, even though major problems remained unresolved.

Records reviewed by Fox News Digital show Treasury had questioned whether Crescent Dunes was ready for use months before approving the grant payment.

In September 2016, Treasury questioned a claim by Tonopah Solar Energy that Crescent Dunes had been ready for use since February of that year. The agency pointed to a July commissioning report suggesting the builder, Cobra Thermosolar Plants, had not yet formally handed control of the facility over to Tonopah.

In a Sept. 21 response to Treasury's questions, Tonopah Solar Energy defended its claim, arguing that the plant had passed key tests and was capable of generating electricity. It also acknowledged an earlier extended shutdown caused by problems with the plant's salt-piping system.
The following month, the plant's hot molten-salt storage tank failed, forcing the plant offline for months.
Despite that breakdown, Tonopah and Cobra went ahead with the revised handover agreement in December.

On March 7, 2017, just weeks into the first Trump administration, Treasury approved a $243.7 million grant payment — even though Crescent Dunes remained shut down nearly five months after the tank failure.
The plant would not resume generating electricity until July 2017.

A timeline shows how Crescent Dunes faced questions over its readiness for operation, suffered a major molten-salt tank failure in October 2016 and remained shut down when Treasury approved a $243.7 million grant payment in March 2017. An additional $31.9 million was approved in February 2018, bringing total grant awards to approximately $275.6 million. The approvals are central to disputed fraud allegations brought by private investors. (Fox News)

The approval letter said Treasury was still reviewing some of the project's claimed costs before deciding whether to release additional money.

In February 2018, Treasury approved an additional $31.9 million, bringing the total grant awards to approximately $275.6 million, according to newly obtained federal records. The additional payment was scheduled for disbursement within seven business days.
But Treasury was not the only federal agency involved.

The Department of Energy, which had backed Crescent Dunes with a $737 million federal loan guarantee, also had a say in major construction decisions. DOE approved the revised December handover despite unfinished repairs. It also waived certain missed deadlines, allowing the plant to be formally recognized as operational under its loan agreement.
That approval did not automatically qualify Crescent Dunes for the separate Treasury grant.

A separate December 2016 financing agreement involving Tonopah Solar Energy and DOE required the Treasury grant money to go first toward repaying the project’s short-term federal borrowing, including principal and accrued interest.
Documents obtained by Fox News Digital show that Tonopah Solar Energy made a $218.9 million payment toward a federal loan in March 2017, shortly after Treasury approved its initial grant award.
"So in a sense, the federal government just paid themselves, right? So they're still out the money, right," Hogan told Fox News Digital.

On April 12, 2017, while Crescent Dunes was still offline, DOE published an article celebrating the plant as a breakthrough in solar technology without mentioning that it had been shut down for months.

What remains unclear is whether Treasury officials knew about the October breakdown, unfinished repairs and December contract changes when they authorized the initial grant payment — information that could have affected whether the plant qualified for the grant.
Fox News Digital has asked DOE and Treasury about the grant's approval process, the plant's condition and taxpayer losses, but neither agency has provided a full accounting.
In a statement, the Trump administration's Department of Energy criticized previous administrations' handling of the project, saying it had resolved its financial interests in Crescent Dunes in 2020.

"It is unfortunate that previous administrations irresponsibly managed taxpayer dollars in their support of the Green New Scam," a DOE spokesperson said. "Since 2020, DOE has had no ownership, operational, or financial interest in the Obama-era project."
Fox News Digital has also filed Freedom of Information Act requests seeking grant payment records, loan accounting and communications between the agencies.

The Crescent Dunes solar plant near Tonopah, Nevada, features a central tower surrounded by more than 10,000 mirrors that direct sunlight toward a receiver to generate electricity. The Obama-era project, backed by more than $1 billion in federal support, went bankrupt twice before selling for $7 million in July 2026. (Getty Images)

In January 2020, Hogan's investment group, CMB, which had lent $90 million to a company tied to Crescent Dunes developer SolarReserve, sued Tonopah Solar Energy and companies tied to Spanish construction giant ACS, accusing them of defrauding the federal government.

The lawsuit was filed under the False Claims Act, which allows private whistleblowers to sue on the government's behalf and receive a share of any money recovered. Known as "qui tam" cases, the lawsuits can be taken over or dismissed by the Justice Department.
After investigating CMB's allegations for more than three years, Biden's Justice Department declined to take over the lawsuit in June 2023, leaving CMB to pursue it alone.

On Nov. 7, 2024, just two days after Trump's election victory, Biden's Justice Department moved to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that continuing the case would burden the Treasury, Energy and Justice departments.
CMB challenged the move, arguing that Biden's DOJ had failed to explain what had changed since it allowed the investors to proceed.
Then, in July 2025, six months into Trump's second term, a federal judge granted DOJ's request and dismissed the lawsuit without deciding whether the fraud allegations were true.
CMB appealed to the Ninth Circuit, where Trump's Justice Department defended the dismissal in an April 2026 court filing.

Matt Dunn, an attorney at Covington & Burling who specializes in False Claims Act litigation, described DOJ's decision to intervene after initially allowing the case to proceed as "unusual, but not extraordinary."
Dunn said the government may have its own assessment of a lawsuit's potential value that differs from the whistleblower's.
"The government might privately have a different view of the merits of the case or the potential value of the case that it doesn't necessarily share publicly," Dunn said.

Dunn said the Supreme Court has given the government substantial discretion to dismiss such cases, describing the legal hurdle for whistleblowers seeking to overturn a dismissal as "an extraordinarily high bar for a relator to overcome."
Hogan, meanwhile, has a financial stake in the outcome. He says his investors lost the $90 million they lent to the SolarReserve-linked company.

If the lawsuit is revived and CMB ultimately succeeds, the government theoretically could recover up to three times its proven damages under the False Claims Act, and CMB could receive a share, potentially offsetting its investors' losses.
"That's my job for my investors to leave no stone unturned to try to make sure that, in fact, I get their money back," Hogan said.

The Ninth Circuit must now decide whether the lawsuit can move forward — potentially opening the door for the government to recover hundreds of millions of dollars in disputed funds — or whether DOJ's decision to shut it down will stand.
The Justice Department's handling of the case has also drawn scrutiny on Capitol Hill.
In February 2025, Reps. Lance Gooden, R-Texas, and Carol Miller, R-W.Va., urged Attorney General Pam Bondi to investigate why the Biden administration moved to shut down the lawsuit.

Gooden later urged Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to consider suspending federal contracts with companies tied to Spanish construction giant ACS, whose subsidiary Cobra built the plant and held a stake in Tonopah Solar Energy. He also called for an investigation into ACS and Banco Santander's roles in the project's financing and bankruptcy amid the allegations of fraud involving federal funds.

"When taxpayers are defrauded to a scale this massive, our government has a responsibility to get the facts and hold those responsible to account," Gooden told Fox News Digital. "That is why I have asked Secretary Hegseth to pause contracts with ACS-affiliated entities until these allegations are fully reviewed and every avenue to recover taxpayer money has been pursued."

In February 2025, Reps. Lance Gooden, R-Texas, and Carol Miller, R-W.Va., urged Attorney General Pam Bondi to investigate why the Biden administration moved to shut down the lawsuit. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Rep. Carol Miller, R-W.Va., leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 29, 2023. Miller has questioned the collapse of the federally backed Crescent Dunes solar plant and the potential loss of taxpayer money. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

One such contract involves a $2.84 billion Navy dry dock project at Pearl Harbor awarded to a joint venture involving ACS subsidiary Dragados. The project completion date has been delayed from September 2027 to March 2029, according to the Government Accountability Office. Dragados is not accused of fraud in the Crescent Dunes lawsuit.
Miller, meanwhile, also questioned how a project backed by nearly $1 billion in federal financing could end up selling for $7 million.

"That's not good math," Miller told Fox News Digital. She suggested another congressional letter could be warranted, saying that "if we can recover any of that taxpayer money, that would be wonderful."

In April 2026, Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, a longtime defender of whistleblowers who helped strengthen the False Claims Act in 1986, demanded answers from DOJ over its handling of fraud lawsuits, particularly cases it shut down despite whistleblowers wanting to press ahead.

In a July 10 response obtained by Fox News Digital, DOJ revealed that Crescent Dunes was one of just 12 cases in which it moved to shut down a lawsuit after initially allowing it to proceed — fewer than 0.3% of nearly 5,000 whistleblower cases received between 2020 and 2025.

DOJ also confirmed that other federal agencies can push to have such lawsuits dismissed, including to avoid the burden of producing evidence. But it did not say whether Treasury or DOE pushed to kill the Crescent Dunes case — or what investigators found when they examined the fraud allegations.

In April 2026, Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, a longtime defender of whistleblowers who helped strengthen the False Claims Act in 1986, demanded answers from DOJ over its handling of fraud lawsuits, particularly cases it shut down despite whistleblowers wanting to press ahead. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
The companies accused of fraud have backed DOJ's effort to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that federal law gives the government broad authority to shut down whistleblower cases.

Tonopah Solar Energy, which filed for bankruptcy in January 2026, has also fiercely rejected CMB's allegations, accusing the investors of pursuing a "scorched earth mission" through repeated legal challenges against the company.
"The reality is there is no merit to CMB's claims whatsoever," the company argued in an April 2026 bankruptcy filing.

Tonopah Solar Energy made those arguments while winding down its affairs in bankruptcy, before selling the plant's assets in July. The new owners had no involvement in the alleged 2016 fraud, and the bankruptcy sale generally shielded them from the former owner's legal liabilities.

In a separate 2020 lawsuit, Hogan's investors sought to recover an allegedly unpaid $90 million loan, suing companies tied to Crescent Dunes after SolarReserve failed to repay much of the money. They suffered a setback in 2024 when an arbitration panel rejected five of their claims and ordered them to pay $2.44 million in legal fees and costs.
The companies did not respond to Fox News Digital's repeated requests for comment.
The dispute was separate from the whistleblower lawsuit alleging fraud involving the $275 million Treasury grant.
Despite years of investigation, the Justice Department has never publicly disclosed what it uncovered.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Nearly seven years after Hogan's investors filed their lawsuit, the fraud allegations have never been tested at trial. And despite President Trump's pledge to crack down on fraud and wasteful green-energy spending, his Justice Department is still defending the Biden administration's decision to shut down the case.
"If we're wrong, the evidence will show it," Hogan said. "But don't let a Biden-era dismissal prevent the merits from ever being heard."
Michael Dorgan is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business.

title: NYC college put on notice after Jewish campus group shunned by student government: 'Rude awakening'
summary: Shabbos Kestenbaum decries anti-Jewish discrimination after a City University of New York school canceled a Cultural Arts Night, citing Title VI.
story: Shabbos Kestenbaum called for Hunter College to lose federal funding after its student government was accused of shutting down an event involving Jewish students.

A Jewish American activist in New York City decried what he calls "anti-Jewish discrimination" after the student government at a school that is part of the City University of New York (CUNY) system, canceled an event that was supposed to include the school's Hillel group when it received backlash from other student organizations.

Hunter College's undergraduate student government (USG) canceled a "Cultural Arts Night" involving several student groups, including Hunter Hillel, the Chinese Student & Scholar Association, the Taiwanese Student Association and the Center for Puerto Rican Studies, according to the New York Post. The radical far-left group Students for Justice in Palestine reportedly took part in planning the event.
In a statement to The Post, the school itself admitted that some of those groups withdrew from the event because Hunter Hillel was planning to participate.
Protesters rallied outside Hunter College on Nov. 19, 2026, after student leaders scrapped an event featuring Hillel. (#EndJewHatred)
JEWISH CAMPUS LIFE AT A ‘CROSSING POINT’ AS STUDENTS WEIGH ANTISEMITISM RISKS, NEW REPORT SHOWS

"They were establishing a cultural arts night, which I might add also included countries with far worse civil rights violations, like China, and none of that was a problem until, of course, the Jewish organization was involved," said Shabbos Kestenbaum, who described himself as a Jewish American activist and who works for PragerU.
"So this is blatant anti-Jewish discrimination, and we as New Yorkers, we as Americans, and yes, we, as Jews, will do our best to hold the university accountable," he said.
The USG apologized for sponsoring the event, saying it had "failed" and that the event "should never have moved forward.

"To be clear, USG does not endorse this event or this collaboration," the apology said. "We hear what the student body has said, and we have made the decision to cancel the event as it doesn’t align with our values or the values of the students we represent as the Hunter Community. We apologize to the clubs and students who were affected by this instance."
Hunter College faced claims of antisemitism after student leaders canceled an event featuring Hillel, a Jewish organization. (Rachel Wolf/Fox News Digital)
JUSTICE DEPARTMENT LAUNCHES TITLE VI INVESTIGATION INTO DEI PROGRAMS AT ARIZONA STATE UNIVERSITY
The apology said the group was actively working to ensure that such a mistake never happened again.

Kestenbaum believes that the school might have run afoul of anti-discrimination laws, including Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits any entity receiving federal funding from engaging in discrimination based on sex, race, ethnicity or other immutable characteristics.
He advocated for the federal government to pull its funding from Hunter College.

"It's just enforcing the laws already on the books," he said, adding that President Donald Trump and his administration have been making progress on punishing discriminatory behavior on college campuses.

Graduates of Hunter College walk out of graduation ceremonies to protest Israel's continued war in Gaza on May 30, 2025, outside Barclays Center in Brooklyn, N.Y. (Andrew Lichtenstein/Corbis via Getty Images)

"It's not something you pick and choose if you feel good that morning," he said. "It's the law and the expenditure of federal dollars is a representation of our values. And so if you're at university and you're discriminating against American citizens based on their ethnicity, based on the religion, based on their politics — not only is that a violation of law, but that's not a representation of where we want our money to go to."
Hunter Hillel responded to the cancellation in a statement to Fox News Digital.
BACK TO SCHOOL SHOULD NOT MEAN BACK TO FEAR FOR JEWISH STUDENTS

"Hillel students were looking forward to taking part in the Cultural Arts Night, and our organization had no role in the student government’s decision to cancel it. Antisemitism has no place at Hunter College," the statement said. "The antisemitic response to the cancellation notice has been egregious and inappropriate. Rita Levine Rabin Hillel at Hunter remains committed to building joyful, strong, and vibrant Jewish life on campus."

Kestenbaum also referenced Rep.-elect Darializa Chevalier, D-N.Y., a prominent anti-Israel activist who took part in the infamous 2024 Columbia University encampment, and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, himself a former anti-Israel activist.
He said students at New York's colleges are simply following the examples set for them by their elected officials.
CUNY has previously settled with the Department of Education after discrimination claims.
TRUMP ADMIN OPENS CIVIL RIGHTS PROBES INTO 15 COLLEGES OVER DEI GRANTS
Columbia University students participate in a pro-Palestinian encampment on their campus on April 25, 2024, in New York City. (Stephanie Keith/Getty Images)

"And all these elitist universities that think that they're higher and better than the law, they're in for a rude awakening," Kestenbaum said. "And again, you don't need to radically pass pieces of legislation that overhauls the bureaucracy. All you need to do is make it incredibly clear to these colleges, we are not giving you money if you discriminate. It is literally that simple."
The CUNY system did not return a request for comment.

"There is no place for discrimination and harassment in our college community," Hunter College told the New York Post. "We have policies in place to safeguard that principle and will not hesitate to enforce them."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Neither Hunter College nor its USG returned Fox News Digital's comment requests.
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Jeffries calling Jerusalem NYC's ‘sixth borough’ resurfaces as progressives swing against Israel
summary: Hakeem Jeffries once called Jerusalem the "6th Borough" in a resurfaced AIPAC clip, raising questions as he heads toward a January House speaker vote.
story: The top Democrat in the House of Representatives defends Israel in a 2020 AIPAC speech where he acknowledges that the country has to wrestle with regional instability, adversaries
Hakeem Jeffries once called his deep ties to Jerusalem an extension of his representation of New York City as he touted his support for Israel and the Jewish community.

But those comments from 2020, recently resurfaced and going viral, may come back to bite the Democratic House leader as the progressive wing of the party — and even some establishment members — continue to further break with the U.S. maintaining support for the Jewish state.
"Someone said to me, ‘Hakeem, you’re going to Israel a 5th time?’" Jeffries recalled in an interview with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) more than six years ago.
"I said, ‘listen, I’m from New York City' — and back home in New York City, we consider Jerusalem to be the 6th Borough. And so, I’m just trying to catch up with my constituents."
The comments resurfaced just after he won his party's nomination to be speaker of the House in the next Congress.
JEFFRIES SURVIVES DEM VOTE TO SECURE SPEAKER POSITION AS PROGRESSIVE RESISTANCE CLOUDS HIS CHANCES

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks before a House vote on funding for the Department of Homeland Security, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on March 5, 2026. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)

The remarks from 2020 contrast starkly with a growing faction of the Democratic Party that has condemned AIPAC and the political favor Israel has historically enjoyed among lawmakers. The clip also raises questions over how far Jeffries will go to placate calls for a more critical review of U.S.-Israel relations in light of his previous support for the Jewish state.

Jeffries won the secret-ballot vote to remain leader of the House’s Democratic Caucus with just 11 in the caucus voting against his leadership and 251 voting in favor. The result secured his nomination ahead of the full House floor vote in January, where he will need a simple majority of the chamber's 435 members to become speaker.
During his AIPAC speech, Jeffries noted that some of his support stemmed from the uniquely challenging geopolitical environment around Israel.
"I think when you’re on the ground, for me it’s always been clear that Israel lives in an incredibly tough neighborhood," Jeffries said.

"When you think about the dangerous situation in the Sinai to the south, Hamas in Gaza, Hezbollah to the north, Syria and chaos to the east, Iraq still a mess, Iran with nuclear ambitions and a tremendously bad actor — I grew up in Brooklyn in the late 80s and early 90s, I know from tough neighborhoods that Israel lives in a tough neighborhood," Jeffries said.
HOUSE DEMOCRATS FRACTURE BADLY OVER MASSIE AMENDMENT TO CUT $3.3B IN U.S. AID TO ISRAEL

The stance clashes forcefully with at least eight members set to be a part of the 120th Congress with ties to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). The group aims to "end all military and economic aid to Israel [and] prosecute U.S. and Israeli leaders responsible for the genocide in Gaza."
Two other members outside of the group, Democratic Reps.-elect Brad Lander and Scott Wiener have similarly called for a full embargo of Israel.
American flags on either side of an Israeli flag (Debbie Hill/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
Jeffries’ own tone on Israel has changed over the years since the beginning of its war with Hamas in Gaza in October 2023, citing alarm at Israel’s civilian casualties.
In July, Jeffries argued in a letter to his colleagues that "a meaningful change in direction is needed."
"Israel has an advanced economy and is capable of paying for its own sophisticated weapons, as the Prime Minister recently acknowledged," Jeffries wrote.

"Accordingly, any future security arrangement between our two countries should be structured consistently with defense agreements that exist with our other Western allies and strictly adhere to our human rights laws and values," Jeffries wrote.
FETTERMAN WARNS THERE IS NO LONGER 'COMMON GROUND' WITH FAR-LEFT DEMOCRATS OVER ISRAEL
Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., joined by fellow House Democrats, speaks at a press conference outside the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 30, 2025, in Washington, D.C.

Even so, Jeffries has steered clear of calling the conflict a genocide — a growing characterization from within the progressive wing — and has rejected a blanket discontinuation of U.S. aid to Israel.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In his letter, Jeffries also condemned efforts by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., to cut off all forms of assistance, advocating for a $3.3 billion military aid package to Israel included in the U.S. 2027 State Department appropriations bill.
"America’s commitment to Israel’s right to exist as a Jewish and democratic state and homeland for the Jewish people must remain ironclad," Jeffries said in his letter.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Apex predator at center of farmers vs environmentalists fight as Trump weighs major move: 'Out of control'
summary: Minnesota farmer Shayne Isane says gray wolves killed three calves in one night, costing thousands as Trump moves to reconsider federal protections.
story: Fox News Digital spoke to farmers grappling with devastating livestock losses from gray wolves and experts weighing in on Trump’s push to reconsider federal protections for the apex predator.

A powerful apex predator has reignited a fierce battle between farmers demanding greater control over gray wolves killing their livestock and environmentalists fighting to keep them shielded — a decision the Trump administration must now weigh that could shape the future of wildlife management.

One longtime Minnesota farmer has spent years grappling with the loss of several of his calves killed by gray wolves, also known as timber wolves, roaming around his property in the middle of the night.

"We can walk right outside of our door and hear the howling of these timber wolves, and it'll send shivers down your spine because you have seen what they can do, and they're the top-of-the-line predator," Shayne Isane told Fox News Digital.
"There's nothing that hunts them. No other animals they are afraid of."
ARCTIC WOLF ATTACKS CHILD DURING ZOOKEEPER EVENT, GIRL AIRLIFTED TO HOSPITAL
Farmers across the Great Lakes region are grappling with gray wolves killing their livestock, reigniting a fierce debate over wildlife management. (Courtesy of Jonathan Miller and Shayne Isane)

Isane, who has farmed for nearly four decades, said he is one of many farmers struggling to defend his livestock from gray wolves. Despite losing thousands of dollars and fearing for the safety of his nearly 300 cattle, Isane said he is unable to handle the threat himself.

"Even if we see them attacking our livestock, we can't shoot or try to help out our animals," he said. "It's just against the law. We can't do it, only in the case of the threat of human life, which is a tough sell for us, because when you see them very close to your livelihood, your families and your livestock, it's a huge concern."

As President Donald Trump moves to reconsider federal protections, Isane said he is one of many farmers hoping to gain more control over the growing threat. The plan could affect states across the country, including Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, California and Colorado.

The Interior Department has until Dec. 3 to determine whether gray wolves and their subspecies, Mexican wolves, have met the recovery criteria under the Endangered Species Act. If the criteria are met, the department must begin the process of removing or reducing federal protections.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, a department spokesperson said the department had no updates on that decision but "recognizes the importance of effective wildlife management and the challenges wolf depredation can pose for livestock producers."
NATIONAL PARK SERVICE DIRECTOR CALLS YELLOWSTONE'S WILD BISON RECOVERY AN 'INCREDIBLE CONSERVATION STORY'
Environmentalists have long opposed delisting gray wolves, arguing it could lead to culling, trapping and trophy hunting and threaten their recovery. (iStock)

One of Isane's largest losses came when three of his young calves were killed in a single night. He said the wolves often drag away or dispose of the carcasses themselves, making it difficult to confirm the attack to state investigators.
In Minnesota, a farmer must have the carcass of their livestock in order to confirm a suspected wolf attack and report the loss within 48 hours to receive reimbursement.
"To lose one animal or two animals is $3,000 a piece, and so that really can affect our bottom line," he said.

A Minnesota Department of Agriculture spokesperson told Fox News Digital its program "provides 100% reimbursement of verified losses at full market value" and pointed to its Wolf Livestock Depredation Grant.
"While we can assist farmers with livestock prevention and loss, wolf management does not fall under the work of the Minnesota Department of Agriculture," the spokesperson wrote.

But Isane said keeping the livestock alive is only part of the "constant battle." He said wolves can cause "added stress" to the herd. "They're constantly being harassed by the wolves," he said. "We see it in weights. They lose weight, they are constantly on edge, and it affects their overall health."
Isane said many deterrent methods suggested by the state have proven unsuccessful, saying wolves are able to "outsmart" them.
"They just don't work," he said.
Isane emphasized that environmentalists aren’t seeing the full picture. He said the wolf population had spiraled "out of control."
"The first 30 years of my life, I hardly saw a timber wolf, and now I've seen multiple ones, 50 to 100, probably in the last 25 years," Isane said. "It's gotten increasingly worse."
OREGON BALLOT MEASURE THAT WOULD HAVE CRIMINALIZED HUNTING AND FISHING FAILS TO QUALIFY FOR VOTE
President Donald Trump is moving to reconsider federal protections for gray wolves as farmers push for greater control over the apex predator. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
According to the Minnesota DNR, there were about 2,400 gray wolves in Minnesota in 2026, with no statistically significant change from last year.

"The Minnesota DNR is very confident in our wolf research and population estimates, which indicate a stable population, not one of unconstrained or rapid population growth," a spokesperson said in a statement to Fox News Digital.
Isane said he welcomes Trump's efforts to fix a problem that has "no method of controlling."
White House deputy press secretary Taylor Rogers told Fox News Digital the Biden administration’s "radical environmental policies" left ranchers defenseless as "predators wiped out their livestock."

"As a result, the national cattle herd reached a 75-year low, driving up prices for consumers," Rogers wrote. "As promised, President Trump is reversing these harmful policies and is fighting for America’s ranchers."
Shawn Regan, C3 Journal editor and Manhattan Institute senior fellow, said states can effectively manage recovered wolf populations without them being listed under the Endangered Species Act.

"It's not the best tool for continuing to manage recovered populations into the future," Regan said. "There's a reason why the act has a delisting process to allow for transition of those species to state management."
Delisting gray wolves has long been part of Trump's agenda.

During his first term, the administration removed federal protections for the species across most states. Six environmental groups, represented by environmental law group Earthjustice, sued the Trump administration in 2021 over the decision.

A federal judge overturned the decision in 2022, restoring protections across most states except in the Northern Rockies, where states still have control. The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals is currently weighing whether that ruling should be upheld.

Some environmental groups involved in the lawsuit told Fox News Digital Trump’s executive order could reverse years of recovery efforts and urged the administration to focus on other issues facing farmers.

"The administration is offering up wolves as a bargaining chip while failing to address the real economic pressures burdening American farmers and ranchers," Sara Amundson, president of Humane World Action Fund, said.

Eric Clewis, senior Northern Rockies representative for Defenders of Wildlife, echoed this, saying, "Framing wolves as the villain distracts from policies actually squeezing the ranching industry, particularly because wolves account for less than 1% of total livestock loss."

Collette Adkins, a senior attorney and director of the Center for Biological Diversity’s carnivore program, worries the implications could stretch even further, saying removing federal protections could "erase decades of recovery work."
WASHINGTON'S GRIZZLY BEAR POWER GRAB IS FINALLY COMING TO A LONG-OVERDUE END
Cows on Minnesota farmer Shayne Isane's farm, where he has lost several calves to gray wolf attacks over the years. (Courtesy of Shayne Isane)
She added that the "tiny fraction of livestock operators" who have conflicts with wolves can help by doing "a better job" learning to live with them peacefully.
Environmentalists have advocated for years against delisting, arguing it could lead to culling, trapping and trophy hunting and reduce populations they believe have not fully recovered.

Independent Women’s Forum Center for Energy and Conservation Director Gabriella Hoffman told Fox News Digital there is a possibility that the move to delist gray wolves may only be a short-term solution once it heads to Congress.

"Do we have to worry about lawsuits potentially blocking this from going into effect?" Hoffman, who also recently investigated wolf attacks in Wisconsin for a conservation documentary, said. "Congress not following through with their duty to codify this permanently and ensure this doesn't go back and forth?"
Hoffman said delisting could actually prevent the species from becoming endangered again.

"Leaning too much on emotions would undermine the science and also I think put the wolf in further danger and make it even more imperiled than it is if you have a management system in place," she said.
She added that wolf attacks on livestock are a sign of thriving conservation efforts.
"While it is problematic that wolf depredation or attacks by wolves is increasing, that's actually a positive sign, as counterintuitive as it sounds, of their status as a species," she said.
Jonathan Miller, a Michigan dairy farmer since the 1970s who switched to raising a herd of roughly 100 cattle, said protective fencing has created a "balance" with wolves.
"It's very effective to keep them away," he said.
He said the attacks haven’t hurt his business financially, but managing the fencing has added some extra challenges.
"It's a lot of extra work management trying to move the fence, keep it electrified so that it's effective," he said.
Earlier this month, Miller found the carcasses of two of his healthy sheep, which he blamed on his "lack of management" in putting up the barrier.
"You hate to see a wolf take one of your animals, but we lose animals, and it's just another factor," he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
When the family lost their first calf to a wolf in the early 2000s, Miller said it "kind of changed things."
It was the first time he laid eyes on the predator that "probably only weighed about 60 pounds, but was big enough to drag a calf across the yard."

Miller said wolf sightings in people's yards have become less common since locals began handling the issue themselves. However, he supports Trump's push for state management rather than "local people illegally controlling the numbers of the wolves."
He hopes the move can help farmers and wolves finally coexist.
"I don't want to eliminate the wolves," he said. "I love to see wolves. I try to get pictures, but there has to be control."
