title: States put speed-limiting devices in reckless drivers' cars
summary: Virginia's GPS speed limiter program is already active for reckless driving offenders, but early users report glitches that apply wrong speed limits.
story: A LifeSafer GPS-powered speed limiter displays a 35 mph limit and helps prevent the driver from accelerating beyond the posted speed limit. (LifeSafer ISA)

We've all seen it. You're driving down the highway when someone flies past you at a ridiculous speed. Maybe they're weaving through traffic while everyone else tries to stay out of their way. Now, states are turning to speed-limiting devices that could stop some of the most dangerous drivers from doing it again.

Virginia has already started installing GPS-powered devices in vehicles used by certain reckless-driving offenders. Washington, D.C., has a similar program, and more jurisdictions are exploring the technology. The idea sounds promising. Instead of simply telling someone to slow down, the device can actually restrict how fast their car accelerates.

However, there's a catch. Some drivers using these systems have reported GPS glitches that mistakenly apply the speed limits of nearby roads. And that raises a question worth asking. What happens when your car refuses to accelerate because its GPS thinks you're somewhere else?
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
SILICON VALLEY DEVELOPER ACCUSED OF MURDER AFTER INVESTIGATORS SAY TESLA REACHED 142 MPH BEFORE FATAL CRASH
How speed-limiting devices stop reckless drivers

The technology is called Intelligent Speed Assistance (ISA). It uses GPS location information and digital maps to determine the posted speed limit. Here's how it works. Let's say you're traveling on a road with a 45 mph speed limit. As your vehicle reaches 45 mph, the device restricts additional acceleration. Pressing harder on the gas pedal won't normally make the car accelerate beyond that limit.

However, the system doesn't automatically slam on the brakes or shut off the engine. Instead, it limits the vehicle's ability to accelerate. That means a vehicle traveling downhill could still exceed the posted limit because of gravity.

Some systems also allow brief overrides when additional acceleration is necessary for safety. Think of it as a speed governor that automatically adjusts as you move between roads. The important difference comes down to control. Many newer vehicles already recognize speed limits and warn drivers when they're going too fast. These aftermarket devices take things further by restricting acceleration.
Virginia is already putting speed limiters in cars

Virginia launched its Intelligent Speed Assistance Program on July 1. The state allows courts to require speed-limiting technology for certain driving offenses, including reckless driving and racing. The Virginia DMV can also require participation in qualifying cases involving excessive demerit points. For eligible drivers, the program offers a way to maintain restricted driving privileges rather than face a full license suspension. According to a Nov. 2 report, approximately 100 devices had been installed in Virginia since July. Many participants faced reckless-driving charges or convictions. Some cases involved speeds exceeding 100 mph.

The restrictions are serious. Qualifying drivers may need the equipment installed in every vehicle they own or co-own. They must also comply with restrictions on which vehicles they can operate. Then there's the cost. Participants generally pay installation and ongoing service fees, although financial assistance may be available for those who qualify. The goal is to let certain drivers continue essential travel while reducing the risk of dangerous speeding.
More states are moving toward speed-limiting technology

Virginia has company in exploring this approach. Washington, D.C. launched its Intelligent Speed Assistance Program on Oct. 1, 2025. Under the program, D.C. driver's license holders convicted of aggravated reckless driving must enroll and operate only authorized vehicles equipped with the technology.

Washington state passed legislation in 2025 requiring speed-limiting devices in certain cases involving dangerous speeding and driving restrictions. However, those requirements won't take effect until Jan. 1, 2029. Meanwhile, New York City is considering a proposal introduced on Oct. 22. It would require vehicle owners who accumulate 16 school-zone speeding violations within 12 months to install speed-limiting devices. The New York City proposal remains in committee and has not become law. These programs differ in scope. Still, they show how policymakers are increasingly considering technology as a response to dangerous driving.
JOE BIDEN MANDATED ALL NEW VEHICLES COME INSTALLED WITH A 'KILL SWITCH.' THIS REPUBLICAN WANTS TO REPEAL IT
LifeSafer's Intelligent Speed Assistance device uses GPS and digital maps to identify speed limits and restrict vehicle acceleration. (LifeSafer ISA)
GPS glitches are raising serious safety concerns

GPS technology is incredibly useful. But anyone who's followed navigation directions onto the wrong road knows it can make mistakes. Consider this situation. You're driving on a highway with a 65 mph speed limit. A service road running alongside it has a 35 mph limit. If your GPS mistakenly places you on the service road, the speed limiter could apply the lower limit. Your vehicle wouldn't suddenly brake, but it could restrict additional acceleration even though you're traveling on a highway with a higher speed limit. That's the type of GPS problem some Virginia participants have reported.

Early users reportedly experienced situations where their devices applied lower limits from nearby roads. Officials acknowledged the complaints and said they were working on fixes. To be clear, the reports establish that location errors have occurred. They do not establish a pattern of crashes caused by those errors. That could become a safety concern when a driver needs additional acceleration to merge into traffic, but the vehicle won't respond as expected. That's a potential safety concern officials need to address before these systems become more widespread.
Can drivers override a speed limiter in an emergency?

Some systems provide temporary overrides when drivers need additional acceleration. Virginia's proposed technical standards outline specific limits for emergency overrides, although those requirements have not yet been finalized. Under the proposal, an override would last no longer than 30 seconds, permit a maximum of 5 mph above the posted speed limit and allow no more than two overrides per driving cycle.

Those specifications appear in regulations published Oct. 19. The rules remain proposed, with public comments accepted through Dec. 18. The limits are intended to balance safety with the program's goal of preventing excessive speeding. However, they also show that an emergency override may provide much less acceleration than a driver expects. That's why clear instructions and reliable operation are so important.
Why officials believe speed limiters could save lives

There's a serious reason states are considering these devices. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, 11,288 people died in speeding-related traffic crashes in 2024. Speeding contributed to 29% of all U.S. traffic fatalities that year. Those numbers help explain why officials want something more effective than another speeding ticket.

A driver who repeatedly ignores speed limits may continue taking risks after paying fines. And suspending someone's license doesn't physically prevent that person from getting behind the wheel. Speed-limiting technology offers another option. A properly functioning device can prevent certain excessive speeds while allowing qualifying drivers to continue traveling to work or handling essential responsibilities.

However, speed limits tell only part of the safety story. Someone can drive recklessly without exceeding the posted limit. Following too closely can still cause a crash. Bad weather can also make a legally permitted speed dangerous. So, these devices may help reduce extreme speeding, but they cannot guarantee safe driving.
NEW BIG RIG SAFETY TECH COULD SAVE YOUR LIFE
A driver operates a vehicle equipped with a LifeSafer speed limiter showing a 30 mph speed limit and a current speed of 29 mph. (LifeSafer ISA)
Could speed limiters eventually be required in every car?

That's the bigger question. For now, these enforcement programs focus on drivers who meet specific legal criteria. There is no nationwide requirement forcing every U.S. driver to install one of these aftermarket speed-limiting devices. However, many newer vehicles already offer speed-limit recognition and warnings. That means some of the technology has become familiar to drivers.

The bigger step involves allowing software to actively restrict acceleration. As more jurisdictions test these programs, lawmakers could consider expanding eligibility. But any expansion would require additional policy decisions. And public acceptance could become a major obstacle. After all, there's a big difference between your dashboard warning you that you're speeding and your car preventing you from accelerating.
Speed-limiting devices also raise privacy questions

There's another issue I think deserves more attention. What happens to all the driving information these systems collect? GPS-based speed limiters need location data to determine which speed limit applies. Depending on the program, they may also record speeding events and other information used to monitor compliance.

Virginia's proposed regulations would require service providers to report certain vehicle events and speed violations, including GPS locations. The proposal also contains a significant additional requirement. Beginning July 1, 2027, new installations would need cameras capable of photographing the driver's seat when the device records a speeding event, if the proposed rules take effect as written.

That raises questions about who can access the information and how long it remains stored. We explored similar privacy concerns in our article, Is it worth saving money to let a car insurance company track your every move? Insurance tracking programs serve a different purpose. However, both technologies show how much information connected vehicles can generate about the people driving them. And once that information exists, clear rules about its collection and use become especially important.
Kurt's key takeaways

I understand why states want to take this approach. We've all shared the road with someone driving so recklessly that you wonder how they still have a license. And if technology can prevent someone from driving 100 mph through traffic, I see the appeal. What concerns me is putting that much authority in the hands of a GPS system that can make mistakes. I've seen enough technology glitches over the years to know that even sophisticated systems sometimes get things wrong. That's inconvenient when your phone sends you to the wrong address. It's a much bigger concern when you're behind the wheel. I also think states need to be careful about how they expand these programs. Targeting repeat dangerous drivers makes sense. Requiring everyone to surrender control of their vehicle would raise a very different set of questions. Before we go further, I'd like to see stronger evidence that these devices reduce crashes without creating new safety problems. Because ultimately, the goal should be safer roads. And that means making sure the technology earns our trust before we depend on it.

Would you feel safer knowing reckless drivers have speed limiters in their cars, or does the idea of a GPS system controlling your accelerator worry you even more? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: The VPN setting that keeps your printer and apps working
summary: VPN split tunneling lets your banking app skip the encrypted tunnel while other apps stay protected, and the Allow LAN setting can fix printer issues.
story: Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson warned of worrying privacy clauses in smart devices in a recent episode of the "Beyond Connected" podcast.

If you use a VPN, you've probably run into this at least once. You turn it on to protect your privacy, and suddenly something stops working. Maybe your printer won't connect. Maybe your banking app keeps asking you to verify your identity. Or perhaps a website refuses to load.

So you do what a lot of us would do. You turn off the VPN to fix the problem. Everything starts working again, and you forget to turn the VPN back on. That's the problem. You've disabled a privacy tool because it was getting in your way.

Fortunately, there's a setting that can help. It's called VPN split tunneling, and it lets you choose which apps use your VPN and which ones connect normally. There's also a separate setting worth checking if your printer stops working. Here's how both work and how to set them up with a VPN.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
TRAVEL MISTAKE PUTS PHONE, LAPTOP AND STREAMING ACCOUNTS AT RISK
A VPN helps protect your online privacy, but certain settings can interfere with apps and devices you use every day. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why VPNs can cause problems with banking apps and printers

A virtual private network, or VPN, encrypts your internet traffic between your device and the VPN server. It also hides your usual public IP address from the websites you visit. That added privacy can be especially useful on public Wi-Fi. However, some apps and websites don't always cooperate with VPN connections.
Why banking apps sometimes block VPNs

When you connect through a VPN, your bank may see an IP address associated with a different location or one shared by other VPN users. That can trigger additional security checks. Your bank might ask you to verify your identity again, block a login attempt or temporarily restrict access. The bank is trying to protect your account. Still, those interruptions can get frustrating when you're simply trying to check your balance or pay a bill.
Why your printer might disappear

Your printer works differently from your banking app. Most wireless printers communicate with your computer through your home Wi-Fi network. That connection typically stays inside your local network instead of traveling out to the internet. Some VPN settings can interfere with this communication, particularly when access to local devices is restricted.

The result? Your printer may suddenly appear offline even though it's connected to Wi-Fi and working normally. Here's the important distinction. Split tunneling can help with certain app connections, but printer problems often require a separate local network setting.
What is VPN split tunneling and how does it work?

Think of split tunneling as giving certain apps permission to take a different route. Normally, when your VPN is connected, supported internet traffic travels through the encrypted VPN tunnel. With split tunneling, you can choose which apps or connections bypass that tunnel. For example, you might want your browser and email to continue using your VPN. However, if your banking app repeatedly triggers security checks, you could allow that app to use your regular internet connection.

Both types of connections can operate at the same time. That means you don't have to disconnect your entire VPN whenever one app has trouble. There is one trade-off to understand. Apps that bypass the VPN use your regular IP address and lose the extra privacy provided by the VPN tunnel. Secure websites can still encrypt their traffic using HTTPS, but your VPN no longer shields those excluded connections. For that reason, I recommend keeping most apps on the VPN and excluding only the ones that actually need it.

Many VPN services offer split tunneling, but not all of them include it. The available controls also depend on your device, operating system and VPN app. Some let you exclude individual apps, while others allow you to create rules for websites or IP addresses.

Before getting started, open your VPN app and look for a setting called Split Tunneling, App Exclusions or something similar. If you don't see one, check your VPN provider's support website to find out whether the feature is available for your device. Here's how the setup generally works across different platforms.
On Windows and Mac, some VPN apps let you choose which applications use the VPN and which connect directly to the internet. The exact steps depend on your VPN provider.

Open your VPN app on your computer.Go to Settings, Preferences or the app's connection settings.Look for Split Tunneling or a similarly named feature.Turn on split tunneling if your VPN supports it.Choose the option to exclude selected apps from the VPN connection.Add the app that's having trouble, such as your banking app.Keep your other apps routed through the VPN unless you have a specific reason to exclude them.Save your changes and reconnect to the VPN if the app requires it.
Open your VPN app on your computer.
Go to Settings, Preferences or the app's connection settings.
Look for Split Tunneling or a similarly named feature.
Turn on split tunneling if your VPN supports it.
Choose the option to exclude selected apps from the VPN connection.
Add the app that's having trouble, such as your banking app.
Keep your other apps routed through the VPN unless you have a specific reason to exclude them.
Save your changes and reconnect to the VPN if the app requires it.
Some VPNs also let you create routing rules for specific IP addresses or websites. However, most people will find app-based controls easier to manage when they're available.

Keep in mind that split tunneling support varies on Mac. Some VPNs may require additional permissions, a particular connection protocol or an updated version of the app. If you can't find the setting, check your VPN provider's instructions before changing anything else.
SHOULD YOU USE A SEPARATE COMPUTER FOR ONLINE BANKING?
VPN split tunneling lets you choose which apps bypass the encrypted connection while keeping other internet traffic protected. (trumzz/Getty Images)
Android supports app-based VPN routing, and many VPN services offer split tunneling through their Android apps. However, the feature and its settings vary by provider.

Open your VPN app on your Android phone or tablet.Go to Settings or Connection Settings.Find Split Tunneling, App Exclusions or a similar option.Choose the setting that allows selected apps to bypass the VPN.Select the apps you want to exclude from the VPN connection.Save your changes and reconnect to the VPN if prompted.
Open your VPN app on your Android phone or tablet.
Go to Settings or Connection Settings.
Find Split Tunneling, App Exclusions or a similar option.
Choose the setting that allows selected apps to bypass the VPN.
Select the apps you want to exclude from the VPN connection.
Save your changes and reconnect to the VPN if prompted.
If your VPN supports this type of split tunneling, the selected apps should use your regular internet connection while the remaining apps continue using the VPN.

One thing to watch for: Android has a system setting called Block connections without VPN. If you've enabled it, apps configured to bypass the VPN may lose internet access because Android blocks traffic that doesn't use the VPN.

Disabling that restriction can allow split tunneling to work, but it also changes your protection if the VPN connection drops. If you depend on that stricter security setting, consider leaving it enabled.

Here's an important difference for Apple users. Split tunneling options are generally more limited on iPhones and iPads than on Windows or Android devices. Many consumer VPN apps do not offer a way to choose individual apps that bypass the VPN.

Some VPN services may support certain network or IP address exclusions, but these features vary by provider. There is no universal setting on an iPhone that lets you select a banking app and automatically exclude it from your VPN connection.
Here's what to check:

Open your VPN app on your iPhone or iPad.Look under Settings or Connection Settings for Split Tunneling, Exclusions or a similar option.If the feature is available, review which types of traffic your VPN allows you to exclude.Follow your VPN provider's instructions before adding any exceptions.Reconnect to your VPN if required and test whether the original problem has been resolved.
Open your VPN app on your iPhone or iPad.
Look under Settings or Connection Settings for Split Tunneling, Exclusions or a similar option.
If the feature is available, review which types of traffic your VPN allows you to exclude.
Follow your VPN provider's instructions before adding any exceptions.
Reconnect to your VPN if required and test whether the original problem has been resolved.

There are limitations. Some VPNs support exclusions based on IP addresses rather than individual apps. Large websites and banking services often use multiple IP addresses that can change. As a result, excluding one IP address may not solve your problem.

Excluding public IP addresses can also create privacy risks because unrelated websites sometimes share the same network infrastructure. Avoid making these changes unless you understand which connections will bypass your VPN.

For most iPhone users, I recommend checking whether switching VPN servers resolves the problem before trying more advanced settings. If your VPN doesn't support split tunneling on iOS, you may need to use another troubleshooting method.

Linux users should also check their VPN app's settings. Some Linux VPN applications support split tunneling for individual apps or IP addresses, although the available features depend on the provider and Linux distribution.
3 VPN SETTINGS TO CHECK BEFORE YOUR NEXT TRIP
A dedicated VPN IP address gives users a consistent online identity that may reduce CAPTCHAs and repeated login verification requests. (Photo by Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Printer still not working? Check this VPN setting first
If your wireless printer stops responding while your VPN is connected, split tunneling may not be the first setting you need.

Some VPN services include an option that allows your computer or phone to communicate with devices on your local network, even while the VPN remains active. It may be called Allow LAN Access, Allow Local Network Access or something similar.
Here's what to look for on your device:

Open your VPN app.Go to Settings, Preferences or Connection Settings.Look for an option related to LAN access or local network connections.If available, enable access to devices on your local network.Save your changes and reconnect to the VPN if required.Try printing again to see whether the connection works.
Open your VPN app.
Go to Settings, Preferences or Connection Settings.
Look for an option related to LAN access or local network connections.
If available, enable access to devices on your local network.
Save your changes and reconnect to the VPN if required.
Try printing again to see whether the connection works.

This setting can allow your computer to communicate with trusted devices on your home network while your VPN remains connected. Some VPN apps already permit local network access by default. Others may restrict it depending on your security settings, including certain kill switch configurations.
If you don't see a local network option, check your VPN provider's support instructions. The feature may use a different name or may not be adjustable in your version of the app.

One security tip: Only allow local network access when you trust the network. On public Wi-Fi, blocking communication with nearby devices can provide additional protection. If your printer still doesn't appear, check that both devices are connected to the same home network. Restart the printer and temporarily disconnect your VPN to see whether your computer can find it. This can help determine whether the VPN is causing the connection problem. Remember to reconnect your VPN after testing.
On a Mac, you can also try adding the printer manually using its IP address under System Settings > Printers & Scanners.
What if your banking app still doesn't work?

Split tunneling can help with banking app problems caused by VPN IP addresses, but it won't resolve every login issue. Before excluding your banking app, try connecting to another VPN server. Sometimes the problem involves a particular server address.

You can also check whether your banking service offers guidance about VPN connections. If you regularly encounter security checks, another option is a dedicated VPN IP address. Unlike a shared VPN address, a dedicated IP stays assigned to you. That consistency can reduce some verification requests without requiring you to bypass VPN protection.

Some VPN services offer dedicated IP addresses, either as part of certain plans or as an additional paid feature. Whatever you choose, don't disable your bank's security alerts or two-factor authentication to make logging in easier.
Why VPN split tunneling is worth checking
Here's what I like about this feature. You don't have to sacrifice your entire VPN connection because one app refuses to cooperate. Instead, you can make a targeted adjustment.

Your browser can continue using the VPN while an app that needs a direct connection bypasses it. And if the problem involves your home printer, you can check the local network access setting before changing anything else.

Just remember that excluded apps won't receive the same VPN protection. The idea is to make your VPN easier to use without unnecessarily giving up the privacy benefits you installed it for in the first place.
For the best VPN software, see my expert review of the best VPNs for browsing the web privately on your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
Kurt's key takeaways

I can understand why someone would turn off their VPN when a banking app won't open or a printer suddenly stops working. You want to get on with what you're doing. But I don't like the idea of turning off a privacy tool every time something goes wrong. That's why I think split tunneling is worth knowing about. If your VPN supports it, you can keep most of your internet traffic protected while making exceptions for apps that need a direct connection. And if you're having trouble printing, check that local network setting before doing anything else. Just be careful about which apps you exclude. I would rather make one small adjustment than leave my VPN turned off and forget about it.
Has your VPN ever stopped a banking app, printer or another device from working? What did you do to fix it? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Georgia officer shoots 13-year-old after traffic stop linked to earlier shooting, police say
summary: A 13-year-old suspected in a Jones County, Georgia, shooting was later wounded by a Milledgeville Police officer during a traffic stop at Milledgeville Mall, police say.
story: A Milledgeville, Georgia, police officer shot a 13-year-old during a traffic stop involving a vehicle linked to a separate robbery and shooting, authorities said.
A Georgia police officer shot and wounded a 13-year-old Sunday night while conducting a traffic stop linked to an earlier shooting, according to authorities.
The teenager is suspected of being involved in a Jones County robbery and shooting that left one man with a gunshot wound.

Jones County Sheriff Butch Reece said the teenager had met with four men from Macon for a gun sale on Etheridge Road when the group allegedly tried to rob the teenager. The teenager then opened fire, shooting one of the men.
GEORGIA DEPUTY FIRED AFTER HARASSING MOM WITH FAKE FACEBOOK PAGE
A Georgia police officer shot and wounded a 13-year-old Sunday night while conducting a traffic stop linked to an earlier shooting. (Milledgeville Police Department)

Authorities said the teenager fled the scene before being tracked down to the Milledgeville Mall parking lot, where Milledgeville police attempted to stop a vehicle determined to be linked to the Jones County shooting.
During the traffic stop, an officer shot the teenager, who sustained a single gunshot wound, Milledgeville Police said. A firearm was also recovered at the scene.
The teenager was alert and conscious following the shooting and was transported to a hospital in the Macon area for medical treatment. (Milledgeville Police Department)

The teenager was alert, conscious and speaking following the shooting and was transported to a Macon-area hospital for medical treatment, where the juvenile was listed in stable condition, Milledgeville police said.

title: Man convicted for role in Tessa Majors' 2019 NYC killing released on parole
summary: Luchiano Lewis, convicted in the 2019 murder of Barnard College freshman Tessa Majors, was freed on conditional parole after serving fewer than seven years behind bars.
story: Fox News correspondent CB Cotton reports on the parole release of a man convicted in the 2019 killing of a Barnard College freshman on ‘Fox Report.’

One of the three then-teenagers convicted in connection with the 2019 murder of Barnard College freshman Tessa Majors in New York City has now been released on conditional parole supervision, according to the New York State Department of Corrections and Community Supervision.

Luchiano Lewis, now 21, was released on Oct. 14 under conditional release and placed under community supervision after serving fewer than seven years behind bars for his role in the robbery and killing in Manhattan's Morningside Park in December 2019, state correction records show.

Lewis, who was released from the Franklin Correctional Facility, had been sentenced to nine years to life after pleading guilty in 2021 to second-degree murder and first-degree robbery in connection with Majors' killing.
MARYLAND MAN ACCUSED OF GIRL'S FATAL SHOOTING RELEASED FROM PRISON DAYS BEFORE
A split of Tessa Majors and Luchiano Lewis. (Fox News | Pool photo)

Under New York State law, Lewis' conditional release did not require him to go before the State Board of Parole because eligible inmates can qualify for conditional release after serving two-thirds of their minimum sentence, subject to applicable requirements and good-time allowances.
Majors, who was 18 when she was killed, was attacked on Dec. 11, 2019, near a staircase in Morningside Park.

Prosecutors said a group of teens confronted Majors in an attempted robbery, during which she was stabbed multiple times. She was eventually able to climb a set of stairs and reach the street before collapsing. She was taken to a hospital, where she died from her injuries.
JUDGE SENTENCES LILY PETERS' KILLER 4 YEARS AFTER 10-YEAR-OLD FOUND DEAD IN WOODS
Tessa Majors was killed on Dec. 11, 2019, near a staircase in Morningside Park. (Provided by Majors family)

After the crime, then-14-year-old Lewis and another 14-year-old were both tried as adults for the attack. Prosecutors said Lewis held Majors in a headlock while the other 14-year-old stabbed her multiple times.
While Lewis was not holding the knife in the attack, prosecutors said he played a key role in the robbery that killed Majors.
At Lewis' sentencing, Manhattan Supreme Court Justice Robert Mandelbaum said the killing "tore at the fabric of the entire city."
"The defendant was and is extremely young. He has his whole life ahead of him, but Tessa Majors does not," he added.
A makeshift memorial stands for 18-year-old Barnard College freshman Tessa Majors in Morningside Park on December 26, 2019, in New York City. (David Dee Delgado/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Majors' parents described the lasting impact of the loss of their child during Lewis' sentencing, remembering her as a talented student, musician and writer whose future was tragically ended too soon.

The two other teenagers convicted in connection with the killing — Rashaun Weaver, who was 14 at the time of the crime, and Zyairr Davis, who was 13 at the time — remain behind bars. Weaver was sentenced to 14 years to life in prison for murder and robbery, while Davis pleaded guilty to robbery and was sentenced to 18 months in juvenile detention. Davis completed his juvenile sentence but is now being held on an unrelated attempted murder case.

title: Purdue professor, 2 daughters killed in apparent murder-suicide after daughter’s terrifying 911 call
summary: Purdue University professor Julie Tkach and her two teenage daughters died in an apparent murder-suicide in West Lafayette, Indiana, authorities say.
story: Julie Tkach, a Purdue University professor, and her daughters, ages 16 and 17, were found dead alongside the father in their Indiana home.
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

A Purdue University professor and her two teenage daughters were killed in an apparent murder-suicide last week after the father reportedly opened fire on his family before turning the gun on himself, according to Indiana authorities.

Preliminary autopsy results identified the mother as Julie Tkach, 53, of West Lafayette, who died from multiple gunshot wounds, with her death ruled a homicide, the Tippecanoe County Coroner’s Office said Friday. Julie was a clinical assistant professor in Purdue University's Department of Hospitality and Tourism Management, according to her LinkedIn profile.

The father, Thomas Tkach, 51, died by suicide from a gunshot wound to the head, officials said. He was employed by the Tippecanoe County Sheriff's Office as a courthouse security officer after previously serving as a jail deputy, according to local outlet Star City News., according to local outlet Star City News.
KANSAS CONVICTED FELON, SEX OFFENDER ALLEGEDLY KILLS FELLOW FAMILY MEMBERS BEFORE TAKING HIS OWN LIFE: POLICE
Julie and Thomas Tkach and their daughters, Katharyn and Lauren, pose for an undated photo in Indiana. (Tom Tkach/Facebook)
Their daughter, Katharyn, 17, died from multiple gunshot wounds to the head, while their other daughter, Lauren, 16, died from multiple gunshot wounds, the coroner's office said.

West Lafayette Police said the family members were found inside their West Lafayette-area home Wednesday evening, Nov. 18, after officers responded to a 911 call shortly after 8:30 p.m. The coroner's office was subsequently notified of multiple deaths at roughly 1:50 a.m. Thursday.

According to emergency dispatch audio obtained by Star City News, authorities received a separate concerning call shortly before the bodies were discovered. A dispatcher described receiving a call from one of the daughters.
"She advised that her father had a gun and was threatening to shoot the family. I heard multiple gunshots go off and the line is now silent," the recording said.
TWO TEEN SUSPECTS HELD AFTER 5 FAMILY MEMBERS KILLED IN 'TARGETED MASS SHOOTING'
Julie Tkach and her daughters, Katharyn, 17, and Lauren, 16, were killed in an apparent murder-suicide at their West Lafayette, Indiana, home. (Julie Tkach/Facebook)

While officials have not disclosed a motive behind the killings, the coroner’s office urged anyone struggling with mental health challenges to seek help through available resources. Residents can call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.
Indiana State Police is leading the investigation because Thomas Tkach was employed by the Tippecanoe County Sheriff's Office.

The West Lafayette Police Department described the incident as a "terrible night" that deeply affected its personnel, as well as those at the Tippecanoe County Sheriff's Office, which also responded to the scene.
"Many people on my team and other teams have had a very difficult time with the incident that took place on Wednesday night," the sheriff’s office said.
"The things seen and heard the other night will be remembered for the rest of their lives," the office added.
DISPATCH AUDIO RELEASED IN MICHIGAN FAMILY MURDER-SUICIDE AS TROUBLED FAMILY'S SECRETS EMERGE
Julie Tkach, a Purdue University professor, and her husband, Thomas Tkach, a courthouse security officer, were found dead in their West Lafayette, Indiana, home last week. (Julie Tkach/Facebook)

According to LinkedIn, Julie had spent more than 20 years teaching and mentoring students in the hospitality industry. Prior to Purdue, she worked at South Dakota State University for eight years as a lecturer and instructor.
In a statement to Fox News Digital, Purdue offered its condolences and said it would provide support to those affected.
"We are saddened by this tragedy and the death of Julie and her family. We offer our condolences and support to her colleagues, peers, students and all who are affected," the university said.

"The Tippecanoe County Coroner’s Office extends its deepest condolences to all who have been impacted by this tragedy. These deaths have affected many people across our community, including friends, neighbors, and others who knew the family," the office said.

The emergency response required a multi-agency effort involving the Tippecanoe County Sheriff's Office, West Lafayette Police Department, Indiana State Police, emergency medical services, fire crews and the coroner's office, according to West Lafayette police.
Fox News Digital reached out to the Tippecanoe County Sheriff's Office and Purdue University for more information.

title: FAA lifts ground stop on Atlanta-bound Delta flights after system outage
summary: Delta Air Lines says crews are using manual workarounds after an outage in its weight-and-balance system reportedly delayed at least 3,500 flights.
story: Fox News' Madison Scarpino reports on a Delta Air Lines technology issue that triggered a ground stop at Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport in Atlanta, causing hundreds of flight delays.

A Sunday morning outage in Delta Air Lines' automated weight-and-balance system forced the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to briefly halt Atlanta-bound flights and reportedly delay at least 3,500 Delta flights across major hubs, including Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport and New York's LaGuardia Airport.
The technical failure rippled through Sunday's travel schedule, with the ground stop leading to roughly an hour delay before being lifted.
"Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation," Delta told Fox News in a statement earlier.
"We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism."
UNITED AIRLINES SAYS TECHNOLOGY ISSUE RESOLVED AFTER ‘WIDESPREAD SYSTEM OUTAGE’

Delta issued an update later Sunday and apologized to its customers for the delays, with the airline confirming that its automated system for calculating departing flights' weight and balance was back working.
Approximately 5,000 Delta and Delta Connection flights were scheduled, Delta said.

"Delays and cancellations as noted by FlightAware are accurate – approximately 70% of these are connected to the automation; the remaining are attributable to inclement weather and ensuing ATC programs in NYC and in the U.S. Northeast," Delta said in a statement.
Delta also said it was rebooking customers on the next available itinerary and providing meals and hotel rooms where necessary.
"For customers facing a canceled flight and don’t wish to travel, refunds are being given," the company said.
Delta said its teams were also focused on completing the rest of Sunday's schedule and said cancellations, "as always, are a last resort when all other options have been exhausted."
20,000 BAGS STRANDED AFTER TECHNICAL ISSUE AT MAJOR AIRPORT LEAVES TRAVELERS SCRAMBLING
Delta issued an update later Sunday and apologized to its customers for travel delays.
Earlier, the FAA had stressed the outage was specific to Delta and "not related" to air traffic control systems.
"Delta is working to resolve issues with the airline’s weight and balance automation system," the FAA said.
"These delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems. Please check with Delta for the latest information."

Before any commercial aircraft can take off, crews must verify that its total weight and center of gravity fall within strict safety limits – a process that relies heavily on baggage and cargo data. With the automated system offline, Delta staff were calculating weight and balance figures manually for departing flights while technicians work to bring the software back online.
DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK
The Delta Air Lines weights and measures outrage impacted travel up to New York's LaGuardia Airport on Sunday morning. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)

The airline coordinated with air traffic controllers to manage the flow of planes and prevent congestion at airport gates and on the tarmac at its Atlanta hub. A ground delay for Atlanta had remained in effect for Delta only after the ground stop had been lifted, the airport said in a statement.

"Hartsfield-Jackson is aware of operational issues affecting Delta flights at ATL. Based on our latest information, the ground delay applies to Delta departures only. It is not airportwide," the statement said. "Delta is managing the issue with its operations team."

The issue comes more than a week after a historic nationwide FAA ground stop and an ensuing week of ongoing cybersecurity issues from reported system upgrades and patches throughout the U.S. The issues caused panic online that percolated into the stock market, causing massive dips in tech and artificial intelligence stocks.

title: Mississippi mother, caregiver face charges after refusing to give cancer treatment to toddler
summary: Destiny Schliefert faces felony murder charges after police say she refused cancer treatment for her 3-year-old son, who weighed 24 pounds when he died.
story: Fox News correspondent Madison Scarpino reports on ‘The Faulkner Focus’ after Susan Smith was denied parole for a second time for drowning her two sons in South Carolina in 1994.
A Mississippi mother is facing multiple felony murder charges after she refused to give her 3-year-old son his cancer treatment, authorities say.
The mother, Destiny Schliefert, reported the death of her son to police on July 31, saying the boy had stopped breathing. He weighed just 24 pounds by the time of his death, police said.

The boy had been diagnosed with cancer at Children’s Mercy Hospital in Kansas City in March 2024. Schliefert told police that the boy's health began to rapidly decline in May, with him losing the ability to eat and walk.
STARVING TODDLER ATE DIAPERS AND DRYWALL BEFORE DYING IN FILTHY ROOM WHILE PARENTS LIVED CLEAN, POLICE SAY
Destiny Schliefert, left, and Debbie Potter, right, face multiple charges of child neglect for the death of Schliefter's 3-year-old son. (Courtesy: Christian County Sheriff's Office)
Police say she claimed he had stopped eating because he'd been impacted by his grandfather's death in 2025.
She did not pursue any treatment for the boy's cancer after his diagnosis in 2024.
SOUTH CAROLINA MOM COULDN'T REMEMBER LAST TIME SHE FED 2 DAUGHTERS BEFORE THEY WERE FOUND DEAD: AFFIDAVITS

A doctor told investigators that the boy, who has not been identified, likely would have lived if he had received treatment. Schliefert herself admitted that medical care "probably" would have helped him.
Destiny Marie Schliefert is facing multiple felony murder and child neglect charges in the death of her 3-year-old son. (Courtesy: Christian County Sheriff's Office)

She told police that she and another caregiver, Debbie Potter, drove the boy to the hospital in early July but didn't bring him in, fearing they would be reported for poorly caring for the boy, according to Ozark First.
PARENTS OF 7-YEAR-OLD WHO DIED WEIGHING 255 POUNDS CHARGED WITH MURDER IN SUSPECTED NEGLECT CASE
Phone records indicate that Schliefert searched "fastest way to get a toddler to gain weight fast" on July 2, just weeks before the boy died.
Schliefert faces charges of second-degree murder, second-degree felony murder and child abuse or neglect resulting in death.
OHIO MOM ARRESTED FOR HAVING 16 KIDS IN 'EVIL' LIVING CONDITIONS WANTS TO BE REUNITED WITH CHILDREN: LAWYER
Debbie Potter faces charges of child neglect for the death of a 3-year-old boy she was helping care for. (Courtesy: Christian County Sheriff's Office)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Schliefert also has two additional children, ages 7 and 15. She faces additional child endangerment charges in connection to their care.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: Illegal immigrant avoids charges after Florida grandmother killed outside grocery store, enraging family
summary: Prosecutors dropped all charges against Carlos Suarez-Contreras in Deborah Murphy's death at a Panama City Beach Publix, citing hurdles under Florida law.
story: Surveillance video shows the moments before Venezuelan national Carlos Suarez-Contreras allegedly backed his SUV into Deborah Murphy and killed her in the parking lot of a Publix store in Panama City, Florida. (Florida Highway Patrol)
The criminal case against an illegal immigrant accused of backing over and killing an elderly woman in a grocery store parking lot has been dismissed.
He will not face any charges for the accident, Larry Basford, state attorney for Florida’s Fourteenth Judicial Circuit, told Fox News Digital.
Several factors prevented prosecutors from pursuing and securing charges under Florida law, Basford said.
‘VIBRANT’ FLORIDA GRANDMA ALLEGEDLY KILLED BY ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT OUTSIDE PUBLIX, FAMILY FIGHTS FOR JUSTICE
Deborah Murphy, 82, was killed in Florida on May 17, 2026. (Courtesy of Amy Edge)
"I think everyone would agree that what he did was careless and it was negligent," Basford said.
But, "not every tragedy amounts to a crime."
That’s heartbreaking news for the family of 82-year-old Deborah Murphy, said Murphy’s daughter, Amy Edge.
Both sets of tires crushed her body before the car stopped, she and her twin sister Beth Schulz told Fox News Digital.
THREE-TIME DEPORTED ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED WITH KILLING NORTH CAROLINA GIRL, 6, AFTER RUNNING STOP SIGN

On May 17, Murphy walked back to her car carrying a bag after a brief stop at Publix in Panama City Beach. Surveillance video shows her striding through the crosswalk toward her car, when she was struck by a Toyota 4Runner moving in reverse, according to court records.
She was facing away from the vehicle as she walked, the video shows. She apparently didn’t see it coming.
FLORIDA DMV WORKER FACES 360 FELONIES FOR ALLEGEDLY HELPING ILLEGAL ALIENS GET LICENSES WITHOUT DRIVING TESTS

The driver, Carlos Suarez-Contreras, was a 26-year-old from Venezuela who was in the United States illegally, arrest records show. He was driving the vehicle with a canceled Georgia license, arrest records show.
Carlos Suarez-Contreras was arrested after Deborah Murphy's death. (Bay County Sheriff’s Office)
Murphy was pushed to the ground by the SUV. But it didn’t stop.
ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT TRUCKER CHARGED IN CRASH THAT KILLED MOM, 2 YOUNG SONS HEADING TO AIRPORT
The car continued backing up, "running over Ms. Murphy," according to an arrest affidavit submitted by the Florida Highway Patrol.
Suarez-Contreras was charged with driving with a canceled license and causing a death, a third-degree felony.
ICE LODGES DETAINER FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED IN WRONG-WAY MARYLAND CRASH THAT KILLED MOM, DAUGHTER
He was held without bond because of his immigration status and because he was thought to be a "potential flight risk," Florida Highway Patrol records show.
Murphy was taken to the hospital and died from blunt force injuries less than an hour later, her daughters said.
Prosecutors worked on the case for almost six months, searching for answers that could lead to a conviction.
"We tried not to leave any stone unturned," Basford said.
ILLEGAL ALIEN'S ‘INEXCUSABLE’ CRIME SPARKS INTERSTATE CLASH BETWEEN GOP SEN, DEM GOV: ‘YOU SHOULD BE ASHAMED’
They found that Suarez-Contreras’ driver’s license had been canceled. But it became invalid only a day before the accident.
The Georgia Department of Driver Services confirmed to Fox News Digital that Suarez-Contreras' license had been canceled.
Citing privacy concerns, an agency spokeswoman would not say when it had been canceled, or when he would have been notified.
A non-U.S. citizen establishing residency in Georgia "must obtain a Georgia driver’s license within 30 days," according to the Georgia Department of Driver Services website.

A non-U.S. citizen is considered a resident if he or she "accepts employment or engages in trade in Georgia, and enrolls his or her children in a private or public school within ten days after the commencement of employment," according to the agency.
A person can also be considered a "resident" of Georgia if he or she is "present in the state for 30 or more days."
Prosecutor’s dilemma
The question of whether Suarez-Contreras knew the license had been canceled is what proved problematic for prosecutors in Florida.
"Under the law, we have to prove that the individual knew his license was suspended," Basford said.
Prosecutors considered charging him with vehicular homicide and manslaughter, Basford said. But they couldn’t establish the culpable negligence needed for that.
Using the surveillance video that captured the fatal accident, investigators re-enacted the scene.
Considering that information, they decided the SUV wasn’t backing quickly enough to prove Suarez-Contreras was driving "recklessly" when he drove over Murphy.
At the scene, the passenger of the car, Luis Sanabria, gave sworn testimony to a law enforcement officer that it was Suarez-Contreras who "was operating the vehicle at the time of the crash."

Sanabria was found to have an expired visa, according to the incident report. He was released into the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Jacob Navarro, public affairs specialist for the Bay County Sheriff’s Office, told Fox News Digital.
Luis Sanabria, an illegal immigrant, was a passenger in the car when Deborah Murphy was killed outside a Publix in Panama City Beach, Florida, police said. (Bay County Sheriff’s Office)

In considering charges for Suarez-Contreras, prosecutors looked to a Florida law passed in 2023. It invalidates a driver’s license issued to an illegal immigrant in certain states, such as California, Connecticut and Delaware.
Unfortunately, the legislation does not designate Georgia as one of "those liberal states that gave licenses out so freely to individuals," Basford said.
Murphy’s family is devastated that there’s no chance of justice, Edge said.
"We feel incredibly let down by the state of Florida, who vowed to seek justice on her behalf," she said. "It's like experiencing the loss all over again."
Murphy was in great health and presumably had many more years with the family, Edge said.Now, she won't attend her grandchildren’s weddings, or meet any more of her great-grandchildren, she said.
"That's been taken away."
Fighting for change
Murphy’s two daughters are incredulous that Florida isn’t pursuing a trial. It could have set a new precedent for this type of case, Edge said.

At the beginning of the investigation the prosecution team had been very optimistic about securing multiple charges for Suarez-Contreras, she said. The only question in their minds at the time was the length of the prison sentence he would receive if convicted, she said.
She and her sister question the way their mother’s death was investigated and why so much weight was given to a re-enactment of the incident.
"We know the man killed her," Edge said. "He never got out of the car. He never ran to her aid. He never stopped. He wasn't reversing from a spot. He drove backwards."

The family also questions why Suarez-Contreras wasn’t tested for drugs or alcohol and why his phone records weren’t reviewed. Yet, Murphy’s body was subjected to a toxicology evaluation, her daughters said.
Deborah Murphy with her husband, retired Air Force Colonel George Murphy, and their grandchildren on a Florida beach. (Courtesy of Amy Edge)
The sisters will continue to fight to bring positive changes from the tragedy. They may pursue changes to Florida law or the way law enforcement officers conduct similar investigations.
SEND US A TIP
"There's a lot of different questions we have that we'll continue to explore, but not in a vengeful way," Edge said. It’s "more in that we don't want this to happen to someone else."
GOT A TIP?
There’s some comfort knowing Suarez-Contreras is in ICE custody awaiting deportation, she said.
"We don't want him to be able to do this to anyone else in the United States. Our drive now is to ensure that he is deported."
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
Suarez-Contreras’ defense attorney, Russell Ramey, told Fox News Digital that he’s pleased the charges were dropped.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
After the case was dropped, Suarez-Contreras was transferred into ICE custody on Nov. 15, according to the Bay County Jail. Fox News Digital could not reach him for comment.
Murphy's family has launched a petition urging State Attorney Larry Basford to reconsider his decision not to pursue criminal charges in her death.

title: Harvard scientist may never prove mysterious space object’s origin after mission scrapped
summary: Avi Loeb claims JAXA's canceled Hayabusa2 landing mission on 1998 KY26 ends the only chance to prove the object is the lost Soviet probe Phobos 1.
story: Avi Loeb breaks down why he believes asteroid 1998 KY26 may actually be the lost 1988 Phobos 1 spacecraft — and why JAXA’s sudden decision to scrap its 2031 rendezvous leaves key questions unanswered.

A Harvard astrophysicist who claims a mysterious object speeding through our solar system is actually a lost Soviet spacecraft says scientists may never be able to get a clear look at it after Japan abruptly scrapped a planned mission to land on the target.

Avi Loeb told Fox News Digital that the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's decision to cancel its 2031 Hayabusa2 rendezvous with the object known as 1998 KY26 removes the only opportunity to capture high-resolution images of its surface and settle whether it is a natural space rock or the missing 1988 Soviet probe Phobos 1.

"There is no way by which we can actually resolve the object, or get a high-resolution image of its surface, without coming close to it — without a flyby — because even with the Webb telescope or the biggest telescopes we have on Earth, the object is not close enough to be resolved into multiple pixels in an image," Loeb said.
MYSTERIOUS OBJECT MOVING THROUGH SPACE COULD BE LOST SOVIET PROBE AS NASA WEIGHS IN ON THEORY

The cancellation came just days after NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman dismissed speculation about the roughly 36-foot-wide object during an appearance on "Fox & Friends," saying, "I've not seen any evidence to suggest this is ... anything other than an asteroid."
A concept image of an asteroid passing Earth. (iStock)

Loeb pushed back on that assessment, arguing KY26 is "not an asteroid" because it accelerates in a way gravity alone cannot explain and predicting that when Japan's spacecraft lands on it in July 2031, scientists would find a label reading "Made in the USSR" instead of ice or rock.
NASA CHIEF CONFIRMS AGENCY HAS UNEXPLAINED UFO IMAGERY: 'WE DON'T KNOW WHAT IT IS'

Japan's space agency reported to the Cabinet Office's Space Policy Committee on Nov. 16 that it was abandoning the 2031 rendezvous after the last normally functioning main ion engine on Hayabusa2 malfunctioned in mid-August, according to the Japanese newspaper Yomiuri Shimbun.

"I was surprised that the cancellation by JAXA occurred just a day or two after I spoke about it publicly, because the malfunction in the engine was known for several months," Loeb said. "The probability that we're dealing with a coincidence where within a day after my public discourse, JAXA decides to cancel this mission is a day divided by the duration over which it was known that the fourth engine is malfunctioning – and that was over 100 days or so.
TRUMP HIGHLIGHTS NASA NUCLEAR-POWERED MARS SPACECRAFT MISSION PLANNED FOR 2028

A model of Phobos 1, the Soviet spacecraft that lost contact with Earth while traveling to Mars in 1988. Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb and his colleagues have examined whether the mysterious object 1998 KY26 could be the lost probe. (Credit: NASA)
"So, I would argue that the probability for a chance coincidence is less than 1%, but it could still be a coincidence," he added.

Loeb noted that Hayabusa2 was designed over several years and questioned why Japanese engineers did not attempt an Earth gravity-assist maneuver to compensate for the lost engine thrust rather than pivoting to another target.

JAXA officials said in their report that reaching KY26 in 2031 already required an Earth gravity assist, and that combining working parts from two damaged engines left the 12-year-old spacecraft without enough thrust to perform the necessary orbital changes, prompting a redirect to a 2028 flyby of asteroid 2015 BM510 instead, the newspaper added.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Even without a close-up flyby, Loeb said astronomers still have one major tool left to test his theory from afar by using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope to measure the heat radiating off KY26 and analyze its chemical spectrum.
SCIENTISTS DISCOVER POTENTIALLY MASSIVE DWARF PLANET CANDIDATE HIDING BEYOND PLUTO
An illustration shows the Soviet Phobos 1 spacecraft, which was launched toward Mars in July 1988 but lost after a faulty command caused it to shut down. (Credit: NASA)

"So far, we detected a reflection of sunlight from this object, but the Webb telescope can potentially detect the heat emitted by the object, and that will offer us an opportunity to learn both about the size, the surface temperature of the object, as well as the composition of the object," Loeb said.
While mainstream scientists have suggested KY26 is an ordinary rock or comet, Loeb noted the object rotates about once every five minutes and is far brighter than expected.
EIFFEL TOWER-SIZED ASTEROID APOPHIS TO PASS CLOSER TO EARTH THAN MANY SATELLITES IN 2029, NASA SAYS
Avi Loeb speaks during the SALT conference in Manhattan, New York City, on September 14, 2022. (David 'Dee' Delgado)
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"This object reflects about half of the sunlight that is impinging on it, whereas a typical rock or iceberg reflects about 5% of the sunlight impinging on it," Loeb said, adding that the object's brightness is "surprising."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

NASA previously told Fox News Digital that a 2025 orbital study led by the agency's Center for Near-Earth Object Studies concluded KY26's complex trajectory is driven by solar radiation forces – "the natural push of sunlight and thermal emission on its non-spherical shape" – rather than hidden comet-like activity.
SEND US A TIP

Loeb and his colleagues, however, found KY26's trajectory closely resembles that of Phobos 1 – a Soviet spacecraft launched toward Mars in July 1988 that shut down after a faulty command – and calculated that sunlight reflecting off its solar panels could produce the observed push without any signs of a "dark comet" tail.
GOT A TIP?

"It could be a comet shedding some gas backward that is pushing it forward, but in that case we should have seen the gas," Loeb said. "We should have seen the dust because for comets we see a tail and the dust particles are being pushed away from the sun by the solar radiation."
TRUMP SAYS AIR FORCE PILOTS DESCRIBED A ROUND UFO FLYING THREE TIMES FASTER THAN AN F-22 FIGHTER JET
In this handout photo provided by SpaceX, a Tesla roadster launched from the Falcon Heavy rocket with a dummy driver named "Starman" heads towards Mars. (Photo by SpaceX via Getty Images)
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Loeb added that KY26 orbits the sun at a distance of a fraction to a few times the separation between Earth and the sun and poses no threat of hitting Earth, though he argued space agencies must remain open-minded when tracking unexplained objects.
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

He noted that in January 2025, astronomers briefly cataloged an object near Earth as an asteroid before realizing it was actually the Tesla Roadster launched into space by SpaceX in 2018 – a mistake that was only caught because humans knew its flight path.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Hopefully, the Rubin Observatory in Chile that is funded by the Department of Energy and the National Science Foundation will find dozens of interstellar objects in the coming decade, and we should be curious enough to check whether all of them are rocks or icebergs, because if one of them is technological in origin, that will change our view on our place in the universe," Loeb said.

title: Three killed, one injured in shooting at Ohio baby shower, police say
summary: Three people, including the unborn child's father, were killed at a baby shower shooting at Pandora's Magical Events Venue in Parma, Ohio, police say.
story: A shooting Saturday at an entertainment venue left three people dead in Parma, Ohio. (Google Maps)
Three people were killed and another was injured during a shooting at a baby shower at an Ohio event venue Saturday evening, according to local reports.
The shooting occurred around 6 p.m. inside Pandora's Magical Events Venue, located at 5331 Ridge Road in Parma, Ohio, according to a statement released by the Parma Police Department.
Responding officers determined that four people had been shot during an "exchange of gunfire."
A 17-year-old girl, a 19-year-old man and a 45-year-old man were found dead at the scene, according to police.
PREGNANT MOM JUST 4 DAYS FROM GIVING BIRTH AMONG 8 KILLED IN PENNSYLVANIA MASSACRE: REPORTS

Parma police public information officer Scott Traxler told FOX 8/WJW that the 19-year-old victim was the unborn child's father and the 45-year-old victim was the pregnant woman's father. Police identified the 19-year-old man as one of those involved in the exchange of gunfire.
A fourth victim, a 39-year-old woman, suffered a gunshot wound to the leg that was considered non-life-threatening, police said.

Police also said a 29-year-old man allegedly involved in the exchange of gunfire was taken into custody following the shooting. Authorities have not publicly identified the man in custody or announced a possible motive.
Traxler told Fox News Digital that authorities were continuing to verify additional details surrounding the shooting.
Multiple firearms were recovered from the scene, according to police.
In a social media post, the Parma Police Department said officers were investigating a shooting involving multiple victims in the 5300 block of Ridge Road.
"Parma Police Department extends its deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives in this tragic incident," the department wrote.
"There is no danger to the public," police added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Police said the families of those killed have been notified.
The Parma Police Department's Detective Bureau is investigating the shooting.
This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

title: Florida man sentenced to death for 'cold, calculated' murder of attorney whose body was never found
summary: Former Florida plastic surgeon Tomasz Kosowski got the death penalty for murdering lawyer Cozzi, whose remains were never recovered after the 2023 killing.
story: Tomasz Kosowski asked the judge for a courtroom demonstration during his murder trial. The Florida plastic surgeon represented himself against charges that he killed attorney Steven Cozzi. The judge found him guilty. (FOX 13)
A former Florida plastic surgeon acting as his own attorney was sentenced to death Friday for the 2023 murder of an opposing lawyer whose remains were never recovered, court records show.

Pinellas County Judge Joseph Bulone imposed the death penalty on Tomasz Kosowski, 47, after denying a last-minute motion by Kosowski to disqualify the judge from the case, according to the Pinellas County court docket.

"The court has given great weight to the aggravating factor that the homicide was committed in a cold, calculated and premeditated manner, without any pretense of moral or legal justification," Bulone said in court, FOX 13 Tampa Bay reported, ruling that the nature of the killing alone outweighed all mitigating factors.
FLORIDA PUTS 77-YEAR-OLD MAN TO DEATH FOR DEPUTY'S MURDER AS STATE CLOSES IN ON EXECUTION RECORD
Tomasz Kosowski was accused of killing Steven Cozzi. (Pinellas County Sheriffs Office)
Bulone had found Kosowski guilty of first-degree murder in September following a non-jury trial, court records show.

The two men crossed paths through a civil lawsuit dating back to 2019, over medical billing money Kosowski claimed he was owed. Steven Cozzi represented corporate clients Kosowski had sued, and prosecutors said Kosowski grew increasingly hostile toward the attorney during years of litigation.

Cozzi disappeared on March 21, 2023, minutes before a scheduled 10 a.m. teleconference hearing in the case, leaving his phone, keys and wallet on his desk at the Blanchard Law Firm in Largo, court records show.

Prosecutors said Kosowski killed Cozzi inside the firm's bathroom — where spattered blood mixed with Kosowski's DNA was found — and wheeled Cozzi's remains out in a heavy wagon covered with a reddish-orange blanket to a silver Toyota Tundra.
UNLICENSED MIAMI SURGEON 'DR. FRANKENSTEIN' VANISHES DAYS BEFORE TRIAL OVER BOTCHED PROCEDURES: AUTHORITIES
Authorities say Steven Cozzi was killed at this law office in Florida. (Google Maps)

Surveillance cameras tracked the truck to Kosowski's Tarpon Springs home, where investigators executing a search warrant found Cozzi's DNA in the truck bed and on the garage floor, along with a vial of the paralytic drug succinylcholine tied to Kosowski's Miami plastic surgery practice, court records show.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Cellphone records placed Kosowski near a dumpster in Collier County near the Everglades, and investigators searched the landfill where its contents were taken after more than 6,000 tons of garbage had been piled onto the load, prosecutors said.
Cozzi's remains were never found, and the Public Defender's Office was appointed to represent Kosowski in his appeal, according to court records.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: NYC suspect in Chinatown fatal beating had 5 open cases as Mamdani pushes plan to close Rikers
summary: Alexander Florentino faced five open cases before the fatal Chinatown attack, arriving as Zohran Mamdani unveiled a plan to close Rikers Island by 2032.
story: The announcement comes after local reports that the mayor has been asking prosecutors recently about ways to free inmates held on bail.

A 25-year-old homeless New York City man charged with beating a 62-year-old woman to death and assaulting a man in Manhattan's Chinatown was free despite five open criminal cases — including three arrests in November alone — just as Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled a plan to close the city's Rikers Island jail.
NYPD officers arrested Alexander Florentino at 11:30 a.m. Saturday in the 5th Precinct on charges of murder, attempted murder, two counts of strangulation, burglary, assault and attempted assault.

New York State Unified Court System records show Florentino was awaiting Dec. 14 court appearances across five pending Manhattan Criminal Court dockets, meaning he had been released ahead of Friday's fatal attack.
ILLEGAL ALIEN ACCUSED OF ATTEMPTED MURDER AT LARGE AFTER RIKERS RELEASE DESPITE ICE DETAINER: DHS

Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks with inmates on Rikers Island while they watch a World Cup soccer match on July 15, in New York. Mamdani announced this week his plan to shutter the notorious jail on the East River. (Seth Wenig/AP Photo, File)

Most recently, police arrested Florentino on Nov. 18 in connection with an incident two days earlier, court records show. NYPD Transit Bureau officers also arrested him twice on Nov. 11 in separate cases tied to incidents on Nov. 11 and Aug. 3, and he had two open arrests from Sept. 2 and Sept. 28.

The repeat arrests came just a day after Mamdani unveiled a six-year plan to shutter Rikers Island by 2032 by cutting the jail population from roughly 6,700 to 4,100 and expanding alternatives to detention.

"Too many New Yorkers have experienced our criminal legal system as a revolving door, where they cycle in and out of jail because there is too little energy expended towards helping them rebuild their lives," Mamdani said Friday. "We have a legal and moral obligation to close Rikers."
PENN STATION STABBING VICTIM SLAMS MAMDANI, DA BRAGG FOR SUSPECT BEING FREE ON STREETS
A view of Rikers Island in Queens, N.Y. (Andrew Lichtenstein/Corbis via Getty Images, File)

Police said officers responded to 27 Catherine St. around 3: 22 p.m. Friday and found the 62-year-old woman unconscious and unresponsive with trauma to her face and neck. Emergency medical workers transported her to NYC Health + Hospitals/Bellevue, where she was pronounced dead.
Officers also found a 66-year-old man with a laceration to the right side of his face after being struck over the head with a glass bottle, police said. He was taken to Bellevue in stable condition.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled a six-year plan to close Rikers Island jail complex in Queens, N.Y., by the end of 2032. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

Authorities have not released the woman's identity pending family notification, and the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner will determine her cause of death. Police have not disclosed a possible motive or said whether Florentino knew the victims.

The Manhattan District Attorney's Office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Inside the 'Lion’s Den': Real estate brothers bragged about 'hunting' women before 30-year prison terms
summary: New Peacock docuseries "The Wolves of Real Estate" reveals texts in which Oren Alexander wrote of "hunting" women before his 30-year sex trafficking sentence.
story: Attorney Michael Willemin says private jets, superyachts and powerful connections helped the convicted brothers operate for years and left women fearful of coming forward.

The Alexander brothers sold multimillion-dollar mansions, mingled with the wealthy and lived like real estate golden boys. But behind the luxury and excess, prosecutors said, was a decades-long pattern of sexual abuse.
In text messages presented at trial and featured in a new docuseries, the brothers and their associates discussed "hunting" for women.
"We are running out of prey," Oren wrote in one message.

Convicted of federal sex trafficking offenses and each sentenced to 30 years in prison, Tal, Oren and Alon Alexander are the subjects of a new Peacock true crime docuseries, "The Wolves of Real Estate: The Alexander Brothers," which features accounts from women who say the trio sexually assaulted them.
ALEXANDER BROTHERS ALLEGEDLY PAID FOR COVERAGE OF SEX-TRAFFICKING TRIAL AS WRITERS DENY FAVORABLE TREATMENT

Oren Alexander, center, and his twin brother, Alon, right, attend their bond hearing at the Richard E. Gerstein Justice Building Dec. 13, 2024, in Miami, Florida. Alon, Oren and Tal Alexander were each sentenced to 30 years in federal prison Oct. 27, 2026. (Matias J. Ocner/Pool via Reuters)

"The brothers at trial, they said, 'We're not predators, we were just playboys,’" director Emma Schwartz told Fox News Digital. "But, at the same time, you see their own words. Oren says he would hunt women like he hunts a client. And that's not exactly language about seducing people. The word 'hunt' was used a lot in their messages.

"The prosecutor's theory to the jury, and the public, was that these men invited women out to the Hamptons, women who traveled through New York, and the whole purpose was to sexually assault or rape them," Schwartz said. "There were messages like, 'Let's orgy them out,' with a clear intent that sex was involved."

In this courtroom sketch, prosecutor Madison Smyser questions Katie Moore (pseudonym) during the federal sex trafficking trial of high-profile real estate agent brothers Tal Alexander, Alon Alexander and Oren Alexander, sitting before Judge Valerie E. Caproni, in New York City Jan. 27, 2026. (Jane Rosenberg/Reuters)

The Alexander brothers, born into wealth, grew up to be real estate golden boys. Oren and Tal, former star brokers at Douglas Elliman, later co-founded their own real estate firm specializing in luxury properties in Miami, New York City and Los Angeles.

The brothers were involved in high-profile real estate transactions, including a nearly $240 million penthouse sale in 2019 that set a record for the most expensive residential sale in U.S. history. They co-founded the luxury real estate firm Official in 2022.

In a courtroom sketch, defense attorney Teny Geragos speaks near Oren Alexander at the start of the federal sex trafficking trial of high-profile real estate agent brothers Tal Alexander, Alon Alexander and Oren Alexander in New York City Jan. 27, 2026. (Jane Rosenberg/Reuters)
Alon was an executive at his family's private security company.

Together, they moved in elite circles and hosted lavish parties in Miami, New York City, the Hamptons and Aspen. Court filings previously obtained by Fox News Digital alleged that the brothers used "the promise of luxury experiences, travel and accommodations" to lure women to locations where they were then sexually assaulted.
Oren Alexander and Tal Alexander speak at a panel at the Rockstars of Real Estate event Sept. 3, 2013, in New York City. (Amy Sussman/Invision for Details Magazine/AP Images, File)

According to the docuseries, the brothers exchanged messages in secret group chats, including one message that read, "Welcome to the Lion's Den." The conversations included discussions about "hunting" for women and what the participants expected in return.

Brothers Oren, Alon and Tal Alexander at an exclusive VIP venue. Prosecutors say they used their glamorous lifestyle of luxury travel and nightclubs as a hunting ground to drug and sexually assault women, leading to their 2026 conviction and 30-year prison sentences. (Peacock)
"All content in this chat stays in the chat," one text shown in the film warned.

In another text shown in the film, Oren said "boys need to hunt" because "we are running out of prey." He appeared to write, "Met a cute Canadian and took her back to the crib and trained her." When one person texted, "No is not an option," Oren replied, "Nope."
Tal Alexander and Oren Alexander on a yacht, circa 2013. (Patrick McMullan via Getty Images)
In a separate group chat, Oren warned that the "boys are hungry," while Tal wrote, "Girls look fresh," according to court documents.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Real estate titans Oren and Tal Alexander, along with brother Alon, enjoyed a lifestyle of private jets, superyachts and A-list VIP access that made them fixtures of the New York and Miami social scenes. (Peacock)

In an exclusive interview, Gage urged the incoming Democrat-controlled Congress to build on President Donald Trump's designation of illicit fentanyl as a weapon of mass destruction and treat emerging synthetic drugs as a biodefense priority.
"If you look at the overdose crisis like any other health crisis, really as a disease, you'll know the best way to treat a crisis is by preventing it altogether," Gage said.
