title: Swift assurances from officials after wave of nationwide outages raises questions, expert says
summary: SMET CEO Danny Cooper says ruling out a cyberattack too fast risks missing hackers after the JPMorgan Chase, Microsoft outages and air travel ground stop.
story: As federal officials and major institutions called a string of critical infrastructure disruptions isolated technical glitches, a longtime security veteran warns that hasty assurances can mask stealth intrusions, and give adversaries room to linger undetected.

Amid a slew of high-profile disruptions that struck major pillars of American life over the past week, including a nationwide ground stop that halted air travel, banking outages at JPMorgan Chase and other lenders, and a service disruption at Microsoft, officials were quick to reassure the public that nothing nefarious was behind the failures.

During the ground stop, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the homeland and the banking system remained secure, insisting that the disruptions showed no signs of a cyberattack or malicious activity.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton similarly stated that officials saw no evidence of a coordinated or state-sponsored attack, pointing instead to routine patching and system upgrades.
DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE'

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton testified Wednesday to reiterate intelligence shows the recent outages are neither related nor a result of a 'state-sponsored' attack. (Brendan Smialowski / AFP)

"Based on what we know today … these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes," Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday. "They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack."
Major companies, including Microsoft and JPMorgan Chase, also attributed the disruptions to internal technical issues or software bugs rather than malicious intrusions.
US INFRASTRUCTURE CRUMBLES AS ADVERSARIES POWER UP – LEAVING AMERICANS DANGEROUSLY EXPOSED: CYBER EXPERT
To Danny Cooper, CEO of critical infrastructure security firm SMET, the speed with which those assurances were issued poses a problem.
"A blanket statement like 'there's no malicious activity associated with any of the outages' is almost impossible from a probability perspective," Cooper told Fox News Digital.
THE OUTAGES AMERICA HAS SUFFERED WEREN'T AN ATTACK, BUT THE NEXT FAILURE COULD BE
A Chase ATM is pictured outside the bank as technology disruptions impact banking services. (Ava Palschakov for Fox News Digital)

Public anxiety tends to spike around a single question in the aftermath of a major disruption: Was it a coincidence or an attack? Public skepticism is understandable given how many critical systems stumbled within a five-to-six-day window, Cooper said.

"How plausible is it that all these pillars or whatever all suffered major independent technical failures within a five- or six-day window?" Cooper asked. "I think highly improbable. And I understand why the American public is calling this into question and deeply empathize with that. The pattern recognition is there."
DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK

Even when officials point to routine maintenance or aging hardware, Cooper argued that ruling out foul play too quickly skips investigative steps that take time to execute properly, which could potentially undermine efforts to fix vulnerabilities and prevent future incidents.

A person looks at a departures board showing delays and cancellations at LaGuardia airport on Nov. 13, in New York City. The Federal Aviation Administration had ordered a nationwide ground stop on all departing flights, one of several critical infrastructure that experienced outages or issues last week, raising questions about the cause of the stoppages. (Getty Images)

"If a company or the government is making a statement that is as bold as 'we are certain there is no malicious activity here' without having the time to actually do an appropriate investigation, in the case of this sort of cyber domain, some cyber forensics and a full audit of what transpired, that's not quite how it works," she said.
PERPETUAL PARALYSIS: WHY EVERYTHING IS GRINDING TO A HALT

"On the physical side, being able to fully interrogate what has happened in the environment, who was there, and so on about what is happening in the periphery and what led up to that moment in time, those things take time."
An instant "nothing to see here" message can also deepen public suspicion, Cooper said, particularly when multiple institutions and agencies echo that conclusion before audits can be completed.
JOIN THE CHAT: RECENT TECH OUTAGES LOOM OVER MULLIN TESTIMONY ON WORLDWIDE THREATS
The Democratic National Committee (DNC) also sounded the alarm over conflicting statements coming from the Trump administration.

A general view of Charlotte Douglas International Airport in Charlotte, North Carolina, United States, on November 13, 2026, as passengers face delays and strandings after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stop for all flights. (Peter Zay/Anadolu via Getty Images)

"The administration has repeatedly offered conflicting statements about the causes of the outages," DNC Deputy Communications Director Kendall Witmer said in a statement. "Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested that SI – Trump’s preferred name for Artificial Intelligence (AI) – is responsible for the multiple outages that have occurred in recent days, according to a "very smart" tech guy he talked to. Then, yesterday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio contradicted Mullin and would not attribute the outages to AI."
MICROSOFT’S MASSIVE OUTAGE OFFERS A LESSON IN HOW TO BRING THE WORLD BACK ONLINE

Much of the official explanation surrounding the November disruptions centered on software updates and system upgrades. Organizations frequently schedule maintenance and can experience downtime when rolling out changes at scale, especially if teams move too quickly, Cooper noted.
However, those windows are what sophisticated adversaries watch closely, she warned.
"If companies are disproportionately moving to execute these sorts of upgrades en masse, then yes, it's possible that you would have a higher number of downtime or outages," she said.

"But it's also quite possible that, particularly given the sophistication of cyber adversaries, whether it's hackers, whether it's non-state entities, whether it's nation-state entities, it's also possible that they are using those software updates or upgrades or patches and in those moments actually injecting malware and exploits and so on."

title: MICHAEL RUIZ: Half of California's DAs sue Newsom over death row clemency
summary: Gavin Newsom faces a lawsuit from 29 district attorneys and victims' families who say his mass clemency for 548 death row inmates skipped victim notice.
story: With just 60 days left in his term, Gov. Gavin Newsom's plan to commute every California death row inmate's sentence is facing a lawsuit from half of the state's current DAs and victims' families.

District attorneys in half of California's 58 counties have signed onto a lawsuit alongside victims' families and law enforcement groups against term-limited Gov. Gavin Newsom over his lame-duck move to grant clemency to 548 death row inmates in the Golden State.
Many of the prosecutors had publicly condemned the governor's move shortly after he announced it earlier this month.
"Only this Court can stop the Governor’s disregard of the law — his abuse of power," former Sacramento District Attorney Anne Marie Schubert wrote in the 58-page petition, filed Monday.
MICHAEL RUIZ: CALIFORNIA PROSECUTORS REVOLT AFTER NEWSOM ORDERS STATE'S WORST KILLERS OFF DEATH ROW

"His eleventh-hour decision to grant commutation en masse intentionally disregarded the statutorily required notice to the victims of these heinous crimes and the prosecutors who obtained those convictions and penalties, and it even interfered with this Court’s mandatory duty to meaningfully review his decisions."

Schubert, who said she worked through the weekend on the filing, is the president and CEO of the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, which is spearheading the lawsuit on behalf of 29 district attorneys and the families of more than two dozen victims.
Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks March 26, 2025, in Los Angeles. (Frazer Harrison/WireImage)
"The governor’s assurance that the perpetrators will never be released is obviously cruelly false."

Marc Klaas, whose 12-year-old daughter Polly was kidnapped at knifepoint from a slumber party at her mother's house and strangled to death in 1993, is among the petitioners. Polly's killer, Richard Allen Davis, has been on death row since 1996.

Other victims' families include those of slain 8-year-old Gabriel Fernandez, Placer County Sheriff's Detective Mike Davis, Pittsburg Police Officer Larry Lasater, Sacramento Deputy Danny Paul Oliver and five U.S. Forest Service firefighters killed battling the 40,000-acre Esperanza Fire in 2006 — among others.

Convicted murderer Richard Allen Davis is restrained by lawyer Barry Collins as he gestures in the courtroom after he was found guilty on all counts in the murder of Polly Klaas in San Jose, Calif., June 18, 1996. (Reuters/John Burgess/Pool)
Read the filing:
MICHAEL RUIZ: DA IDENTIFIES 49 LOCAL KILLERS SLATED FOR NEWSOM"S DEATH ROW CLEMENCY — AND THEIR CRIMES

"Given what so many of these families have been through for so long, the impact in this case is exceptionally severe, as documented in the declarations filed with this petition," Schubert wrote in the filing. "The Governor’s assurance that the perpetrators will never be released is obviously cruelly false."

The move has even caught the attention of the White House, with President Donald Trump, Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel expected to meet with some of the victims' families Monday.

"Governor Newsom is failing these innocent victims and their families by refusing to carry out justice against these heinous murderers," said Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman. "He is playing politics with public safety. President Trump will always stand with innocent victims and will continue to restore law and order and deliver safer communities."

California hasn't carried out an execution in 20 years despite having the largest death row in the country, and Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra is expected to continue the moratorium when he takes office. The death penalty remains on the books as more than a symbolic punishment, however, and condemned inmates are excluded from benefiting from some of the state's criminal justice reforms.
CALIFORNIA SUED OVER POLICY THAT COULD FREE SERIAL KILLERS AS LACI PETERSON'S FRIEND SOUNDS ALARM

Thousands of jurors and hundreds of judges set aside their personal views on the merits of the death penalty to render judgments based on the evidence and the law. Governor Newsom decided his personal views should override all those who actually participated in the process, followed and applied the law.
BIDEN CLEMENCY BLITZ LEFT DOJ SCRAMBLING AS MANY COMMUTATIONS BYPASSED NORMAL VETTING, EMAILS SHOW

Newsom has argued that the prisoners in question are not eligible for other reforms that could eventually lead to further sentence reductions or even their release. His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit.

title: USDA releases decades of Bigfoot files, including 1982 Forest Service investigation in Washington state
summary: The USDA's Bigfoot/Sasquatch Records include an official 1982 Forest Service probe into footprints in Washington state's Umatilla National Forest.
story: The U.S. Forest Service released files detailing so-called sightings of Bigfoot dating back to the 1940s.
The Trump administration has slowly released a trove of government documents about one of the biggest and most enduring mysteries in American folklore: Bigfoot.

On Oct. 15, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) released three files from its "Bigfoot/Sasquatch Records," The Washington Post first reported, adding fresh intrigue to the legend of the towering, hair-covered creature said to roam North American forests without ever being captured.

A metal sculpture of Bigfoot welcomes visitors to Happy Camp in the Klamath Forest near Yreka, Calif., Aug. 2, 2022. The folklore of the hairy mythical creature has spawned intrigue for decades. (Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
NASA CHIEF PULLS BACK CURTAIN ON TRUMP UFO FILES AFTER BIZARRE FINDS SURFACE IN BURIED FED RECORDS

The records include an official U.S. Forest Service (USFS) investigation from June 1982 into reported Bigfoot footprints discovered in the Mill Creek Watershed of Washington state's Umatilla National Forest.
Investigators documented track measurements, took color photographs and made plaster casts across several field sites to preserve the unusual physical evidence.
NEW JERSEY COUPLE REPORT SEEING 8-FOOT TALL BIGFOOT STEPPING OUT IN FRONT OF THEIR CAR: 'WE KNOW WHAT WE SAW'

Another file details a reported encounter with the creature in Montana dating back to the 1940s. Separately, USFS staff once hosted a Bigfoot in Your Backyard forum in California's Stanislaus National Forest to discuss local sightings, noting at the time the agency could neither confirm nor deny the creature's existence.

This photo shows what former rodeo rider Roger Patterson said is the American version of the Abominable Snowman. He said pictures of the creature, estimated at 7½ feet tall, were taken northeast of Eureka, Calif. (Getty Images/Bettmann/Contributor)

A six-page document included in last month's release, which was written in 1980, recounts a historical report from Petty Creek, Montana, by Leo Kinney, who described spotting a large set of tracks alongside three hunters in the 1940s.
FOLLOW US ON X

"At this point we held a conference and decided that we were not particularly anxious to catch up to whatever it was, and though we didn't confess it at this time, in later conversations we found out that we all had a very uneasy feeling and could feel chills running up and down our backs," Kinney wrote.
The release also includes details of a 2003 sighting in Sanders County, Montana.
IDAHO DEER HUNTER REPORTS BIGFOOT ENCOUNTER IN REMOTE WOODS AFTER HE 'SMELLS THE SMELL'
In an interview with The Washington Post, Jeremiah Byron of the "Bigfoot Society" questioned the timing of the federal disclosures.
"Why is all this cryptid and Bigfoot-related stuff happening now?" Byron asked. "I’m hoping what this means is that they could be ramping up government entities to start releasing information."
While Bigfoot lore has traditionally centered on the Pacific Northwest, the creature has also surfaced in pop culture, with players reporting sightings in the video game Grand Theft Auto VI.
A metal sculpture of Bigfoot welcomes visitors to the tiny community of Happy Camp in the Klamath Forest.  (Luis Sinco/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
Gamers have shared clips of the cryptid wandering the woods of Leonida, a fictional U.S. state based on Florida, before sprinting away in a panic when spotted, according to GameSpot.

title: Zoo shares autopsy findings following Fiona the hippo’s heartbreaking death
summary: Cincinnati Zoo’s director of animal health, Dr. Mike Wenninger, said a postmortem examination has revealed where the hat was lodged inside Fiona’s digestive tract.
story: Dr. Mike Wenninger, the Cincinnati Zoo’s director of animal health, revealed where the hat was lodged inside Fiona’s digestive tract. (Cincinnati Zoo)
The Cincinnati Zoo on Friday released new autopsy findings after the death of Fiona, the hippo whose battle after swallowing a visitor's hat left people across the nation heartbroken.

A postmortem examination determined that a foreign object, confirmed to be a hat zoo officials said was accidentally thrown into her enclosure, was lodged deep inside the hippo's massive digestive tract, according to the zoo's director of animal health, Dr. Mike Wenninger.
The hat was located halfway through the small intestine, about 25 feet from the beginning of her intestinal tract and 50 feet from where it would have exited her body as waste.
FIONA THE HIPPO HONORED BY US SENATE IN UNANIMOUS RESOLUTION PRAISING CINCINNATI ZOO STAFF
Fiona, a Nile hippopotamus, eats a specialty birthday cake to celebrate turning 3 years old Jan. 23, 2020, in Cincinnati. (AP Photo/John Minchillo)

The findings settle lingering questions about the hat's exact location after care teams spent days trying to locate it using various methods, including ultrasounds and upper and lower gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopies.
Care teams even obtained 9-foot-long endoscopy tools but were still unable to reach her intestines through her mouth.
"The upper GI endoscopy couldn't even reach out of her large sacculated stomach," Wenninger said.
BELOVED HIPPO FIONA DIES AT CINCINNATI ZOO AFTER SWALLOWING VISITOR'S HAT
During Fiona's early weeks as a premature hippo, Cincinnati Zoo staff provided 24/7 critical care to keep her warm and fed until she grew strong enough to thrive. (Cincinnati Zoo)
"Given her anatomy and the attachments from her intestinal tract to body wall, there's no place, no way to get in there with specialized endoscopes," he added.

The hat's location and Fiona's anatomy also made surgical removal impossible, Wenninger said, explaining that even laparoscopic procedures, in which a scope is inserted into the abdomen through a small incision, were not feasible.

"Laparoscopic surgery wasn't possible given the location and a laparotomy, so (an) open incision in a hippo that size with an incision that's that long would have been a death sentence for her," he said.
Zoo officials added that the findings confirm the care team did everything possible, and the complications left no viable options for additional operations.
Born six weeks premature in January 2017, Fiona weighed just 29 pounds, 25 pounds lighter than the lowest recorded birth weight for Nile hippos. (Cincinnati Zoo)
"No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked," Wenninger said.

Following Fiona's death, the facility said the zoo remains open, but the area around the Hippo Cove enclosure will be closed through the weekend to give the animal care team the space it needs during this time.
"Keepers, vets, staff and volunteers are shaken and trying to navigate this loss. She meant a lot to a lot of people," the zoo said in a statement.
FUN FACT: FIONA THE HIPPO BECAME THE SMALLEST NILE HIPPO KNOWN TO SURVIVE
Fiona, a 9-year-old Nile hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo, died Thursday after ingesting a knitted hat that accidentally landed in her habitat. (Cincinnati Zoo)
While most hippos in captivity live up to 50 years, Fiona was just 9 years old when her condition rapidly deteriorated in November.

She first made headlines in 2017 after defying the odds as a premature hippo. She was born six weeks early, weighing just 29 pounds. By comparison, healthy newborn hippos typically weigh between 50 and 120 pounds at birth.

Zoo officials said Fiona became ill after a visitor tossed a hat into the air near her enclosure. The hat became caught in a ceiling fan, which propelled it over the viewing windows.

title: Verdict reached in Los Angeles retrial over 2025 Pacific Palisades wildfire that killed 12 people
summary: Jonathan Rinderknecht was convicted of federal arson in the Pacific Palisades fire that killed 12 and destroyed nearly 7,000 homes after a mistrial.
story: Fox News correspondent Matt Finn reports on the verdict a jury reached Friday in the retrial of a California man facing federal arson charges in the 2025 Palisades wildfires.

A man accused of sparking the deadly 2025 Pacific Palisades wildfire that killed 12 people and destroyed nearly 7,000 homes was found guilty on all counts Friday after a federal retrial in Los Angeles, months after his first trial ended in a mistrial.

Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, a former Uber driver with dual U.S.-French citizenship, had been charged with two federal arson counts — including destruction of property by means of fire — in U.S. District Court.
He was retried on a scaled-down grand jury indictment after his initial three-week trial ended in a hung jury in June.

Ahead of the second trial, federal prosecutors dropped one of the original three charges against Rinderknecht, and modified the two remaining federal arson counts, reducing his maximum possible prison sentence from 45 years to 40 years.
PALISADES FIRE SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY DRIVEN BY 'SOCIETAL REVENGE,' BEHAVIORAL ANALYST TESTIFIES IN COURT
Jonathan Rinderknecht, 29, was charged with igniting the blaze that eventually became the Palisades Fire in Los Angeles. (USAttyEssayli/X)

Following the verdict, a juror in the case — identified only by his first name, Cameron, who served as Juror No. 3 — told reporters that deliberations stretched across roughly two days as the panel systematically reviewed every piece of testimony and video evidence from the first day of court to the last.

"I’ll be honest, I was the person who found him not guilty. Originally, I was the one who stood out on that. So it took a lot for me to be convinced otherwise," he said, noting the initial tally stood at 10 guilty, one not guilty and one undecided.

Cameron said his initial hesitation centered on a "technical review" of the fire investigation and whether investigators properly followed protocol when linking the initial blaze to the later inferno. He said the jury ultimately concluded the defendant's own testimony — placing himself alone on the hill on a clear, calm night while smoking and carrying a lighter — pointed to him starting the first fire, which then smoldered into the Jan. 7 disaster.

"What I will say is that his intent was to start a fire," Cameron said. "What that fire did after his actions, whether he can say or whether no one can say, like who knows? Only he will know and only God himself. And so the result of his fire is what ultimately led to January 7th [2025]."
DEFENSE TEAM TRIES TO TIE NBA CHAMPION CHIS BOSH TO PALISADES ARSONIST CASE, CITING FIREWORK EVIDENCE: REPORT
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said in a statement following the conviction that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured."

"Nearly two years ago, the Palisades Fire devastated our city, taking innocent lives, destroying thousands of homes, and changing so many lives and Los Angeles forever," Bass said. "So many are still struggling to rebuild. For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality.
"Los Angeles will always stand with Pacific Palisades."

Los Angeles City Councilwoman Traci Park, who represents the Pacific Palisades, said the verdict "puts a bookend on one piece of this saga," though she emphasized that thousands of residents remain displaced and locked in disputes with insurance companies nearly two years later.

"The emotions that come with it really are a mixed bag, because at the end of the day, no amount of courtroom justice will ever restore what was lost or repair the harm that was caused," Park told reporters.
SPENCER PRATT UNITES WITH KAREN BASS' BROTHER TO SUE THE LA MAYOR OVER PALISADES FIRE DESTRUCTION
A drone image shows damage from the Palisades Fire in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of Los Angeles on Jan. 28, 2025. (Myung J. Chun / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
Park also argued the conviction does not absolve local officials of systemic failures during the disaster.

"I don't think this takes heat off of the authorities," she said, pointing to breakdowns in infrastructure, evacuation routes, water systems and public safety staffing when the blaze rekindled. "And in my view, the real accountability comes in what we do next to prevent something like this from happening again."

Prosecutors accused Rinderknecht of "maliciously" sparking a brush fire on Jan. 1, 2025 — initially dubbed the Lachman Fire — that was quickly extinguished, only to smolder underground in brush roots before strong winds fanned it into a massive inferno days later.
The blaze tore through the seaside enclave of Pacific Palisades, leveling entire neighborhoods and causing property damage estimated between $35 billion and $150 billion.

Federal prosecutors also alleged in court filings that Rinderknecht was partly inspired by Luigi Mangione, who pleaded guilty to federal charges in the December 2024 murder of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in New York City.
PALISADES FIRE SUSPECT WAS ALLEGEDLY 'FIXATED' ON LUIGI MANGIONE AND HELD 'RESENTMENT OF THE RICH': COURT DOCS
An aerial view of the fire damage caused by the Palisades Fire is shown in the Pacific Palisades, Calif., Jan. 22, 2025. (Mike Blake/Reuters, File)

According to prosecutors, Rinderknecht searched online for phrases including "free LuigiMangione," "let's take down all the billionaires" and "reddit lets kill all the billionaires" in mid-December 2024.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

When investigators asked Rinderknecht why someone might set a fire in the affluent Pacific Palisades, he allegedly said it would stem from resentment of the rich, adding that "we’re basically being enslaved by them" and comparing the act to the killing Mangione committed.

Mangione’s attorney, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, previously told Fox News Digital in a statement that her client "does not support violent actions and does not condone past or future political violence," calling attempts to link him to unrelated crimes "irresponsible, dangerous and prejudicial."
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
An aerial view shows homes destroyed in the Palisades Fire with the Pacific Ocean in the distance, Jan. 27, 2025, in Pacific Palisades, Calif. (Mario Tama/Getty Images, File)

Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty and maintained his innocence, contending in a court filing earlier this year that he merely witnessed the Jan. 1 fire after hiking up a hill to watch New Year's fireworks and immediately called 911.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB
His defense attorney, Steve Haney, argued that prosecutors lacked physical evidence tying his client to arson and contended the massive Jan. 7 blaze was set separately by someone else.

The first trial collapsed in late June after jurors deadlocked 10-2 in favor of acquittal. Following that mistrial, a woman identifying herself as Juror No. 4 told reporters there was "no proof" and said the prosecution's "holdover fire" theory didn't work for her, calling a retrial a "waste of our American dollars."

Burned homes are reduced to skeletal outlines days after the Palisades Fire swept through the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of Los Angeles. (Fox News, File)

U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli vowed at the time to press forward, writing on X that the evidence was strong and prosecutors fully intended to "retry this case before a new jury and obtain guilty verdicts on all charged counts."

The Palisades blaze erupted around the same time as the deadly Eaton Canyon fire roughly 30 miles east in Altadena, which killed 19 people and was later blamed on sparks from an electrical transmission tower. title: Judge rejects Alex Murdaugh's push to toss murder indictment over blood and ammo claims
summary: A judge refused to dismiss murder charges against Alex Murdaugh, rejecting defense claims that SLED investigator David Owen misled the grand jury on blood spatter.
story: Alex Murdaugh returns to a South Carolina courtroom for a pretrial hearing as his defense team seeks to dismiss the original murder indictments against him. Defense attorney Jim Griffin argues that a South Carolina Law Enforcement Division (SLED) investigator presented false testimony to the grand jury regarding alleged blood spatter on Murdaugh’s shirt. Prosecutors deny the allegations as Murdaugh prepares for a retrial in the murders of his wife and son.
The judge overseeing Alex Murdaugh’s double murder retrial has refused to dismiss the charges against him, dealing another legal blow to the disgraced former attorney ahead of his April court date.

Attorneys for Murdaugh argued on Friday, Nov. 13, during a pre-trial hearing that South Carolina Law Enforcement Division (SLED) investigator David Owen gave misleading testimony regarding blood-spatter evidence and shotgun ammunition, saying it undermined the integrity of the grand jury proceedings.

In her ruling on Friday afternoon, South Carolina Circuit Court Judge Debra R. McCaslin said that while there were major errors in the state's presentation of evidence to grand jurors, other evidence overwhelmingly supported the indictment.

"Even if the challenged testimony concerning the blood spatter on the T-shirt and shotgun ammunition were excluded from consideration by the grand jury, the remaining unchallenged evidence overwhelmingly established probable cause," McCaslin wrote.
ALEX MURDAUGH MAKES 'EXPLOSIVE' BID TO BLOW UP MURDER CASE HINGING ON DNA, DIRTY MONEY AND LIES: EXPERT
Alex Murdaugh, right, is shown here with his family. (Fox News)
While McCaslin refused to dismiss the murder indictment, she criticized the state's lead investigator on the case.

"The Court does not take lightly Special Agent Owen’s failure to recognize and account for a laboratory report addressed directly to him prior to presenting testimony in this case," she wrote. "Oversights of this nature undermine public confidence in the integrity of the criminal justice system."
McCaslin also acknowledged that evidence regarding ammunition presented to the grand jury wasn't accurate, but says there's no evidence that it was intentional.
ALEX MURDAUGH LAWYERS ALLEGE ‘FABRICATED’ EVIDENCE WAS USED TO SECURE MURDER INDICTMENTS

"Even accepting that the challenged testimony was inaccurate, the record presented does not establish intentional fabrication or prosecutorial misconduct," she said.
The judge said Murdaugh's defense can challenge the disputed evidence at trial in April.

"Any inconsistencies in prior investigative statements or forensic conclusions are matters properly addressed through cross-examination and impeachment at the upcoming trial, rather than through the pretrial dismissal of facially valid indictments," McCaslin wrote.
The South Carolina Attorney General’s Office said after McCaslin's ruling: "We continue to prepare for the retrial in April."

Murdaugh's defense attorneys argued that Owen misled the grand jury about alleged blood-spatter evidence found on the shirt Murdaugh was wearing on June 7, 2021, when his wife, Maggie, and son, Paul, were murdered at the family's Moselle property in Colleton County.
Owen claimed that blood spatter found on Murdaugh's shirt linked him to the killings, despite earlier testing that failed to detect human blood in samples taken from the garment.
At Murdaugh's first murder trial, Owen said he had no intention of misleading the grand jury and stated that he did not see the final SLED lab report until after the indictment had been issued.
ALEX MURDAUGH FACES STATE PUSHBACK ON MAGGIE DNA TESTING AND PRISON LAPTOP REQUEST

Prosecutors reiterated during the Nov. 13 hearing that the negative test results regarding the blood didn't necessarily invalidate the blood-spatter findings, and pointed to additional testing done by the state's expert which suggested earlier chemical treatment could have produced false negatives.

Alex Murdaugh is pictured in court. (Tracy Glantz of The State and Henry Taylor of The Post and Courier)

Prosecutors said the expert continued to stand behind his conclusions and that Owen's testimony before the grand jury accurately captured investigators' understanding of the evidence at that point in time.
ALEX MURDAUGH DEFENSE SAYS MURDER WEAPON MAY BE TIED TO SEPARATE KILLING AS JUDGE SEEKS ANSWERS

Owen also told grand jurors that shotguns found on the Murdaugh property were loaded with the same combination of ammunition used to kill Paul, a claim the defense argues was false. Murdaugh's attorneys maintained that none of the recovered shotguns contained the exact combination of shells found at the murder scene.

Prosecutors acknowledged that Owen's description of the ammunition to the grand jury may have been imprecise but argued that he had not intentionally misled jurors.

"This was not overtly false. This was what the agent understood at the time," lead prosecutor Creighton Waters said.

title: Suspect in alleged rape of LSU student killed by car fights to keep mom’s warning texts out of December trial

story: Madison Brooks was a student at LSU when she was allegedly gang-raped then struck and killed by a car in Louisiana. title: EXCLUSIVE: NIH funded foreign labs with troubling safety lapses, including deadly bat virus experiment
summary: PETA alleges the National Institutes of Health funded foreign animal labs with biosafety failures, including a halted Hendra virus bat study in Australia.
story: State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott joins 'Fox & Friends' to confirm the U.S. is ending funding for dangerous gain-of-function research globally following Dr. Anthony Fauci's repeated invocation of the Fifth Amendment during a Senate hearing.

FIRST ON FOX: The National Institutes of Health (NIH) awarded millions of taxpayer dollars to foreign animal research facilities where significant biosafety, containment and staffing failures allegedly took place — including a bat virus experiment in Australia that was abruptly halted after animal containment broke down, according to federal records obtained by People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) and reviewed by Fox News Digital.

The internal agency records and noncompliance reports show that federal health officials repeatedly approved funding or failed to identify major safety and oversight vulnerabilities until after taxpayer-funded animal experiments were already underway.

In response to the findings, PETA on Monday sent a formal complaint to NIH Director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, demanding that the agency immediately halt all federal funding for animal experiments conducted outside the U.S.

The newly released information comes amid mounting scrutiny on Capitol Hill regarding foreign research oversight and renewed calls for the bipartisan Cease Animal Research Grants Overseas (CARGO) Act, which would permanently prohibit NIH from bankrolling animal experiments in foreign countries.
GABBARD SAYS DECLASSIFIED BIOLAB RECORDS VALIDATE CONCERNS PREVIOUSLY DISMISSED AS MISINFORMATION

Fundación Centro de Primates (FUCEP): An Aotus monkey in a nest covered with feces in a rusty cage. The photo was taken by an inspector on Nov. 24, 2021, and obtained by PETA through a public records request to Corporación Autónoma Regional del Valle del Cauca, or CVC. (PETA)
Deadly bat virus experiment halted over biosafety lapses

According to federal documents, the NIH funded a study on Hendra virus — a lethal, bat-borne pathogen — at the Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness, operated by Australia's national science agency, CSIRO. The project, "Shining a light on bat cellular immunity following virus infection," was suspended by the facility’s Animal Ethics Committee after serious operational failures surfaced.

Internal records show the facility suffered from insufficient appropriately trained personnel capable of conducting animal procedures at the required biocontainment level, an absence of adequate contingency planning, unclear protocols and prolonged confinement of flying foxes without proper enrichment.
RIDGLAN FARMS BEAGLES BEGIN LEAVING WISCONSIN FACILITY AFTER RESCUE GROUPS STRIKE DEAL FOR RELEASE

After a single flying fox tested positive for Hendra virus, staff were forced to kill all eight bats housed together because the room could not be elevated to Biosafety Level 4 (BSL-4) containment. A ninth flying fox housed separately at BSL-4 was later killed after also testing positive.

The primary investigator alerted the NIH to the infections in May 2023, leading the ethics board to suspend the study weeks later. However, the NIH’s Office of Laboratory Animal Welfare (OLAW) did not receive even a preliminary report of the suspension until April 2024 — more than 10 months after the shutdown, according to records.

The documents show the Australian bat study was not an isolated incident. At Newcastle University in the United Kingdom, where researchers conducted NIH-funded brain and stroke research on nonhuman primates, a 2025 federal review ordered the facility to reevaluate its personal protective equipment standards, tuberculosis screening and emergency procedures for testing potential human exposures to the deadly Herpes B virus.

Fundación Centro de Primates (FUCEP): Dirty cages seen on cracked, concrete flooring covered with black and green mold. Waterers seem to be repurposed disposable soda bottles, one of which still seems to have its original label. Two pieces of guadua bamboo seem to be the only things keeping the structure from collapsing. Fibers from the construction mesh and debris from trees hang down from the top of the structure. An electrical, portable stove sits next to the guadua bamboo, and its cable seems to be attached to the "ceiling" of the structure. Something that appears to be an animal corpse is wedged between the chain-link roof and the plastic sheet that covers it. The photo was obtained by PETA from a whistleblower. (PETA)
'Enhanced' inspections run on institution-controlled cameras

Following past international scandals — including a shuttered Colombian facility that received $17 million in U.S. funding while keeping monkeys in squalor — the NIH pledged to implement "enhanced oversight" of foreign institutions in line with Government Accountability Office (GAO) recommendations.
However, PETA’s review of 124 federal files obtained through the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) shows the NIH’s oversight relies almost entirely on self-reporting and scripted virtual site visits.

Records show that virtual visits were announced months in advance, allowing overseas facilities ample time to prepare. At Newcastle University, the facility received notice in May 2025 for a virtual visit that did not happen until December.
Notification letters outlined prearranged planning sessions, document reviews and camera tours where foreign personnel controlled what government monitors could see on screen.

The format gave federal regulators no ability to conduct unannounced walk-throughs, inspect arbitrary rooms, review records in real time or conduct confidential staff interviews, according to records.

Out of 70 annual reports examined regarding active NIH-backed animal research across foreign labs between 2023 and 2025, 67 self-reported zero violations, reflecting a system almost entirely dependent on foreign labs self-policing their own programs.
HARVARD-CHINA LINKS UNEARTHED AS CONGRESS FINDS 140 PAPERS CO-AUTHORED BY CCP MILITARY UNIVERSITIES
NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya testifies during the House subcommittee hearing on oversight of the National Institutes of Health in Rayburn building on March 17, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc)
Unapproved labs, unaccounted animals and missing assurances
The records also document widespread administrative failures, including grants flowing to institutions that lacked basic federal authorization:

The NIH awarded a $13 million tuberculosis vaccine adjuvant contract to the University of Sydney in 2022, but the animal testing was outsourced to the Centenary Institute in Australia, an entity lacking the required NIH Foreign Animal Welfare Assurance.
The unauthorized setup went unnoticed by the NIH for years until the university inquired about the death of an experimental mouse in 2025.
HUNDREDS OF ACTIVISTS FACE PEPPER SPRAY IN VIOLENT CLASH WITH DEPUTIES AT WISCONSIN BEAGLE RESEARCH FACILITY

The NIH also confirmed that it could find "no records of an assurance" for multiple foreign entities carrying out U.S.-funded animal studies, including Australian biotech firm Kinoxis Therapeutics, which conducted opioid withdrawal experiments on 80 dogs, 314 rats and 1,485 mice under a grant active through May 2026.
Similar record absences occurred for grants involving animal testing at institutions in Canada, Kenya and Israel.

Fundación Centro de Primates (FUCEP): Employees performing a procedure on an Aotus monkey, who has been placed on the dirty surface of a table, which is standing on a cracked, concrete floor covered with green mold. The photo was obtained by PETA from a whistleblower. (PETA)

At the Research Center in Clinical Biochemistry and Immunology in Argentina, the NIH funded a multi-year Chagas disease study. A 2026 preprint co-authored by the lead researcher detailed mice experiencing continuous whole-body tremors and hind-limb paralysis — conditions mandating euthanasia under the approved protocol.

However, the lab reported that untreated animals died over an extended 120-day timeframe and admitted it does not generate animal monitoring or veterinary records, leaving federal regulators with no documentation of how animal deaths were tracked.
WHITE HOUSE REBUKES CBS INTERVIEW AFTER HOST BATTLES NIH DIRECTOR OVER LOSS OF TRUST IN PUBLIC HEALTH
PETA, lawmakers call to cut off overseas animal lab funding
In her letter Monday to Bhattacharya, Dr. Magnolia Martínez, PETA’s lead projects manager and congressional liaison, argued that the NIH's foreign monitoring regime is fundamentally broken.

The organization noted that an Animal Welfare Assurance represents a baseline administrative requirement that does not ensure animal welfare or clinical applicability to human health, urging the agency to halt funding foreign animal tests and redirect resources toward human-biology-based research methods.
Fox News Digital reached out to the NIH for comment on the reported biosafety lapses, the oversight timeline and calls to halt overseas animal grants, but did not immediately receive a response.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Lawmakers in Washington are similarly ramping up efforts to cut off foreign funding through the CARGO Act, emphasizing that American taxpayers should not be underwriting unaccountable and hazardous research in foreign jurisdictions.

Fox News Digital reached out to bipartisan sponsors of the CARGO Act — including Sens. Rick Scott, R-Fla., Cory Booker, D-N.J., and Dina Titus, D-Nev. — asking whether the newly revealed foreign laboratory failures will prompt renewed legislative action and oversight hearings to permanently ban federal funding for overseas animal experiments.
Alexandra Koch is a Fox News Digital Editor, with a focus on high-impact events that shape national conversation.
She has covered major national crises, including the L.A. wildfires, Potomac and Hudson River aviation disasters, Boulder terror attack, and Texas Hill Country floods.

title: Zelenskyy hails ‘exemplary Ukrainian operation’ sinking Russian warship off Libya
summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy shared video of Ukraine's naval drones sinking Russia's corvette Merkury off Libya, as peace talks resume after a nine-month pause.
story: Video released by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy shows strikes on the Russian corvette Merkury and a dry cargo ship he says transported weapons. (State Security Service of Ukraine via AP)

The war between Russia and Ukraine continues to spill outside the countries' boundaries, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy shared a video of a drone striking and sinking Russian weapons ships off the coast of Libya.

"We continue our operations in designated waters," Zelenskyy wrote early Monday morning in a statement on X. "We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukraine weapons. Glory to Ukraine!"

The strikes come as President Donald Trump is pushing for peace, but Ukraine has remained steadfast in not only fighting off Russian gains in south and east of Ukraine, but also taking the fight to Russia "in designated waters" around the globe.
RUSSIAN WARSHIP SINKS OFF LIBYA AS SUSPECTED UKRAINIAN STRIKES TAKE WAR BEYOND BLACK SEA

"An exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war," the post began. "I thank the warriors of the Security Service of Ukraine and all our Defense Forces of Ukraine who took part in carrying out these tasks. I received detailed briefings on the operation’s steps yesterday and today – the targets we set were achieved. It all took place off the coast of Libya.

"Our warriors deployed seven Ukrainian-made naval drones. Despite all the enemy’s efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk. It’s one of their newest ships, commissioned in 2023, during the full-scale war. A Ka-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed along with the corvette. Our second target was the Russian dry cargo vessel MV ANGARA, which the enemy used to transport weapons. Result: target hit."
UKRAINE POUNDS BLACK SEA FLEET’S ‘LAST MAJOR STRONGHOLD’ WHILE PUTIN FLEXES NAVAL POWER IN PACIFIC

Sunday's drone strike hit the Russian vessel while it was docked at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya – a region controlled by military commander Khalifa Haftar, whose Libyan National Army maintains ties with Russia. The Institute for the Study of War reported that the Merkury had stopped at Benghazi for several days under a cooperation agreement to refuel and resupply while escorting Russian cargo vessels capable of carrying military supplies back to Russia.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the Baltic Sea incident part of a "dangerous trend of increasing terrorist activity" and urged regional nations to warn Kyiv against such operations. Russian, Estonian and Finnish vessels fought the blaze after the Sparta II drifted into Finnish waters before a Russian vessel began towing it away Sunday.
UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS

Osama Hamad, prime minister of Libya's eastern-based government, said he asked the United Nations to investigate "suspicions that the boats had been launched from western Libya" and to verify whether Ukrainian military experts are operating there. Western Libya is governed by the internationally recognized Government of National Unity in Tripoli, which did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
UKRAINE’S DRONE REVOLUTION SHOWS RUSSIA IS DANGEROUSLY UNPREPARED. BUT, SO IS AMERICA
This file photo shows the newly sunken Russian navy corvette, Merkury, participating in a naval military exercise in the Baltic Sea on July 16, 2023. (Russian Defense Ministry Press Service via AP)
The Benghazi operation follows earlier maritime incidents far outside the Black Sea theater.

March Mediterranean tanker fire: Russia's Transport Ministry alleged in March that Ukrainian naval drones launched from Libya attacked the Arctic Metagaz, a liquefied natural gas carrier sailing from Murmansk that later sank between Libya and Malta. Kyiv never claimed responsibility for that incident.Gulf of Finland strike: A Saturday drone attack set fire to the Sparta II, a Russian cargo ship operated by the Russian defense logistics firm Oboronlogistika, in international waters in the Gulf of Finland. Finland's military said Ukraine likely carried out the strike, which forced the evacuation of all 16 crew members and left one slightly injured.

March Mediterranean tanker fire: Russia's Transport Ministry alleged in March that Ukrainian naval drones launched from Libya attacked the Arctic Metagaz, a liquefied natural gas carrier sailing from Murmansk that later sank between Libya and Malta. Kyiv never claimed responsibility for that incident.

Gulf of Finland strike: A Saturday drone attack set fire to the Sparta II, a Russian cargo ship operated by the Russian defense logistics firm Oboronlogistika, in international waters in the Gulf of Finland. Finland's military said Ukraine likely carried out the strike, which forced the evacuation of all 16 crew members and left one slightly injured.
UKRAINE'S ZELENSKYY ON DEFYING US IN ATTACKING RUSSIAN OIL: 'OUR RESPONSE MUST BE PAINFUL'

The expanding naval strikes come as U.S.-backed peace talks between Moscow and Kyiv resumed this month after a nine-month pause. The sticking point remains Russian annexation of occupied Ukrainian in exchange for potential NATO-like security guarantees. Zelenskyy had told Fox News of some potential negotiation of land for security, but has since balked at giving up on the land bridge sought by Vladimir Putin to connect Russia to the Black Sea.

The overland route connecting Russia to the Black Sea coast and Crimea runs through occupied southern Ukraine – specifically the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions – alongside the 19-kilometer (12-mile) Crimean Bridge across the Kerch Strait.
UKRAINE RELEASES VIDEO SHOWING DAMAGE TO PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE FOLLOWING 'UNPRECEDENTED OPERATION' IN CRIMEA
Ukraine strategically struck the Crimean Bridge while Trump was getting ready to meet with Putin and China's Xi Jinping. The meeting came thereafter and did not result in any movements toward peace.
Mykola Bielieskov of the National Institute for Strategic Studies in Kyiv told Reuters that Ukraine is seeking leverage through "horizontal escalation."

"Since neither side is able to compel the other to accept terms of settlement through the battlefield only, both try to find new ways to pressure each other," he said.

title: Russian warship sinks off Libya as suspected Ukrainian strikes take war beyond Black Sea
summary: The Russian corvette Merkury capsized at Benghazi Naval Base after suspected Ukrainian sea drones struck, injuring ten people, Libyan officials say.
story: Russia faces a record Ukraine drone attack as more than 1,400 drones strike overnight, damaging the prized Crimean Bridge. Host Harris Faulkner covers the escalating war before analyzing the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt in the Middle East. Retired Blackhawk helicopter pilot Lt. Col. Darin Gaub joins 'The Focus' to discuss these rising global conflicts and U.S. military positioning.
A Russian warship capsized and sank Sunday after suspected Ukrainian sea drones struck a naval base in eastern Libya, triggering an explosion and fire, according to Libyan officials.
Hours later, a second drone attack also hit a commercial ship off the coast of Benghazi, Reuters reported.

The first ship, the Russian navy corvette Merkury, was docked at Benghazi Naval Base when two explosive-laden sea drones struck the vessel, according to Libyan military officials who spoke to The Associated Press.
UKRAINE POUNDS BLACK SEA FLEET’S ‘LAST MAJOR STRONGHOLD’ WHILE PUTIN FLEXES NAVAL POWER IN PACIFIC
Fire burns after an explosion aboard a Russian ship docked at Benghazi port in Libya. (Reuters)
At least four other drones were intercepted and destroyed, the officials said.

Satellite images showed most of the warship capsized and submerged, with only its bow remaining above water. Smoke could be seen rising from the ship's superstructure, and debris was scattered along the pier.
Ten people, including Russian and Libyan nationals, suffered minor injuries in the attack and were receiving treatment in Benghazi, medical sources told Reuters.
The warship had stopped at the port to refuel and resupply while returning to Russia under a maritime cooperation agreement with Libya's eastern-based government, officials said in a statement.
Libyan military officials said an initial investigation indicated that Ukrainian sea drones had been launched from a base in western Libya, according to The AP.
UKRAINE STRIKES DEEP INTO RUSSIA’S ARCTIC GAS HEARTLAND AS TRUMP PUSHES PUTIN TOWARD PEACE
The port of Benghazi after an explosion aboard a Russian ship docked at the Benghazi naval base. (Vantor/Handout via REUTERS)
Hours after the warship was struck, a Maltese-flagged commercial ship was also hit by a sea drone off Benghazi, two Libyan military sources told Reuters.
Libyan naval forces rescued the commercial ship's crew, while health officials reported that some crew members sustained minor injuries and were in stable condition.
Libyan naval and air forces also intercepted more than 20 drone boats off Benghazi on Sunday evening, the military sources told Reuters.
The attacks prompted Libya's eastern-based government to seek an international investigation.

Prime Minister Osama Hamad said his government had submitted a formal request to the United Nations General Assembly and Security Council to investigate the attacks, including suspicions that the drones were launched from western Libya.
RUSSIA DEPLOYS NORTH KOREAN MISSILE UNIT TO UKRAINE; MOSCOW-PYONGYANG AXIS DEEPENS: REPORT
A Russian corvette before and after the explosion in Benghazi, with Libya's eastern-based government saying the explosion was caused by a suspected drone attack. (VANTOR/ Reuters)
Hamad also called for an investigation into the possible presence of Ukrainian military experts in Libya and requested an explanation from Kyiv about their activities.
The eastern government insisted that Libya was not a party to the war between Russia and Ukraine and condemned attempts to use its territory to settle foreign conflicts.
"The Libyan government will not allow Libyan ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts," the government said.
Benghazi is controlled by forces loyal to Gen. Khalifa Haftar, whose self-styled Libyan National Army dominates eastern and southern Libya and maintains close ties with Russia.
Libya has been divided since the 2011 NATO-backed uprising that toppled longtime dictator Moammar Gadhafi.
UKRAINE UNLEASHES MORE THAN 400 DRONES NEAR MOSCOW IN ONE OF WAR'S BIGGEST ATTACKS
Putin is testing the boundaries of NATO with aircraft incursions, allied states say. (Ramil Sitdikov/Pool/Reuters)
A U. N. recognized government operates from Tripoli, while a rival administration controls much of the east.

The suspected attacks also come as Ukraine has expanded its campaign against Russian naval assets beyond the Black Sea. In December 2025, Ukraine said it struck a Russian-linked oil tanker with aerial drones in the Mediterranean Sea.
In March 2026, Russia accused Ukraine of attacking a Russian liquefied natural gas tanker with naval drones launched from the Libyan coast.

Libyan officials previously told the AP that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating from military facilities in western Libya, including an air base in Misrata and sites in Tripoli and Zawiya.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Ukrainian forces have used explosive-laden sea drones and missiles to strike Russian warships and naval installations, primarily in the Black Sea.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Trump says Iran unleashed missile, drone surge after midterms
summary: President Donald Trump says Iran launched more missiles and drones over the past week than at any point in over a year, and all were knocked down with no damage.
story: President Donald Trump claimed that the war with Iran will end "right after" the midterm elections in the U.S.

President Donald Trump said Sunday that Iran has launched more missiles and drones over the past week than at any point in more than a year, adding that U. S. forces shot them down without any damage and as tensions escalate following the U.S. midterm elections.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump also tied the surge in Iranian attacks to the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress amid voter frustration over the war with Iran and rising fuel costs.
"As everyone remembers, I predicted two things concerning the November 3rd Midterm Elections," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
TRUMP RESPONDS AFTER VANCE BLAMES IRAN WAR FOR MIDTERM LOSSES, VP SAYS HIS JOB IS TO SUPPORT PRESIDENT

President Donald Trump said Iran has launched more missiles and drones over the past week than at any point in more than a year, claiming U.S. forces intercepted them all without damage. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

"One, that if the Democrats win, the Stock Markets would go down, substantially, which they have, and two, that the Islamic Republic of Iran, which has killed 81,000 protestors as of today, will grow more aggressive in their attacks, which has also occurred. "
Trump also said that Iran launched "more drones and missiles over the past week than at any time for over a year," though he said U.S. defenses neutralized the threat.
"Don't worry, they've all been knocked down, and done no damage," Trump said.
"Iranian leaders consider the Democrats weak, ineffective, and Country destroying, but I won't let that happen!" he added.
The remarks also came days after the Senate rejected a war powers resolution in a 48-51 vote on Nov. 19, leaving Trump's military authority intact.
TRUMP WARNS OF NEW STRIKES AGAINST IRAN AFTER NEW YEAR, CALLS NEGOTIATORS ‘PROFESSIONAL TAP DANCERS’
President Donald Trump monitors U.S. military operations in Iran following an Israeli strike in Tehran on Saturday, Feb. 28, 2026. (@WhiteHouse/X)

Speaking to Fox News earlier Sunday, Trump said he is inclined to resume strikes on Iran after the new year if diplomatic talks fail to produce a deal, warning that Iranian vessels testing the U.S. naval blockade would end up "at the bottom of the sea like the rest of the navy."

In his social media post Sunday, Trump accused both Democrats and Iran of trying to keep fuel prices high ahead of the midterm elections and separately questioned the integrity of the vote without providing evidence.

"Both the Dems and Iran fought like hell to keep the Oil price up as long as possible and, since the Election, the Oil price has dropped by a record level," Trump wrote, adding that it was too bad voters "didn't understand this before they pulled the trigger."

"The whole Election was very 'strange,'" he said. "In the end, America will win! "

title: Trump dares Iran to breach US port blockade as Tehran reportedly readies 14 oil tankers
summary: Iran reportedly positioned 14 tankers at Kharg Island to breach the U.S. blockade, as President Donald Trump dared Tehran to test American naval forces in the Gulf.
story: United Against Nuclear Iran senior adviser Charlie Brown dismisses Iranian convoy threat to run US Navy blockade as ‘farcical’.

Reports that Iran plans to send more than a dozen tankers through the U.S. blockade of its ports raised fears of a wider conflict Sunday, as a maritime security expert warned of a risky confrontation and President Donald Trump dared Tehran to test American forces deployed across the Gulf.

"I hope they do, they'll all be at the bottom of the sea like the rest of the navy," Trump told Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst when asked whether Iran would attempt to breach the blockade, first imposed in April.
The warning came as reports indicated Iran was preparing a convoy of tankers to breach the blockade from Kharg Island, a critical oil export hub.
TRUMP DETAILS SWEEPING 'ALL OR NOTHING' BLOCKADE OF STRAIT OF HORMUZ AFTER FAILED IRAN TALKS
U.S. Marines aboard USS New Orleans (LPD 18) stand watch in the Arabian Sea during naval blockade operations against Iran. (U.S. Central Command)

Maritime security experts warned the vessels could face U.S. naval forces right across the Indian Ocean, while the Institute for the Study of War cautioned that an attempted breakout could perhaps trigger a wider war.

The reported operation would involve tankers sailing from Kharg Island, which handles most of Iran's crude oil exports, toward the Gulf of Oman and with crews reportedly assigned to the vessels and Iranian flags raised ahead of a possible attempt to breach the blockade.

Charlie Brown, a senior adviser to United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI) and maritime sanctions enforcement expert, dismissed the reported operation as "propaganda" and said the plan was unlikely to succeed if ever attempted.
"This supposed plan by the Iranians to suddenly deploy 14 vessels to try to breach the blockade in a convoy — it's farcical," Brown told Fox News Digital on Sunday.
"The blockade is enforced not merely as a line that is crossed, but the ability of the United States Navy to enforce this blockade extends across the entire Indian Ocean and beyond."
BLOCKADE 101: AMERICAN SEA POWER ON DISPLAY AS TRUMP CORNERS IRAN AND WARNS OFF CHINA
Satellite view of Kharg Island, located in the Persian Gulf off the coast of Iran. (Gallo Images/Orbital Horizon/Copernicus Sentinel Data 2024)
"If ships try to get out of the area that is managed by the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet, the U.S. Navy's 7th Fleet is the next area command that has responsibility over the Indian Ocean," he said.
"And they have ships and aircraft that are there right now, and they'll just take up the mission."

The potential confrontation comes amid rising maritime tensions. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported Sunday that a tanker was involved in an incident with military forces in the Gulf of Oman but did not identify the vessel or connect it to the reported Iranian convoy.
"UKMTO has received a report of an incident involving a tanker and military forces in the Gulf of Oman," the agency said in an advisory.
"Vessels are advised to consider the latest maritime security information and maintain awareness of the evolving operational environment."
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) also warned Iran could attempt to break the blockade within days as mounting economic pressure leaves Tehran with few options.
"Iran's deteriorating economic situation is increasingly dire, which is forcing Iranian officials to reckon with the necessity of breaking the US blockade," the institute said in an update.
The assessment followed a Nov. 20 report by Hamshahri, a Tehran municipality-affiliated outlet, claiming Iran had positioned 14 tankers at Kharg Island to breach the blockade.
TRUMP BLOCKADE SQUEEZING IRAN SO HARD REGIME MAY BE DUMPING OIL INTO GULF, EXPERTS SAY
Iran seized two foreign oil tankers in the Persian Gulf on Thursday, allegedly carrying 1 million liters of smuggled fuel. (GIUSEPPE CACACE/AFP via Getty Images)

"Attempting to run the blockade would expose Iran to significant risk that ranges from the destruction of a tanker fleet at minimum to possibly resuming a larger-scale conflict with the United States, or both," the institute said.
"Iran's willingness to accept these risks demonstrates the degree to which the regime views the current economic situation as both dire and unsustainable."
Brown, however, questioned whether Tehran would send the tankers, suggesting the reported operation was an attempt to project defiance rather than a viable strategy.

"This supposed run of the blockade by several Iranian ships that's discussed is most likely propaganda — another one of a series of similar propaganda statements that don't turn out to be true and are easily debunked," he said.
Brown also disputed reports that the tankers were loaded and preparing to depart, citing satellite monitoring of Kharg Island.
"We carefully watched Kharg Island loading by satellite imagery, and there's really no indication that there's been any significant loading there in quite some time."

Brown said coordinating a 14-vessel convoy would also pose major logistical challenges, requiring lead and trailing ships, coordinated communications and procedures for responding to U.S. military orders.
Civilian crews could face significant danger if they refused orders to stop, he warned.
TRUMP WARNS OF NEW STRIKES AGAINST IRAN AFTER NEW YEAR, CALLS NEGOTIATORS ‘PROFESSIONAL TAP DANCERS’
A drone view shows vessels anchored in the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, May 25, 2026. (Stringer TPX IMAGES OF THE DAY via Reuters)
"They would obviously be going into an area of great risk, and they would have to decide whether to comply with the instructions to stop or face action," Brown said.

In a Nov. 18 advisory, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) warned that ships receiving Iranian cargo through ship-to-ship transfers could face interception or seizure, extending the blockade beyond vessels departing Iranian ports, Reuters reported.
Brown said U.S. forces would likely contact the tankers by radio from Navy ships or aircraft and order them to stop. Refusal could trigger an escalated military response.
He said the Navy could transfer responsibility between regional commands, making it difficult for Iranian tankers to escape by sailing farther into the Indian Ocean.
"There's an administrative boundary, a geographic boundary between the 5th Fleet and the 7th Fleet, between CENTCOM and INDOPACOM," Brown said.
"But the U.S. Navy is a global Navy, and they're able to handle these transfers of responsibility when a target or ship of interest crosses that boundary."

Brown said U.S. forces have the ships, aircraft and procedures to intercept multiple vessels at once, while the open waters of the Indian Ocean offer more room to maneuver than the narrow Strait of Hormuz.
"It's a mission of the United States, not merely a mission in CENTCOM," Brown said. "So they have the forces in place."

"So if they do try to make an attempt with multiple ships, I'm quite confident all or most — probably all — would be interdicted," he added.
